EXAMPLE 4: Evaluation of potato cold chipping qualities before and after cold storage
[0055]	Chipping attributes of the wild type and CISCOM lines were tested by frying chips after fresh harvest and after 30 days of cold storage. Potato tubers were sliced into 1.5 to 2.0 mm pieces and deep-fried at 184℃ in groundnut oil. Colour of the fried chips were scored visually in a scale of 1-10 based on reference colour chart for potato chips developed by Ezekiel et al. (2003). The lightest-coloured chips are those with a colour score of 1, while the darkest-coloured chips are those with a score of 10.
[0056]	At fresh harvest, all RNAi transgenic lines and wild-type control produced light-coloured chips with a score of 1.0 to 1.5. Chip colour scores varied significantly after 30 days of cold storage, ranging from 1.5 to 6.5. After 30 days of cold storage, the KC1 and KC3 wild-type tubers produced the darkest coloured chips with colours core of 8 and 7, respectively. However, chip colour in all the six selected CISCOM RNAi lines was much lighter after cold storage and acceptable compared to that of the respective wild type. Chips colour score for all the six selected transgenic lines were between 1.5 to 2.0 after 30 days of cold storage as shown in Figure 5. These six lines were further characterized.

EXAMPLE 5: Sugar estimation of the selected transgenic lines
[0057]	Total sugar was extracted based on the protocol of Viola & Davies (1992) and Jaiswal et al. (2023) with minor modifications. In brief, 200 mg of finely grounded tuber sample was taken in a 2 ml Eppendrof  tube and 1 ml of 80% ethanol was added and mixed well by vortexing. Then the mixture was boiled at 80℃ for 10 minutes and left to cool down at room temperature. The tubes were centrifuged at 3000xg for 2 min and supernatant containing soluble sugars were transferred to fresh tubes. Remaining sugar was extracted from the precipitate by repeating the above step twice. The collected clarified supernatant was dried in a vacuum evaporator at 40℃ to evaporate ethanol completely. Vacuum dried sugar was dissolved in 200 µl of double distilled water and glucose, fructose and sucrose content were measured by Sucrose/D-Fructose/D-Glucose Assay Kit as per manufacturer’s instruction. All the assay reactions were performed in triplicate with different dilution of sugar sample (10 to 20 times) as required to get the absorbance values within the desired limit.
[0058]	Soluble sugars, glucose, fructose and sucrose were quantified for the selected transgenic and wild-type control plants. Reducing sugar (glucose and fructose) (RS) content of the selected transgenic lines and that of wild-type lines were comparable just after fresh harvest, but after 30 days of cold storage RS level in the tuber tissue rose to 206.37±5.14 mg 100 gm FW-1 for KC1 wild-type, and that for KC3 wild-type it was 236.10±12.37 mg 100 gm FW-1. While the transgenic lines maintained a very low level of RS. The RS levels for KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104 lines were 9.85±0.24, 15.09±0.64 and 23.63±0.55 mg 100 gm FW-1 , respectively. The RS content of the KC3 transgenic lines were 10.80±0.16, 18.36±1.10, 10.98±0.73 mg 100 gm FW-1. These data show up to 95% reduction in RS level in the transgenic lines of both KC1 and KC3 compared to the wild type after cold storage, as shown in Figure 5 (a) and (b) of the present disclosure. On the other hand, sucrose level in all transgenic tubers was dramatically reduced compared to the respective wild-type tubers, at fresh harvest as well as after cold storage. At fresh harvest reduction of sucrose in the three selected KC1 lines was 80.55%, 62.50%, and 81.40% respectively, that for KC3 transgenic lines was 65.72%, 46.37%, and 71.89% respectively. The same level of reduction in sucrose content has also been maintained in the selected transgenic lines after cold storage for one month. The mean sucrose content of KC1 and KC3 wild-type tuber after cold storage was 505.19±34.63 and 528.09±23.22 mg 100 gm FW-1, while the sucrose content in the selected KC1 transgenic lines remained 51.93±4.99, 132.97±7.66, 72.31±3.49 mg 100 gm FW-1 and that of selected KC3 transgenic lines were 75.04±6.16, 126.69±5.93, 69.07±7.12 mg 100 gm FW-1, as shown in Figure 6 (c) and (d) of the present disclosure.

EXAMPLE 6: Estimation of acid invertase activity of the selected transgenic lines
[0059]	Crude protein was extracted by grounding 200 mg of tuber samples after fresh harvest and after 30 days of cold storage at 4℃ in 1 ml extraction buffer containing 50 mM sodium acetate, pH 4.75 (adjusted with acetic acid), 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT and 1 mM PMSF. Samples were mixed thoroughly by vortexing and centrifuged at 12000 x g for 15 minutes at 4℃. Supernatant containing the crude enzyme extract, was collected in a fresh tube without disturbing the pellet and immediately used for measuring acid invertase activity. Protein concentration in the crude extract was determined by Bradford method. For measuring acid invertase activity 20 µl enzyme extract was incubated with 180 µl of assay buffer (30 mM sucrose and 30 mM sodium acetate, pH 4.75) at 37℃ for 30 minutes. After incubation enzyme was heat inactivated in boiling water bath for 10 minutes and centrifuged at 12000 x g for 2 minutes. Supernatant was collected in a fresh tube for glucose estimation as described previously. Zero minute control was taken for all samples for omitting residual enzyme activity and background absorbance. Invertase activity was calculated as nmol glucose formed min-1 mg protein-1.
[0060]	The acid-invertase activity of transgenic tubers showed reduction to a great extent compared to the wild-type, both at fresh harvest and after 30 days of cold-stress conditions. The acid-invertase activities in the transgenic lines, KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104 were 0.22, 0.23, and 0.13 nM glc min-1 mg protein-1, respectively, at fresh harvest. The acid-invertase activity in the transgenic lines, KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104 were 0.50, 0.63, and 0.59 nM glc min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively after cold storage. While the acid-invertase activity in the freshly harvested and cold-stored KC1 wild-type tubers were 0.87 and 3.48 nM glc min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively. The acid-invertase activities in the KC3 transgenic tubers, KC3 CIS5, KC3 CIS14, and KC3 CIS20 were 0.39, 0.55 and 0.27 nM glc min-1 mg Protein-1 at fresh harvest condition, and 0.68, 0.76 and 0.37 nM glc min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively, after 30 days of cold storage. The same in the freshly harvested and cold-stored KC3 wild-type tubers were 2.27 and 4.66 nM glc min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively. This demonstrates that silencing the StVaInv transcript significantly reduced acid-invertase activity in transgenic tubers, with KC1 transgenic tubers losing up to 85% and KC3 transgenic tubers losing up to 95% of enzyme activity after cold storage, as shown in Figure 7 (a) and (b) of the present disclosure.

EXAMPLE 7: Estimation of UGPase enzyme activity of the selected transgenic lines
[0061]	Tuber samples (200 mg) were crushed into fine power with liquid nitrogen and enzyme was extracted by 1 ml buffer containing 100 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 2 mM EDTA, 1 mM PMSF and 1 % TritonX 100 (v/v). After proper mixing by vortexing, mixture was centrifuged at 12000 x g for 15 minutes at 4℃, and supernatant containing enzyme extract was taken into fresh tube and used for measurement of UGPase activity. Total protein was measured by the Bradford method. UGPase activity was determined following Sowokinos (1976), with slight modifications. The assay reaction mixture contained 1 mM of UDP-Glc, 1 mM of NADP+, 5 mM of MgCl2, 0.8 mM of glycyl-glycine, 0.2 mM of L-cysteine, 0.02 mM of glucose-1,6-bisphosphate, 1 unit of phosphoglucomutase, 1 unit of Glc-6-P dehydrogenase, 100 mM Tris-Cl, pH 7.5. The enzyme extract and assay reaction mixture were used in a 1:4 ratio to determine UGPase enzyme activity. The reaction was started by adding 2.5 mM PPi. The enzyme was assessed spectrophotometrically at 25°C (pyrophosphorolytic direction, using PPi and UDP-Glc as substrates) by measuring the reduction of NADP+ at 340 nm using a BioTek Epoch 2 Microplate spectrophotometer. One unit (U) of UGPase activity was defined as 1 μmol of NADPH formed per minute.
[0062]	The UGPase enzyme activity, measured in the wild-type and transgenic tubers, was also found to be lower in the transgenic tubers in both the conditions, i.e. fresh harvest and 30 days of cold storage. UGPase enzyme activity levels in the freshly harvested KC1 transgenic tubers, KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104, were 0.31, 0.56 and 0.38 U min-1 mg Protein-1 , respectively. The same for KC3 transgenic tubers, KC3 CIS5, KC3 CIS14, and KC3 CIS20, were 0.20, 0.21, and 0.31 U min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively. While, the UGPase activity levels in the wild-type KC1 and KC3 tubers were 2.01 and 1.04 U min-1 mg Protein-1 , respectively, at fresh harvest condition. UGPase enzyme activity levels in the cold-stored KC1 transgenic tubers, KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104, were 0.51, 0.73 and 0.85 U min-1 mg Protein-1, respectively. The same for KC3 transgenic tubers, KC3 CIS5, KC3 CIS14, and KC3 CIS20, were 0.24, 0.25, and 0.37 U min-1 mg Protein-1. But the UGPase activity levels in the wild-type KC1 and KC3 tubers after cold storage increased to 2.90 and 1.25 U min-1 mg Protein-1, as shown in Figure 7(c) and (d) of the present disclosure. The data shows up to 85% and 80% reduction in UGPase activity in KC1 and KC3 transgenic tubers, respectively.

EXAMPLE 8: Quantitative real time-PCR for expression of StUGPase and StVaInv
[0063]	qRT-PCR analysis was carried out using StUGPase-specific and StVaInv-specific primers of SEQ ID NO: 4-11, as shown in above Table 1. EXAMPLE 9: Southern blot analysis 
[0065]	Southern hybridization was performed to verify transgene integration and transgene copy number in the genome of CISCOM RNAi transgenic potato lines. Each genomic DNA sample of about 15 μg was fully digested in a 50 μl reaction using 5 μl of EcoRI (EcoRI-HF® 20U/μl) and resolved on a 0.8% agarose gel (without ethidium bromide) in 1X TAE buffer. Using a positively charged nylon membrane (Hybond N+, Amersham, U.K.), the Southern blot preparation process was carried out in accordance with Sambrook et al. (2001). The digested DNA was transferred by capillary action to the membrane overnight (16 hour) at room temperature. After taking out the gel carefully, the membrane was rinsed in 2X SSC (0.3 M NaCl, 0.03 M Trisodium Citrate, pH 7.0) and then spread out on Whatman 3 paper to dry by air. The membrane was fixed with Stratalinker UV-crosslinker (Stratagene, U.K.) at 22 J/cm for 90 seconds. A 790 bp DIG-labeled probe was amplified via PCR using primers specific to the nptII gene. The protocol provided by the DIG Luminescent Detection Kit (Roche) was followed for probe preparation, prehybridization, hybridization, and detection. Under dark conditions, the hybridised membrane was exposed to X-ray film (Fujifilm, Kodak) in an intensifying cassette. After 45 minutes of exposure, the X-ray film was developed in a darkroom and the results were visualized.
[0066]	Southern hybridization was performed to confirm gene integration and copy number in 6 potato CISCOM RNAi lines. Genomic DNA isolated from leaves of the RNAi transgenic lines and non-transformed KC1 and KC3 wild-type plants was digested with EcoRI, which recognizes a single site within the T-DNA region of the pBI121::CISCOM binary vector. A 790 bp nptII fragment was amplified using PCR and labelled with DIG-dUTP to serve as a probe. The six CISCOM RNAi transgenic potato lines contained 1 to 9 copies of the transgene in their genome. KC1 transgenic lines, KC1 CIS102, KC1 CIS103, and KC1 CIS104, contained 9, 2 and 8 copies of transgenes, respectively; while KC3 transgenic lines, KC3 CIS5, KC3 CIS14, and KC3 CIS20, contained 1, 2, and 2 copies of trans-gene, respectively, as shown in Figure 9 of the present disclosure.

EXAMPLE 10: Small RNA expression analysis by Northern hybridization
[0067]	Total RNA was isolated from the cold-stored tubers following a trizol-based protocol (Paul et al., 2023). A 5% metaphor gel was prepared and 80 μg total RNA per sample was loaded for separation. RNA samples were separated at 70-75 V at 4°C for 2-2.5 hr and then transferred to a positively charged nylon membrane (N+, Bright Star-Plus, Applied Biosystem) through capillary blotting setup, same as described for Southern blot transfer in the previous section. RNA was transferred to the membrane by running capillary blotting setup for seven to eight hours, with the transfer buffer kept at 4°C. Instead of using UV cross-linking, the EDC reagent was utilized, following the instructions provided by Pall et al. (2008). Using StUGPase-specific and StVaInv-specific primers, 500 nt long probe (Supplementary Table) specific to the target sequences were PCR labelled using a PCR DIG-Probe Synthesis Kit with DIG-dUTP (Roche), in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. The DIG Luminescent Detection Kit (Roche) protocol was followed for pre-hybridization, hybridization, and small RNA expression detection.
[0068]	Small RNA northern hybridization was used to detect siRNA accumulation in RNAi transgenic lines. RNA from cold-stored tubers was resolved on an 5% metaphore agarose gel and blotted onto a membrane. The membrane was then probed with randomly labelled StVaInv and StUGPase cDNA. The 21-nt oligos which served as forward primer for amplification of StVaInV and StUGpase probe were used as a positive control. Accumulation of siRNA (21-24 nt) targeting StVaInv and StUGPase can be seen in the X-ray plate as dark bands, as shown in Figure 10 of the present disclosure.

title: A REINFORCEMENT STRUCTURE FOR A CHASSIS OF A VEHICLE
abstract: Disclosed herein is a reinforcement structure (100) for a chassis of a vehicle. The reinforcement structure (100) includes a first reinforcement member (102) disposed at rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along longitudinal direction of the vehicle. One end (112) of the first reinforcement member (102) is proximal to rear suspension area of the vehicle. A second reinforcement member (104) is disposed at the rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along longitudinal direction of the vehicle. One end (114) of the second reinforcement member (104) is proximal to rear suspension area. A rear coil stiffener (106) is disposed at rear suspension area and between opposite ends of the first reinforcement member (102) and the second reinforcement member (104). The rear coil stiffener (106) attach the first reinforcement member (102) and the second reinforcement member (104) to the rear floor of the vehicle.
specification:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION
[0001]	The present disclosure relates to vehicle framework and more particularly, to a reinforcement structure for a chassis of a vehicle.
BACKGROUND
[0002]	A vehicle framework can be divided into a sub-structure and a super-structure. The sub-structure includes a chassis that forms a load-bearing part of the vehicle. The chassis is adapted to attach essential and auxiliary components, such as wheels, suspension components, and the like, to ensure smooth operation and movement of the vehicle. The super-structure is attached on top of the chassis. The super-structure includes a body structure including a vehicle frame, a cabin space, a cargo space, and a floor of the vehicle.
[0003]	Typically, during the motion of the vehicle, due to irregularities of the road, vibrations may be transmitted from the road into the cabin space of the vehicle, via the chassis of the vehicle. In particular, vibrations may be transmitted from the road to the wheels, from wheels to a suspension attachment area of the chassis, and from the suspension attachment area to a floor of the super-structure causing structural vibration. The structural vibration of the super-structure gets transmitted into the cabin space of the vehicle resulting in vibrational noises called vibro-acoustic noise. Further, the structural vibrations transmitted to the super-structure may vary at the front of the vehicle and at the rear of the vehicle. 
[0004]	Conventionally, the chassis of the vehicle includes reinforcement structures to enhance the vehicle’s structural integrity, stability, and overall performance. The conventional reinforcement structures positioned at the rear of the vehicle include a continuous long bar. The continuous long bar of the conventional reinforcement structures may help in maintaining structural alignment, however, fails to prevent the transmission of structural vibrations into the cabin of the vehicle. 
[0005]	Hence, it is desirable to develop a reinforcement structure for the chassis of the vehicle that may prevent vibro-acoustic noise from reaching the cabin space.
[0006]	The drawbacks and limitations of the conventional techniques explained in the background section are just for exemplary purposes and the invention would never limit its scope only such limitations. A person skilled in the art would understand that this invention and below mentioned description may also solve other problems or overcome the other drawbacks/disadvantages of the conventional arts which are not explicitly captured above.
SUMMARY
[0007]	This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts, in a simplified format, that are further described in the detailed description of the invention. This summary is neither intended to identify key or essential inventive concepts of the invention and nor is it intended for determining the scope of the invention.
[0008]	In an embodiment of the present disclosure, a reinforcement structure for a chassis of a vehicle is disclosed. The reinforcement structure includes a first reinforcement member, a second reinforcement member, and a rear coil stiffener. The first reinforcement member is adapted to be disposed at a rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along a longitudinal direction of the vehicle. In an embodiment, one end of the first reinforcement member is proximal to a rear suspension area of the vehicle. The second reinforcement member is adapted to be disposed at the rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along the longitudinal direction of the vehicle. In an embodiment, one end of the second reinforcement member is proximal to the rear suspension area. The rear coil stiffener is adapted to be disposed at the rear suspension area and between opposite ends of the first reinforcement member and the second reinforcement member. In an embodiment, the rear coil stiffener is adapted to attach the first reinforcement member and the second reinforcement member to the rear floor of the vehicle.
[0009]	In an embodiment of the present disclosure, a vehicle is disclosed. The vehicle includes a body structure, and a chassis adapted to be disposed under the body structure. The chassis includes a suspension area adapted to attach a suspension device, and a reinforcement structure. The reinforcement structure includes a first reinforcement member, a second reinforcement member, and a rear coil stiffener. The first reinforcement member is adapted to be disposed at a rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along a longitudinal direction of the vehicle. In an embodiment, one end of the first reinforcement member is proximal to the rear suspension area of the vehicle. The second reinforcement member is adapted to be disposed at the rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along the longitudinal direction of the vehicle. In an embodiment, one end of the second reinforcement member is proximal to the rear suspension area. The rear coil stiffener is adapted to be disposed at the rear suspension area and between opposite ends of the first reinforcement member and the second reinforcement member. In an embodiment, the rear coil stiffener is adapted to attach the first reinforcement member and the second reinforcement member to the rear floor of the vehicle.
[0010]	Accordingly, the reinforcement structure of the present disclosure having the rear coil stiffener adapted to attach the first reinforcement member and the second reinforcement member to the rear floor of the vehicle, may advantageously arrest the movement of the rear floor in the vehicle in the vertical direction to the motion of the vehicle. As a result, a significant reduction in the structural vibration may be observed in the vehicle deployed with the reinforcement structure of the present disclosure. Therefore, present disclosure advantageously vibro-acoustic noise inside the cabin space of the vehicle. 
[0011]	Further, the reinforcement structure of the present disclosure may be constructed in three parts, i.e., the first reinforcement member, the second reinforcement member, and the rear coil stiffener. Accordingly, having the reinforcement structure constructed in three parts may improve the adaptability of the reinforcement structure, allowing its implementation in a variety of vehicle models.

It is appreciated that these drawings depict only typical embodiments of the invention and are therefore not to be considered limiting of its scope. The invention will be described and explained with additional specificity and detail with the accompanying drawings.

[0025]	Embodiments of the present invention will be described below in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings.
[0026]	Figure 1 illustrates an exploded view of a reinforcement structure 100 for a chassis of the vehicle, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0027]	The vehicle may include a body structure, and the chassis adapted to be disposed under the body structure. The chassis may act as a main support structure of the vehicle that may provide a foundation for mounting all other components, including an engine, a transmission, and a super-structure of the vehicle. The chassis may further include a suspension attachment area adapted to secure a suspension system. The suspension attachment area may be adapted to handle stresses and forces exerted by the suspension system. The suspension system may include helical coil springs, shock absorbers, and linkages that work together to absorb shocks from the road, thereby providing a smooth ride and maintaining the stability of the vehicle.
[0028]	The chassis of the vehicle may be reinforced with the reinforcement structure 100 to enhance the vehicle’s structural integrity, stability, and overall performance. In an embodiment, the reinforcement structure 100 may be oriented in a longitudinal direction of the vehicle. The reinforcement structure 100 may include a first reinforcement member 102, a second reinforcement member 104, and a rear coil stiffener 106. 
[0029]	The first reinforcement member 102 may be adapted to be disposed at a rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along the longitudinal direction of the vehicle. Further, on assembly of the the reinforcement structure 100, one end 112 of the first reinforcement member 102 may be proximal to the rear suspension area of the vehicle. The second reinforcement member 104 may be adapted to be disposed at the rear floor of the vehicle and oriented along the longitudinal direction of the vehicle. Further, on assembly of the the reinforcement structure 100, one end 114 of the second reinforcement member may be proximal to the rear suspension area of the vehicle. The rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to be disposed at the rear suspension area, and between opposite ends of the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 of the reinforcement structure 100. In an embodiment, the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to attach the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 to the rear floor of the vehicle. 
[0030]	Accordingly, the reinforcement structure 100, in particular the attachment of the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 to the rear floor via the rear coil stiffener 106, may advantageously arrest the movement of the rear floor in the vehicle in the vertical direction to the motion of the vehicle. As a result, the reinforcement structure 100 may prevent transmission of the structural vibration to the rear floor of the vehicle. Accordingly, transmission of vibro-acoustic noise into a cabin space of the vehicle may be prevented. 
[0031]	As shown in Figure 1, the reinforcement structure 100 may be constructed in three parts, in contrast to a single longitudinal reinforcement structure of the conventional art. The three parts may include the first reinforcement member 102, the second reinforcement member 104, and the rear coil stiffener 106. Accordingly, having the reinforcement structure 100 constructed in three parts may improve the adaptability of the reinforcement structure 100, allowing its implementation in a variety of vehicle models. 
[0032]	Figures 2A to 2C illustrate different views of the rear coil stiffener 106. Figure 2A illustrates a top planar view of the rear coil stiffener 106, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 2B illustrates a bottom perspective view of the rear coil stiffener 106, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 2C illustrates another bottom perspective view of the rear coil stiffener 106, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figures 2A-2C are described in conjunction hereinafter for ease of explanation.
[0033]	As shown, the rear coil stiffener 106 may include a U-shape structure having a base member 202, a first stiffener member 210, a second stiffener member 220, a third stiffener member 230, and a fourth stiffener member 240. The base member 202 may include a pair of longitudinal edges and a pair of lateral edges. The first stiffener member 210 may protrude from a first longitudinal edge of the pair of longitudinal edges of the base member 202. The second stiffener member 220 may protrude from a second longitudinal edge of the pair of longitudinal edges of the base member 202. The third stiffener member 230 may protrude from a first lateral edge of the pair of lateral edges of the base member 202. The fourth stiffener member 240 may protrude from a second lateral edge of the pair of lateral edges of the base member 202.
[0034]	In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be perpendicular to the base member 202. In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to abut the first reinforcement member 102. In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 may further include a first set of flaps 212, 214, and 216 protruding perpendicularly from edges of the first stiffener member 210. In an embodiment, the first set of flaps 212, 214, and 216 may be adapted to overlap a portion of an outer surface of the first reinforcement member 102. 
[0035]	In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be perpendicular to the base member 202. In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to abut the second reinforcement member 104. In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 may further include a second set of flaps 222, 224, and 226 protruding perpendicularly from edges of the second stiffener member 220. In an embodiment, the second set of flaps 222, 224, and 226 may be adapted to overlap a portion of an outer surface of the second reinforcement member 104. 
[0036]	In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be planar to the base member 202. In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to abut a wheel housing of the vehicle. In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 may further include a third flap 232 protruding perpendicularly from an edge of the third stiffener member 230, in a direction opposite to the first stiffener member 210 and the second stiffener member 220. In an embodiment, the third flap 232 may be adapted to abut the wheel housing. 
[0037]	In an embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 240 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be planar to the base member 202. In an embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 240 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to abut the rear floor of the vehicle.
[0038]	In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may abut the first reinforcement member 102. In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may be adapted to rigidly attach to the first reinforcement member 102. In particular, the first set of flaps 212, 214, and 216 of the first stiffener member 210 overlapping the portion of the first reinforcement member 102 may be rigidly attached to the first reinforcement member 102. In an embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 and the first reinforcement member 102 may be rigidly attached at one or more first attachment points. The one or more first attachment points corresponds to points of contact between the first stiffener member 210 and the first reinforcement member 102 at which a rigid attachment may be formed. In one embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 and the first reinforcement member 102 may be spot welded at the one or more first attachment points. In another embodiment, the first stiffener member 210 and the first reinforcement member 102 may be attached via fasteners at the one or more first attachment points.
[0039]	In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may abut the second reinforcement member 104. In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 may be adapted to rigidly attach to the second reinforcement member 104. In particular, the second set of flaps 222, 224, and 226 of the second stiffener member 220 overlapping the portion of the second reinforcement member 104 may be rigidly attached to the second reinforcement member 104. In an embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 and the second reinforcement member 104 may be rigidly attached at one or more second attachment points. The one or more second attachment points corresponds to points of contact between the second stiffener member 220 and the second reinforcement member 104 at which a rigid attachment may be formed. In one embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 and the second reinforcement member 104 may be spot welded at the one or more second attachment points. In another embodiment, the second stiffener member 220 and the second reinforcement member 104 may be attached via fasteners at the one or more second attachment points.
[0040]	In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may abut the wheel housing of the vehicle. In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 may be adapted to rigidly attach to the wheel housing of the vehicle. In particular, the third flap 232 of the third stiffener member 230 that abuts the wheel housing may be rigidly attached to the wheel housing of the vehicle. In an embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 and the wheel housing of the vehicle may be rigidly attached at one or more third attachment points. The one or more third attachment points corresponds to points of contact between the third stiffener member 230 and the wheel housing at which a rigid attachment may be formed. In one embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 and the wheel housing of the vehicle may be spot welded at the one or more third attachment points. In another embodiment, the third stiffener member 230 and the wheel housing of the vehicle may be attached via fasteners at the one or more third attachment points.
[0041]	In an embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 240 of the rear coil stiffener 106 may abut the rear floor of the vehicle. In an embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 240 may be adapted to rigidly attach to the rear floor of the vehicle. In an embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 230 and the rear floor of the vehicle may be rigidly attached at one or more fourth attachment points. The one or more fourth attachment points corresponds to points of contact between the fourth stiffener member 230 and the rear floor at which a rigid attachment may be formed. In one embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 230 and the rear floor of the vehicle may be spot welded at the one or more fourth attachment points. In another embodiment, the fourth stiffener member 230 and the rear floor of the vehicle may be attached via fasteners at the one or more fourth attachment points.
[0042]	Additionally, the non-uniform structure formed at the rear coil stiffener 106 may further improve crash performance of the vehicle. In particular, in an event of a rear crash, the rear coil stiffener 106 may crumble in its entire length, and consequently, the rear coil stiffener 106 may absorb crash energy within its structure. Accordingly, the transmission of the crash energy may be prevented from passing onto the first reinforcement member 102, thereby preventing damage to the cabin space of the vehicle.
[0043]	In addition, the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure being rigidly attached to the wheel housing area and the rear floor of the vehicle, may arrest the movement of the rear floor in the vehicle in the vertical direction. As a result, a significant reduction in the structural vibration may be observed in the vehicle deployed with the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure. 
[0044]	Further, the structural vibrations experienced by the rear floor of the vehicle deployed with the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure may be significantly lower than the structural vibration experienced by the rear floor of the vehicles deployed with conventional continuous long reinforcement structure.
[0045]	In particular, the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 being rigidly secured to the rear floor and the wheel housing area of the vehicle via the first attachment points, the second attachment points, the third attachment points, and the fourth attachment points of the rear coil stiffener 106 may arrest the movement of the rear floor in vertical direction thereby, preventing the transmission of structural vibrations to the rear floor of the vehicle.
[0046]	In a non-limiting example, when dynamic loading may be applied to the rear suspension attachment area of the vehicle having the reinforcement structure of the present disclosure, then, the accumulation of stress near the rear suspension attachment area of the vehicle deployed with the reinforcement structure may be significantly less in comparison with the vehicle deployed with conventional continuous long reinforcement structure. Therefore, the rigid attachment of the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure with the rear floor of the vehicle may result in a significant decrease in the accumulation of stress in the rear suspension attachment area of the vehicle. In particular, the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 being rigidly secured to the rear floor and the wheel housing area of the vehicle via the first attachment points, the second attachment points, the third attachment points, and the fourth attachment points of the rear coil stiffener 106 may arrest the movement of the rear floor in vertical direction thereby, preventing the transmission of structural vibrations to the rear floor of the vehicle.
[0047]	The present disclosure may further include several advantages over the existing techniques. For example, the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure having the rear coil stiffener 106 adapted to attach the first reinforcement member 102 and the second reinforcement member 104 to the rear floor of the vehicle, may advantageously arrest the movement of the rear floor in the vehicle in the vertical direction. As a result, a significant reduction in the structural vibration may be observed in the vehicle deployed with the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure. Therefore, present disclosure advantageously prevents vibro-acoustic noise from reaching the cabin space of the vehicle. 
[0048]	Further, the reinforcement structure 100 of the present disclosure may be constructed in three parts, i.e., the first reinforcement member 102, the second reinforcement member 104, and the rear coil stiffener 106, Accordingly, having the reinforcement structure 100 constructed in three parts may improve the adaptability of the reinforcement structure 100, allowing its implementation in a variety of vehicle models.
[0049]	Furthermore, the rear coil stiffener 106 of the present disclosure may crumble in its entire length in an event of a rear crash, and consequently, the rear coil stiffener 106 may absorb crash energy within its structure. Accordingly, the transmission of the crash energy may be prevented from passing onto the first reinforcement member 102, thereby preventing damage to the cabin space of the vehicle.

title: LIFTING SYSTEM FOR MOBILE ROBOTS
abstract:
ABSTRACT
A lifting assembly is described, comprising a support frame and at least one lifting platform arranged on the support frame. The at least one lifting platform comprises a scissor mechanism having a lower end pivotally mounted to the support frame and an upper end supporting a platform surface. At least one linear motion guide rail is arranged vertically on the support frame to provide guidance for vertical movement of the scissor mechanism. At least one cam mechanism actuates the scissor mechanism. The scissor mechanism provides vertical stroke while maintaining the platform surface parallel to the support frame through guidance of the linear motion guide rail. The lifting assembly is configured for implementation in material handling systems requiring controlled vertical positioning capabilities.

FIELD OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE
[0001]	The present disclosure relates generally to the field of material handling equipment and lifting mechanisms. More specifically, the present disclosure pertains to lifting assemblies incorporating scissor mechanisms with cam actuation systems for automated applications, particularly those requiring precise vertical positioning capabilities while maintaining a compact form factor.

BACKGROUND
[0002]	In modern manufacturing and material handling operations, automated lifting systems play an important role in streamlining production processes and improving operational efficiency. These systems are extensively used for material handling in warehouses, distribution centres, assembly lines, and various industrial applications. The ability to adjust working heights during material handling operations is a requirement for automated systems, as it enables operators and automated equipment to access different areas including storage racks, assembly stations, and perform various tasks ergonomically and efficiently.
[0003]	Several challenges exist in implementing lifting mechanisms for automated systems in industrial operations. A primary constraint is the overall height limitation of the lifting system, as excessive height can interfere with other equipment and compromise operator accessibility or automated system functionality. Additionally, the lifting mechanism must provide sufficient vertical stroke to accommodate various working heights while maintaining stability throughout the range of motion. The need to synchronize multiple lifting points for balanced platform elevation, coupled with space constraints and the requirement for position control, presents significant engineering challenges in automated environments.
[0004]	Conventional solutions to these challenges typically employ hydraulic lifting systems, traditional scissor mechanisms, and pneumatic actuators. Hydraulic systems offer high load capacity and smooth operation but require complex fluid power circuits, pumps, reservoirs, and regular maintenance of hydraulic components. Traditional scissor lift mechanisms, while mechanically simpler, often demand substantial installation height to achieve desired stroke lengths, making them unsuitable for applications with height constraints. Pneumatic systems provide clean operation but may struggle with precise position control and synchronization between multiple lifting points, particularly in applications requiring exact positioning.
[0005]	While the conventional solutions mentioned above may provide some operational capability, they often fall short in achieving consistent performance required for automated systems. Hydraulic systems require extensive maintenance and present potential fluid leakage issues that can contaminate work environments. Traditional scissor mechanisms without proper actuation control lack the precision needed for automated operations and may not provide adequate synchronization when multiple lifting points are required. Pneumatic systems, while clean, often lack the positional accuracy and holding capability required for automated applications, and compressed air systems can be energy-intensive and noisy.
[0006]	Therefore, there exists a need for an improved lifting assembly specifically designed for automated systems that can efficiently address the technical problems associated with the conventional systems.

SUMMARY
[0007]	In an exemplary embodiment, a lifting assembly is described, comprising: a support frame; at least one lifting platform arranged on the support frame, the at least one lifting platform comprising: a scissor mechanism having a lower end pivotally mounted to the support frame and an upper end supporting a platform surface; at least one linear motion (LM) guide rail arranged vertically on the support frame to provide guidance for vertical movement of the scissor mechanism; and at least one cam mechanism to actuate the scissor mechanism.
[0008]	In some embodiments, the at least one cam mechanism comprises a rotatable cam and at least one cam follower, wherein the cam follower engages with the rotatable cam and is coupled to a central portion of the scissor mechanism.
[0009]	In some embodiments, the lifting assembly further comprises a drive assembly configured to operate the cam mechanism, wherein the drive assembly comprises a motor and a gearbox coupled to the motor.
[0010]	In some embodiments, the at least one lifting platform comprises a first lifting platform and a second lifting platform, and wherein the drive assembly further comprises a drive shaft coupled to the gearbox and connecting cam mechanisms of the first lifting platform and the second lifting platform, wherein rotation of the drive shaft causes synchronized rotation of rotatable cams to actuate scissor mechanisms of both lifting platforms.
[0011]	In some embodiments, the scissor mechanism comprises: a plurality of link plates arranged in a crossed configuration; a plurality of pivot joints connecting the link plates at intersection points; and a plurality of bearing assemblies mounted at the pivot joints to facilitate rotational movement between the link plates during extension and retraction of the scissor mechanism.
[0012]	In some embodiments, the lifting assembly further comprises at least one LM guide block mounted to the central portion of the scissor mechanism, wherein the at least one LM guide block engages with the at least one LM guide rail to maintain vertical alignment during lifting operation.
[0013]	In some embodiments, the at least one cam follower comprises: a roller bearing assembly mounted on a shaft; a bearing housing enclosing the roller bearing assembly; and a mounting bracket connecting the bearing housing to the central portion of the scissor mechanism.
[0014]	In some embodiments, the drive shaft comprises: a first end portion coupled to the cam mechanism of the first lifting platform; a second end portion coupled to the cam mechanism of the second lifting platform; and a coupling assembly connecting the gearbox to the drive shaft for transferring rotational motion from the motor.
[0015]	In some embodiments, the motor comprises: an encoder for monitoring angular position of a motor shaft; a drive controller for synchronized operation of the at least one lifting platform; and a braking mechanism for maintaining the at least one lifting platform at intermediate positions between a fully retracted position and a fully extended position.
[0016]	In some embodiments, the scissor mechanism, when actuated from a fully retracted position to a fully extended position through rotation of the at least one cam mechanism, provides a vertical stroke while maintaining the platform parallel to the support frame through guidance of the at least one LM guide rail.
[0017]	In some embodiments, the support frame includes a first mounting region for supporting the first lifting platform, a second mounting region for supporting the second lifting platform, and a central region between the first mounting region and the second mounting region for housing the drive assembly.
[0018]	In another exemplary embodiment, a system is described, comprising: a platform; the lifting assembly according to claim 1 mounted on the platform; and a control unit configured to coordinate lifting operations of the lifting assembly.
