title: SMART BIO-ACOUSTIC DUST NEUTRALIZER USING HARMONIC RESONANCE FIELDS FOR URBAN AIRSPACES
abstract: The present invention discloses a Smart Bio-Acoustic Dust Neutralizer designed to reduce airborne particulate matter in open urban environments through directed harmonic resonance fields. The system comprises a phased acoustic emitter array, environmental and bio-indicator sensors, an AI-driven optimization unit, a micro-seeding subsystem, and a wireless mesh communication interface. Real-time sensor data enables the AI controller to dynamically adjust acoustic frequency, amplitude, and phase to form steerable resonance corridors that induce particle agglomeration. Optional micro-seeding enhances collision rates in low-concentration conditions. Safety and compliance modules continuously monitor sound-pressure levels and human presence to ensure regulatory adherence. Multiple nodes coordinate through a mesh network to expand coverage, target pollution hotspots, and optimize energy use. The invention provides an adaptive, filter-less, scalable solution for urban air-quality improvement, achieving effective particulate neutralization while minimizing noise, power consumption, and environmental impact.
specification:
The present invention provides a Smart Bio-Acoustic Dust Neutralizer, comprising a modular, intelligent, and networked system configured to actively mitigate airborne particulate matter in open urban environments through controlled acoustic energy, artificial intelligence, environmental sensing, and optional micro-seeding techniques. The invention is specifically designed to overcome the limitations of conventional acoustic particulate control technologies that are restricted to enclosed chambers, ducts, or industrial filtration systems. In contrast, existing systems, the disclosed invention generates steerable harmonic resonance corridors in open air, enabling localized agglomeration and neutralization of suspended particulate matter while maintaining safety for humans, animals, and surrounding infrastructure. The system operates as a distributed network of autonomous nodes capable of individually or cooperatively treating pollution hotspots in urban environments such as roadsides, construction sites, industrial perimeters, transportation hubs, public spaces, and smart city installations.
[0026]		Each deployable node of the system comprises a phased acoustic emitter array, an environmental sensing subsystem, an optional bio-indicator sensing module, an optional micro-seeding subsystem, an embedded processing and artificial intelligence controller, communication interfaces, power management circuitry, and multiple safety mechanisms. The phased acoustic emitter array consists of a plurality of individually addressable transducer elements arranged in linear, circular, planar, or other suitable geometries. Each transducer is independently controlled with respect to phase, frequency, amplitude, and timing, thereby enabling dynamic beamforming and the creation of steerable harmonic resonance corridors within open-air environments. These harmonic corridors concentrate acoustic energy in predetermined spatial regions, increasing the probability of collisions among suspended particulate matter and promoting agglomeration into larger particles that subsequently settle naturally or become easier to remove through existing environmental processes.
[0027]		The acoustic subsystem further includes driver circuits, waveform amplifiers, impedance matching circuitry, thermal protection components, and a digital signal processing module configured to generate multi-frequency acoustic signals across audible and ultrasonic frequency ranges. The digital signal processor synthesizes harmonic waveforms and applies beamforming algorithms in accordance with control instructions generated by the embedded artificial intelligence engine. The processor continuously modifies phase delays, amplitude distributions, and frequency combinations to optimize the acoustic field in response to changing environmental conditions. Consequently, the system provides highly localized and adaptive acoustic treatment while minimizing unnecessary energy consumption and acoustic exposure outside the intended treatment zone.
[0028]		Each node incorporates a comprehensive sensing subsystem to support intelligent operation. The sensing subsystem includes one or more particulate sensors configured to measure airborne particle concentration and size distribution across multiple particulate ranges, including ultrafine particles, PM1.0, PM2.5, and PM10. Meteorological sensors, including wind speed sensors, wind direction sensors, humidity sensors, temperature sensors, and barometric pressure sensors, continuously monitor atmospheric conditions affecting particle dispersion and residence time. Optional bio-indicator sensors, such as bio aerosol detectors, fluorescence-based biological sensors, passive biological samplers, or chemical biosensors, may additionally detect biological particulate content present within the atmosphere. Acoustic microphones and sound pressure level sensors continuously monitor both emitted and ambient sound levels, thereby enabling closed-loop regulation of acoustic emissions. Human and wildlife detection devices, including passive infrared sensors, proximity sensors, radar sensors, or privacy-preserving imaging systems, further detect the presence of people or animals to ensure safe operation within populated environments.
[0029]		The invention may further comprise an optional micro-seeding subsystem configured to improve acoustic agglomeration efficiency under conditions where ambient particulate concentration is insufficient for effective particle collision. The micro-seeding subsystem includes sealed reservoirs containing environmentally compatible hygroscopic or coagulation-promoting materials, precision metered dispensers, piezoelectric spray actuators, dosing controllers, containment structures, and chemical safety mechanisms. The artificial intelligence controller selectively activates the micro-seeding subsystem only when predetermined environmental conditions indicate that acoustic treatment alone would be ineffective. The released material is dispensed in extremely low concentrations sufficient to promote particle nucleation while remaining within environmental safety regulations. Safety interlocks prevent accidental release and ensure that only approved materials are utilized.
[0030]		The embedded controller forms the computational core of each node and comprises one or more processors executing artificial intelligence algorithms, optimization routines, digital signal processing software, and real-time operating systems. The controller receives continuous streams of information from the sensing subsystem and generates optimized acoustic control strategies based on environmental conditions, particulate concentration, meteorological data, historical operating records, and safety constraints. Local memory stores operational logs, learned environmental models, calibration information, and machine learning parameters, while cloud-connected storage may provide centralized model updates, long-term environmental analysis, and regulatory reporting.
[0031]		Multiple nodes communicate through secure wireless mesh networks, low-power wide-area networks, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or equivalent communication technologies. The communication subsystem enables synchronized beam steering, cooperative treatment of large pollution zones, coordinated energy management, and distributed environmental sensing across multiple deployment locations. The network architecture allows neighbouring nodes to exchange sensor information, transfer treatment responsibilities, coordinate harmonic corridor formation, and optimize overall system efficiency. A cloud-based or edge-based orchestration platform may supervise network-wide operation while allowing each node to retain autonomous decision-making capability in the event of communication interruption.
[0032]		The invention further provides an operator interface accessible through web-based or mobile applications. The operator interface permits authorized users to configure operational parameters, schedule treatment sessions, monitor system health, access environmental data, review regulatory compliance reports, manually override automated functions when required, and perform remote diagnostics. Firmware updates, software upgrades, calibration routines, and fault detection procedures may be performed remotely using secure over-the-air communication mechanisms, thereby reducing maintenance requirements and improving long-term operational reliability.
[0033]		In operation, each node normally remains in a low-power monitoring state during which environmental sensors continuously acquire particulate, meteorological, biological, and acoustic information at predefined sampling intervals. Upon detection of elevated particulate concentrations or scheduled activation conditions, the system increases sensor sampling rates and initiates environmental characterization. Sensor fusion algorithms combine particulate measurements, atmospheric parameters, and optional biological information to estimate the three-dimensional distribution, density, particle-size spectrum, and anticipated residence time of the airborne particulate cloud. These parameters are supplied to the artificial intelligence optimization engine for treatment planning.
[0034]		The artificial intelligence engine generates multiple candidate acoustic treatment strategies using learned environmental models, physical acoustic simulations, surrogate prediction models, and optimization algorithms. Each candidate strategy specifies acoustic frequencies, harmonic combinations, phase distributions, beam steering angles, emission timing, power levels, and optional micro-seeding parameters. The optimization engine evaluates each candidate according to multiple objective functions including particulate agglomeration efficiency, energy consumption, acoustic safety, environmental compatibility, operational cost, and regulatory compliance. The strategy providing the highest predicted effectiveness while satisfying all safety constraints is selected for execution.
[0035]		Before acoustic emission begins, the safety supervision subsystem performs comprehensive validation of the selected treatment strategy. Human presence detectors, wildlife sensors, sound pressure level estimators, geofencing databases, and regulatory constraints are simultaneously evaluated. Sensitive areas including hospitals, schools, residential zones, wildlife habitats, and densely occupied pedestrian regions are automatically identified. If projected sound levels exceed permissible limits or protected areas intersect the intended harmonic corridor, the artificial intelligence engine recalculates the treatment plan by modifying beam orientation, reducing acoustic power, selecting alternative frequencies, or temporarily suspending operation until safe conditions exist. Where micro-seeding is enabled, additional authorization procedures verify approved materials, allowable dosage limits, and proper dispenser functionality before release is permitted.
[0036]		Following successful safety verification, the digital signal processing engine converts the optimized treatment plan into synchronized drive signals for each transducer element of the phased acoustic array. The phased array then generates one or more steerable harmonic resonance corridors within the targeted atmospheric region. When required, the optional micro-seeding subsystem releases precisely metered quantities of environmentally compatible nucleation agents synchronized with the acoustic emission to enhance particle collision probability. Throughout operation, microphones, sound pressure level sensors, particulate detectors, and environmental sensors continuously provide feedback to the controller. Closed-loop algorithms dynamically modify frequencies, phase relationships, amplitudes, and beam orientation in real time to compensate for changing wind conditions, atmospheric turbulence, shifting pollution sources, and evolving particulate distributions.
[0037]		The invention further supports coordinated operation among multiple nodes. Neighbouring units exchange localization information, environmental measurements, beamforming parameters, and operational status through the communication network. Cooperative algorithms distribute treatment responsibilities among multiple nodes to create extended harmonic resonance corridors covering larger geographic areas while minimizing redundant energy expenditure. Nodes may sequentially transfer treatment responsibilities as pollution plumes move with prevailing winds, thereby enabling continuous mitigation across extensive urban regions.
[0038]		Upon completion of the treatment cycle, the controller compares post-treatment particulate measurements with predefined performance objectives. If desired particulate reduction has not been achieved, the optimization process repeats using updated environmental information until target conditions are satisfied or predefined operating limits are reached. After successful treatment, acoustic emission ceases, optional micro-seeding is terminated, and the node returns to standby monitoring mode. All operational data, including sensor measurements, acoustic parameters, optimization decisions, environmental conditions, safety events, and treatment effectiveness, are securely stored within local memory and optionally transmitted to centralized databases for long-term analysis, predictive modelling, and continuous machine learning refinement. The accumulated operational history enables the system to progressively improve future treatment strategies for specific geographic locations and recurring environmental conditions.
[0039]		The system incorporates multiple redundant safety features to ensure reliable operation under all environmental conditions. Continuous sound pressure monitoring automatically attenuates acoustic output whenever predefined thresholds are approached. Human or animal detection immediately reduces acoustic intensity, redirects beam patterns, or suspends operation. Hardware diagnostics continuously monitor transducer health, sensor functionality, communication integrity, and power system status. In the event of component failure, communication loss, or abnormal operating conditions, the controller automatically transitions to conservative operating modes or safely suspends treatment while notifying maintenance personnel. Immutable operational logs support regulatory audits, maintenance planning, and environmental compliance verification.
[0040]		The invention may be installed on existing urban infrastructure including lighting poles, traffic signals, building facades, transportation shelters, industrial structures, mobile platforms, autonomous vehicles, or unmanned aerial systems. Installation procedures include acoustic calibration using reference microphones, environmental sensor calibration using certified standards, communication network configuration, and safety verification. Routine maintenance consists primarily of inspection of acoustic transducers, sensor verification, replenishment of optional micro-seeding reservoirs, software updates, and periodic recalibration. The filter-less architecture substantially reduces maintenance requirements compared with conventional air filtration systems.
[0045]		Alternative embodiments of the invention include mobile particulate mitigation platforms mounted on service vehicles or drones, hybrid systems combining acoustic beamforming with electrostatic collection devices, coordinated deployment with vegetative pollution barriers, centralized cloud-based citywide orchestration systems, adaptive selection of environmentally compatible micro-seeding agents, and fallback operating modes utilizing conservative preconfigured beamforming profiles during sensor failures. Accordingly, the disclosed Smart Bio-Acoustic Dust Neutralizer provides an intelligent, scalable, adaptive, and environmentally safe solution for mitigating airborne particulate pollution in open urban environments through coordinated acoustic resonance, advanced sensing, artificial intelligence, and distributed network operation. ,

title: DISPLAY DEVICE
abstract:
A display device including a bendable display panel in which a plurality of sub-pixels are arranged, a support portion overlapping at least a portion of the display panel, a first attachment portion that attaches at least a portion of the display panel to at least a portion of the support portion, and a coating layer overlapping at least a portion of the display panel and disposed on at least a portion of a side surface of the support portion is provided. In this configuration, the display panel is more resistant to cracking when reshaped.

CROSS REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION

BACKGROUND
[0002]	FIELD
[0003]	Embodiments of the invention relate generally to a display device.  More particularly, a new way to construct conventionally flat display devices such that they can be bent or assume curved shapes without damage is disclosed.
[0004]	DISCUSSION OF THE BACKGROUND
[0005]	As the era of advanced information technology has arrived, the field of display technology, which visually represents electrical information signals, has rapidly developed. In response to this trend, various display devices having excellent characteristics such as reduced thickness, lightweight, and low power consumption have been developed. Specific examples of such display devices include a liquid crystal display (LCD), a plasma display panel (PDP), a field emission display (FED), and an organic light-emitting display (OLED).
[0006]	As applications for these display devices have multiplied, manufacturers have sought to increase their adaptability and expand the range of physical forms and shapes that displays can assume.  New uses continue to arise for displays that can be curved, folded, or rolled.  Devices that include displays can be made more compact and portable.  An improved range of viewing angles can be supported in a great range of applications.  Wearable devices with curved or rolled displays, including watches and clothing items, are becoming more popular.  Designers of smartphones, tablets, automotive display screens and medical diagnostic devices are eager to incorporate new bendable display technologies in order to offer consumers electronic devices in forms that are more appealing or practical for their needs.
[0007]	For example, various components may be mounted in a display device, and structures having various display layouts have been developed to protect such components.
[0008]	However, the most useful display technologies, including LCD, PDP and OLED technologies, were initially developed to provide flat, non-flexible screens.  There remains a need in the art to adapt these display technologies to new market needs for displays that can be curved, folded, or rolled.
[0009]	The above information disclosed in this Background section is only for understanding of the background of the inventive concepts, and, therefore, it may contain information that does not constitute prior art.

[0010]	Embodiments of the present disclosure meet the above-described need in the art for a display device in which a display panel is bent.  Such bending is made practical by a narrow bezel, which is preferred by designers for the modern, minimalist look that it imparts to displays.  A narrow bezel also offers the advantage of minimizing any gap between adjacent screens.

[0055]	Referring to FIG. 1, the display device 100 according to an embodiment of the present disclosure may include a display panel 110 in which a plurality of gate lines GL and data lines DL are connected and a plurality of sub-pixels SP are arranged in a matrix form, a gate driving circuit 120 that drives the plurality of gate lines GL, a data driving circuit 130 that supplies data voltages through the plurality of data lines DL, a controller 140 that controls the gate driving circuit 120 and the data driving circuit 130, and a power management circuit 150.
[0056]	The display panel 110 displays an image based on scan signals and light-emission control signals delivered from the gate driving circuit 120 through the plurality of gate lines GL, and data voltages delivered from the data driving circuit 130 through the plurality of data lines DL.
[0057]	In the case of a liquid crystal display, the display panel 110 may include a liquid crystal layer formed between two substrates and may operate in any known mode such as a twisted nematic (TN) mode, a vertical alignment (VA) mode, an in-plane switching (IPS) mode, or a fringe field switching (FFS) mode. On the other hand, in the case of an organic light-emitting display, the display panel 110 may be implemented in a top emission type, a bottom emission type, or a dual emission type.
[0058]	The display panel 110 may include a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix form, and each pixel may include sub-pixels SP of different colors, for example, a white sub-pixel, a red sub-pixel, a green sub-pixel, and a blue sub-pixel. Each sub-pixel SP may be defined by the plurality of data lines DL and the plurality of gate lines GL.
[0059]	One sub-pixel SP may include a thin film transistor (TFT) formed in a region where one data line DL and one gate line GL intersect, a light-emitting device such as an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) that charges a data voltage, and a storage capacitor that is electrically connected to the light-emitting device to maintain the voltage.
[0060]	The gate driving circuit 120 is controlled by the controller 140 and controls the driving timing of the plurality of sub-pixels SP by sequentially outputting scan signals to the plurality of gate lines GL disposed in the display panel 110.
[0061]	In this case, the gate driving circuit 120 may include one or more gate driving integrated circuits (GDICs), and may be disposed only on one side of the display panel 110 or on both sides depending on a driving method. Alternatively, the gate driving circuit 120 may be embedded in a bezel region of the display panel 110 and implemented in a gate-in-panel (GIP) form.
[0062]	The data driving circuit 130 receives image data DATA from the controller 140, converts the received image data DATA into data voltages in an analog form, and then outputs the data voltages to the respective data lines DL in synchronization with the timing at which scan signals are applied through the gate lines GL. Accordingly, each sub-pixel SP connected to the data lines DL displays a light-emission signal having a luminance corresponding to the data voltage.
[0063]	Similarly, the data driving circuit 130 may include one or more source driving integrated circuits (SDICs), and the source driving integrated circuits SDICs may be connected to bonding pads of the display panel 110 by a tape automated bonding (TAB) method or a chip-on-glass (COG) method, or may be directly disposed on the display panel 110.
[0064]	The controller 140 supplies various control signals to the gate driving circuit 120 and the data driving circuit 130 and controls operations of the gate driving circuit 120 and the data driving circuit 130. That is, the controller 140 controls the gate driving circuit 120 to output scan signals according to timing implemented in each frame, and on the other hand, delivers the image data DATA received from outside to the data driving circuit 130.
[0065]	In this case, the controller 140 receives, from an external host system 160, various timing signals including a vertical synchronization signal (Vsync), a horizontal synchronization signal (Hsync), a data enable (DE) signal, and a main clock (MCLK), together with the image data DATA.
[0066]	The host system 160 may be any one of a television (TV) system, a set-top box, a navigation system, a personal computer (PC), a home theater system, a mobile device, and a wearable device.
[0067]	Accordingly, the controller 140 generates a control signal using various timing signals received from the host system 160 and transmits the control signal to the gate driving circuit 120 and the data driving circuit 130.
[0068]	For example, the controller 140 outputs various gate control signals, including a gate start pulse (GSP), a gate clock (GCLK), and a gate output enable signal (GOE), to control the gate driving circuit 120.
[0069]	In addition, the controller 140 outputs various data control signals, including a source start pulse (SSP), a source sampling clock (SCLK), and a source output enable signal (SOE), to control the data driving circuit 130.

title: METHOD AND APPARATUS FOR CLEANING CONTAINERS WITH ULTRASONIC TRANSDUCER AND MONITORING SYSTEM
abstract:
The present invention relates to a method for cleaning containers, preferably reusable bottles, wherein ultrasonic vibrations are generated by at least one ultrasonic transducer and applied to the containers during cleaning. According to the invention, it is provided for a state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be monitored by a monitoring system, wherein the state is a mechanical state, an optical state and/or an electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. The invention also relates to an apparatus for carrying out the method.
FIG. 1
specification:
METHOD AND APPARATUS FOR CLEANING CONTAINERS WITH ULTRASONIC TRANSDUCER AND MONITORING SYSTEM

[0001]	The present invention relates to a method for cleaning containers, preferably reusable bottles, according to claim 1, and to an apparatus for cleaning containers according to claim 14.

PRIOR ART

[0002]	Methods for cleaning containers, preferably reusable bottles, are known in the prior art. The containers are cleaned of germs and dirt using a plurality of spray nozzles and immersion baths with cleaning medium, for example consisting of water and alkali. In addition, the labels stuck onto the containers are removed during cleaning.

[0003]	Since the containers have to be cleaned in a wide variety of soiling conditions, from almost clean to completely covered in sand, mud and mold, and since a plurality of label materials, different adhesives used to attach the labels to the reusable bottles, and layer and/or label finishes are used which can inhibit/slow down the penetration of the cleaning medium through the label, the cleaning method must be such that even hard-to-remove soiling and labels are still reliably removed. This is resource intensive.

[0004]	In the prior art, as shown for example in CN104338708A, it is therefore known to generate ultrasonic vibrations during cleaning by at least one ultrasonic transducer and to apply them to the containers. This can improve the cleaning of the containers, as some soiling can be loosened and labels can be perforated by the ultrasonic vibrations, which can improve the penetration of the labels by the cleaning medium. This allows the method to be carried out in a more resource-efficient manner.

[0005]	Nevertheless, there is still a need for improvement regarding the reliability of the container cleaning method and the required resource utilization, and in particular regarding possible unforeseen process shutdowns.

OBJECT

[0006]	Based on the known prior art, the technical object to be achieved is therefore to specify a method and an apparatus for cleaning containers that enables improvements with regard to the above-mentioned need.

SOLUTION

[0007]	This object is achieved according to the invention by the method for cleaning containers according to claim 1 and the apparatus for cleaning containers according to claim 14. Advantageous developments of the invention are disclosed in the dependent claims.

[0008]	The method according to the invention for cleaning containers, preferably reusable bottles, wherein ultrasonic vibrations are generated by at least one ultrasonic transducer and applied to the containers during cleaning, is characterized in that a state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer is monitored by a monitoring system, wherein the state is a mechanical state, an optical state and/or an electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer.

[0009]	This allows defects in the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be detected early and/or the expected remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be determined. This allows for a more efficient layout of the method and enables timely maintenance breaks to be scheduled to avoid unexpected process stoppage.

[0010]	Preferably, the state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer is monitored by the monitoring system during cleaning of the containers and while ultrasonic vibrations are being generated by at least one ultrasonic transducer. This allows defects to be detected as quickly as possible. Furthermore, the monitoring system can also be used to check the correct control of the at least one ultrasonic transducer.

[0011]	In one embodiment, it can be provided for the containers to be passed through at least one immersion bath filled with cleaning medium and for the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be arranged in the at least one immersion bath. Preferably, the cleaning medium consists of water and alkali. The combination of ultrasonic vibration within the immersion bath results in a synergistic increase in the effectiveness of the cleaning effect by the ultrasonic vibrations and the immersion bath.

[0012]	The containers can be passed through the immersion bath and the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be arranged in the immersion bath such that the at least one ultrasonic transducer is directed towards the containers, preferably towards bottoms of the containers. This allows the ultrasonic vibration to act directly on the containers and the dirt and labels to be removed, wherein an as large as possible container surface is covered by directing the ultrasonic vibration towards the bottoms of the containers. The containers can further preferably be arranged in transport cells during cleaning, which comprise a fixing mechanism, so that there is a gap between a transport cell wall and the containers. This prevents the containers from touching the transport cell wall, which leads to an uneven distribution of cavitation bubbles generated by the ultrasonic vibration and thus to a certain deterioration of the cleaning effect. In addition, this allows for a more flexible arrangement of the at least one ultrasonic module in relation to the containers passing by it, since the touching of the transport cell wall by the containers occurs in particular if the bottoms of the containers do not point vertically downwards within the transport cells.

[0013]	In one embodiment, the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be measured by at least one vibration sensor of the monitoring system to monitor the mechanical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. The vibration sensor allows for efficient monitoring of the mechanical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can continuously monitor the vibrations emitted by the at least one ultrasonic transducer during cleaning. This allows unexpected defects in the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be quickly identified. Instead, and also preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can intermittently monitor the vibrations emitted by the at least one ultrasonic transducer, further preferably during cleaning. This can increase the service life of the vibration sensor. Preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can be attached directly to the outside of the at least one ultrasonic transducer, or integrated into its housing. Attaching it directly to the outside allows for a very precise measurement of the ultrasonic vibration. When integrated into the housing, the vibration sensor is protected from contamination.

[0014]	In this process, a self-learning system of the monitoring system can evaluate a vibration pattern of the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer, which is measured by the at least one vibration sensor, and, based on a sufficient data basis, determine a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. This allows unexpected process stoppages to be efficiently avoided.

[0015]	In a further embodiment, a surface of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be detected by at least one camera or at least one laser scanner of the monitoring system to monitor the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Since wear and tear of the at least one ultrasonic transducer over time is also accompanied by surface changes, which can manifest themselves, for example, in the form of surface defects such as craters, pores, or other changes in structure, the state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be efficiently monitored by monitoring its optical state using at least one camera or at least one laser scanner. Preferably, the optical state can be evaluated by the self-learning system of the monitoring system and, based on a sufficient data basis, a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be determined. Preferably, the at least one camera or the at least one laser scanner is arranged in relation to the at least one ultrasonic transducer such, and has a resolution such, that changes in the surface in the order of 0.01 mm, further preferably 0.001 mm, are detectable. In one embodiment of the method, the cleaning medium is drained from the immersion bath and the at least one ultrasonic transducer is cleared of the cleaning medium before the at least one camera or the at least one laser scanner of the monitoring system detects the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. This allows for a particularly accurate determination of the optical state.

[0016]	In a further embodiment, a current density flowing through the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be measured by the monitoring system and compared with an applied potential in order to monitor the electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Damage to the at least one ultrasonic transducer leads to a change in the ratio of current density to applied potential, whereby the state, in particular the electrical state, of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be efficiently monitored by determining such ratio. Preferably, the electrical state can be evaluated by the self-learning system of the monitoring system and, based on a sufficient data basis, a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be determined.

[0017]	Furthermore, a power applied to the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be controlled by the monitoring system based on the monitored state. This allows for improved and more reliable cleaning with lower resource consumption, as the applied power can be adapted to the state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer and thus to the ultrasonic vibrations that can actually be applied. This ensures that sufficient ultrasonic vibrations are generated while simultaneously preventing excessive power from being applied to the at least one ultrasonic transducer, thereby increasing the service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Preferably, the at least one ultrasonic transducer is configured such that, in a fully functional state, the at least one ultrasonic transducer generates the ultrasonic vibrations required for cleaning at a reduced power compared to a maximum power of the at least one ultrasonic transducer, further preferably at 60 to 80% of the maximum power of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. This has the advantage that the service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer is significantly longer when operating at reduced power, and that the applied power can be increased if the state of the ultrasonic transducer makes this necessary.

[0018]	An apparatus according to the invention for cleaning containers, preferably reusable bottles, with at least one ultrasonic transducer, which is configured such that ultrasonic vibrations can be generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer and applied to the containers during cleaning, is characterized in that the apparatus comprises a monitoring system which is configured to monitor a state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer, wherein the state is a mechanical state, an optical state and/or an electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer.

[0019]	The apparatus enables early detection of defects in the at least one ultrasonic transducer and/or the determination of an expected further service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. This allows for a more efficient configuration of the apparatus and enables timely maintenance breaks to be scheduled to avoid unexpected apparatus stoppage.

[0020]	The apparatus is preferably configured such that the state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer is monitored by the monitoring system during cleaning of the containers and while ultrasonic vibrations are being generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer.

[0021]	The apparatus can comprise at least one immersion bath filled with cleaning medium, wherein the at least one ultrasonic transducer is arranged in the at least one immersion bath and the apparatus is configured such that the containers can be passed through the at least one immersion bath. Preferably, the cleaning medium consists of water and alkali. The combination of ultrasonic vibration within the immersion bath results in a synergistic increase in the effectiveness of the cleaning effect by the ultrasonic vibrations and the immersion bath.

[0022]	The apparatus can be configured and the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be arranged in the immersion bath such that the at least one ultrasonic transducer is directed towards the containers, preferably towards bottoms of the containers. This allows the ultrasonic vibrations to act directly on the containers and the dirt and labels to be removed, wherein a container surface, which is as large as possible, is covered by directing the ultrasonic vibration towards the bottoms of the containers. The apparatus can further preferably include transport cells in which the containers can be arranged during cleaning and which comprise a fixing mechanism, so that there is a gap between a transport cell wall and the containers when the containers are arranged in the transport cells. This prevents the containers from touching the transport cell wall, which leads to an uneven distribution of cavitation bubbles generated by the ultrasonic vibration and thus to a certain deterioration of the cleaning effect. In addition, this allows for a more flexible arrangement of the at least one ultrasonic module in relation to the containers passing by it, since the touching of the transport cell wall by the containers occurs in particular if the bottoms of the containers do not point vertically downwards within the transport cells.

[0023]	In one embodiment of the apparatus, the monitoring system can have at least one vibration sensor which is configured to measure the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer in order to monitor the mechanical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. The vibration sensor allows for efficient monitoring of the mechanical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can be configured such that the at least one vibration sensor continuously monitors the vibrations emitted by the at least one ultrasonic transducer during cleaning. This allows unexpected defects in the at least one ultrasonic transducer to be quickly identified. Instead, and also preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can be configured such that the at least one vibration sensor intermittently monitors the vibrations emitted by the at least one ultrasonic transducer, further preferably during cleaning. This can increase the service life of the vibration sensor. Preferably, the at least one vibration sensor can be attached directly to the outside of the at least one ultrasonic transducer, or integrated into its housing. Attaching the apparatus directly to the outside allows for a very precise measurement of the ultrasonic vibration. When integrated into the housing, the vibration sensor is protected from contamination.

[0024]	A self-learning system can be integrated into the monitoring system, which is configured to evaluate a vibration pattern of the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer, which is measured by the at least one vibration sensor, and, based on a sufficient data basis, determine a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. This allows unexpected process stoppages to be efficiently avoided.

[0025]	In one embodiment of the apparatus, the monitoring system can include at least one camera or at least one laser scanner configured to capture a surface of the at least one ultrasonic transducer in order to monitor the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Since wear and tear of the at least one ultrasonic transducer over time is also accompanied by surface changes, which can manifest themselves, for example, in the form of surface defects such as craters, pores, or other changes in structure, the state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be efficiently monitored by monitoring its optical state using at least one camera or at least one laser scanner. Preferably, the self-learning system can be integrated into the monitoring system, which is configured to evaluate the optical state and, based on a sufficient data basis, determine a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. Preferably, the at least one camera or the at least one laser scanner is arranged in relation to the at least one ultrasonic transducer such and has a resolution such that changes in the surface on the order of 0.01 mm, further preferably 0.001 mm, are detectable. [0026]	In one embodiment of the apparatus, the monitoring system can be configured such that a current density flowing through the at least one ultrasonic transducer can be measured by the monitoring system and compared with an applied potential in order to monitor the electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE FIGURES

[0028]	Fig. 1 shows a schematic illustration of a section of an apparatus for cleaning containers or of a method step for cleaning containers according to one embodiment.

[0029]	Fig. 2 shows a detailed view of the section of the apparatus or of the method step according to the embodiment with a partial section through a transport cell.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE FIGURES

[0030]	Fig. 1 shows a schematic illustration of a section of an apparatus for cleaning containers 1, preferably reusable bottles, or of a method step for cleaning containers according to one embodiment. According to the invention, during cleaning, ultrasonic vibrations are generated by at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 and applied to the containers 1, wherein a state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 is monitored by a monitoring system 3, wherein the state is a mechanical state, an optical state and/or an electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2.

[0031]	As shown in Fig. 1, the containers 1 can be passed through at least one immersion bath 4 filled with cleaning medium 12 and the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 can be arranged in the at least one immersion bath 4. The containers 1 can be passed through the immersion bath 4 and the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 can be arranged in the immersion bath 4 such that the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 is directed towards bottoms of the containers 1.

[0032]	The containers 1 can be arranged in transport cells 5 during cleaning, which comprise a fixing mechanism 6, so that there is a gap 7 between a transport cell wall 8 and the containers 1. This is shown in particular in the detailed view shown in Fig. 2 of the section of the apparatus or the method step according to the embodiment with a partial section through a transport cell 5. In an embodiment not shown, transport cells 5 can also be omitted.

[0033]	As in the embodiment shown in Fig. 1, the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 can be measured by a vibration sensor 9 of the monitoring system 3 to monitor the mechanical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. As shown in Fig. 1, the at least one vibration sensor 9 can be attached directly to the outside of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. Alternatively, the at least one vibration sensor 9 can also be integrated into the housing of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. Furthermore, a self-learning system 14 can be integrated into the monitoring system 3, by which a vibration pattern of the ultrasonic vibrations generated by the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2, which is measured by the at least one vibration sensor 9, is evaluated, and, based on a sufficient data basis, a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 is determined.

[0034]	As also shown in the embodiment depicted in Fig. 1, a surface 10 of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 can be detected by at least one camera 11 of the monitoring system 3 in order to monitor the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. In an embodiment not shown, the monitoring system 3 can also comprise a laser scanner with which the surface 10 of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 is detected in order to monitor the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. The self-learning system 14 of the monitoring system 3 can evaluate the optical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 and, based on a sufficient data basis, determine a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2.

[0035]	Furthermore, as also shown in the embodiment depicted in Fig. 1, a current density flowing through the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2 can be measured by the monitoring system 3 and compared with an applied potential in order to monitor the electrical state of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 2. For this purpose, monitoring system 3 includes, for example, a power meter 13. The electrical state can also be evaluated by the self-learning system 14 of the monitoring system 3, so that, based on a sufficient data basis, a remaining service life of the at least one ultrasonic transducer 9 can be determined by the self-learning system 14.

title: DRIVING EVENT DETECTION USING ALIGNED VIDEO AND TEXT ENCODERS
abstract:
A method for detecting a driving event includes receiving video data from one or more vehicle-mounted cameras. The method includes generating one or more video embeddings in an embedding space based on the video data. The method includes generating one or more text embeddings of a natural language input in the embedding space. The natural language input corresponds to a driving event description. The method includes comparing the one or more video embeddings and the one or more text embeddings in the embedding space. The method includes determining at least one similarity value between the one or more video embeddings and the one or more text embeddings based on the comparison. The method includes detecting the driving event when the at least one similarity value is above a detection threshold.

FIELD OF INVENTION
[0002]	The present disclosure relates to driving monitoring systems, and more particularly to methods and systems for the detection of driving events using aligned video and text encoders that enable real-time classification of driving behaviors through comparison of video embeddings with natural language driving event descriptions in a shared embedding space.

BACKGROUND
[0003]	The information disclosed in this background section is only for the enhancement of understanding of the general background of the disclosure and should not be taken as an acknowledgement or any form of suggestion that this information forms the prior art already known to a person skilled in the art.
[0004]	Driving event detection is a basis for vehicle safety systems that may help drivers improve their awareness of safe and unsafe driving habits. Distracted driving is a concern worldwide, contributing to road accidents, injuries, and fatalities each year. With the increasing use of mobile devices and other in-vehicle technologies, drivers may be prone to distractions that can lead to lapses in attention. Detection systems that rely on manual observation or sensor-based approaches may face challenges in addressing the complexity and variety of distracted behaviors.
[0005]	Detection systems may rely on pre-trained models that utilize datasets and training processes. Such models may face difficulties adapting to new or uncommon driving behaviors, which may involve retraining and updates. This may limit effectiveness and scalability, making it challenging to keep pace with the evolving nature of driving behaviors.
[0006]	Another challenge in developing effective driving behavior detection systems is the handling of corner cases, rare or atypical scenarios that may not be well-represented in training data. These corner cases can lead to false positive rates, which may reduce reliability and user trust in the system. Detection systems may lack the agility to address such specific and nuanced scenarios dynamically.
[0007]	Moreover, existing systems may not incorporate real-time feedback from drivers, which can be useful for refining detection criteria and minimizing false positives. Drivers' experiences and feedback can provide insights into the system's performance under real-world conditions. However, existing systems may not leverage this feedback effectively, resulting in models that do not improve based on user interactions.
[0008]	Accordingly, systems and methods that can address at least one or more of these challenges in driving event detection are desired.

[0032]	Certain aspects of the present disclosure relate to an apparatus that uses aligned video and text encoders to detect driving events through comparison of video embeddings with natural language driving event descriptions in a shared embedding space. The apparatus 103 may address challenges associated with detecting distracted driving behaviors by leveraging one/zero-shot encoding approaches that enable real-time detection without extensive retraining.
[0033]	FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary vehicle 100 implementing an apparatus 103 for detecting a driving event. As shown, the vehicle 100 may include one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101 configured to capture video data of a driving environment and users within the vehicle 100. The one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101 may include exterior cameras 101A-101C and one or more interior cameras 101D-101E. The exterior cameras 101A-101C may be positioned on external surfaces of the vehicle 100. The exterior cameras 101A-101C may be configured to capture a view of the driving environment external to the vehicle 100. The exterior cameras 101A-101C may include, but are not limited to, a windshield-mounted exterior-facing camera, a front bumper camera, a grille‑mounted camera, a rear-view camera, side-mounted cameras, roof-mounted cameras, and surround‑view cameras. In an exemplary embodiment, the interior cameras 101D-101E may be positioned within a cabin of the vehicle 100. The interior cameras 101D-101E may be configured to capture video data of a user, such as a driver, within the vehicle 100. The interior cameras 101D-101E may include, but are not limited to, a driver-facing camera, a cabin-monitoring camera, an Infrared (IR) interior camera, and a gesture-recognition camera.
[0034]	In an embodiment, the one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101 may be coupled to an apparatus 103 configured to detect a driving event. In an embodiment, the apparatus 103 may be a part of a control unit of the vehicle 100. In another embodiment, the apparatus 103 may be connected to the control unit.	In another embodiment, the apparatus 103 may be integrated together with a windshield mounted camera.
[0035]	In an embodiment, the driving event refers to a detectable action, behavior, or condition associated with operation of the vehicle 100 or behavior of the driver. In particular, the driving event refers to any identifiable action, behavior, or condition related to how a vehicle is being driven or how the driver is behaving while operating the vehicle. The driving event may be momentary or may occur over a period of time. For example, consider a situation in which the vehicle 100 is in motion and at least one of the interior cameras 101D-101E captures video showing the driver repeatedly raising a hand to the side of the face while holding a rectangular object. The disclosed apparatus 103 processes the video and compares the observed visual patterns with a natural‑language description such as “driver using a mobile phone while driving.” When the similarity between the captured video data and the description exceeds a defined threshold for a sufficient duration, the apparatus 103 determines that a driving event has occurred. In this case, the detected driving event is distracted driving due to phone usage, and the system may respond by recording the event, generating an alert, or taking other appropriate action.
[0036]	Accordingly, in an embodiment, the apparatus 103 may receive video data from the one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101. The apparatus 103 may process the video data using an encoder system comprising aligned video and textual encoders to generate video embeddings in an embedding space. The apparatus 103 may also generate text embeddings of natural language driving event descriptions in the same embedding space. By comparing the video embeddings and the text embeddings, the apparatus 103 may determine similarity values that indicate whether a driving event has occurred.
[0037]	The apparatus 103 may leverage a foundation model pre-trained on a diverse dataset of textual prompts and corresponding video data. The foundation model may serve as a pre-trained base that understands various notions related to driving, including behaviors of a driver within a vehicle, such as whether the driver is holding a phone, eating, or wearing hands-free devices. By utilizing the foundation model, the apparatus 103 may generate new classifiers based on textual prompts without requiring extensive retraining.
[0038]	In a further embodiment, the apparatus 103 may employ zero-shot learning to detect previously unseen driving events based on pre-trained knowledge of vehicle-related scenarios. Zero-shot learning may allow the apparatus 103 to describe and understand a video of a driving event without having been explicitly trained on examples of that specific event. The apparatus 103 may leverage pre-trained knowledge and generalize from related concepts learned during training.
[0039]	In a further embodiment, the apparatus 103 may employ one-shot learning to detect driving events using a single example of a specific driving event. One-shot learning may be useful when obtaining more examples is difficult or costly, such as when driving events are rare. The apparatus 103 may adapt to new information from a single example to detect other examples that are similar.
[0040]	The apparatus 103 may dynamically generate and compare encoded vectors from textual prompts and live video clips, enabling real-time detection of new distracted behaviors without extensive retraining. For instance, if a regulatory change requires detection of hands-free device usage, the apparatus 103 may immediately adapt by generating a prompt such as "Is the driver wearing a hands-free device?" and encoding the prompt into a vector using a text encoder. The apparatus 103 may then compare the encoded prompt with encoded video clips of the driver to detect the specified behavior in real-time.
[0041]	The apparatus 103 may also track behaviors over time. For instance, if the apparatus 103 detects that a driver is eating, the apparatus 103 may continuously monitor this behavior. If the detected behavior exceeds a predefined threshold, the apparatus 103 may trigger an alert indicating a confirmed detection. Continuous tracking may help ensure that transient or brief actions are not misclassified.
[0042]	In another embodiment, the apparatus 103 may support audio encoding to enhance detection of behaviors that involve sound, such as singing or laughing. By incorporating audio data, the apparatus 103 may generate prompts like "Is the driver singing?" and compare audio clips against encoded vectors for singing. A multi-modal approach may enable improved detection of various distracted or drowsy behaviors by better distinguishing other behaviors, like singing, which may have a similar visual appearance to other behaviors.

[0055]	FIG. 3 illustrates a functional block diagram of the apparatus 103 with the modules 214 for detecting the driving event, according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. The modules 214 communicate with each other through data buses or shared memory within the apparatus architecture.
[0056]	The transceiver module 302 may be configured to receive the video data from the one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101. The transceiver module 302 may receive the video data from the interior cameras 101D-101E capturing video data of the driver within the vehicle 100. In an exemplary embodiment, the video data may comprise a sequence of frames captured while the vehicle 100 is in motion. The transceiver module 302 may receive the video data through the I/O interface 208 or through direct connection to the one or more vehicle-mounted cameras 101. The transceiver module 302 may store the video data in the database 212 for processing by other modules of the modules 214.
[0057]	Then the generating module 304 may be configured to generate one or more video embeddings in an embedding space based on the video data received by the transceiver module 302. The generating module 304 may process frames or clips from the video data to generate the one or more video embeddings. In an embodiment, the one or more video embeddings may represent visual content of the video data in the embedding space. The generating module 304 may capture semantic information about objects, actions, and behaviors depicted in the video data. In an embodiment, the generating module 304 may utilize an encoder system comprising aligned one or more video encoders and one or more textual encoders to generate the one or more video embeddings. The encoder system may comprise a foundation model pre-trained on a dataset of textual prompts and corresponding video data. The foundation model may serve as a pre-trained base that understands various notions related to driving, including behavior of a driver within the vehicle 100, such as whether the driver is holding a phone, eating, or wearing hands-free devices. 
[0058]	The generating module 304 may further be configured to generate one or more text embeddings of a natural language input in the embedding space. The natural language input may correspond to a driving event description. In an embodiment, the driving event description may specify what driving behavior or event should be detected.
[0059]	In an embodiment, the driving event description may comprise hierarchical event detection parameters. The hierarchical event detection parameters may organize detection criteria in a structured manner that captures relationships between general event categories and specific variations. Each version of driving event description may be maintained in a hierarchical structure that captures the relationships between general event categories and specific variations. The hierarchical structure may enable independent performance metrics to be tracked for each hierarchical level, allowing targeted optimization of detection criteria at different granularities. The hierarchical event detection parameters may include, but are not limited to, a primary event description, common false alarm scenarios, and corner case specifications. The primary event description may define a general category of the driving event to be detected, such as “distracted driving” or “drowsy driving.” The primary event description may serve as a top-level classification that encompasses multiple specific variations of the driving event. The common false alarm scenarios may specify situations that are frequently misidentified as the driving event but that should not trigger detection. For example, the common false alarm scenarios for a “phone usage” detection may include “drinking water,” “scratching face,” or “adjusting sunglasses.’ The corner case specifications may define rare or exceptional conditions that require special handling to ensure accurate detection. The corner case specifications may address subtle behaviors or unusual circumstances that standard detection criteria may not adequately capture.
[0060]	The hierarchical structure of the driving event description may enable the apparatus 103 to apply detection criteria at multiple levels of specificity.
