title: A System for Visualizing Predicted Vehicle Trajectory and Collision Risk
abstract: The present invention relates to a system (100) for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk. The system includes a sensor module (110), a processing unit (120), a control unit (130), and a projection module (140). The sensor module (110) continuously acquires real-time vehicle data and environmental data. The processing unit (120) receives the real-time vehicle data and environmental data from the sensor module (110), determines a predicted vehicle trajectory (122), and determines a collision risk level (124). The control unit (130) generates adaptive projection instructions (132) based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124). The projection module (140), including an LED or laser-based projection system (142), projects on a road surface (144) a dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) showing a predicted turning path (152) and color-coded risk zones (154). The visual representation (150) is updated in real time during a turning maneuver.
specification:
Field of the invention

[0001]	The present invention relates to the field of automotive safety systems. More specifically, the invention relates to a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk.

Background of the invention

[0002]	Vehicles are commonly equipped with turn indicator systems for signalling an intended direction of travel. Conventional turn indicators typically provide only a left-turn signal or a right-turn signal to nearby road users. While such indicators communicate directional intent, they do not convey information regarding the anticipated path of travel, turning radius, maneuvering envelope, or potential interaction with surrounding road users during a turning maneuver. During turning operations, particularly at intersections, narrow roadways, parking facilities, loading zones, and congested traffic environments, a vehicle may occupy a larger area than is readily apparent to surrounding road users.

[0003]	The problem is particularly significant for large vehicles such as buses, trucks, trailers, and commercial transport vehicles that require wider turning radii and greater maneuvering space. Conventional signalling systems do not communicate the extent of the turning arc or the area that may be swept by the vehicle during the maneuver. This lack of information may contribute to uncertainty among nearby road users and may increase the likelihood of unsafe interactions. Various vehicle lighting systems, including adaptive headlights and steering-responsive illumination systems, are known in the art. Although such systems may alter light distribution based on steering angle or vehicle movement, they are generally intended to improve roadway visibility for the driver. These systems do not provide surrounding road users with information relating to the anticipated trajectory or occupied space of the vehicle during a turn.

[0004]	Existing safety systems may detect nearby vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, obstacles, or other road users and may generate warnings or initiate vehicle control actions. However, such systems are primarily directed toward informing the driver or controlling the vehicle itself. As a result, surrounding road users may remain unaware of potential conflict areas associated with the vehicle's intended maneuver. In urban environments, dense traffic conditions, low-light situations, adverse weather conditions, and other complex driving scenarios, it may be difficult for surrounding road users to accurately interpret the future movement of a turning vehicle based solely on conventional turn signals. 

[0005]	The absence of clear information regarding anticipated vehicle movement and occupied road space may reduce situational awareness and contribute to traffic conflicts. Accordingly, a technical problem exists in that conventional vehicle signalling and lighting systems provide limited information regarding the anticipated movement path, turning envelope, and maneuvering space of a vehicle during a turning operation, thereby making it difficult for surrounding road users to accurately assess vehicle behaviour and potential interaction zones.

[0006]	Therefore, there is a need for a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk to overcome a few or all drawbacks of the existing technologies. 

Objects of the invention

[0007]	An object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk.

[0008]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk that develop a context-aware system that predicts vehicle trajectory in real time. 

[0009]	Yet another object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk that dynamically project risk-aware visual zones along with turning path.

[0010]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk that incorporate environment sensing like vehicles, pedestrians, road conditions

[0011]	One more object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk that enhance vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-environment communication.

[0012]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk that to enable adaptive projection behaviour based on real-time risk assessment. 

Summary of the Invention

[0013]	According to the present invention, there is provided a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk. The system may include a sensor module configured to continuously acquire real-time vehicle data and environmental data; a processing unit configured to receive the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data from the sensor module, determine a predicted vehicle trajectory, and determine a collision risk level; a control unit configured to generate adaptive projection instructions based on the predicted vehicle trajectory and the collision risk level; and a projection module including an LED or laser-based projection system configured to project, on a road surface, a dynamic context-aware visual representation showing a predicted turning path of the vehicle and color-coded risk zones. The dynamic context-aware visual representation may be updated in real time based on the predicted vehicle trajectory, the collision risk level, and changes in the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data during a turning maneuver.

Detailed description of the invention 

[0021]	An embodiment of this invention, illustrating its features, will now be described in detail. The words "comprising," "having," "containing," and "including," and other forms thereof, are intended to be equivalent in meaning and be open-ended in that an item or items following any one of these words is not meant to be an exhaustive listing of such item or items, or meant to be limited to only the listed item or items. 

[0022]	The present invention relates to a system for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk, more particularly to a system for context-aware adaptive turn trajectory and risk visualization for vehicles using dynamic road projection. The system can be used in passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, smart vehicles, autonomous vehicles, parking assistance systems, emergency vehicles, and urban traffic systems for visually communicating a predicted turning path, color-coded risk zones, safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space on a road surface during a turning maneuver.

[0023]	The terms “first,” “second,” and the like, herein do not denote any order, quantity, or importance, but rather are used to distinguish one element from another, and the terms “a” and “an” herein do not denote a limitation of quantity, but rather denote the presence of at least one of the referenced item.

[0024]	The disclosed embodiments are merely exemplary of the invention, which may be embodied in various forms.

[0025]	Referring now to figure 1, a system (100) for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk in accordance with the present invention is illustrated. The system (100) includes a sensor module (110), a processing unit (120), a control unit (130), a projection module (140). The sensor module (110) is operatively connected to the processing unit (120). The processing unit (120) is operatively connected to the control unit (130). The control unit (130) is operatively connected to the projection module (140). The projection module (140) is arranged to project a dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on a road surface (144). 

[0026]	The sensor module (110) is configured to continuously acquire real-time vehicle data and environmental data. The sensor module (110) includes a steering angle sensor (112), a vehicle speed sensor (114), an inertial measurement unit (116), and at least one environment sensing device (118). The at least one environment sensing device (118) is selected from a camera, LiDAR or ultrasonic sensor. The steering angle sensor (112) acquires steering angle data of the vehicle during a turning maneuver. The vehicle speed sensor (114) acquires vehicle speed data. The inertial measurement unit (116) acquires yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data of the vehicle. The at least one environment sensing device (118) acquires environmental data relating to surrounding objects present near the vehicle or near the predicted vehicle trajectory.

[0027]	The real-time vehicle data includes steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. The environmental data includes relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects. The surrounding objects may include nearby vehicles, pedestrians, obstacles, or other road users positioned on or near the predicted vehicle trajectory. The real-time vehicle data and the environmental data are continuously supplied from the sensor module (110) to the processing unit (120), further the processing unit (120) receives updated data during the turning maneuver.

[0028]	The processing unit (120) is configured to receive the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data from the sensor module (110). The processing unit (120) determines a predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and determines a collision risk level (124). The predicted vehicle trajectory (122) represents a future movement path of the vehicle during the turning maneuver. The collision risk level (124) represents a level of possible contact or conflict between the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the surrounding objects.

[0029]	The processing unit (120) computes a turning radius using the steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. Based on the computed turning radius and the real-time vehicle data, the processing unit (120) determines the predicted vehicle trajectory. In one implementation, the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) is determined as a curved path corresponding to the turning motion of the vehicle. The curved path may be represented as coordinate points, a projected arc, or a road path corresponding to the expected movement of the vehicle.

[0030]	The processing unit (120) is further configured to refine the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) using a supervised machine learning model based on the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data received from the sensor module (110). The supervised machine learning model is trained using historical driving pattern data, vehicle movement data, and environmental data. The supervised machine learning model assists in refining the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) where actual road movement may differ from a purely calculated turning radius due to steering variation, speed variation, road geometry, or movement of surrounding objects. The supervised machine learning model  receives at least the steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, inertial measurement unit data, relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects as input values and outputs a refined predicted vehicle trajectory.

[0031]	The processing unit (120) is also configured to estimate the collision risk level (124) based on relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and overlap between the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and positions of surrounding objects. The processing unit (120) compares the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) with the position of surrounding objects. If the surrounding object is outside the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and outside the required maneuvering space, the collision risk level (124) may be determined as safe or low. If the surrounding object is near the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or near the required maneuvering space, the collision risk level (124) may be determined as moderate risk. If the surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or is moving toward the predicted vehicle trajectory, the collision risk level (124) may be determined as high collision risk. The overlap is determined by comparing the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) with the positions of surrounding objects on or near the road surface (144).

[0032]	Further, the control unit (130) is configured to generate adaptive projection instructions based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124). The adaptive projection instructions control the projection module (140) for producing the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on the road surface (144). The adaptive projection instructions may include instructions relating to size, shape, intensity, brightness, color, position, and update timing of the projected visual representation. The control unit (130) continuously receives the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124) from the processing unit (120), and updates the adaptive projection instructions during the turning maneuver.

[0033]	Furthermore, the projection module (140) includes an LED or laser-based projection system (142). The projection module (140) is configured to project, on the road surface (144), the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) showing the predicted turning path (152) of the vehicle and color-coded risk zones (154). The projection module (140) receives the adaptive projection instructions (132) from the control unit (130) and projects the predicted turning path (152), the color-coded risk zones (154), a turning arc, safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space on the road surface (144).

[0034]	Referring now to figure.2 the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is adaptively modified in size, shape, intensity, and brightness based on vehicle speed, steering angle, environmental conditions, weather conditions, and the collision risk level. For example, when the vehicle speed increases during a turn, the projected turning path  may be extended to indicate a longer predicted vehicle trajectory. When the steering angle increases, the projected turning path may become sharper or may form a smaller turning radius. When the environmental conditions or weather conditions indicate low visibility, rain, fog, darkness, or night-time condition, the brightness or intensity of the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) may be increased for clearer visibility on the road surface (144).

[0035]	The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) further includes color-coded risk zones (154) including green indicating safe, yellow indicating moderate risk, and red indicating high collision risk. A green risk zone may be projected when no surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or required maneuvering space. A yellow risk zone may be projected when a surrounding object is near the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or is moving toward the required maneuvering space. A red risk zone may be projected when the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) overlaps with the position of a surrounding object or when the relative velocity and motion direction indicate a high possibility of collision.

[0036]	The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) communicates vehicle movement intent and collision risk to nearby road users during the turning maneuver. The predicted turning path (152) informs nearby road users about the expected movement direction of the vehicle. The turning arc informs nearby road users about the turning angle and turning radius of the vehicle. The safe maneuvering boundaries indicate the boundary within which the vehicle is expected to move. The required maneuvering space indicates the road space required by the vehicle for completing the turning maneuver. The color-coded risk zones (154) inform nearby road users about safe, moderate risk, and high collision risk regions near the vehicle.

[0037]	In an operation, the sensor module (110) continuously acquires real-time vehicle data and environmental data. The real-time vehicle data includes steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. The environmental data includes relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects. The processing unit (120) receives the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data from the sensor module (110). The processing unit (120) computes a turning radius and determines the predicted vehicle trajectory. The processing unit (120) estimates the collision risk level (124)  based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and surrounding objects. The control unit (130) generates adaptive projection instructions based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124). The projection module (140) projects the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on the road surface (144). The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is updated in real time based on the predicted vehicle trajectory, the collision risk level (124), and changes in the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data during the turning maneuver.

[0038]	In the alternative embodiment, the environmental data may further include road geometry or lane curvature detected by the at least one environment sensing device (118) or received from a vehicle system. The road geometry or lane curvature may be used by the processing unit (120) while determining the predicted vehicle trajectory, further  the projected predicted turning path, turning arc, safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space correspond to the actual road condition near the vehicle.

[0039]	In the alternative embodiment, the collision risk level (124)  determined by the processing unit (120) may be classified into a low collision risk, a moderate collision risk  and a high collision risk. The low collision risk  corresponds to a safe condition in which no surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or the required maneuvering space. The moderate collision risk corresponds to a caution condition in which a surrounding object is near the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or moving toward the required maneuvering space. The high collision risk corresponds to a condition in which a surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or is positioned within the required maneuvering space.

[0040]	In the alternative embodiment, the projection module (140) may operate in a continuous projection mode or in an event-triggered projection mode. In the continuous projection mode, the projection module (140) projects the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) during vehicle movement. In the event-triggered projection mode, the projection module (140) projects the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) during a turning maneuver, U-turn maneuver, parking maneuver, reverse turning maneuver, or any maneuver requiring visual communication of the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124).

[0041]	In the alternative embodiment, in low-visibility conditions including night-time condition, fog condition, rain condition, or darkness, the control unit (130) may generate adaptive projection instructions for increasing the intensity and brightness of the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150), further the predicted turning path (152), the color-coded risk zones (154), safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space remain visible on the road surface (144).

[0042]	In the alternative embodiment, the system (100) may include or communicate with a vehicle-to-vehicle or vehicle-to-infrastructure communication arrangement for sharing the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or the collision risk level (124) with nearby vehicles or infrastructure. The visual road projection may be used together with such communication for conveying vehicle movement intent and collision risk to nearby road users.

[0043]	In the alternative embodiment, the system (100) may be connected with an autonomous driving system of the vehicle. In such implementation, the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124) generated during autonomous operation may be supplied to the control unit (130), and the projection module (140) may project the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on the road surface (144) for external communication with nearby road users.

[0044]	In the alternative embodiment, the system (100) may be used during turning maneuver, U-turn maneuver, parking maneuver, reverse turning maneuver, and urgent turning maneuver. The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) may be projected continuously or only when the vehicle enters a maneuvering condition requiring communication of the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124).

[0045]	In the alternative embodiment, the system (100) may also be implemented as a retrofit kit or modular add-on device for existing vehicles. In such implementation, the sensor module (110), processing unit (120), control unit (130), and projection module (140) may be mounted on the vehicle and connected to available vehicle data sources or separate sensors.

[0046]	By way of a non-limiting example, a vehicle fitted with the system (100) begins a left turning maneuver at an intersection. The steering angle sensor (112) acquires the steering angle, the vehicle speed sensor (114) acquires the vehicle speed, and the inertial measurement unit (116) acquires yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. At the same time, the at least one environment sensing device (118) detects a pedestrian near the left side of the road surface (144) and a nearby vehicle approaching from behind. The processing unit (120) receives the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data and computes a turning radius. The processing unit (120) determines the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and checks relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and overlap between the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the positions of the pedestrian and the nearby vehicle. Since the pedestrian is near the predicted vehicle trajectory, the processing unit (120) determines a moderate risk  for the region near the pedestrian. 

[0047]	Further, the control unit (130) generates adaptive projection instructions for projecting the predicted turning path, safe maneuvering boundaries, required maneuvering space, and a yellow risk zone near the pedestrian. If the pedestrian moves into the predicted vehicle trajectory, the processing unit (120) updates the collision risk level (124) to high  risk, and the control unit (130) changes the adaptive projection instructions further the projection module (140) projects a red risk zone on the road surface (144). If the pedestrian moves away from the predicted vehicle trajectory, the collision risk level (124) is changed to safe, and the color-coded risk zones (154) are shown in green. The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is therefore continuously updated during the turning maneuver.

[0048]	Referring now to figure 3, a method (200) for visualizing predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk in accordance with the present invention is illustrated. The method (200) is described in conjunction with the system (100) including the sensor module (110), the processing unit (120), the control unit (130), and the projection module (140). The method (200) continuously acquires real-time vehicle data and environmental data, determines a predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and a collision risk level (124), generates adaptive projection instructions (132), projects a dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on the road surface (144), and updates the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) in real time during a turning maneuver.

[0049]	The method (200) starts at step (210).

[0050]	 At step (220), the sensor module (110) continuously acquires real-time vehicle data and environmental data. The real-time vehicle data includes steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. The environmental data includes relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects (180). The steering angle is acquired using the steering angle sensor (112). The vehicle speed is acquired using the vehicle speed sensor (114). The yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data are acquired using the inertial measurement unit (116). The environmental data is acquired using at least one environment sensing device (118) selected from a camera, LiDAR or ultrasonic sensor.

[0051]	At step (230), the processing unit (120) receives the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data from the sensor module (110). The processing unit (120) receives the steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, inertial measurement unit data, relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects. The received data is used for determining the predicted vehicle trajectory (122)  and the collision risk level (124) during the turning maneuver.

[0052]	Further, the processing unit (120) determines the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) based on the real-time vehicle data received from the sensor module (110). The processing unit (120) computes a turning radius using the steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. Based on the computed turning radius, the processing unit (120) determines the predicted vehicle trajectory (122)  of the vehicle. The predicted vehicle trajectory (122)  represents the expected path of movement of the vehicle during the turning maneuver.

[0053]	Further,  the processing unit (120) refines the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) using the supervised machine learning model. The supervised machine learning model receives the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data from the sensor module (110). The supervised machine learning model may use steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, inertial measurement unit data, relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of surrounding objects as input values. Based on the input values, the supervised machine learning model  provides the a refined predicted vehicle trajectory (122).

[0054]	Further, the processing unit (120) determines the collision risk level (124) based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122)  and the environmental data. The collision risk level (124) is estimated based on relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and overlap between the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and positions of surrounding objects. The processing unit (120) compares the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) with the positions of surrounding objects on or near the road surface (144). When no surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or required maneuvering space, the collision risk level (124) is determined as safe. When a surrounding object is near the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or moving toward the required maneuvering space, the collision risk level (124) is determined as moderate risk. When a surrounding object overlaps with the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) or is positioned within the required maneuvering space, the collision risk level (124)  is determined as high collision risk.

[0055]	At step (240), the control unit (130) generates adaptive projection instructions (132) based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the collision risk level (124). The adaptive projection instructions (132) include instructions for controlling size, shape, intensity, brightness, color, position, and update timing of the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150). The control unit (130) supplies the adaptive projection instructions (132) to the projection module (140).

[0056]	At step (250), the projection module (140) projects, on the road surface (144), the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150). The projection module (140) includes the LED or laser-based projection system (142). The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) shows the predicted turning path (152) of the vehicle and color-coded risk zones (154). The color-coded risk zones (154) include green indicating safe, yellow indicating moderate risk, and red indicating high collision risk. In an implementation, the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) further includes the predicted vehicle trajectory (122), a turning arc, safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space on the road surface (144).

[0057]	At step (260), the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is updated in real time based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122), the collision risk level (124), and changes in the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data during the turning maneuver. When the steering angle changes, the turning radius and the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) are updated by the processing unit (120), and the projected predicted turning path (152) and turning arc are changed accordingly. When the vehicle speed changes, the size or length of the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is changed. When the collision risk level (124) changes, the color-coded risk zones (154) are changed. When environmental conditions or weather conditions indicate low visibility, rain, fog, darkness, or night-time condition, the intensity or brightness of the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) is changed.

[0058]	The method (200) ends at step (270).

[0059]	By way of a non-limiting example, a passenger vehicle approaches a busy urban intersection during evening traffic and initiates a left turn. The sensor module (110) continuously acquires real-time vehicle data including steering angle, vehicle speed, yaw rate, orientation data, and inertial measurement unit data. Simultaneously, the at least one environment sensing device (118) detects surrounding objects including a pedestrian approaching a crosswalk and a bicycle moving along the side of the road. The environmental data includes relative distance, relative velocity, motion direction, and position of the detected surrounding objects. The processing unit (120) receives the real-time vehicle data and the environmental data and determines a predicted vehicle trajectory (122) corresponding to the intended left turn. The processing unit (120) evaluates the positions and movements of the pedestrian and the bicycle relative to the predicted vehicle trajectory and the required maneuvering space. Because the pedestrian is approaching the projected turning path (152), the processing unit (120) determines the collision risk level (124) as moderate risk.

[0060]	 Further, based on the predicted vehicle trajectory (122) and the determined collision risk level (124), the control unit (130) generates adaptive projection instructions (132). The projection module (140) projects the dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) on the road surface (144). The dynamic context-aware visual representation (150) includes the predicted turning path (152), the turning arc, safe maneuvering boundaries, required maneuvering space, and a yellow color-coded risk zone (154) indicating the moderate risk area near the pedestrian. As the vehicle continues the turning maneuver, the pedestrian enters closer to the predicted vehicle trajectory (122). The processing unit (120) correspondingly increases the collision risk level (124) to high collision risk. The control unit (130) updates the adaptive projection instructions (132), and the projection module (140) changes the color-coded risk zones (154) from yellow to red on the road surface (144). When the pedestrian safely clears the turning area, the collision risk level (124) is reduced and the color-coded risk zones (154) change to green.

[0061]	The present invention has the advantage of providing a system (100) that externally communicates predicted vehicle trajectory and collision risk using dynamic road projection. The system provides real-time visualization of a predicted turning path, color-coded risk zones, safe maneuvering boundaries, and required maneuvering space on the road surface. The system  also accounts for real-time vehicle data, environmental data, environmental conditions, weather conditions, and collision risk level. The system reduces ambiguity associated with conventional turn indicators by visually indicating both vehicle movement intent and collision risk to nearby road users during a turning maneuver.

title: A System for Data Management and Analytics for Civilian and Governmental Infrastructure Monitoring
abstract: The present invention relates to a system (100) for data management and analytics for civilian and governmental infrastructure monitoring. The system (100) includes a field sensor network (10), an edge gateway (20), an ingestion layer (30), an analytics layer (40), a real-time alerts unit (50), a distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60). The distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60) stores sensor readings in a time-series table having a composite partition key comprising the sensor identifier and the temporal bucket, and a clustering key comprising the timestamp, so that the sensor readings are stored in bounded time-based partitions. The distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60) stores a latest sensor state in a latest sensor state table having a partition key including a location identifier and the sensor type, and a clustering key including the sensor identifier, so that a current condition of each sensor is retrievable per location.
specification:
Field of the invention

[0001]	The present invention relates to the field of IoT monitoring for traffic and city infrastructure. More specifically, the present invention relates to a system for data management and analytics for civilian and governmental infrastructure monitoring.

Background of the invention

[0002]	Civilian and governmental infrastructure systems are increasingly using sensors and connected devices for monitoring traffic, environmental conditions, utilities, parking, public transport, pedestrian movement, emergency situations, and other city operations. Such sensors generate large amounts of real-time data from different locations such as roads, intersections, parking areas, public transport routes, utility zones, pollution monitoring points, and other public infrastructure areas. The collected data is useful for city authorities, traffic departments, environmental departments, utility operators, and emergency response teams for monitoring present conditions and taking suitable decisions. 

[0003]	Further, existing infrastructure monitoring systems commonly use separate monitoring arrangements for different departments or services. For example, traffic monitoring data may be handled by one system, pollution monitoring data may be handled by another system, and utility data may be stored in a different system. Due to such separation, the data remains scattered across different platforms. Such scattered data makes it difficult for authorities to obtain a combined view of the actual condition of the city or infrastructure environment. As a result, decision-making becomes slow, and coordination between departments becomes difficult.  

[0004]	Further, many existing systems also use centralized databases or conventional relational databases for storing sensor data. Such databases may work properly when the number of sensors is limited. However, when thousands of sensors continuously send data every few seconds or minutes, the database may become slow due to a high number of write operations. The centralized database may also require expensive hardware upgrades to handle increasing data load. Further, if the central database fails, the monitoring system may lose access to important sensor data, which is not suitable for traffic control, emergency response, public safety, and other time-sensitive applications. 

[0005]	Further, existing systems also face difficulty in handling time-series sensor data. Sensor readings are usually generated continuously with timestamps, and such data keeps increasing over time. If such data is not stored in a properly divided time-based manner, the storage tables may become very large and slow to search. Retrieval of historical sensor readings for a particular sensor, road segment, location, or time period may take more time. This limitation affects historical analysis, reporting, planning, and policy evaluation.  

[0006]	Another limitation of existing systems is that current sensor status and historical sensor data are often stored together or accessed through the same data structure. Due to this, retrieving the latest condition of a sensor may require searching through a large amount of past data. Such delay is not suitable for real-time dashboards, alert generation, traffic signal control, pollution alerts, utility fault detection, or emergency response. A system that separately maintains current sensor states and historical sensor readings is therefore required for faster access and better monitoring. 

[0007]	Further, existing systems also do not always provide a proper data flow from field sensors to dashboards and control systems. Some systems collect data from sensors, but do not properly validate the data, add metadata, or prepare the data for efficient storage. Missing timestamps, incorrect sensor identifiers, incomplete sensor data, and lack of location or road segment information can reduce the usefulness of the collected data. Without proper preprocessing and metadata addition, the data may not be suitable for accurate analysis, reporting, and control actions.

[0008]	Further, many known systems are mainly focused on either monitoring or display of information. Such systems may not provide a complete arrangement for collecting sensor data, forwarding the data through an edge gateway, validating and preparing the data through an ingestion layer, processing the data through an analytics layer, generating real-time alerts, controlling infrastructure devices, storing real-time and historical sensor data, and displaying the information through dashboards and reports. Due to this, such systems may not be suitable for large-scale civilian and governmental infrastructure monitoring.

[0009]	Existing traffic and smart city systems may also suffer from delayed responses because the sensor data is transmitted to a remote server without local handling or structured processing. Network delay, poor connectivity, and unstructured data transmission may affect timely control of traffic signals, public alerts, emergency response equipment, and utility devices. In applications such as traffic congestion detection, pollution alert generation, or emergency route management, delayed action may reduce the effectiveness of the monitoring system.

[0010]	Therefore, there is a need for a system for data management and analytics for civilian and governmental infrastructure monitoring to overcome a few or all drawbacks of the existing technologies.

Consider a scenario where, the field sensor network (10) includes vehicle detectors, speed sensors, and queue length sensors installed at an urban road intersection. The field sensor network (10) collects vehicle count, speed information, and queue length as real-time sensor data. The edge gateway (20) receives the real-time sensor data from the vehicle detectors, adds the local timestamp and sensor identifier, and forwards the real-time sensor data to the ingestion layer (30). The ingestion layer (30) validates the real-time sensor data, adds metadata including road segment, location, sensor type, and timestamp, computes the temporal bucket, and prepares write operations. 

[0063]	Further, the distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60) stores the sensor readings in the time-series table and updates the latest sensor state table. The analytics layer (40) processes the real-time sensor data over a rolling time window and determines that the congestion level has crossed a predetermined threshold. The real-time alerts unit (50) generates a congestion alert and controls a traffic signal controller to increase the green signal duration for the congested road. The API and query layer (70) retrieves the latest congestion level and historical vehicle count from the distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60). The dashboards and reports (80) display the congestion alert, current traffic condition, and historical traffic trend to the traffic operator.

[0064]	In another scenario, the field sensor network (10) includes air quality sensors, temperature sensors, humidity sensors, and noise sensors deployed in a city zone. The field sensor network (10) collects pollution level, temperature, humidity, and noise level as real-time sensor data. The edge gateway (20) receives the real-time sensor data and forwards the real-time sensor data to the ingestion layer (30) after adding the local timestamp and sensor identifier. The ingestion layer (30) validates the real-time sensor data, adds metadata including location, region, sensor type, and timestamp, computes the temporal bucket, and prepares write operations. 

[0065]	Further, the distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60) stores the real-time sensor data and historical sensor data. The analytics layer (40) compares the pollution level over a rolling time window with a predetermined pollution threshold. The real-time alerts unit (50) generates a pollution alert when the predetermined pollution threshold is crossed. The API and query layer (70) retrieves current pollution level and historical pollution trend from the distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60). The dashboards and reports (80) display real-time pollution status and historical pollution trends for environmental monitoring and governmental decision-making.

[0066]	Therefore, the present invention has the advantage of providing the system (100) for data management and analytics for civilian and governmental infrastructure monitoring. The system (100) provides a single connected arrangement for monitoring many types of infrastructure conditions. The system (100) supports both real-time monitoring and historical analysis. The system (100) reduces delay in decision-making because the latest sensor state table provides current sensor conditions per location. The system (100) supports long-term analysis because the time-series table stores historical sensor readings in bounded time-based partitions. The system (100) improves reliability because the distributed Apache Cassandra cluster (60) replicates sensor readings and latest sensor states across a plurality of nodes. The system (100) supports civilian and governmental use cases, including traffic management, environmental monitoring, utility monitoring, emergency response, parking management, public transport monitoring, urban planning, and policy evaluation.

title: HAND REHABILITATION SYSTEM AND METHOD
abstract: A hand rehabilitation system (100a) includes a hand exoskeleton device configured to be worn on a patient's hand, an input interface, and a processing unit. The input interface allows selection of a rehabilitation mode based on an impairment level of the patient. The rehabilitation modes include a first mode (108), a second mode (112), a third mode (116), and a fourth mode (118). The processing unit receives real-time hand movement data from one or more sensors associated with the selected rehabilitation mode, computes joint angles from the real-time hand movement data, compares the computed joint angles with reference joint angle sequences to generate similarity metrics, and determines an error value based on a difference between the computed joint angles and the reference joint angle sequences. A feedback module (134) provides real-time feedback based on the similarity metrics.
specification:
FIELD OF INVENTION
	The present disclosure relates to rehabilitation systems and methods, and more particularly to a multi-modal hand rehabilitation system and method thereof.
BACKGROUND
	Hand motion disorders commonly arise from neurological and musculoskeletal conditions such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, peripheral nerve injury, and post-fracture stiffness. These impairments may lead to partial or complete loss of conscious hand mobility, resulting in degradation of overall hand performance. Rehabilitation of such disorders traditionally incorporates repetitive physiotherapy exercises aimed at achieving a proper range of motion and muscle coordination.
	Traditional rehabilitation techniques are heavily dependent on human assistance and constant supervision of physiotherapists. Although these methods may be effective, they can require a significant amount of time and may be subject to human errors. Furthermore, the accuracy of motion replication may degrade over multiple training sessions, indirectly leading to inconsistencies that could adversely affect long-term rehabilitation outcomes.
	Existing technologies in the field of rehabilitation and assistive exoskeleton systems cover a range of approaches such as motor-driven multi-joint actuation, virtual-reality-based rehabilitation platforms, EMG-guided mirror-training systems, biofeedback-driven adaptive controllers, and force-feedback exoskeletons designed to support passive, assistive, or active training modes. However, many existing systems focus on isolated aspects of rehabilitation and may lack multi-modal flexibility with intelligent control. Patients with different conditions may benefit from different modes of operation, yet existing systems may not provide such adaptability.
	Existing hand therapy solutions may exhibit limitations such as non-adaptive exercise routines, restricted motion assistance, and single-device feedback approaches. Traditional rehabilitation systems may lack real-time motion monitoring, patient-specific adaptive intensity control, autonomous and reliable motion control, and extensible assistance based on the degree of neuromuscular impairment.
	Additionally, patients with missing fingers or abnormal finger structures may present challenges for traditional computer-vision-based tracking systems, which may have difficulty capturing accurate landmarks in such cases. Existing systems may not adequately address the rehabilitation of specially-abled patients who cannot follow visually guided exercises or who have anatomical variations that interfere with conventional motion tracking approaches.
	Therefore, in view of the above-mentioned problems, it is desirable to provide a hand rehabilitation system and method that can eliminate one or more of the above-mentioned problems associated with the existing art. 
SUMMARY
	This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts, in a simplified format, that are further described in the detailed description of the invention. This summary is neither intended to identify key or essential inventive concepts of the invention and nor is it intended for determining the scope of the invention.
	In accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure, a hand rehabilitation system is disclosed. The hand rehabilitation system includes: a hand exoskeleton device configured to be worn on a patient's hand; an input interface configured to allow selection of a rehabilitation mode based on an impairment level of the patient, wherein the rehabilitation modes include a first mode, a second mode, a third mode, and a fourth mode; a processing unit configured to: receive real-time hand movement data from one or more sensors associated with the selected rehabilitation mode; compute joint angles from the real-time hand movement data; compare the computed joint angles with reference joint angle sequences to generate similarity metrics; determine an error value based on a difference between the computed joint angles and the reference joint angle sequences; and a feedback module configured to provide real-time feedback based on the similarity metrics.
	In an embodiment, providing multiple rehabilitation modes that can be selected based on the impairment level of the patient enables the system to accommodate patients across a spectrum of conditions, from severe paralysis to mild muscle stiffness. Computing joint angles and comparing them with reference joint angle sequences allows for objective measurement of rehabilitation progress, while real-time feedback based on similarity metrics enables patients to adjust their movements during exercise sessions.
	The first mode includes a motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode for severe impairments, the second mode includes an optical tracking mode for specially-abled patients, the third mode includes a position tracking glove for moderate impairments, and the fourth mode includes a vision-based hand tracking mode for minor impairments. Providing distinct modes tailored to different impairment levels ensures that patients receive appropriate therapy support matched to their specific condition, whether they have severe paralysis requiring motor-driven assistance, anatomical variations requiring optical tracking, moderate impairments benefiting from sensor-based tracking, or minor impairments suitable for camera-based tracking without wearable hardware.
	The hand rehabilitation system further includes a closed-loop adaptive control module configured to continuously adjust actuation commands based on the error value using a proportional control mechanism to enable real-time error correction. Continuously adjusting actuation commands based on the error value using a proportional control mechanism enables the system to dynamically correct hand movements during rehabilitation exercises, improving the accuracy of motion replication and reducing inconsistencies that could adversely affect long-term rehabilitation outcomes.
	The first mode further includes a soft robotic actuation assembly including tendon-driven finger modules, one or more servo motors, and position tracking sensors, wherein the finger modules are configured to enable controlled flexion and extension of fingers. Tendon-driven finger modules with servo motors and position tracking sensors enable precise control of finger movements for patients with severe impairments who have minimal hand mobility, allowing the system to guide the patient's hand through rehabilitation exercises with controlled flexion and extension.
	The first mode further includes an emergency stop mechanism configured to immediately stop actuation upon activation. An emergency stop mechanism that immediately stops actuation upon activation provides a safety feature that prevents injury or strain during motor-driven rehabilitation sessions.
	The first mode further includes a temperature-controlled therapeutic glove configured to provide thermal assistance during rehabilitation, wherein temperature is monitored and regulated within predefined threshold values. A temperature-controlled therapeutic glove that monitors and regulates temperature within predefined threshold values provides thermal support to the patient's hand during rehabilitation, which enhances therapeutic outcomes while maintaining safe operating conditions.
	The optical tracking mode of the second mode includes one or more optical markers configured to track hand movement of patients having missing or abnormal fingers, wherein the optical markers include at least one of active light-emitting markers and passive visual markers. Optical markers configured to track hand movement of patients having missing or abnormal fingers address the challenge of rehabilitating specially-abled patients who cannot be accurately tracked using traditional computer-vision-based systems, enabling motion tracking regardless of anatomical variations.
	Selected optical markers corresponding to unavailable anatomical landmarks are excluded from motion analysis. Excluding selected optical markers corresponding to unavailable anatomical landmarks from motion analysis enables the system to provide accurate rehabilitation feedback for patients with missing fingers by dynamically adjusting which landmarks are tracked based on the patient's specific hand configuration.
	The position tracking glove of the third mode includes one or more position tracking sensors configured to capture angular displacement data of fingers, and the processing unit is further configured to detect sensor failure when no sensor data is received for a predefined time period. Position tracking sensors that capture angular displacement data provide accurate angular measurements during rehabilitation exercises, while detecting sensor failure when no sensor data is received for a predefined time period ensures reliable operation and alerts users to potential equipment issues.
	The vision-based hand tracking mode of the fourth mode is configured to extract hand landmarks from a live camera feed using a computer vision model and compute joint angles geometrically from the extracted hand landmarks. Extracting hand landmarks from a live camera feed using a computer vision model enables rehabilitation for patients with minor impairments without requiring wearable hardware, reducing equipment complexity and patient burden.
	The processing unit is further configured to determine speed-invariant similarity using Dynamic Time Warping. Determining speed-invariant similarity using Dynamic Time Warping enables accurate comparison of patient movements with reference movements regardless of variations in movement speed, accommodating patients who perform exercises at different paces during rehabilitation.
	The reference joint angle sequences are extracted from predefined hand movement profiles stored in a reference database; the predefined hand movement profiles being derived from demonstration videos. Extracting reference joint angle sequences from predefined hand movement profiles stored in a reference database enables clinicians to create and store customized exercise demonstrations, providing flexibility in defining rehabilitation exercises tailored to individual patient conditions.
	The hand rehabilitation system further includes a network-based interface configured to enable clinician-based patient assessment, rehabilitation mode selection, and configuration of therapy parameters including number of cycles and movement speed. A network-based interface that enables clinician-based patient assessment, rehabilitation mode selection, and configuration of therapy parameters allows clinicians to remotely monitor and configure rehabilitation sessions, improving accessibility and enabling efficient management of multiple patients.
	In accordance with another embodiment of the present disclosure, a method for hand rehabilitation is disclosed. The method includes: selecting, by a processing unit, a rehabilitation mode from a plurality of rehabilitation modes based on an impairment level of a patient; receiving, by the processing unit, real-time hand movement data from one or more sensors associated with the selected rehabilitation mode; computing, by the processing unit, joint angles from the real-time hand movement data; comparing, by the processing unit, the computed joint angles with reference joint angle sequences to generate similarity metrics; determining, by the processing unit, an error value based on a difference between the computed joint angles and the reference joint angle sequences; and providing, by a feedback module, real-time feedback based on the similarity metrics.
	Selecting a rehabilitation mode based on the impairment level of the patient and providing real-time feedback based on similarity metrics enables adaptive therapy that accommodates patients with varying levels of hand impairment while providing objective performance measurements during rehabilitation exercises.
	The method further includes continuously adjusting, by a closed-loop adaptive control module, actuation commands based on the error value using a proportional control mechanism. Continuously adjusting actuation commands based on the error value using a proportional control mechanism enables real-time correction of hand movements during rehabilitation, improving the accuracy and consistency of exercise execution.
	The plurality of rehabilitation modes includes a first mode including a motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode for severe impairments, a second mode including an optical tracking mode for specially-abled patients, a third mode including a position tracking glove for moderate impairments, and a fourth mode including a vision-based hand tracking mode for minor impairments. Providing multiple rehabilitation modes including motor-driven, optical tracking, position tracking, and vision-based systems ensures that the method can be applied to patients across a range of conditions, from severe paralysis requiring motor assistance to minor impairments suitable for non-contact vision-based tracking.

	Figure 1A illustrates a method 100 for therapy mode selection within a hand rehabilitation system. The hand rehabilitation system comprises a hand exoskeleton device worn on a patient's hand. The hand rehabilitation system further comprises an input interface and a processing unit. The input interface allows selection of a rehabilitation mode based on an impairment level of the patient. The rehabilitation modes comprise a first mode 108, a second mode 112, a third mode 116, and a fourth mode 118.
	The method 100 begins at a step 102 where a patient presents with a finger injury. The patient is enrolled into the hand rehabilitation system for assessment and treatment.
	At a step 104, a doctor analyzes the patient's condition based on clinical evaluation of the patient's motion impairment. The doctor assesses the degree of impairment in the fingers and determines an appropriate rehabilitation mode for the patient.
	Further, the method 100 proceeds through a hierarchical decision process to select one of the four rehabilitation modes. At a decision 106, the processing unit evaluates whether the patient has a severe injury. Severe injuries include conditions such as stroke, major neuromuscular injury, or minimal hand mobility. If the patient has a severe injury, the method 100 proceeds along the Yes branch to a mode 108. The first mode 108 comprises a motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode for severe impairments. The motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode assists patients in performing physical exercises through motorized actuation.
	If the patient does not have a severe injury, the method 100 proceeds along the No branch from decision 106 to a decision 110. At decision 110, the processing unit evaluates whether the patient is specially-abled. Specially-abled patients include patients who have missing fingers or abnormal finger structures that make traditional computer-vision-based tracking difficult. If the patient is specially-abled, the method 100 proceeds along the Yes branch to a mode 112. The second mode 112 comprises an optical tracking mode for specially-abled patients. The optical tracking mode uses physical markers attached to a glove to track hand movements, enabling motion tracking regardless of anatomical variations.
	If the patient is not specially-abled, the method 100 proceeds along the No branch from decision 110 to a decision 114. At decision 114, the processing unit evaluates whether the patient has a moderate issue. Moderate issues include conditions where the patient does not require a hand exoskeleton system but still benefits from structured monitoring to avoid motion errors. If the patient has a moderate issue, the method 100 proceeds along the Yes branch to a mode 116. The third mode 116 comprises a position tracking glove for moderate impairments. The position tracking glove captures angular data during exercises to provide precise motion measurement.
	If the patient does not have a moderate issue, the method 100 proceeds along the No branch from decision 114 to a mode 118. The fourth mode 118 comprises a vision-based hand tracking mode for minor impairments. The vision-based hand tracking mode uses a computer vision model for patients with minor impairments and does not require wearable hardware. The vision-based hand tracking mode relies on camera-based landmark extraction for guiding rehabilitation exercises.
	The hierarchical decision process through decision 106, decision 110, and decision 114 enables clinician-based patient assessment and rehabilitation mode selection based on the level of impairment. The processing unit is configured to select a rehabilitation mode from the plurality of rehabilitation modes based on the impairment level of the patient, ensuring that patients across a spectrum of conditions from severe paralysis to mild muscle stiffness receive appropriate therapy support.
	Figure 1B illustrates a block diagram of a hand rehabilitation system 100a. The hand rehabilitation system 100a implements the method 100 described with reference to Figure 1A. The hand rehabilitation system 100a comprises a hand exoskeleton device 120, an input interface 122, and a processing unit 124. The hand exoskeleton device 120, the input interface 122, and the processing unit 124 communicate with one another over a network 136.
	The hand exoskeleton device 120 is configured to be worn on a patient's hand. The hand exoskeleton device 120 carries the one or more sensors associated with the selected rehabilitation mode. The hand exoskeleton device 120 captures real-time hand movement data of the patient during a rehabilitation exercise. The hand exoskeleton device 120 transmits the real-time hand movement data to the processing unit 124 over the network 136.
	The input interface 122 allows selection of a rehabilitation mode based on the impairment level of the patient. The input interface 122 receives a clinician input that indicates the selected rehabilitation mode. The selected rehabilitation mode is one of the first mode 108, the second mode 112, the third mode 116, and the fourth mode 118 described with reference to Figure 1A. The input interface 122 communicates the selected rehabilitation mode to the processing unit 124 over the network 136.
	The processing unit 124 comprises a receiving module 126, a computing module 128, a generate module 130, a determine module 132, and a feedback module 134. Each module performs a respective function during the rehabilitation exercise. The processing unit 124 thereby controls the hand rehabilitation system 100a in the selected rehabilitation mode.
	The receiving module 126 receives the real-time hand movement data from the one or more sensors associated with the selected rehabilitation mode. The computing module 128 computes joint angles from the real-time hand movement data. The generate module 130 generates similarity metrics by comparing the computed joint angles with reference joint angle sequences. The determine module 132 determines an error value based on a difference between the computed joint angles and the reference joint angle sequences. The feedback module 134 provides real-time feedback based on the similarity metrics.
	The network 136 couples the hand exoskeleton device 120, the input interface 122, and the processing unit 124. The network 136 enables remote operation of the hand rehabilitation system 100a. A clinician thereby assesses the patient, selects the rehabilitation mode, and configures therapy parameters through the input interface 122. The feedback module 134 returns the real-time feedback to the input interface 122 over the network 136 for display to the patient and the clinician.
	Figure 2A depicts an account creation interface 200a for the hand rehabilitation system. The account creation interface provides a web-based interface for user registration and authentication.
	The account creation interface comprises a header bar positioned at the top of the interface. The header bar contains navigation options including a login option and a sign up button. The sign up button is configured to initiate the account creation process. The header bar displays the system title on the left side and the navigation options on the right side.
	The main content area of the account creation interface may display a create account form. The create account form includes a title and subtitle text that guides users through the registration process. The create account form is configured to collect user information through a multi-step process.
	The create account form includes a progress indicator to display three steps in the account creation process. A first step is labeled “Account Type” and indicates the currently active step. A second step is labeled “Personal Information” and a third step is labeled "Credentials." The progress indicator provides visual feedback to users regarding the current position within the multi-step account creation process.
	The create account form includes a doctor card and a patient card for role selection. The doctor card displays a medical cross icon with the label "Doctor" beneath the icon. The patient card displays a human figure icon with the label "Patient" beneath the icon. The doctor card and the patient card are configured as selectable options that enable users to specify the account type during registration. Selection of the doctor card initiates a registration flow for clinician accounts, while selection of the patient card initiates a registration flow for patient accounts.
	The create account form includes a next button to advance the user to the subsequent step in the account creation process upon activation. A back option is positioned adjacent to the next button to enable navigation to a previous step.
	The account creation interface includes a sign in link accompanied by text indicating ”Already have an account?” and is configured to redirect existing users to a login interface. The login interface provides secure authentication for registered users before redirecting authenticated users to a main dashboard of the hand rehabilitation system.
	Figure 2B depicts a doctor dashboard interface 200b for the hand rehabilitation system. The doctor dashboard interface provides a centralized view for clinicians to monitor and manage patients assigned to the respective doctor. The hand rehabilitation system uses a PostgreSQL database to store patient information, with different doctors having particular patients assigned to the respective doctor.
	The doctor dashboard interface comprises a header section containing a title and subtitle indicating the purpose of monitoring patient progress and upcoming sessions. An add new patient button is positioned in the upper right area of the header section. The add new patient button is configured to initiate a patient registration workflow, enabling the doctor to enroll new patients into the hand rehabilitation system and assign the new patients to the doctor's patient roster.
	Statistics cards are arranged horizontally below the header section. The statistics cards comprise a plurality of summary cards, each displaying an icon and a corresponding metric. A first card of the statistics cards displays a total patients count. A second card of the statistics cards displays an active goals count. A third card of the statistics cards displays a scheduled sessions count. A fourth card of the statistics cards displays a success rate percentage. The statistics cards provide an overview of the doctor's patient management metrics and rehabilitation outcomes.
	The doctor dashboard interface includes a recent patients table to display patient information retrieved from the PostgreSQL database. The recent patients table comprises column headers for patient name, progress, last session date, status, and actions. Each row of the recent patients table corresponds to a patient assigned to the doctor and displays the patient's rehabilitation progress as a percentage value, the date of the patient's last session, a status indicator showing the current state of the patient's rehabilitation, and action icons for viewing and editing patient information.
	The doctor dashboard interface displays all details of patients assigned to the doctor, including medical history, rehabilitation progress, and past session exercise data. Upon selecting a patient from the recent patients table, the doctor is presented with a detailed overview of the patient's medical history, rehabilitation progress, and past session exercise data. The doctor dashboard interface enables the doctor to select a therapy mode for the patient based on clinical evaluation of the patient's condition.
	Figure 2C depicts a user interface screen 200c for selecting and initiating a rehabilitation mode for a patient within the hand rehabilitation system. The user interface screen forms part of a network-based interface configured to enable clinician-based patient assessment, rehabilitation mode selection, and configuration of therapy parameters.
	The user interface screen comprises a sessions panel positioned in an upper portion of the interface. The sessions panel includes a first button labeled "View Sessions" and a second button labeled "View Progress." The sessions panel is configured to provide access to historical session data and patient rehabilitation progress information. Selection of the first button retrieves session history from the PostgreSQL database, while selection of the second button displays progress metrics for the patient.
	The sessions panel includes an exercise dropdown configured to enable selection of exercises from a reference database. The exercise dropdown displays a currently selected exercise and provides a list of available exercises stored in the reference database when activated. The exercises available through the exercise dropdown correspond to predefined hand movement profiles derived from demonstration videos recorded by clinicians.
	Mode selection buttons are arranged horizontally below the exercise dropdown. The mode selection buttons comprise five selectable options corresponding to the rehabilitation modes of the hand rehabilitation system. A first button of the mode selection buttons is labeled "Mode 1" and corresponds to the first mode 108 comprising the motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode for severe impairments. A second button of the mode selection buttons is labeled "Mode 2 (Active)" and corresponds to an active optical sensing configuration of the second mode 112 for specially-abled patients. A third button of the mode selection buttons is labeled "Mode 2 (Passive)" and corresponds to a passive optical sensing configuration of the second mode 112 for specially-abled patients. A fourth button of the mode selection buttons is labeled "Mode 3" and corresponds to the third mode 116 comprising the position tracking glove for moderate impairments. A fifth button of the mode selection buttons is labeled "Mode 4" and corresponds to the fourth mode 118 comprising the vision-based hand tracking mode for minor impairments.
	The mode selection buttons enable the clinician to select a rehabilitation mode based on the impairment level of the patient as determined during clinical evaluation. Upon selection of a mode from the mode selection buttons, the network-based interface initiates the corresponding rehabilitation process and presents configuration options for therapy parameters. The therapy parameters for the motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode of the first mode 108 include a number of cycles specifying the repetition count for the exercise and a movement speed specifying the pace at which the exercise is performed. The configuration of therapy parameters through the network-based interface enables clinicians to customize rehabilitation sessions according to individual patient conditions and treatment objectives.
	Figure 3 illustrates a method 300 for motor-assisted rehabilitation within the hand rehabilitation system. The method 300 provides a structured process for guiding patients with severe hand impairments through rehabilitation exercises using the motor-driven hand exoskeleton mode of the first mode 108.
	The method 300 begins at a mode 1 302 entry point, which corresponds to the first mode 108 described with reference to Figure 1. The mode 1 302 is selected when a patient presents with severe impairments such as stroke, major neuromuscular injury, or minimal hand mobility.
	Following the mode 1 302 entry point, the method 300 proceeds to a reference video decision 304. At the reference video decision 304, the processing unit determines whether a clinician selects a previously recorded reference video from a library or creates a new reference video. The error calculation module 334 computes the instantaneous angular error for each finger and thumb according to the following relationship:
e(t)=θ_ref (t)-θ_actual (t)

The corrected servo command for each finger and thumb is calculated according to the following relationship:
θ_cmd (t)=θ_servo (t)+k_p e(t)
	where θ_cmd (t) represents the corrected servo command at time t, θ_servo (t) represents the servo actuation command generated by the angle conversion module 332, k_p represents the proportional gain constant, and e(t) represents the instantaneous angular error computed by the error calculation module 334. The corrected servo command is calculated as the sum of the servo actuation command and the product of the proportional gain constant and the instantaneous angular error. The proportional gain constant k_p determines the magnitude of the correction applied to the servo actuation commands in response to the computed error values.

title: A BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM HAVING SoC CONFIDENCE EVALUATION MODULE
abstract:
ABSTRACT
Title : A Battery Management System having SoC Confidence Evaluation Module
A Battery Management System (1000) having an integrated chemistry aware State-of-Charge (SoC) module and a process for chemistry-aware State-of-Charge confidence evaluation and adaptive battery management are disclosed. The Battery Management System (1000) comprises a battery sensing module (102), a signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103), a battery management controller (105), a State-of-Charge estimation engine (106), a chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107), an adaptive battery control module (108), battery actuation interfaces (109) and a communication interface module (110). The State-of-Charge estimation engine (106) executes one or more State-of-Charge estimation algorithms to generate one or more estimated State-of-Charge values. The chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107) identifies battery chemistry, evaluates chemistry-dependent electrochemical observability, estimator divergence, thermal stability, aging, State-of-Health and signal consistency, and generates a dynamic State-of-Charge confidence value. The adaptive battery control module (108) utilizes the estimated State-of-Charge and evaluated confidence information to generate adaptive battery control commands and establishes a closed-loop feedback path for estimator recalibration, adaptive estimator selection, confidence evolution and continuous improvement in the reliability of State-of-Charge estimation during battery operation.

“A BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM HAVING SoC CONFIDENCE EVALUATION MODULE”
