The following specification describes the nature of the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed.
 
Field of Invention

	    The present invention relates generally to Battery Management Systems (BMS) for rechargeable battery packs of vehicles.   More particularly, the present invention relates to a Battery Management System configured to have an integrated chemistry aware State-of-Charge (SoC) confidence evaluation module.  

Background of the Invention

	    Battery Management Systems (BMS) play a vital role in ensuring the safe, reliable and efficient operation of rechargeable battery packs employed in electric vehicles (EVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), battery energy storage systems (BESS), renewable energy storage platforms and other electrochemical energy storage applications.   Modern battery-powered systems require accurate estimation of battery operating states, particularly the State-of-Charge (SoC), to facilitate charging control, power limitation, energy management, range estimation, thermal management and safety protection.  These requirements necessitate advanced battery management systems capable of continuously monitoring battery operating conditions and adapting control strategies under varying environmental, electrical and electrochemical conditions.

	     Conventional Battery Management Systems estimate the State-of-Charge using techniques such as Coulomb Counting, Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) estimation, model-based estimation, Kalman filtering, Extended Kalman Filtering (EKF) and hybrid estimation methods.   Although these estimation techniques provide reasonable SoC predictions under ideal operating conditions, the estimation accuracy is significantly influenced by sensor inaccuracies, measurement noise, battery aging, temperature variation, cell imbalance, partial charge-discharge cycling and electrochemical characteristics of different battery chemistries. Consequently, conventional Battery Management Systems generally assume that the computed SoC value is inherently reliable and employ the estimated SoC directly for battery control decisions without assessing the reliability of the estimation itself.

	       There exist numerous technical challenges associated with conventional State-of-Charge estimation techniques.   The electrochemical behaviour of different battery chemistries varies considerably resulting in different estimation characteristics.   For example, Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries exhibit extended flat Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) regions that significantly reduce voltage observability, whereas Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) batteries exhibit hysteresis behaviour and chemistry-dependent voltage variations that adversely affect estimation accuracy.   Furthermore, conventional estimation methods do not adequately account for estimator disagreement, thermal instability, battery degradation, State-of-Health (SOH), impedance variation or measurement consistency during battery operation.    As a result, estimation uncertainty increases considerably under partial charging and discharging conditions, battery aging and dynamically changing operating environments.

	      Existing Battery Management Systems generally treat the estimated State-of-Charge as a deterministic parameter and lack any mechanism for determining the confidence or reliability associated with the estimated value.   Consequently, battery control decisions including charge termination, discharge limitation, fast charging, regenerative braking, battery balancing, thermal management and safety protection are performed without considering the uncertainty associated with the estimation process.   This often results in erroneous State-of-Charge jumps, premature charge termination, incorrect power limitation, unstable fast-charging behaviour, reduced battery service life and compromised operational safety, particularly under low-observability operating conditions encountered in certain battery chemistries.

	        Several advanced battery estimation techniques have been proposed to improve State-of-Charge estimation accuracy by employing adaptive observers, machine learning algorithms, hybrid estimation methods and electrochemical battery models.    However, many of these approaches primarily focus on improving estimation accuracy and do not dynamically evaluate the confidence associated with the estimated State-of-Charge.   Moreover, existing confidence-aware approaches generally fail to incorporate chemistry-specific observability characteristics, estimator divergence behaviour, thermal operating conditions, battery aging, State-of-Health degradation and signal consistency into a unified confidence evaluation framework.   These methods further do not employ the evaluated confidence as a closed-loop control parameter for adaptive battery management functions including estimator arbitration, recalibration, adaptive charging, thermal protection and battery safety intervention.

	      Hence, there exists a need for an improved Battery Management System that integrates battery sensing hardware, chemistry identification, State-of-Charge confidence evaluation, confidence evolution and adaptive battery control within a unified embedded architecture. 

Objectives of the Present Invention

	     The main objective of the present invention is to provide a chemistry-aware Battery Management System (BMS) that dynamically evaluates the confidence associated with battery State-of-Charge (SoC) estimation and utilizes the evaluated confidence as an adaptive control parameter for battery management operations.

	     Another objective of the present invention is to provide a hardware-based SoC confidence evaluation framework that integrates battery sensing circuitry, chemistry identification hardware, confidence evaluation modules and adaptive battery control circuitry to improve the reliability and accuracy of battery State-of-Charge estimation.

	      Another objective of the present invention is to provide a chemistry-aware confidence determination mechanism that dynamically identifies the battery chemistry and evaluates electrochemical observability characteristics.

	      Another objective of the present invention is to provide an adaptive confidence evaluation framework that continuously evaluates estimator divergence, thermal stability, battery aging, State-of-Health (SOH), signal consistency and rest-validation information.

	       Another objective of the present invention is to provide a confidence fusion mechanism configured to combine a plurality of battery operating parameters into a dynamic State-of-Charge confidence value for supporting intelligent battery management decisions.

	        Yet, the objective of the present invention is to provide an adaptive battery control system that dynamically regulates charging current, discharge current, fast charging, regenerative braking, battery balancing, thermal management and battery protection functions in accordance with the evaluated State-of-Charge confidence level.
	         Yet, another objective of the present invention is to provide a confidence evolution framework that continuously updates the SoC confidence value using confidence decay and confidence recovery mechanisms, thereby improving estimation robustness throughout battery operation.

	        Further, the objective of the present invention is to provide an automatic estimator arbitration mechanism capable of dynamically recalibrating, selecting or switching between multiple SoC estimation algorithms according to battery chemistry, operational conditions and evaluated confidence levels.

	       Yet, the objective of the present invention is to provide a confidence-aware battery management framework that enhances battery safety, operational reliability, charging efficiency and battery service life by utilizing dynamically generated confidence information to govern adaptive battery control decisions in electric vehicles and hybrid electric vehicles.

Brief Description of the Drawings

	     This invention is illustrated in the accompanying drawings, throughout which reference letters indicate corresponding parts in the various figures.  The embodiments herein and advantages thereof will be better understood from the following description when read with reference to the following drawings, wherein

	     Figure 1 shows the system architecture of a chemically aware SoC confidence-based Battery Management System as per the present invention.
 
	      Figure 2 decribes an example process flow for determining SoC confidence and implementing adaptive battery control actions in accordance with the present invention.

	      Figure 3 presents the confidence evolution state machine, which helps track dynamically the accuracy of the estimated State-of-Charge (SoC).

	      Figure 4 illustrates an adaptive battery control decision framework based on SoC confidence evaluation of the present invention.

	       Figure 5 describes the validation characteristics of the proposed chemistry aware SoC confidence framework in accordance with the present invention.
     
Detailed Description of the Present Invention

	      The invention will now be described in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings which must not be viewed as restricting the scope and ambit of the invention.        Referring to Fig. 1, the Battery Management System (1000) having an integrated chemistry aware SoC confidence evaluation module is configured to have a battery sensing module (102),  signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103), a battery management controller (105), a State-of-Charge (SoC) estimation engine (106), a chemistry aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107), an adaptive battery control module (108), a battery actuation interfaces (109) and a communication interface module (110).    The SoC estimation engine (106) communicates with the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) to receive conditioned battery measurements comprising battery voltage, current, temperature, impedance and other operational parameters and computes the battery State-of-Charge using one or more estimation techniques including Coulomb counting, Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) estimation, Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) estimation, model-based estimation, machine-learning based estimation or combinations thereof.     The SoC estimation engine (106) is configured to execute a plurality of estimation algorithms simultaneously to generate multiple SoC estimates for subsequent confidence evaluation.     The estimated SoC values together with the processed battery measurements are communicated internally to the chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107).

	             The battery sensing module (102) comprises one or more voltage sensing circuits, current sensing circuits, temperature sensing circuits, impedance measurement circuits, analogue front-end circuitry and signal acquisition interfaces configured to continuously acquire battery operating parameters from the battery pack (101).   The battery sensing module (102) further comprises hardware sampling circuitry configured to synchronously acquire battery measurements and communicate digitized measurement data to the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) through one or more internal communication buses.

	         The State-of-Charge estimation engine (106) comprises an embedded estimation processor, estimator memory, arithmetic processing circuitry and estimator execution logic configured to execute one or more State-of-Charge estimation models.    The estimation engine (106) is configured to receive conditioned battery measurements from the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) and electronically generate one or more estimated State-of-Charge values, which are temporarily stored within one or more estimator registers prior to communication with the chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107).
	      The chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107) is configured to comprise a chemistry identification module (107a), an observability analysis module (107b), an estimator divergence engine (107c), a thermal stability evaluation module (107d), an aging and State-of-Health analysis module (107e), a signal consistency evaluation module (107f), a confidence fusion engine (107g), a confidence evolution engine (107h) and a confidence threshold evaluation module (107i).     The chemistry identification module (107a) receives the conditioned battery measurements and estimated battery states from the SoC estimation engine (106), compares the measured battery characteristics with stored battery chemistry models and determines the battery chemistry corresponding to Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP), Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC), Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum Oxide (NCA), Lithium Titanate Oxide (LTO), Lithium Sulfur or other rechargeable battery chemistries.    The identified battery chemistry is communicated to the observability analysis module (107b), which evaluates chemistry-dependent electrochemical observability using parameters including Open Circuit Voltage-State-of-Charge (OCV-SoC) slope, voltage plateau characteristics, hysteresis behaviour, relaxation characteristics and voltage sensitivity.   Simultaneously, the estimator divergence engine (107c) receives multiple SoC estimates from the SoC estimation engine (106) and determines the degree of divergence between the estimation algorithms.

	        The thermal stability evaluation module (107d) communicates with the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) to receive battery temperature information and determines thermal stability based on battery operating temperature, thermal gradients and thermal loading conditions.    The aging and State-of-Health analysis module (107e) receives battery health information including State-of-Health, impedance variation, cycle count and capacity degradation from the SoC estimation engine (106) and evaluates battery aging characteristics.   Further, the signal consistency evaluation module (107f) receives voltage, current and temperature measurements from the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) to determine measurement consistency, sensor reliability and operational stability.     The outputs generated by the observability analysis module (107b), estimator divergence engine (107c), thermal stability evaluation module (107d), aging and State-of-Health analysis module (107e) and signal consistency evaluation module (107f) are communicated to the confidence fusion engine (107g), which combines the plurality of confidence-related parameters to generate a dynamic State-of-Charge confidence value associated with the estimated SoC.

	          The generated confidence value is communicated to the confidence evolution engine (107h), which dynamically updates the confidence value using confidence decay and confidence recovery mechanisms based on changes in battery operating conditions.   The updated confidence value is thereafter communicated to the confidence threshold evaluation module (107i).     This evaluation module (107i) compares the computed confidence value with predefined confidence thresholds and classifies the battery operating condition into high confidence, medium confidence or low confidence regions.   The evaluated confidence information is subsequently communicated to the adaptive battery control module (108).

	      The adaptive battery control module (108) is configured to receive the estimated State-of-Charge from the SoC estimation engine (106) together with the evaluated confidence information from the confidence threshold evaluation module (107i) and generates adaptive battery control commands accordingly.     The adaptive battery control module (108) generates the adaptive battery control commands to perform battery management functions including charge current regulation, discharge current limitation, fast charging enablement or restriction, end-of-charge confirmation, regenerative braking limitation, estimator arbitration, recalibration management, thermal protection, diagnostics and safety intervention based on the evaluated confidence level.      The generated control commands are communicated to the battery actuation interfaces (109) comprising charger controllers, inverter systems, DC-DC converters, contactors, battery protection circuits, balancing circuits and cooling systems for execution of the adaptive battery control actions.     The communication interface module (110) further communicates battery status, estimated SoC, confidence information and diagnostic data between the Battery Management System controller (105) and external vehicle controllers, supervisory controllers, cloud-based battery management platforms and other communication networks.    The adaptive battery control module (108) further establishes a closed-loop feedback path with the SoC estimation engine (106) to enable estimator recalibration, estimator selection, confidence evolution and continuous improvement in the reliability of battery State-of-Charge estimation during battery operation.    The communication interface module (110) comprises one or more CAN controllers, CAN-FD controllers, LIN interfaces, Ethernet controllers, UART interfaces, SPI interfaces, I²C interfaces and wireless communication modules configured to communicate battery operating information, diagnostic information and confidence information between the Battery Management System controller (105), vehicle electronic control units, cloud servers and supervisory battery management platforms.

	         The adaptive battery control module (108) comprises a hardware control processor configured to generate hardware control signals based on the evaluated confidence level.    The generated control signals are communicated to one or more battery actuation interfaces (109) for regulating battery charging, battery discharging, cell balancing, regenerative braking, thermal management and battery protection functions.

	        The Battery Management System controller (105) comprises one or more embedded processors, microcontrollers, digital signal processors (DSP), application specific integrated circuits (ASIC) and peripheral interfaces configured to execute battery management functions.   The controller (105) further comprises volatile memory, non-volatile memory, register banks, hardware timers, interrupt controllers and direct memory access (DMA) controllers for real-time execution of battery management operations.

	       Referring again to Fig. 2, the process flow for chemistry-aware State-of-Charge (SoC) confidence evaluation and adaptive battery management comprises a series of sequential steps of:
Step 201: The battery sensing module (102) continuously acquires battery operational parameters including cell voltage, pack voltage, charging current, discharging current, cell temperature, pack temperature, battery impedance and other operational measurements from the battery pack (101). These measured signals are communicated to the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) where filtering, signal conditioning, normalization and sensor validation operations are performed to generate conditioned measurement data for subsequent processing.
Step 202: The conditioned battery measurements are communicated to the State-of-Charge estimation engine (106), which executes one or more State-of-Charge estimation algorithms including Coulomb Counting, Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) estimation, Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) estimation, model-based estimation, machine-learning based estimation or combinations thereof to compute one or more battery State-of-Charge (SoC) estimates. The computed SoC estimates together with the processed battery measurements are subsequently communicated to the chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107).  
Step 203: The chemistry identification module (107a) receives the estimated battery states and conditioned battery measurements, analyzes battery voltage response, impedance characteristics, thermal behaviour and electrochemical signatures, and compares the measured characteristics with stored battery chemistry models to identify the battery chemistry. The identified chemistry, corresponding to Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP), Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC), Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum Oxide (NCA), Lithium Sulfur, Lithium Titanate Oxide (LTO) or other rechargeable battery chemistries, is communicated to the observability analysis module (107b) for chemistry-dependent confidence evaluation.  
Step 204: The observability analysis module (107b) evaluates chemistry-specific electrochemical observability by determining parameters including Open Circuit Voltage-State-of-Charge (OCV-SoC) slope, voltage plateau characteristics, hysteresis behaviour, voltage sensitivity and relaxation characteristics to determine the extent to which the battery operating conditions permit reliable SoC estimation. The evaluated observability information is communicated to the confidence fusion engine (107g).  
Step 205: Simultaneously, the estimator divergence engine (107c) receives the plurality of SoC estimates generated by the State-of-Charge estimation engine (106) and computes estimator divergence by comparing the outputs of the respective estimation algorithms. The computed estimator divergence is subsequently communicated to the confidence fusion engine (107g).  
Step 206: The thermal stability evaluation module (107d) receives battery temperature information from the signal conditioning and preprocessing module (103) and evaluates thermal stability based on battery operating temperature, temperature gradients, thermal loading and thermal transients. Concurrently, the aging and State-of-Health analysis module (107e) evaluates battery aging characteristics including State-of-Health (SOH), impedance rise, capacity degradation and battery cycle count, while the signal consistency evaluation module (107f) determines sensor reliability and operational consistency based on voltage, current and temperature measurements.  In certain embodiments, rest-validation information corresponding to battery relaxation conditions may also be evaluated.  The outputs generated by the thermal stability evaluation module (107d), aging and State-of-Health analysis module (107e), signal consistency evaluation module (107f) and rest-validation analysis are communicated to the confidence fusion engine (107g).  
Step 207: The confidence fusion engine (107g) integrates the chemistry observability, estimator divergence, thermal stability, battery aging, State-of-Health, signal consistency and rest-validation information to determine a dynamic State-of-Charge confidence value according to the following relationship:
C_SOC=f(O_chem ,D_est ,T_stab,H_SOH ,S_sig ,R_val )
where:
Ochem represents chemistry observability; 
Dest represents estimator divergence; 
Tstab represents thermal stability; 
HSOH represents battery State-of-Health related information; 
Ssig represents signal consistency; and 
Rval represents rest-validation information. 

	      The generated SoC confidence value is communicated to the confidence evolution engine (107h) and the subsequent steps being executed are:
Step 208: The confidence evolution engine (107h) dynamically updates the computed SoC confidence value using confidence decay and confidence recovery mechanisms according to changes in battery operating conditions. The updated confidence value is subsequently communicated to the confidence threshold evaluation module (107i), which compares the computed confidence value with predefined threshold values and classifies the battery operating condition into high-confidence, medium-confidence or low-confidence operational regions.   
Step 209: The classified confidence information is communicated to the adaptive battery control module (108) together with the estimated State-of-Charge generated by the State-of-Charge estimation engine (106). Based on the evaluated confidence level, the adaptive battery control module (108) determines battery management actions including charge current regulation, discharge current limitation, fast charging enablement or restriction, end-of-charge confirmation, regenerative braking limitation, estimator arbitration, recalibration management, thermal protection, diagnostics and battery safety intervention. The generated control commands are thereafter communicated to the battery actuation interfaces (109) for execution by charger controllers, inverter systems, contactors, balancing circuits, battery protection circuitry and cooling systems.   
Step 210: A closed-loop feedback mechanism is established wherein the updated confidence information, adaptive control status and diagnostic information are continuously communicated back to the State-of-Charge estimation engine (106) and the chemistry-aware SoC confidence evaluation framework (107). The feedback mechanism enables estimator recalibration, adaptive estimator selection, confidence evolution and continuous improvement in the reliability of State-of-Charge estimation, thereby ensuring robust battery management under varying battery chemistries, thermal conditions, aging characteristics and operating environments.

	      Referring further to Figs. 4a to 4c, simulation and performance evaluation were conducted on the chemistry-aware State-of-Charge (SoC) confidence evaluation framework implemented within the Battery Management System (1000).    Referring to Fig. 4a, the simulation results demonstrate that the proposed Battery Management System (1000) dynamically adjusts the computed SoC confidence according to battery observability, thermal behaviour and degradation characteristics, thereby maintaining reliable State-of-Charge estimation under varying electrochemical operating conditions.   Referring to Fig. 4b, the temperature-based evaluation indicates that the proposed confidence evaluation framework maintains higher estimation reliability within the normal battery operating temperature range while progressively reducing the confidence value under thermal stress conditions, thereby enabling adaptive charging, discharge limitation and battery protection before significant estimation errors occur.   Referring to Fig. 4c, the aging analysis illustrates that the computed SoC confidence gradually decreases with increasing battery degradation, impedance rise and capacity fade, thereby allowing the adaptive battery control module to automatically initiate estimator recalibration, power derating and safety protection mechanisms as the battery State-of-Health deteriorates.

	      The battery management system, as per the present invention provides the following technical advantages that contributes to the advancement of technology leading to establish the inventive step:
	It enables real-time chemistry-aware State-of-Charge (SoC) confidence evaluation, thereby improving the reliability and accuracy of battery state estimation under varying operating conditions.
	It dynamically adapts battery charging, discharging, balancing and thermal management operations according to the evaluated SoC confidence level, thereby improving operational safety and reducing the likelihood of erroneous battery control decisions.
	It improves estimation robustness by simultaneously evaluating chemistry observability, estimator divergence, battery aging, thermal stability, signal consistency and rest-validation information, thereby reducing uncertainty associated with conventional deterministic State-of-Charge estimation methods.
	It enables automatic confidence-based estimator arbitration, recalibration and adaptive estimator management, thereby maintaining reliable battery state estimation throughout battery aging, temperature variation and partial charging or discharging operations.
	It ensures safer battery operation by generating hardware control signals for charger controllers, contactor driver circuits, balancing circuits, thermal management controllers and battery protection circuitry whenever low-confidence operating conditions are detected, thereby preventing unsafe charging, over-discharge and abnormal battery operation.
	It improves battery lifetime by adaptively limiting charging current, discharge current, regenerative braking and fast-charging operations according to the evaluated confidence level, thereby minimizing battery degradation, thermal stress and capacity fade.
	It enhances the stability of Battery Management System operation by maintaining a continuously evolving confidence state using dedicated confidence registers, hardware threshold comparators and confidence state update circuitry, thereby preventing abrupt transitions between different battery operating modes.
	It provides a closed-loop confidence-aware battery management architecture wherein updated confidence information is continuously communicated back to the State-of-Charge estimation hardware, enabling automatic recalibration, estimator convergence and continuous improvement in estimation accuracy during battery operation.
	It facilitates reliable operation under adverse operating environments by incorporating battery temperature monitoring, impedance analysis, degradation evaluation and signal validation within the confidence evaluation process, thereby improving battery performance under thermal stress and aging conditions.
	It reduces computational uncertainty by implementing confidence evaluation using dedicated embedded hardware modules, confidence fusion circuitry and threshold comparison hardware, thereby providing deterministic and repeatable battery management decisions suitable for safety-critical automotive applications.

	      While attempt has been made to describe the construction and working of the invention to the fullest possible extent, minor changes that do not detract from the outline established in this document are still possible.    Such changes can be considered as obvious to a person skilled in the art and must hence not be viewed to be taking any front fork with all the other features as covered by this description outside the scope of the claims of this specification.

title:
METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR QUANTUM-SECURE IMAGE
ENCRYPTION
abstract:
ABSTRACT
METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR QUANTUM-SECURE IMAGE
ENCRYPTION
A method (200) for quantum-inspired image encryption and secure image 5
transmission comprises receiving (201), by an image acquisition module (102), an
input image for secure transmission; converting (202), by a bit processing module
(104), the input image into a plurality of bit-level image components; generating
(203), by a key generation module (106), one or more encryption keys using a
chaotic map and a Differential Phase Shift protocol; scrambling (204), by an 10
image transformation module (108), the bit-level image components using a three- dimensional transformation process; encrypting (205), by an encryption module
(110), the scrambled image components to generate an encrypted image; and
transmitting (206), by a communication module (112), the encrypted image to an
authorized receiver for secure decryption and reconstruction.
specification:
FIELD
The present disclosure relates to a system and a method for encrypting an image. BACKGROUND
With the rapid growth of digital communication systems, secure transmission and 5
storage of digital images have become increasingly important in various sectors
including defence, healthcare, surveillance, and cloud computing. Sensitive
images transmitted through communication networks are vulnerable to
interception, tampering, unauthorised access, and cyber-attacks. Conventional
encryption systems often face limitations in handling high-dimensional image 10
data efficiently while maintaining strong security against modern attack
techniques. Existing image encryption approaches primarily rely on traditional cryptographic
algorithms that may become vulnerable against advanced computational systems 15
and emerging quantum computing technologies. Further, many existing systems
suffer from insufficient randomness, predictable key generation, high
computational complexity, and weak resistance against statistical and differential
attacks. Certain conventional scrambling techniques also fail to provide adequate
protection against unauthorised image reconstruction. 20
Accordingly, there exists a need for an improved image encryption framework
capable of providing highly secure, random, and multi-layered encryption using
quantum-inspired communication techniques, chaotic key generation mechanisms, and advanced image transformation processes for secure image transmission and 25
storage. SUMMARY
The present disclosure provides a method for encrypting an image comprising
receiving an input image for secure transmission, converting the input image into 30
a plurality of bit-level image components, generating one or more encryption keys
3
using a chaotic map and a Differential Phase Shift protocol, scrambling the bit￾level image components using a three-dimensional transformation process, encrypting the scrambled image components using the generated encryption keys
to generate an encrypted image, and transmitting the encrypted image to an
authorized receiver for secure decryption and reconstruction. 5
The present disclosure also provides a system for encrypting an image comprising
an image acquisition module configured to receive an input image, a bit
processing module configured to convert the input image into a plurality of bit￾level image components, a key generation module configured to generate 10
encryption keys using a chaotic map and a Differential Phase Shift protocol, an
image transformation module configured to scramble the bit-level image
components using a three-dimensional transformation process, an encryption
module configured to encrypt the scrambled image components to generate an
encrypted image, and a communication module configured to securely transmit 15
the encrypted image to an authorized receiver. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
The following figures are illustrative of particular examples for enabling
embodiments of the present disclosure, are descriptive of some of the 20
embodiments and are not intended to limit the scope of the disclosure. The figures
are not to scale (unless so stated) and are intended for use in conjunction with the
explanations in the following detailed description. Wherever applicable, the words
and phrases used herein should be understood and interpreted to have a meaning
consistent with the understanding of those words and phrases by those skilled in 25
the relevant art. Persons skilled in the art will appreciate that elements in the
figures are illustrated for simplicity and clarity and may not have been drawn to
scale. For example, the dimensions of some of the elements in the figure may be
exaggerated relative to other elements to help to improve understanding of various
exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure. Throughout the drawings, it 30
4
should be noted that like reference numbers are used to depict the same or similar
elements, features, and structures. Fig. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a system for encrypting an image, according
to an embodiment of the present disclosure; 5
Fig. 2 illustrates a flow chart of a method for encrypting an image, according to an
embodiment of the present disclosure; and
Figs. 3 and 4 illustrate exemplary flow charts representing the system and the 10
method. DETAILED DESCRIPTION
The following description with reference to the accompanying drawings is
provided to assist in a comprehensive understanding of exemplary embodiments 15
of the disclosure. It includes various specific details to assist in that understanding
but these are to be regarded as merely exemplary. The terms and words used in the following description are not limited to the
bibliographical meanings, but, are merely used to enable a clear and consistent 20
understanding of the disclosure. Accordingly, it should be apparent to those
skilled in the art that the following description of exemplary embodiments of the
present disclosure are provided for illustration purpose only and not for the
purpose of limiting the disclosure as defined by the appended claims and their
equivalents. 25
Features that are described and/or illustrated with respect to one embodiment may
be used in the same way or in a similar way in one or more other embodiments
and/or in combination with or instead of the features of the other embodiments. 30
5
With the rapid growth of digital communication systems, secure transmission and
storage of digital images have become increasingly important in various sectors
including defence, healthcare, surveillance, and cloud computing. Sensitive
images transmitted through communication networks are vulnerable to
interception, tampering, unauthorized access, and cyber-attacks. Conventional 5
encryption systems often face limitations in handling high-dimensional image
data efficiently while maintaining strong security against modern attack
techniques. Existing image encryption approaches primarily rely on traditional cryptographic 10
algorithms that may become vulnerable against advanced computational systems
and emerging quantum computing technologies. Further, many existing systems
suffer from insufficient randomness, predictable key generation, high
computational complexity, and weak resistance against statistical and differential
attacks. Certain conventional scrambling techniques also fail to provide adequate 15
protection against unauthorised image reconstruction. Referring to figures, Fig. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a system 100 for
encrypting an image, according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. The
present invention relates to the system 100 is configured to provide secure 20
protection of digital images against unauthorized access, interception, statistical
analysis, differential attacks, and reconstruction attempts during communication. The system 100 comprises an image acquisition module 102, a bit processing
module 104, a key generation module 106, an image transformation module 108, 25
an encryption module 110, and a communication module 112. The image acquisition module 102 is configured to receive an input image
intended for secure transmission. The input image may comprise grayscale images, color images, medical images, surveillance images, confidential documents, 30
satellite imagery, or any digital image data requiring secure communication. The
6
image acquisition module 102 may receive the image from a camera, storage
device, computing terminal, cloud repository, or external image source. The
image acquisition module 102 provides compatibility with multiple image sources
and formats, thereby improving deployment flexibility across diverse applications
including defence, telemedicine, surveillance, and secure communications. 5
The bit processing module 104 is configured to convert the input image into a
plurality of bit-level image components. Each pixel value of the input image is
represented in binary form, and the binary representations are decomposed into
multiple binary planes corresponding to individual bit significance levels. For 10
example, an 8-bit grayscale image may be decomposed into eight binary bit
planes. The bit processing module 104 separates the image into these multiple
binary planes to enable fine-grained bit-level encryption operations. This
improves encryption granularity, increases confusion and diffusion properties, and
significantly enhances resistance against reconstruction and cryptanalytic attacks. 15
The key generation module 106 is configured to generate one or more encryption
keys using a chaotic map and a Differential Phase Shift DPS protocol. In one
embodiment, the chaotic map comprises a URUK chaotic map configured to
generate highly random and non-linear encryption keys. The URUK chaotic map 20
utilizes non-linear iterative mathematical transformations to produce pseudo￾random sequences exhibiting high sensitivity to initial conditions, parameter
changes, and sequence unpredictability. The key generation module 106 further utilizes the Differential Phase Shift DPS 25
protocol to securely facilitate encryption key generation and transmission between
communicating entities. The DPS protocol enables secure synchronization of key
parameters between sender and authorized receiver while preventing interception
or key leakage. The encryption keys generated by combining chaotic behavior and
DPS-based secure exchange are used for image encryption. This improves 30
7
randomness, unpredictability, and communication security while reducing risk of
key interception. The image transformation module 108 is configured to scramble the plurality of
bit-level image components using a three-dimensional transformation process. 5
The three-dimensional transformation process comprises a three-dimensional
Arnold transform configured to scramble spatial positions of image pixels across
multiple dimensions. The transform reorders pixel positions according to
deterministic but complex transformation rules, thereby disrupting the original
spatial arrangement of image information. The transformation may be iteratively 10
applied over multiple rounds to increase scrambling complexity. This significantly
increases spatial confusion and makes reverse reconstruction computationally
difficult without transformation parameters. The encryption module 110 is configured to encrypt the scrambled image 15
components using the encryption keys generated by the key generation module
106 to generate an encrypted image. The encryption module 110 performs bit￾level permutation and diffusion operations on the scrambled image components. In permutation operations, bit positions are rearranged according to encryption
key-dependent patterns. In diffusion operations, pixel values or bit values are 20
modified such that minor changes in the input image produce substantial changes
in the encrypted output. The combination of permutation and diffusion produces
the encrypted image. The encrypted image exhibits reduced pixel correlation, uniform histogram distribution, high entropy, and unpredictability. This improves
avalanche effect, strengthens cryptographic robustness, and enhances resistance to 25
differential and statistical attacks. The encrypted image generated by the encryption module 110 is configured to
resist statistical attacks, differential attacks, and unauthorized reconstruction
attempts. Statistical resistance is achieved through entropy enhancement and 30
histogram equalization. Differential attack resistance is achieved through strong
8
diffusion characteristics causing substantial encrypted image variation even for
minimal input image changes. Unauthorized reconstruction resistance is achieved
through combined scrambling, chaotic key generation, and secure key exchange
mechanisms. This ensures suitability for high-security image communication
applications. 5
The communication module 112 is configured to securely transmit the encrypted
image to an authorized receiver. The communication module 112 supports secure
transmission through wireless networks, cloud platforms, local communication
channels, wired networks, or remote transmission systems. The encrypted image 10
may be packetized, serialized, and transmitted through communication protocols
suitable for secure image delivery. This enables flexible deployment across cloud, IoT, defence, surveillance, and telecommunication infrastructures. At the authorized receiver, a decryption module performs decryption using 15
corresponding decryption keys synchronized through the DPS protocol. The
decryption module applies inverse permutation, inverse diffusion, and inverse
three-dimensional transformation operations to reconstruct the original input
image. The reconstructed image corresponds substantially to the original input
image received by the image acquisition module 102. This ensures secure end-to- 20
end communication while preventing unauthorized recovery. Accordingly, the system quantum-inspired image encryption framework that is a
integrates quantum bit-plane Real Ket (QBRK) decomposition, quantum bit-plane
scrambling (QBPS), the URUK chaotic map, and the Differential Phase Shift 25
(DPS) quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol over a Free Space Optics (FSO)
channel. The developed model leverages QBRK-based bit-level processing to
extract pixel-level quantum features, which are scrambled using the final key
generated by combining the URUK chaotic map and DPS protocol. To enhance
spatial diffusion, a 3D non-equilateral Arnold transform (3DNEAT) is applied to 30
the scrambled image, followed by final encryption with a dynamically generated
9
XOR key. The robustness of the developed scheme is validated through multiple
visual and objective analysis metrics including entropy, Number of Pixel Change
Rate (NPCR), Unified Average Changing Intensity (UACI), Peak Signal-to-Noise
Ratio (PSNR), Fourier spectrums, encryption time, Quantum Bit Error Rate
(QBER), fidelity, and eavesdropping detection probability. 5
Fig. 2 illustrates a flowchart of a method 200 for encrypting an image. The
method 200 is configured to be performed by the system 100 of Fig. 1c. The
method 200 will now be described with respect to Figs. 1-2. 10
Referring to Figs. 1 and 2, at step 201, an input image for secure transmission is
received by the image acquisition module 102. The input image may comprise
grayscale, color, surveillance, medical, satellite, or confidential digital images. This supports secure protection of diverse image types. 15
At step 202, the input image is converted by the bit processing module 104 into a
plurality of bit-level image components. The bit-level image components
comprise multiple binary planes generated from pixel values of the input image. This enables fine-grained cryptographic manipulation. 20
At step 203, one or more encryption keys are generated by the key generation
module 106 using a chaotic map and a Differential Phase Shift DPS protocol. The
chaotic map comprises a URUK chaotic map configured to generate random and
non-linear encryption keys. The DPS protocol securely facilitates encryption key
generation and transmission between communicating entities. This enhances key 25
unpredictability and communication security. At step 204, the plurality of bit-level image components are scrambled by the
image transformation module 108 using a three-dimensional transformation
process. The three-dimensional transformation process comprises a three- 30
10
dimensional Arnold transform configured to scramble spatial positions of image
pixels. This improves confusion and spatial security. At step 205, the scrambled image components are encrypted by the encryption
module 110 using the generated encryption keys to generate an encrypted image. 5
The encryption includes bit-level permutation and diffusion operations. This
improves attack resistance and cryptographic robustness. The encrypted image is
configured to resist statistical attacks, differential attacks, and unauthorized
reconstruction attempts. This enables secure deployment in sensitive
communication environments. 10
At step 206, the encrypted image is transmitted by the communication module
112 to an authorized receiver. The communication module 112 securely transmits
the encrypted image through a wireless network, cloud platform, or
communication channel. This supports flexible secure transmission infrastructure. 15
The method 200 further includes a step in which, the encrypted image is
decrypted by a decryption module at the authorized receiver using corresponding
decryption keys to reconstruct the input image. The decryption includes inverse
cryptographic operations corresponding to encryption operations. This ensures 20
authorized end-to-end secure image recovery. Figs. 3 and 4 illustrate exemplary flow charts representing the system and the
method. Referring to Figs. 1-4, it is apparent that the proposed QBRK-QBPS- URUK, DPS, FSO quantum image encryption framework effectively combines 25
quantum-inspired computation, chaotic dynamics, and realistic QKD to ensure
high-security image protection. The DPS protocol enables the secure generation
and distribution of cryptographic keys over quantum channels, ensuring resistance
against eavesdropping attacks. The 3D NEAT offers enhanced pixel position
scrambling in three dimensions, overcoming the periodicity limitations of 30
traditional 2D transforms. Additionally, the URUK Chaotic Map provides strong
11
confusion and diffusion properties, introducing high sensitivity to initial
conditions and system parameters. Performance evaluations, including entropy, 𝑁𝑃, 𝑈𝐴,   𝑃, 𝐵 , 𝑄, and    confirm that the encrypted images exhibit
high randomness, low correlation, and strong resistance to tampering. The
correlation, histogram, and entropy values demonstrate that the proposed 5
approach yields scrambled outputs that withstand statistical scrutiny. It has been
shown that the sensitivity analysis of ciphered images, using 𝑁𝑃 and 𝑈𝐴
measures, is extremely close to theoretical values. This signifies that the designed
approach is resilient to original image attacks. The URUK chaotic map’s sensitive
control parameters allow for a large key space, making it resistant to brute-force 10
attacks. Furthermore, OptiSystem simulations were used to model the performance of the
suggested strategy over optical channels. To confirm system viability and signal
integrity under practical optical transmission conditions, the optical spectrum and 15
time-domain signal waveforms were examined. The approach is shown to be both
theoretically and practically secure for use in secure optical communication
systems by this dual-level validation, which is both cryptographic and optical. The
feasibility of the developed method is supported by forty-seven cutting-edge
methodologies. The suggested technique is validated using subjective and 20
objective evaluations of existing encryption algorithms. The results validate the
practicality and robustness of the designed model for secure quantum
communication systems, making it a strong candidate for future quantum-safe
image encryption and transmission applications. 25
The present invention includes a unique hybridization of DPS-QK Dover FSO, URUK chaotic diffusion, QBRK-based bit-plane logic, selective MSB scrambling
(QBPS), and non-equilateral 3DNEAT permutation, producing a multilayer, noise-enhanced key generation workflow and non-periodic scrambling pipeline. Accordingly, the present invention offers multiple advantages over conventional 30
quantum, chaotic, and classical image encryption techniques:
12
1. Higher Key Entropy Through Hybrid Key Generation
2. Selective High-Impact Encryption Using QBRK and QBPS
3. Enhanced Resistance Against Differential and Chosen-Plain text Attacks
4. Quantum-Level Security Without Full Quantum Hardware Requirements
5. Improved Practicality for Real-Time Imagery (Satellite & Medical) 5
6. FSO-Based Key Distribution Enables Long-Range Secure Communication
7. The framework is interoperable with grayscale and high-resolution images, allowing integration into IoT, CPS, defence, biomedical imaging systems, satellite
telemetry, secure cloud storage, and quantum-resilient encryption pipelines. 10
Therefore, the system 100 and the method 200 provide a multi-layered quantum￾inspired image encryption framework for secure image protection and
transmission. The invention utilizes chaotic map-based key generation to produce highly
random and unpredictable encryption keys. The Differential Phase Shift (DPS) 15
protocol enhances secure key handling and communication security during image
transmission. The three-dimensional image scrambling process significantly
increases image randomness and prevents unauthorized reconstruction. The bit￾level encryption architecture improves diffusion and permutation efficiency for
enhanced image protection. The invention provides improved resistance against 20

analysis. The system 100 and the method 200 support secure transmission of

communication, and secure cloud storage applications. The system 100 and the

different embodiments, the present disclosure is not limited by the disclosed

title: ORAL REHABILITATION DEVICE
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
ORAL REHABILITATION DEVICE 
5 
10 
15 
An Oral Rehabilitation Device (Fig. 2) is disclosed for treating restricted mouth 
opening. The device comprises a handheld housing enclosing a programmable 
control unit, a precision mechatronic actuator driven by a micro-step stepper motor 
and lead screw, and integrated force-sensing and displacement subsystems. The 
control unit executes closed-loop feedback to dynamically adjust stretching 
amplitude, speed, and hold duration based on real-time tissue resistance. The device 
delivers a cyclic, micro-pulsed stretching protocol to safely promote gradual fibrosis 
remodeling while monitoring patient compliance and logging therapy analytics for 
remote clinician review.
specification:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION 
5 
10 
15 
20 
25 
30 
The present disclosure relates generally to medical devices and mechatronic systems 
for physical therapy, and more particularly, to an intelligent, motorized oral 
rehabilitation device and closed-loop control system for delivering controlled 
mandibular mobilization therapy to patients suffering from restricted mouth opening 
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION 
Restricted mouth opening, clinically referred to as trismus, is a debilitating condition 
associated with various maxillofacial disorders, post-surgical jaw stiffness, post
radiation fibrosis, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction, and particularly Oral 
Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF). Oral Submucous Fibrosis is a chronic, progressive, 
and potentially malignant disorder characterized by excessive deposition of collagen 
fibers and the formation of dense fibrotic bands within the oral mucosa and 
underlying connective tissues. As the disease progresses, patients experience a 
gradual loss of tissue elasticity, resulting in a severe reduction in the inter-incisal 
opening distance. This restriction leads to significant clinical complications, 
including impaired mastication, nutritional deficiencies, speech articulation 
difficulties, impaired swallowing, chronic pain, and a substantial reduction in the 
patient's overall quality of life. 
To counteract the progression of fibrosis and restore normal mandibular mobility, 
mechanical stretching of the oral mucosa and surrounding connective tissues is 
clinically necessary. However, existing treatment approaches and devices suffer 
from significant limitations that severely restrict their clinical efficacy, safety, and 
patient compliance. 
A widely utilized manual technique involves the "wooden spatula stacking method," 
where tongue depressors are sequentially forced between the patient's teeth to 
gradually pry the jaw open. This approach is highly subjective, utilizes completely 
uncontrolled stretching forces, and carries an exceptionally high risk of acute tissue 
trauma, mucosal tearing, dental injury, and damage to the TMJ structure. 
Furthermore, because the force application is unstandardized and entirely dependent 
2 
on manual manipulation, patient compliance is extremely poor due to severe pain 
and discomfort. 
5 
10 
15 
20 
25 
30 
Other existing solutions include static mechanical mouth openers or manual hand
operated passive stretching devices. While these devices provide a structured 
mechanical frame, they operate in an open-loop manner. They rely on patient
generated manual force or static screw expansion, completely lacking real-time 
force monitoring, feedback-based adjustment, or active safety intelligence. 
Consequently, there is an ongoing risk of over-stretching the jaw beyond safe 
physiological limits, which can cause micro-tears in the fibrotic bands, leading to 
subsequent inflammation, scarring, and a paradoxical worsening of the restricted 
opening. Additionally, manual devices provide no mechanism to personalize the 
therapy based on individual tissue characteristics or to record and analyze 
rehabilitation data, making it impossible for clinicians to objectively monitor patient 
progress and compliance. 
Surgical interventions, such as the surgical release of fibrotic bands, are often 
required in advanced cases. However, surgical procedures are highly invasive, 
expensive, and carry a substantial risk of post-operative complications. Most 
critically, without structured, highly controlled, and immediate post-operative 
rehabilitation, patients frequently experience a rapid recurrence of fibrosis and 
trismus, leading to a complete relapse and deterioration of surgical gains. 
Conventional physical therapy programs can assist in recovery, but they require 
frequent, costly hospital visits, depend heavily on the subjective expertise of the 
therapist, and lack the objective mechatronic feedback required to precisely quantify 
rehabilitation intensity. 
There is, therefore, an urgent and ongoing clinical need for a portable, motorized, 
and intelligent oral rehabilitation platform that can deliver safe, reproducible, and 
highly precise mandibular mobilization therapy. Specifically, there is a critical need 
for a closed-loop system that can continuously measure tissue resistance and applied 
forces during therapy, dynamically adapt movement parameters in real-time to 
match patient-specific tissue stiffness, prevent over-stretching injuries, and 
objectively log compliance and progress data for remote clinical monitoring.

Referring to Figure 5, the precision actuator assembly 108 is positioned within the 
upper portion of the housing shells 36, 37. The actuator assembly 108 is driven by a 
high-resolution micro-step stepper motor 13, which is secured to the internal chassis

When the stepper motor 13 receives electrical energy, it converts this energy into 
controlled rotational movement. This rotational motion is transmitted through the 
precision lead screw mechanism 9, which converts the rotation into highly accurate 
linear displacement of the lead screw nut 10. The motion transfer linkage 12 
transfers this linear displacement directly to the mandibular movement arm 7, 
thereby driving the lower mandibular pad 5 downward, away from the upper support 
pad 1, to gradually stretch the patient's oral tissues. Due to the high-resolution 
micro-stepping capability of the stepper motor 13 and the fine pitch of the lead 
screw mechanism 9, the device is configured to produce controlled movement 
increments as small as 0.01 mm to 0.05 mm. This sub-millimeter precision allows 
for extremely gradual, smooth stretching of fibrotic oral tissues, completely avoiding 
sudden jerks or uncontrolled impact forces that could cause pain or tissue trauma.

112 comprises a force sensor 3 positioned within a force sensor housing 4. The force

In Figure 2, the closed-loop feedback control architecture 42 and the operational 
method of the device are described. During a therapy session, the patient positions 
the upper support pad 1 and the lower mandibular pad 5 between the upper and 
lower teeth. Upon activation via the start/pause button 28, the adaptive therapy 
control unit 41 executes the selected treatment mode. The control unit 41 sends 
driving signals to the motor driver circuit 19, which drives the stepper motor 13 to 
gradually expand the lower support arm. 
As the lower mandibular pad 5 advances, the force sensor 3 continuously measures 
the tissue resistance encountered during jaw expansion, and the position sensor 16 
measures the actual displacement. These sensor signals are processed in real-time by 
the adaptive therapy control unit 41, which continuously compares the desired 
displacement versus actual displacement and the desired force versus measured 
force. Any deviation is automatically corrected through real-time motor control 
adjustments.

If the measured force approaches a predetermined safety threshold, or if a sudden 
resistance spike is detected, the safety monitoring module 43 automatically slows 
down the movement, pauses the therapy, reduces the displacement speed, or 
terminates the expansion cycle. This prevents excessive stretching forces, minimizes 
the risk of tissue tearing, and protects the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) structures. 
Furthermore, the device incorporates an intelligent adaptive rehabilitation algorithm. 
During each session, the system analyzes the force-displacement relationships 
generated by the patient's fibrotic tissue to create a customized resistance profile 
reflecting tissue stiffness. Based on this profile, the controller automatically adjusts 
the stretching amplitude, expansion speed, hold duration, relaxation intervals, 
number of therapy cycles, and progressive treatment intensity. Patients exhibiting 
high tissue resistance automatically receive gentler, slower expansion protocols, 
while patients demonstrating improved flexibility are progressively advanced to 
higher therapeutic ranges without requiring manual clinician calibration. 
Rather than maintaining a continuous, painful static force, the adaptive therapy 
control unit 41 is programmed to deliver a cyclic Micro-Pulsed Stretching (MPS) 
protocol. Each treatment cycle consists of four distinct, sequential phases: 
1. Phase 1 - Controlled Expansion: The stepper motor 13 is driven to gradually 
increase the distance between the pads 1, 5 at a controlled, incremental rate. 
2. Phase 2 - Short-Duration Tissue Hold: The motor is paused, holding the 
fibrotic tissue at the expanded position for a predefined, short hold duration. 
3. Phase 3 - Controlled Relaxation: The motor is driven in reverse to gradually 
reduce the stretching force and decrease the spacing between the pads. 
4. Phase 4 - Recovery Interval: The device maintains a relaxed, low-force state 
for a brief relaxation period before automatically repeating the cycle. 
This cyclic loading mechanism promotes gradual collagen fiber reorientation and 
fibrosis remodelling, significantly increasing tissue elasticity while reducing patient 
discomfort commonly associated with static stretching.

title: INTEGRATED RESPIRATORY HEALTH MONITORING SYSTEM
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
INTEGRATED RESPIRATORY HEALTH MONITORING SYSTEM 
5 
10 
The present invention relates to a integrated respiratory health monitoring system 
(100) to provide rapid and real-time assessment of respiratory health at the point of 
care. The system (100) comprises a housing (102), a biomarker detection module 
(114) comprising screen-printed electrodes (116) and a potentiostat circuit (118), a 
processing controller (128), a display interface (130), and a communication module 
(132). The integrated system (100) enables early detection and continuous 
monitoring of respiratory disorders in hospitals, clinics, workplaces, remote 
healthcare facilities, and home healthcare environments.
specification:
FIELD 
The present disclosure relates to an integrated respiratory health monitoring system. 
BACKGROUND 
5 
10 
15 
20 
25 
30 
Respiratory diseases including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(COPD), acute lung injury, occupational lung disorders, respiratory infections, and 
pollution-induced lung damage require early diagnosis and continuous monitoring 
for effective disease management. Existing respiratory diagnostic techniques 
generally depend upon separate laboratory-based biomarker analysis and 
standalone spirometry systems. Conventional CC16 biomarker detection is 
primarily performed using laboratory immunoassays such as ELISA, which require 
specialized laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, multiple processing steps, 
and considerable testing time. Similarly, conventional spirometry systems are 
bulky, expensive, require calibration, and are generally operated by trained 
technicians, thereby limiting their use in point-of-care and home healthcare 
applications. 
Furthermore, biochemical biomarker analysis and lung function assessment are 
performed using separate diagnostic systems, resulting in fragmented patient 
information, delayed clinical decision-making, and increased operational 
complexity. Accordingly, there exists a need for an integrated, portable, user
friendly, and cost-effective respiratory health monitoring system capable of 
simultaneously performing biomarker detection, lung function assessment, and 
breath-based analysis within a single platform to facilitate early diagnosis, 
continuous monitoring, and real-time respiratory health assessment. 
Existing respiratory diagnostic systems suffer from several technical limitations, 
including: CC16 biomarker analysis depends upon centralized laboratory-based 
ELISA testing, resulting in delayed diagnosis. Conventional spirometry devices are 
bulky, expensive, and require trained healthcare professionals for operation. 
Biomarker detection and lung function testing are performed using separate

devices, resulting in fragmented patient data. Existing respiratory diagnostic 
systems are not suitable for point-of-care, remote healthcare, or home-based 
monitoring. Conventional systems provide limited integration with digital health 
platforms for continuous patient monitoring. Existing diagnostic procedures 
increase testing time, operational complexity, and overall healthcare cost. 
Conventional systems provide limited support for real-time respiratory health 
assessment and trend analysis. 
SUMMARY 
The present disclosure provides an integrated respiratory health monitoring system. 
The integrated respiratory health monitoring system comprises a housing. The 
integrated respiratory health monitoring system further comprises a respiratory 
health monitoring assembly configured to perform respiratory analysis of a patient. 
The respiratory health monitoring assembly comprises a mouthpiece configured to 
receive exhaled breath from the patient, a particulate mesh filter configured to filter 
the exhaled breath, a nanofiber optic ring sensor configured to detect respiratory 
characteristics, and a spirometry airflow sensing module configured to measure 
pulmonary function parameters. The integrated respiratory health monitoring 
system further comprises a biomarker detection module configured to analyse blood 
or sputum samples of the patient, wherein the biomarker detection module 
comprises a screen-printed electrode assembly and a potentiostat circuit for 
detecting biomarker concentration. The integrated respiratory health monitoring 
system further comprises a signal conditioning circuit comprising a signal 
generator, a differential amplifier, and a current-to-voltage converter configured to 
generate conditioned electrical measurement signals. The integrated respiratory 
health 
monitoring system further comprises a processing controller 
communicatively coupled to the respiratory health monitoring assembly and the 
biomarker detection module for receiving respiratory data and biomarker detection 
data, processing and integrating the received data to generate comprehensive 
respiratory health information. The integrated respiratory health monitoring system 
further comprises a software interface configured to perform respiratory health

analysis, visualization, trend analysis, patient record management, and cloud 
synchronization. The integrated respiratory health monitoring system further 
comprises a display module configured to display respiratory health information, a 
communication module configured to transmit the respiratory health information to 
a remote device for remote monitoring and longitudinal patient analysis, and a 
power supply configured to provide electrical power to the integrated respiratory 
health monitoring system. The integrated respiratory health monitoring system 
enables simultaneous respiratory function assessment and biomarker detection 
within a single portable platform for rapid diagnosis and continuous respiratory

information, delayed clinical decision-making, and increased operational 
complexity. Accordingly, there exists a need for an integrated, portable, user
friendly, and cost-effective respiratory health monitoring system capable of 
simultaneously performing biomarker detection, lung function assessment, and 
breath-based analysis within a single platform to facilitate early diagnosis, 
continuous monitoring, and real-time respiratory health assessment. 
Existing respiratory diagnostic systems suffer from several technical limitations, 
including: CC16 biomarker analysis depends upon centralized laboratory-based 
ELISA testing, resulting in delayed diagnosis. Conventional spirometry devices are 
bulky, expensive, and require trained healthcare professionals for operation. 
Biomarker detection and lung function testing are performed using separate 
devices, resulting in fragmented patient data. Existing respiratory diagnostic 
systems are not suitable for point-of-care, remote healthcare, or home-based 
monitoring. Conventional systems provide limited integration with digital health 
platforms for continuous patient monitoring. Existing diagnostic procedures 
increase testing time, operational complexity, and overall healthcare cost. 
Conventional systems provide limited support for real-time respiratory health 
assessment and trend analysis. 
Referring to Fig. 1, there is illustrated a schematic block diagram of an integrated 
respiratory health monitoring system 100 in accordance with an exemplary 
embodiment of the present disclosure. The integrated respiratory health monitoring 
system 100 is constructed within a compact, portable, and ergonomically designed 
housing 102. The housing 102 is configured to enclose, protect, and mechanically 
support the physical, optical, chemical, and electronic sub-systems of the device, 
enabling point-of-care diagnostics in clinical, hospital, industrial, remote, and home 
healthcare environments. The housing 102 is preferably formed from a lightweight, 
durable, and medically graded material, such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, 
6 
polycarbonate, or carbon-fiber reinforced polymer composites, ensuring structural 
integrity and sanitization compatibility.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the integrated respiratory health monitoring system 100 
comprises a respiratory health monitoring assembly 104 configured for physical 
and functional respiratory analysis of a patient. The respiratory health monitoring 
assembly 104 includes a mouthpiece 106 configured to receive the exhaled breath 
directly from the patient. The mouthpiece 106 is physically coupled to the housing 
102 and can be configured as a detachable, disposable, or sterilizable component to 
maintain hygiene. In fluid communication with the mouthpiece 106, a particulate 
mesh filter 108 is disposed to intercept the exhalation flow. The particulate mesh 
filter 108 is configured to remove salivary droplets, particulate contaminants, and 
other physical debris from the exhaled breath to prevent fouling of downstream 
sensing elements. The particulate mesh filter 108 may be formed from a 
hydrophobic polymer mesh, an electrostatic fiber mesh, or a porous membrane 
having a predetermined pore size, such as between 0.2 microns and 10 microns, to 
optimize particulate capture without creating excessive flow resistance. 
Downstream of the particulate mesh filter 108, a nanofiber optic ring sensor 110 is 
operatively positioned in the exhalation flow channel. The nanofiber optic ring 
sensor 110 is configured to detect and measure physical and chemical 
characteristics of the exhaled breath, such as moisture concentration, temperature, 
or specific gaseous constituents, by monitoring changes in optical properties. The 
nanofiber optic ring sensor 110 may employ silica-based optical fibers or 
polymethyl methacrylate plastic optical fibers functionalized with a sensitive 
polymer cladding, such as polyvinyl alcohol or polyaniline, which exhibits changes 
in refractive index, light attenuation, or spectrophotometric absorption upon contact 
with exhalation components. 
A spirometry airflow sensing module 112 is operatively connected downstream of 
the nanofiber optic ring sensor 110. The spirometry airflow sensing module 112 is

quantitative pulmonary function parameters. These parameters include, but are not 
limited to, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity 
(FVC), peak expiratory flow, and associated respiratory performance indicators or 
performance curves. The spirometry airflow sensing module 112 may utilize a 
differential pressure sensing configuration, a hot-wire anemometer configuration, 
or an ultrasonic transit-time flow sensor configuration to translate physical 
exhalation velocity into high-resolution electrical signals. 
Referring further to Fig. 1, the integrated respiratory health monitoring system 100 
comprises a biomarker detection module 114 designed for biochemical analysis of 
biological fluids of the patient, such as blood, serum, urine, or sputum. The 
biomarker detection module 114 is preferably configured as a Clara Cell Protein 16 
(CC16) biomarker detection module, which provides early detection of lung 
epithelial injury. The biomarker detection module 114 comprises a screen-printed 
electrode assembly 116 and a potentiostat circuit 118. The screen-printed electrode 
assembly 116 is configured to receive a liquid biological sample (such as a blood 
or sputum sample) and provide a highly sensitive electrochemical interface. The 
screen-printed electrode assembly 116 is preferably configured as a disposable, 
single-use test strip that slots into a receiving port defined in the housing 102. 
The screen-printed electrode assembly 116 is fabricated using a series of specialized 
functional inks deposited on an insulating substrate, such as polyester, polyethylene 
terephthalate, polyimide, or paper. The assembly includes a working electrode, a 
counter electrode, and a reference electrode positioned in a coplanar arrangement. 
Conductive tracks and contacts are formed by printing a silver or carbon ink onto 
the substrate, while active electrode areas are defined by printing a dielectric 
insulating ink over the conductive tracks.

To achieve high sensitivity and specificity for target respiratory biomarkers such as 
CC16, the surface of the working electrode of the screen-printed electrode assembly 
116 is modified with a multi-layer biochemical architecture: 
Conductive Polymer Base Layer: Directly coated on the carbon surface of the 
working electrode. This layer acts as the primary conductive path for electron 
transfer between the electrode and the biological sensing elements. Suitable 
conductive polymers include poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene 
sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS), polyaniline, polypyrrole, or polythiophene. 
Nanoparticle Enhancement Layer: Applied over the conductive polymer base layer. 
The nanoparticle enhancement layer comprises gold nanoparticles, silver 
nanoparticles, platinum nanoparticles, magnetic nanoparticles, multi-walled carbon 
nanotubes, single-walled carbon nanotubes, graphene, or graphene oxide. This layer 
significantly increases the electroactive surface area of the working electrode, 
enhances electron transfer rates, and provides a dense array of anchoring sites for 
biomolecules. 
Enzyme-Linked Aptamer Layer: Immobilized on top of the nanoparticle 
enhancement layer. The enzyme-linked aptamer layer comprises aptamers or 
antibodies specific to the target biomarker (such as CC16 or cardiac biomarkers 
such as IGFBP-3). These aptamers or antibodies are conjugated with reporting 
enzymes such as Horseradish Peroxidase (HRP) or Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP). 
This configuration ensures that when the target analyte binds to the immobilized 
aptamer, an enzymatic reaction occurs in the presence of a substrate, producing 
electroactive species detectable at the working electrode. 
Cross-linking Layer: Distributed throughout the biomolecule-containing layers. 
The cross-linking layer stabilizes the enzyme-aptamer complexes on the sensor 
surface, preventing them from degrading or detaching during sample introduction 
and washing. 
Protective Outer Layer: Coated over all the active layers of the working electrode. 
The protective outer layer comprises Nafion or cellulose acetate. This layer acts as 
a selective charge and size barrier, allowing only the target analyte and essential 
9 
redox species to reach the reactive sites while blocking common interfering 
substances and preventing surface fouling by proteins or cells.

such as Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) or Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) are further 
incorporated into the surface chemistry to block any remaining non-specific binding 
sites on the electrode surface. 
The potentiostat circuit 118 is operatively coupled to the screen-printed electrode 
assembly 116 to control the applied electrical potential and measure the resulting 
current generated by specific biochemical binding and redox events. The 
potentiostat circuit 118 is configured to perform spectrophotometric detection, 
amperometric detection, cyclic voltammetry, or a combination thereof for 
determining CC16 biomarker concentration. 
To condition and process the signals, the system 100 includes a signal conditioning 
circuit 120. The signal conditioning circuit 120 comprises a signal generator 122, a 
differential amplifier 124, and a current-to-voltage converter 126. The signal 
generator 122 is configured to generate precise excitation waveforms, such as 
potential steps, linear sweeps, or pulse trains, required for electrochemical analysis. 
The differential amplifier 124 is configured to measure and maintain the potential 
difference between the reference electrode and the working electrode of the screen
printed electrode assembly 116. The current-to-voltage converter 126 is operatively 
connected to the working electrode of the screen-printed electrode assembly 116 
and is configured to translate the low-level, analog current signals from the 
electrochemical reactions into proportional voltage signals. This translation is 
scaled by a resistance multiplier. These voltage signals are subsequently amplified, 
filtered, and stabilized by the signal conditioning circuit 120 before processing by 
the processing controller 128.
