microprocessor or microcontroller running embedded algorithms configured to 
process, align, and integrate the physical lung function data with the molecular 
biomarker data. This integration generates a comprehensive, multi-modal 
respiratory health profile for the patient. 
The processing controller 128 is configured to continuously monitor respiratory 
parameters, compare current respiratory health data with previously stored patient 
data, generate longitudinal health trends, and provide diagnostic support for early 
detection and monitoring of respiratory disorders. This allows the system 100 to 
track the progression of chronic conditions, such as asthma, chronic obstructive 
pulmonary disease (COPD), or occupational lung diseases, and flag acute 
exacerbations before severe clinical symptoms manifest. 
The processing controller 128 is further communicatively coupled to a display 
module 130 and a communication module 132. The display module 130 is 
integrated into the housing 102 to display real-time measurements, diagnostic 
results, historical trends, and user instructions. The display module 130 may be 
configured as an LCD, OLED, or e-paper display with touchscreen capabilities. The 
communication module 132 comprises wired or wireless interfaces, such as 
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Wi-Fi, Zigbee, LoRa, cellular (5G/LTE), or USB, 
configured to transmit the integrated respiratory health information to a remote

management module, is electrically coupled to all active components to provide

The operational mechanism of the integrated respiratory health monitoring system 
100 involves both physical exhalation testing and biochemical liquid sample 
testing. When a patient performs a lung function test, they blow forcefully into the 
mouthpiece 106. The exhaled breath passes through the particulate mesh filter 108, 
which stops large saliva droplets and particulate matter. The filtered breath then 
reaches the nanofiber optic ring sensor 110 and the spirometry airflow sensing 
module 112. The nanofiber optic ring sensor 110 measures gas-phase 
characteristics, while the spirometry airflow sensing module 112 measures FEV1 
and FVC parameters. Concurrently, the exhalation characteristics are logged by the 
processing controller 128. 
For biochemical testing, a liquid sample such as blood, serum, urine, or sputum is 
mixed with pre-measured reagents and applied to the screen-printed electrode 
assembly 116. The screen-printed electrode assembly 116 is inserted into the 
biomarker detection module 114 slot. When the target biomarker (such as CC16) 
binds to the functionalized working electrode, the potentiostat circuit 118 applies a 
constant potential or a voltammetric sweep. The resulting current, which is 
proportional to the concentration of the biomarker in the sample, is measured over 
time (chronoamperometry) or over a swept potential range (cyclic voltammetry). 
The processing controller 128 receives the physical spirometry data and the 
electrochemical biomarker data. By executing integrated clinical decision-making 
algorithms, the processing controller 128 combines the physical exhalation metrics 
(airflow volume and rate) with the biochemical epithelial injury metrics (CC16 
concentration) to generate a holistic, real-time assessment of the patient's 
respiratory health. This integrated result is displayed on the display module 130 and 
transmitted via the communication module 132 to remote healthcare systems to 
support early intervention and personalized disease management.

title: MULTIMODAL NEUROPHYSIOLOGICAL AND BIOCHEMICAL MONITORING SYSTEM
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
MULTIMODAL NEUROPHYSIOLOGICAL AND BIOCHEMICAL 
MONITORING SYSTEM 
5 
10 
15 
A multimodal neurophysiological and biochemical monitoring system illustrated in 
Fig. 2, comprises synchronized electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography 
(ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrochemical neuro-biomarker sensor 
modules. The electrochemical module utilizes a surface-engineered, disposable 
screen-printed electrode strip to detect cellular-level injury, metabolic stress, and 
inflammatory biomarkers. A communicably coupled multimodal data fusion and 
artificial intelligence engine processes these heterogeneous data streams in real time. 
By analyzing temporal relationships and cross-system correlations, the system 
computes predictive neurological risk indices to forecast early neurological 
deterioration, enabling proactive clinical intervention at the point of care.

FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to medical monitoring systems, and more 
particularly to a portable multimodal monitoring system that integrates 
neurophysiological, cardiovascular, hemodynamic, and electrochemical biosensing 
technologies to provide real-time, predictive assessment of neurological status. 
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION 
Early detection and continuous monitoring of neurological dysfunction, traumatic 
brain injury, cerebral hypoxia, stroke progression, and other neurophysiological 
disorders represent critical challenges in modern clinical, emergency, and point-of
care medicine. The human brain is highly dependent on a continuous supply of 
oxygen and nutrients, wherein even brief periods of impaired perfusion or 
oxygenation can initiate a cascade of cellular dysfunction leading to permanent, 
irreversible neuronal damage. Because physiological and biochemical changes at the 
cellular level often precede the manifestation of overt clinical symptoms, a critical 
diagnostic gap exists between the onset of neurological injury and its clinical 
recognition. 
Existing patient monitoring systems deployed in emergency, intensive care, and 
ambulatory settings primarily focus on systemic physiological parameters, such as 
heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and peripheral oxygen saturation. While 
these parameters provide valuable information regarding a patient's general 
hemodynamic status, they offer limited direct insight into the functional and 
metabolic state of the brain. Consequently, a patient may appear clinically stable 
according to conventional vital signs while experiencing progressive, localized 
neurological deterioration at the cellular and functional levels. 
To assess brain health directly, clinical practice typically relies on neuroimaging 
modalities such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI), or electrophysiological assessments such as standard electroencephalography 
(EEG). Although CT and MRI provide high-resolution structural information, they 
are inherently episodic, expensive, require significant infrastructure, and cannot 
provide continuous, real-time functional monitoring at the bedside or during patient 
2 
transport. Traditional EEG systems provide functional cortical data but are generally 
bulky, costly, highly dependent on specialized personnel for electrode placement 
and signal interpretation, and typically restricted to controlled clinical laboratories or 
intensive care units. 
5

30 
Furthermore, existing physiological and biochemical monitoring technologies 
operate in isolation. For example, electrocardiography (ECG) is utilized 
independently to assess cardiac autonomic regulation, photoplethysmography (PPG) 
is used to evaluate peripheral oxygenation, and EEG is used to measure cortical 
electrical activity. Despite the strong biological interdependence between cortical 
function, autonomic regulation, cardiovascular dynamics, and systemic oxygen 
transport, conventional clinical workflows fail to integrate these distinct 
physiological domains into a unified analytical framework. This fragmented 
approach prevents the identification of early, subtle patterns of multi-system 
deterioration. Additionally, conventional biochemical assessments of neurological 
injury rely on centralized laboratory testing of blood samples, which introduces 
significant delays and prevents the real-time correlation of molecular-level 
pathology with electrophysiological changes. 
Accordingly, there exists an ongoing and unmet need for a portable, integrated, and 
continuous 
monitoring 
platform 
capable 
of 
simultaneously 
acquiring 
electrophysiological, cardiovascular, hemodynamic, and neurochemical data at the 
point of care. There is a further need for a system that can dynamically correlate 
these multi-domain signals in real time to generate predictive indicators of 
neurological risk, thereby enabling clinicians to transition from reactive treatment to 
proactive, early-stage intervention before irreversible brain injury occurs. 
OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION 
In one object, the invention provides a portable, integrated multimodal monitoring 
system configured to simultaneously and continuously acquire electrophysiological, 
cardiovascular, hemodynamic, and neurochemical data within a unified platform to 
provide a comprehensive, real-time assessment of brain health.

In another object, the invention provides a point-of-care electrochemical biosensing 
subsystem utilizing disposable surface-engineered screen-printed electrodes 
functionalized with specific biological recognition elements, enabling the rapid and 
highly sensitive detection of molecular biomarkers associated with neuronal injury, 
neurodegeneration, metabolic stress, neuroinflammation, and cerebral hypoxia. 
In another object, the invention provides an artificial intelligence-driven multimodal 
data fusion engine configured to execute advanced machine learning, deep learning, 
and time-series algorithms to analyze temporal relationships and identify hidden 
correlations among heterogeneous physiological and biochemical parameters. 
In another object, the invention provides composite predictive neurological risk 
metrics, including an Early Neuro Risk Index (ENRI), a Neuro-Metabolic Stress 
Index (NMSI), and a Brain-Heart-Oxygen Coupling Index (BHOCI), designed to 
quantify the probability of impending neurological deterioration and cellular 
compromise before the onset of irreversible structural damage or overt clinical 
symptoms. 
In another object, the invention provides a portable, wearable, and modular device 
architecture configured for seamless deployment across ambulances, emergency 
departments, intensive care units, remote healthcare facilities, military 
environments, and home-based settings, thereby extending advanced neurological 
monitoring beyond specialized hospital infrastructure. 
In another object, the invention provides an automated clinical decision support 
system configured to generate real-time alerts and predictive trend visualizations, 
reducing cognitive burden on healthcare professionals and minimizing clinical 
dependence on subjective, intermittent manual neurological assessments.

The present invention addresses the critical limitations of conventional, fragmented 
patient monitoring systems by providing a synchronized, multimodal physiological 
and biochemical monitoring platform . The system is designed to provide 
continuous, real-time, and predictive assessments of brain health at the point of care,

irreversible structural damage occurs .

Referring to Fig. 1, an embodiment of a multimodal neurophysiological and 
biochemical monitoring system 100 comprises an electroencephalography (EEG) 
sensor module 102, an electrocardiography (ECG) sensor module 104, a 
photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor module 106, an electrochemical neuro
biomarker assessment module 108, and a multimodal data fusion and artificial 
intelligence engine 110. The system 100 is configured as a synchronized, portable, 
point-of-care platform that integrates electrophysiological, cardiovascular, 
oxygenation, and biochemical measurements to continuously assess brain health and 
predict early neurological deterioration in real time. 
The EEG sensor module 102 is configured to receive EEG signals from a patient, 
reflecting cortical electrical activity. The ECG sensor module 104 is configured to 
receive ECG signals from the patient, providing insights into cardiac activity and 
autonomic nervous system regulation. The PPG sensor module 106 is configured to 
measure peripheral oxygenation and vascular dynamics of the patient. The 
8

A shielded EEG cable exits the EEG headband assembly 3 and connects directly to

Referring to Fig. 3, the detailed structural, material, and operational parameters of 
the electrochemical neuro-biomarker assessment module 108 and the disposable 
SPE cartridge are illustrated. Panel A of Fig. 3 shows a cross-section of the screen
printed electrode, illustrating a multi-layer microfabricated architecture. The SPE 
cartridge is built upon a substrate layer 5, which is formed from a flexible, 
electrically insulating material such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET), ceramic, or 
polyimide, having a typical thickness of 100 to 250 micrometers. 
A conductive electrode layer 3 is deposited onto the substrate layer 5 using screen
printing technology. The conductive electrode layer 3 is printed using high
conductivity metallic or carbonaceous inks, such as screen-printed carbon, gold, or 
platinum ink, to form a working electrode WE, a reference electrode RE, a counter

A dielectric insulation layer 4, formed from a UV-curable dielectric ink, is deposited 
over the conductive electrode layer 3. The dielectric insulation layer 4 is patterned to 
expose the active sensing area at the distal end of the strip and the contact pads at 
the proximal end, while insulating the intermediate conductive traces. The typical 
thickness of the dielectric insulation layer 4 is 10 to 50 micrometers. 
To enhance the electrochemical properties, sensitivity, and biomolecule 
immobilization efficiency, a nanomaterial layer 2 is deposited onto the active 
surface of the working electrode WE. The nanomaterial layer 2 comprises 
nanostructured conductive materials, including graphene sheets, reduced graphene 
oxide, carbon nanotubes, MXene nanomaterials, gold nanoparticles, platinum

to 2 micrometers.

A biorecognition layer 1 is immobilized onto the nanomaterial layer 2 of the 
working electrode WE. The biorecognition layer 1 comprises specific biological 
recognition elements configured to selectively bind to target neurochemical and 
metabolic biomarkers. These recognition elements include monoclonal antibodies, 
polyclonal antibodies, aptamers, molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs), enzymes, 
peptide receptors, nucleic acid probes, or affinity ligands. The typical thickness of 
the biorecognition layer 1 is 1 to 5 micrometers. 
Panel B and Panel C of Fig. 3 show the top view and perspective view of the SPE 
cartridge layout, respectively. The cartridge has a preferred length of 35 millimeters, 
a width of 12.5 millimeters, and a total thickness of approximately 0.6 millimeters. 
The distal end of the cartridge defines a sample application zone where a biological 
sample, such as blood, plasma, serum, saliva, sweat, tears, interstitial fluid, or 
cerebrospinal fluid, is introduced. 
Panel E of Fig. 3 illustrates the electrochemical cell configuration. When a 
biological sample containing target biomarkers is applied to the sample application 
zone, the electrolyte/sample forms a conductive path bridging the working electrode 
WE, reference electrode RE, and counter electrode CE. The target biomarkers 
selectively bind to the immobilized recognition elements in the biorecognition layer 
1. This highly specific binding event alters the physical and chemical properties at 
the 
electrode-electrolyte interface, causing measurable changes in charge 
distribution, surface capacitance, charge transfer resistance, electron transfer 
kinetics, and interfacial impedance. 
Panel F and Panel G of Fig. 3 illustrate the integration of the SPE cartridge with the 
internal reader of the central console. The central console includes a reader slot with 
spring-loaded pogo-pin contacts configured to align with and press against the 
contact pads of the contact pad layer 6 when the cartridge is inserted. The internal 
cross-section of the device reader reveals a compact electronic assembly mounted on 
a 
printed circuit board, comprising an analog front end, a potentiostat IC 
(electrochemical measurement IC), an MCU/DSP processor, memory, a 
12

The internal potentiostat subsystem is configured to perform highly sensitive 
electrochemical measurements using techniques including cyclic voltammetry (CV), 
differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square wave voltammetry (SWV), and 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). CV is utilized to evaluate redox 
activity by sweeping the applied electrical potential between predetermined limits. 
DPV applies a sequence of voltage pulses superimposed on a slowly changing 
potential to provide highly sensitive quantification of trace concentrations of 
biomarkers. SWV applies alternating square-wave potentials to enable rapid, low
noise measurements. EIS applies small alternating current perturbations across a 
range of frequencies to measure impedance changes associated with label-free 
biomolecular binding events. The measured electrochemical signals are translated 
into quantitative biomarker concentrations. 
The electrochemical neuro-biomarker assessment module 108 is configured to 
simultaneously or sequentially detect a variety of biomarkers, including: 
1. Neuronal Injury Biomarkers: Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP), 
Ubiquitin Carboxyl-Terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1), S100B Protein, and 
Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE). 
2. Neurodegeneration Biomarkers: Neurofilament Light Chain (NfL), Tau 
Protein, and Amyloid Beta. 
3. Metabolic Biomarkers: Lactate, Glucose, and Pyruvate. 
4. Inflammatory Biomarkers: Interleukin-6 (IL-6), Tumor Necrosis Factor 
Alpha (TNF-alpha), and C-Reactive Protein (CRP). 
5. Oxidative Stress Biomarkers: Nitric Oxide Metabolites, Reactive Oxygen 
Species Indicators, and Lipid Peroxidation Products. 
In operational use, the system 100 achieves synchronized signal acquisition across 
all four domains. The EEG sensor module 102 continuously acquires cortical 
electrical signals. The EEG processing engine executes signal amplification, motion

artifact removal, power line interference suppression, baseline drift correction, and 
adaptive noise filtering. It then performs spectral decomposition to determine delta 
band power (0.5 to 4 Hz), theta band power (4 to 8 Hz), alpha band power (8 to 13 
Hz), beta band power (13 to 30 Hz), gamma band power (greater than 30 Hz), 
alpha/theta ratio, spectral entropy, brain symmetry index, cortical slowing metrics, 
functional connectivity metrics, and neurological stress indicators. 
Simultaneously, the ECG sensor module 104 continuously acquires cardiac 
electrical signals. The ECG processing engine identifies the P-wave, QRS complex, 
T-wave, and R-peak positions. It utilizes R-peak detection algorithms to compute R
R intervals and performs Heart Rate Variability (HRV) analysis, extracting time
domain features (such as SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50), frequency-domain features 
(such as LF Power, HF Power, LF/HF Ratio), and non-linear features (such as 
Poincaré plot parameters, approximate entropy, and sample entropy). 
Concurrently, the PPG sensor module 106 continuously acquires optical 
plethysmographic signals. The PPG processing engine derives oxygen saturation 
(SpO2), pulse rate, pulse transit characteristics, perfusion index (PI), pulse wave 
morphology, vascular compliance metrics, and peripheral circulation indicators. 
Advanced waveform analysis is executed to assess arterial stiffness, microvascular 
perfusion, peripheral vasoconstriction, and hemodynamic instability. 
The biochemical data obtained from the electrochemical neuro-biomarker 
assessment module 108 is synchronized with the EEG-derived cortical activity, the 
ECG-derived autonomic regulation metrics, and the PPG-derived oxygenation and 
perfusion metrics. The synchronized data streams are transmitted to the multimodal 
data fusion and artificial intelligence engine 110. 
The multimodal data fusion and artificial intelligence engine 110 employs advanced 
machine learning, deep learning, time-series analysis, neural networks, long short
term memory (LSTM) models, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and 
14 
transformer-based models to analyze temporal relationships and identify hidden 
correlations among the physiological and biochemical parameters.

Based on this integrated, multi-layered analysis, the engine 110 generates 
proprietary, predictive neurological risk indices, including: 
1. Early Neuro Risk Index (ENRI): This index quantifies the probability of 
impending neurological deterioration before clinically observable symptoms 
or structural damage occur, derived from the synchronized analysis of EEG 
parameters, HRV metrics, oxygenation parameters, perfusion indicators, and 
neurochemical/metabolic biomarkers. 
2. Neuro-Metabolic Stress Index (NMSI): This index combines EEG 
abnormalities, oxygenation deficits, and HRV alterations with real-time 
lactate, glucose, and molecular injury marker concentrations to estimate the 
acute metabolic stress burden and cellular compromise of the brain. 
3. Brain-Heart-Oxygen Coupling Index (BHOCI): This index quantifies the 
dynamic functional interactions among cortical activity (EEG), autonomic 
regulation (ECG/HRV), and systemic oxygen delivery mechanisms (PPG). 
Variations in this coupling relationship provide early warning of hypoxic 
stress, cerebral ischemia, neurological injury, autonomic dysfunction, or 
metabolic compromise. 
The computed indices, raw waveforms, and biomarker results are visualized on the 
touchscreen display of the console. The console is further configured to generate 
local acoustic and visual alerts, or transmit alert signals to remote clinical 
dashboards and mobile applications via the integrated wireless communication 
module when any of the predictive indices exceed a predefined risk threshold, 
enabling proactive clinical intervention.

title: COMPUTER-IMPLEMENTED SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR PROVIDING REAL-TIME BIDIRECTIONAL SPEECH INTERPRETATION OVER A PUBLIC TELEPHONE NETWORK
abstract:
COMPUTER-IMPLEMENTED SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR PROVIDING REAL-TIME BIDIRECTIONAL SPEECH INTERPRETATION OVER A PUBLIC TELEPHONE NETWORK
ABSTRACT
 A computer-implemented system and method (1300) for providing real-time bidirectional speech interpretation over public telephone network, are disclosed. A virtual number registry (102) comprising relational database that maintains virtual telephone number profile records. A session manager (106) creates real-time communication session possessing a structured session identifier encoding the virtual telephone number and originating telephone number of caller, and automatically dispatch a speech interpretation agent (108) to the real-time communication session. A carrier trunk selector initiates an outbound call to forwarding telephone number of recipient by selecting between domestic carrier trunk connection and international carrier trunk connection based on whether the forwarding telephone number comprises an international dialing prefix. A speech synthesis engine synthesizes interpreted speech audio with synthesis voice dynamically selected per interpreted segment based on detected output language code rather than a statically-configured language. A sequential audio scheduler (114) delivers interpreted speech audio to respective participant.
FIG. 1
specification:
FIELD OF INVENTION
[0001]Embodiments of the present disclosure relate to real-time speech interpretation systems integrated with public switched telephone networks and voice-over-IP infrastructure, and more particularly to a computer-implemented method for providing real-time bidirectional speech interpretation over a public telephone network using a virtual telephone number interpretation gateway.
BACKGROUND
[0002]Global commerce, immigration, international customer service, and cross-border professional collaboration create urgent demand for real-time spoken language interpretation during telephone calls. While computational translation has advanced substantially for asynchronous text communication, real-time voice interpretation during telephone calls presents technically distinct and largely unsolved challenges: transcription and translation must complete within a latency budget compatible with natural conversational flow; audio quality over telephone networks is significantly lower than studio conditions due to codec compression artifacts, channel noise, and bandwidth limitations; callers frequently switch languages mid-sentence, especially in multilingual communities; telephone infrastructure provides no application programming interface for injecting processed audio into the call path without specialized gateway equipment; and both call participants have a legitimate expectation that the call functions without installing any software.
[0003]Prior art telephony translation systems employ sequential processing pipelines wherein a speech recognition module converts audio to text, a separate translation module converts the text to a target language, and a separate speech synthesis module converts the translated text to audio. This architecture introduces cumulative inter-stage latency because each module must complete and transfer its output before the next stage begins. Independent network calls for recognition and translation services are additive in latency. Translation context cannot flow naturally between stages because they are separate systems with separate state. Error propagation means that recognition errors compound into translation errors. 
[0004]Prior art telephony translation systems operate at the application layer of proprietary software platforms and require all or at least one of the call participants to install and operate software clients. This architecture excludes standard landline telephone users, basic mobile phone users without smartphone capability, payphone users, office PBX fixed-line extension users, users in low-connectivity regions, and any environment where application installation is prohibited or impractical. Prior art interpretation systems require per-call manual configuration of language parameters by one or both participants, either through an application interface before the call or through interactive menus during the call. This requirement is incompatible with calls from standard telephone instruments where no application interface is available. 
[0005]For landline businesses, call centers, and PSTN-based infrastructure, integrating real-time interpretation is particularly difficult because: traditional landlines and PBX systems have no middleware interception point for speech processing; the caller's language is unknown at call setup time; standard telephone infrastructure provides no interface for injecting processed audio streams mid-call; and the recipient cannot install specialized software on fixed-line equipment. Users who need to initiate translated outbound calls but lack smartphones, internet connectivity, or the ability to install applications - including field workers, elderly users, users in low-connectivity regions, and users of landline-only office systems - have no existing solution enabling them to make outbound translated telephone calls from a standard telephone instrument.
[0006]In telephony speech interpretation systems serving multilingual communities, a specific technical problem arises when acoustically similar languages are included together in the language detection candidate set. When a speech recognition system attempts to identify which language a speaker is using, acoustic near-identity between certain language pairs causes systematic misidentification. A misidentified language code causes the speech synthesis system to attempt rendering text in a language for which the selected voice is not trained, resulting in silent or unintelligible audio output for the interpretation channel. No prior art discloses a language hint exclusion policy specifically designed to prevent such systematic acoustic misidentification and the consequent speech synthesis silence failure.
[0007]Hence, there is a need for a computer-implemented system and method for providing real-time bidirectional speech interpretation over a public telephone network using a virtual telephone number interpretation gateway, in order to address the aforementioned issues.
SUMMARY
[0008]This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts, in a simple manner, which is further described in the detailed description of the disclosure. This summary is neither intended to identify key or essential inventive concepts of the subject matter nor to determine the scope of the disclosure
[0009]In accordance with one embodiment of the disclosure, a computer-implemented method for providing real-time bidirectional speech interpretation over a public telephone network using a virtual telephone number interpretation gateway, is disclosed. The computer-implemented method comprises maintaining, in a virtual number registry comprising a relational database, a plurality of virtual telephone number profile records. Each virtual telephone number profile record comprises a virtual telephone number field; a recipient forwarding number field; a first language configuration for an owner; a second language configuration for a caller; a pre-call announcement text field; a keypad-tone automation configuration field; a caller identity display configuration field; a credit authorization state field; and an outbound dial-in authorization configuration comprising an authorized originating telephone number list and an enable flag. 
[0010]The computer-implemented method further comprises receiving, through a carrier trunk interface comprising at least a domestic carrier trunk connection and an international carrier trunk connection, an inbound call directed to one of the virtual telephone numbers from a standard telephone instrument of a caller. The carrier trunk interface is configured to receive inbound calls and initiate outbound calls over telephony networks. The computer-implemented method further comprises creating, by a session manager, a real-time communication session possessing a structured session identifier encoding the virtual telephone number and an originating telephone number of the caller in a deterministic parseable format, and automatically dispatching a speech interpretation agent to the real-time communication session. The computer-implemented method further comprises extracting, by the speech interpretation agent using a session identifier parser, the virtual telephone number and the originating telephone number of the caller from the structured session identifier by splitting on a predefined delimiter.
[0011]The computer-implemented method further comprises retrieving, through a backend authorization client, a virtual telephone number profile associated with the extracted virtual telephone number. The computer-implemented method further comprises synthesizing, by a pre-call announcement engine, an announcement text in a language of the caller using a speech synthesis engine with dynamic voice selection, publishing a dedicated audio channel in the real-time communication session, playing a plurality of synthesized frames, and validating caller connection after playback. The computer-implemented method further comprises initiating an outbound call to a forwarding telephone number of a recipient, comprising: selecting, by a carrier trunk selector, between the domestic carrier trunk connection and the international carrier trunk connection based on whether the forwarding telephone number comprises an international dialing prefix. The computer-implemented method further comprises establishing, by a configurable speech processing pipeline, real-time bidirectional speech interpretation between the caller and the recipient. The computer-implemented method further comprises initializing a first speech interpretation stream for an audio of the caller, configured with translation targeting a first language code of the recipient, with automatic language identification adapted for a speech recognition component to continuously and autonomously identify an actual language spoken by the caller in real time without any declaration and selection from the caller.
[0012]The computer-implemented method further comprises initializing a second speech interpretation stream for an audio of the recipient, configured with translation targeting a second language code of the caller. The computer-implemented method further comprises routing, by a language detection monitor, an original-language output from the speech processing pipeline, detecting changes in a spoken language of the caller during an active call, comparing a detected language against a current translation target, and triggering transparent stream restarts when a mismatch is detected. The computer-implemented method further comprises synthesizing interpreted speech audio with a synthesis voice dynamically selected per interpreted segment based on a detected output language code rather than a statically-configured language. The computer-implemented method further comprises delivering interpreted speech audio to each respective participant through a sequential audio scheduler comprising a bounded input queue configured to receive interpreted output units that comprise at least one of: interpreted text units for speech synthesis and interpreted audio segments for sequential playback, parallel worker tasks each assigned a unique sequence identifier and configured to generate and process corresponding audio segments from the interpreted output units, an ordered audio segment queue, and a single sequential audio player that plays a plurality of audio frames of each audio segment before advancing to a next audio segment, thereby preventing concurrent interpreted audio segments from being played simultaneously.
[0013]The computer-implemented method further comprises archiving, by an interpretation record archival engine, structured records of interpreted speech pairs during a call to cloud object storage with local filesystem fallback upon call termination. The computer-implemented method further comprises executing, by a transcript indexing engine, background jobs that retrieve archived interpretation records, generate vector embeddings of the record content, index the vector embeddings with session metadata and organizational identifiers into a vector search engine, and adapt semantic similarity search and retrieval-augmented generation query answering with access gated by organizational membership.
[0014]In an embodiment, the computer-implemented method further comprises adapting a registered virtual number of an owner to initiate a real-time interpreted outbound telephone call from a standard telephone instrument without requiring internet access, communication device capability, and application software installation on an initiating device, by: (a) maintaining, in a database, a virtual telephone number profile associating a virtual telephone number with at least: a list of authorized originating telephone numbers identifying telephone instruments of a registered owner, an owner language code, and a default target language code; (b) receiving, through a carrier trunk interface, an inbound call to the virtual telephone number from a telephone; (c) determining that an originating telephone number of the inbound call is present in the list of authorized originating telephone numbers, for classifying a session as an owner-initiated outbound dial-in session; (d) playing an interactive voice response (IVR) prompt to the registered owner in the owner language code, synthesized using neural speech synthesis with a voice selected based on the owner language code, instructing the registered owner to enter a destination telephone number using a standard telephone keypad; (e) collecting a sequence of at least one of: dual-tone multi-frequency digit signals and digit signals through speech input, from a telephone audio channel of the registered owner, buffering received digits in reception order, terminating collection upon receipt of a designated terminator character, and upon expiry of a configurable maximum waiting period, forming a destination telephone number string; (f) upon timeout and invalid destination telephone number string, playing an error prompt in the owner language code and offering at least one retry attempt before terminating the session; (g) playing a confirmation prompt to the registered owner in the owner language code indicating the collected destination telephone number string; (h) initiating an outbound call to the collected destination telephone number string, comprising: selecting between a domestic carrier trunk and an international carrier trunk based on a format of the collected destination telephone number string; (i) establishing real-time bidirectional speech interpretation between a telephone of the registered owner and a destination telephone, comprising: initializing a first speech interpretation stream for an audio of the registered owner with translation targeting a language of a destination party, with automatic language identification adapted to detect an actual spoken language of the destination party without requiring either party to declare the actual spoken language; initializing a second speech interpretation stream for an audio of the destination party with translation targeting the owner language code; routing an interpreted output to neural speech synthesis with voice dynamically selected per interpreted segment based on an automatically detected output language code; delivering synthesized interpreted audio to each respective party through the sequential audio scheduler that prevents concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously; and upon call termination, archiving an interpretation record.
[0015]In another embodiment, For establishing the real-time bidirectional speech interpretation between the caller and the recipient, the configurable speech processing pipeline is configured to implement at least one of: comprises: (a) a unified single-session speech recognition and translation pipeline that produces original-language transcription and target-language translation within a same processing session without discrete inter-stage transfers; (b) an automatic speech recognition module coupled with a large language model translation module and a speech synthesis module; (c) the automatic speech recognition module coupled with a neural machine translation module and the speech synthesis module; and (d) a direct speech-to-speech neural translation module.
[0016]In yet another embodiment, the configurable speech processing pipeline is implemented as a unified single-session pipeline in which a single continuous processing session receives audio input frames and produces source-language transcription events and target-language interpretation events within a same session without inter-stage API transfers. Interpretation events are distinguishable from transcription events by a standardized text prefix. The unified single-session pipeline is configured with a one-way translation parameter specifying a target language, producing original-language transcription events carrying an automatically detected source language code identifying an actual spoken language of the caller without a caller input.
[0017]In yet another embodiment, the configurable speech processing pipeline comprises a combination of: (a) an automatic speech recognition module configured to convert an audio stream of the caller to source-language text; (b) a large language model configured to receive the recognized text together with a conversation context buffer and produce target-language translation with awareness of conversational history, cultural register, and domain terminology; and (c) a speech synthesis module configured to convert the translated text to audio, wherein the conversation context buffer maintains a sliding window of recent conversation turns in which oldest entries are removed as new turns arrive, for providing the large language model with bounded recent conversational context for translation coherence without unbounded memory growth.
[0018]In yet another embodiment, the configurable speech processing pipeline comprises a combination of: (a) an automatic speech recognition module configured to convert an audio stream of the caller to source-language text; (b) a neural machine translation module configured to translate the source-language text to a target language; and (c) a speech synthesis module configured to convert translated text to audio.

[0070]The computer-implemented system includes a virtual number registry 102 that comprises a relational database configured to maintain a plurality of virtual telephone number profile records. Each record comprising: a virtual telephone number field; a recipient forwarding number field; a first language configuration for an owner; a second language configuration for a caller; a pre-call announcement text field; a keypad-tone automation configuration field; a caller identity display configuration field; a credit authorization state field; and an outbound dial-in authorization configuration comprising an authorized originating telephone number list and an enable flag. 
[0071]The virtual number registry 102 serves as the central configuration store that transforms ordinary telephone numbers into intelligent language-gateway endpoints. Each virtual telephone number profile record functions as a complete operational blueprint defining how calls to that number should be handled, what languages are involved, where calls should be forwarded, what announcements callers should hear, and who is authorized to use outbound gateway features. The virtual telephone number field stores the assigned gateway number (e.g., +1-888-555-0199) that callers dial to reach the interpretation service. The recipient forwarding number field contains the actual telephone number of the business owner or recipient (e.g., +44-20-7946-0123) to which interpreted calls are connected. The first language configuration specifies the owner's spoken language (e.g., "en-US" for American English), while the second language configuration specifies the expected caller language (e.g., "es-MX" for Mexican Spanish). The pre-call announcement text field stores customizable text played to callers before connection (e.g., "Thank you for calling. Please hold while we connect you with real-time interpretation services."). The keypad-tone automation configuration field stores DTMF sequences (e.g., "1##") for automatically navigating IVR menus at forwarding destinations. The caller identity display configuration field is a boolean controlling whether the original caller's number or the virtual number appears on the recipient's caller ID. The credit authorization state field tracks prepaid balance status. The outbound dial-in authorization configuration contains a list of phone numbers (e.g., +1-555-123-4567, +1-555-987-6543) authorized to use the outbound gateway mode, plus an enable flag to activate this feature.
[0072]In an embodiment, the virtual number registry 102 further stores per virtual telephone number profile record comprising: (a) a keypad-tone automation configuration comprising a stored digit sequence and an enable flag, wherein upon connection of a forwarded outbound call in inbound mode, the speech interpretation agent 108 automatically transmits the stored digit sequence to a recipient SIP participant as keypad-tone signals, adapting automated navigation of interactive voice response (IVR) systems at a forwarded destination without requiring the owner to navigate IVR menus manually; (b) a caller identity display configuration comprising a boolean flag that, when enabled, causes the originating telephone number of the caller to be presented to the recipient as the caller identity, and when disabled, causes the virtual telephone number to be presented, giving organizations control over caller identity transparency; (c) a monthly subscription cost configuration and billing cycle tracking fields; and (d) a subscription status field that, when set to a non-active value, causes credit authorization checks for the virtual telephone number to return a negative result regardless of available credit balance.
[0073]The extended virtual number profile fields comprise additional configuration parameters stored in the virtual number registry 102 for each virtual telephone number profile record, enabling advanced call handling automation, caller identity management, subscription billing, and access control enforcement. The keypad-tone automation configuration comprises a stored digit sequence (a string of DTMF digits such as "1##" or "23#" representing IVR menu selections) and an enable flag (a boolean indicating whether automation is active); upon connection of a forwarded outbound call in inbound mode, when the enable flag is true, the speech interpretation agent 108 automatically transmits the stored digit sequence to a recipient SIP participant as keypad-tone signals, sending RFC 2833 telephone-event packets or in-band DTMF tones to the recipient's phone line; this feature adapts automated navigation of interactive voice response (IVR) systems at a forwarded destination without requiring the owner to navigate IVR menus manually—particularly useful when the forwarding number connects to a corporate phone system, call center queue, or voicemail system that requires pressing digits to reach the actual recipient. The caller identity display configuration comprises a boolean flag controlling what caller ID the recipient sees; when enabled, the originating telephone number of the caller is presented to the recipient as the caller identity (showing the actual foreign caller's phone number, e.g., "+52-55-1234-5678"), while when disabled, the virtual telephone number is presented (showing the gateway number, e.g., "+1-888-555-0199"); this gives organizations control over caller identity transparency—some businesses want recipients to see who is actually calling for callback purposes, while others prefer anonymity or consistent branding by always displaying the virtual number. The monthly subscription cost configuration and billing cycle tracking fields store pricing information (e.g., $29.99/month) and billing dates (subscription start date, next billing date, last payment date) enabling the system to manage recurring subscription charges and generate invoices. The subscription status field stores the account's current standing (values such as "active", "suspended", "cancelled", or "pending"); when set to a non-active value, credit authorization checks for the virtual telephone number return a negative result regardless of available credit balance—this enforcement mechanism ensures that even accounts with substantial prepaid credit cannot place calls if their subscription has been suspended (due to terms of service violation, payment dispute, or administrative action) or cancelled, providing complete access control independent of monetary balance. For example, consider a business customer with virtual number +1-888-555-0199 configured with: keypad-tone automation enabled with sequence "1#" (to skip the company's main greeting and reach the owner's extension directly), caller identity display disabled (so all callers appear to come from the virtual number rather than revealing foreign caller numbers to the receptionist), monthly subscription cost $49.99 with next billing date July 1st, and subscription status "active"; when a Spanish-speaking caller connects, the system forwards to the owner's office number, automatically sends "1#" tones to bypass the IVR menu, displays "+1-888-555-0199" on the recipient's caller ID regardless of the caller's actual number, and allows the interpreted call to proceed; however, if the subscription status were changed to "suspended" due to a failed payment, subsequent calls would be rejected immediately with an appropriate message even if the account had $200 in prepaid credit—the subscription status gate overrides the credit balance check entirely.
[0074]The computer-implemented system further includes a carrier trunk interface 104 comprising at least a domestic carrier trunk connection and an international carrier trunk connection. The carrier trunk interface 104 is configured to receive an inbound call directed to one of the virtual telephone numbers from a standard telephone instrument of a caller. The carrier trunk interface 104 is configured to receive inbound calls and initiate outbound calls over telephony networks. 
[0075]The carrier trunk interface 104 is the telecommunications gateway that connects the interpretation system to public telephone networks, enabling it to receive and place calls over PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network), SIP (Session Initiation Protocol), and VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) infrastructures. The domestic carrier trunk connection is a dedicated circuit or SIP trunk provisioned with a telecommunications carrier for routing calls within a single country (e.g., a Twilio SIP trunk configured for US domestic calls with local number presence). The international carrier trunk connection is a separate circuit or SIP trunk optimized for cross-border calls, typically with different rate structures and routing agreements (e.g., a Bandwidth.com international trunk for calls to Europe, Asia, and Latin America). The interface handles protocol translation between different network types, manages concurrent call capacity, and provides the low-level audio transport over which the interpretation system operates. For example, when a caller in Mexico City dials the virtual number +1-888-555-0199 from their standard landline telephone, the carrier trunk interface 104 receives this inbound call via SIP INVITE, extracts the caller's originating number (+52-55-1234-5678), and routes the call audio to the interpretation system; subsequently, when the system needs to connect to the recipient in London, the interface initiates an outbound call through the international trunk to +44-20-7946-0123.
[0076]The computer-implemented system further includes a session manager 106 configured to create a real-time communication session possessing a structured session identifier encoding the virtual telephone number and an originating telephone number of the caller in a deterministic parseable format, and automatically dispatch the speech interpretation agent 108 to the real-time communication session. 
[0077]The session manager 106 is the orchestration component responsible for establishing, tracking, and coordinating all active interpretation sessions within the system. When a call arrives, the session manager 106 creates a real-time communication session—a logical container that holds all resources, state, and participants associated with that call. The session manager 106 generates a structured session identifier by concatenating the virtual telephone number and caller's originating number using a fixed delimiter (e.g., "+18885550199---+525512345678" where "---" serves as the delimiter). This deterministic format ensures that any component can extract both numbers by simply splitting the identifier string. [0095]The unified single-session pipeline is an integrated speech processing architecture wherein a single continuous processing session handles both speech recognition and translation simultaneously, eliminating the traditional separation between these functions. In conventional architectures, speech-to-text (ASR) operates as one system that produces text output, which is then passed via network API calls to a separate translation system—each stage introducing its own latency, error potential, and state management complexity. The unified pipeline instead employs models capable of simultaneous transcription and translation (such as OpenAI's Whisper with translation mode, or Google's Universal Speech Model), receiving raw audio frames as input and producing both original-language transcription (what the speaker said in their language) and target-language translation (the meaning expressed in the recipient's language) as outputs from the same processing session. The phrase "without discrete inter-stage transfers" emphasizes that there is no separate API call, queue, or network hop between recognition and translation—the model produces both outputs internally. This architecture achieves substantially lower end-to-end latency because there are no cumulative network round trips between stages, no serialization/deserialization overhead between systems, and no independent queuing delays. The outputs are typically distinguishable by standardized prefixes or event types (e.g., transcription events marked with "[TRANSCRIPT]" and translation events marked with "[TRANSLATION]"). For example, when a Spanish-speaking caller says "¿Cuál es el estado de mi pedido?", the unified pipeline receives the audio and produces both the original transcription "¿Cuál es el estado de mi pedido?" and the English translation "What is the status of my order?" from the same model invocation, without sending the Spanish text to a separate translation service.

[0096]The ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline is a modular architecture that leverages the advanced contextual understanding and generation capabilities of large language models (such as GPT-4, Claude, or PaLM) for the translation stage. The automatic speech recognition (ASR) module (such as Google Speech-to-Text, Amazon Transcribe, or Whisper) receives audio input and produces source-language text transcription. This transcription is then passed to the large language model translation module, which receives the text along with a conversation context buffer containing recent conversation history, enabling translation that accounts for conversational context, maintains consistent terminology across turns, adapts to cultural register and formality levels, and handles domain-specific vocabulary intelligently. Unlike traditional neural machine translation, LLMs can be prompted with instructions about tone, context, and domain (e.g., "Translate this customer service conversation, maintaining a polite and helpful tone"). The LLM produces target-language text, which is passed to the speech synthesis module (such as Google Cloud TTS, Amazon Polly, or Azure Neural TTS) to generate spoken audio. The conversation context buffer maintains a sliding window of recent turns to provide bounded context without unbounded memory growth. For example, if a caller says, "I'd like to return the blue one" and the LLM knows from context that the previous exchange discussed "shoes," it correctly translates this as "Quisiera devolver los azules" (referring to shoes) rather than a generic translation that loses the referent—contextual awareness that traditional NMT systems cannot achieve.
[0097]The ASR-NMT-TTS pipeline is a modular architecture employing purpose-built neural machine translation systems (such as Google Translate API, Amazon Translate, DeepL, or Microsoft Translator) optimized specifically for translation tasks. The automatic speech recognition module converts spoken audio to source-language text. This text is passed to the neural machine translation (NMT) module, which employs encoder-decoder transformer architectures trained specifically on parallel text corpora for translation between language pairs. The NMT module produces target-language text, which the speech synthesis module converts to spoken audio. Compared to the LLM-based pipeline, the NMT approach offers advantages in processing speed (NMT models are typically faster than general-purpose LLMs), cost efficiency (translation-specific APIs are often priced lower than LLM APIs), and predictability (NMT systems produce consistent translations for identical inputs, whereas LLMs may vary). However, NMT systems lack the contextual reasoning, cultural adaptation, and domain flexibility that LLMs provide—they translate each segment independently without awareness of conversational history. This pipeline variant is well-suited for high-volume deployments where speed and cost are prioritized over nuanced contextual translation. For example, when a caller says, "What are your business hours?", the ASR produces "What are your business hours?", the NMT translates to "¿Cuáles son sus horarios de atención?", and the TTS synthesizes this as Spanish audio—a straightforward translation that NMT handles efficiently without requiring LLM capabilities.
[0098]The direct speech-to-speech (S2S) neural translation module represents the most advanced and streamlined pipeline architecture, employing end-to-end models (such as Meta's SeamlessM4T, Google's Translatotron, or emerging multimodal models) that directly map source-language speech waveforms to target-language speech waveforms without the intermediate step of text transcription. Traditional pipelines convert speech→text→translated text→speech, with each conversion introducing potential errors and latency. The direct S2S approach bypasses text entirely: neural networks trained on parallel speech corpora learn to transform acoustic features directly from one language to another while preserving speaker characteristics, prosody, emotion, and speaking style. This architecture offers several theoretical advantages: elimination of ASR errors that propagate through text-based pipelines; preservation of paralinguistic information (tone, emphasis, emotion) that text representations lose; potentially lower latency by removing intermediate processing stages; and the ability to handle languages or dialects without standardized written forms. The "without generating an intermediate text representation" constraint is definitional—if the system produces text internally, it is not a true direct S2S system. Current S2S technology is less mature than text-mediated pipelines and may have limitations in vocabulary coverage and translation accuracy for complex content, but represents the cutting edge of speech translation research. For example, when a Mandarin speaker says "这个产品质量很好" with enthusiastic intonation, a direct S2S model produces English audio "This product is very good quality" that preserves the speaker's enthusiastic tone and speaking rhythm, without ever generating Chinese or English text as an intermediate step.

[0107]In an embodiment, the automatic language identification further comprises constructing a language hint set for the speech recognition component of the first speech interpretation stream by: (a) including a configured language code of the caller in the language hint set if and only if the configured language code is actively supported by the speech recognition component; (b) including at least one regionally dominant language as an additional hint to accommodate code-switching behavior common in multilingual communities served by a computer-implemented system; (c) identifying a language code in the language hint set that is acoustically near-identical to another code in the language hint set and whose script is incompatible with a configured speech synthesis voice, wherein inclusion of the language code causes the speech recognition component to systematically misidentify speech in a compatible language as an incompatible language, producing synthesis system input that the configured speech synthesis voice is unable to render, resulting in silent audio output for an interpretation channel; and (d) excluding an identified acoustically confusable code from the language hint set, enforced by a language validation function that returns false for the identified acoustically confusable code, for adapting the identified acoustically confusable code not being included in the language hint set regardless of configuration.
[0108]The automatic language identification feature comprises a sophisticated language hint set construction mechanism that configures the speech recognition component to detect the caller's language accurately while preventing systematic misidentification failures that would render the interpretation channel silent. The critical innovation is the acoustic language disambiguation policy that identifies any language code in the hint set that is acoustically near-identical to another code in the set and whose script is incompatible with the configured speech synthesis voice. "Acoustically near-identical" means the spoken forms of two languages are so similar that speech recognition systems frequently confuse them based on audio alone—examples include Hindi (Devanagari script) versus Urdu (Perso-Arabic script), Serbian written in Cyrillic versus Croatian written in Latin script, or Norwegian Bokmål versus Norwegian Nynorsk. When such a confusable pair exists and one language's script is incompatible with the synthesis voice configured for the target language, inclusion of that code causes the speech recognition component to systematically misidentify speech in the compatible language as the incompatible language. This misidentification produces synthesis system input that the configured speech synthesis voice is unable to render—for example, if the system is configured with a Hindi synthesis voice (expecting Devanagari text) but the recognizer outputs Urdu text (Perso-Arabic script), the synthesis engine cannot render Arabic-script text with a Devanagari-trained voice, resulting in silent audio output for the interpretation channel where the recipient hears nothing instead of interpreted speech. For example, consider a deployment serving a South Asian community where the virtual number is configured with caller language "hi-IN" (Hindi) and the synthesis voice is trained for Devanagari script; the hint set construction includes Hindi (supported, configured) and adds English (regionally dominant for code-switching); the system then evaluates whether to include Urdu ("ur-PK"), which is acoustically near-identical to Hindi but uses Perso-Arabic script incompatible with the Hindi voice; recognizing that including Urdu would cause the recognizer to sometimes output Urdu text that the Hindi voice cannot synthesize (producing silence), the validation function returns false for "ur-PK", excluding it from the hint set entirely, so even if a Hindi-speaking caller's audio has slight Urdu influence, the recognizer is constrained to output Hindi text that the synthesis voice can properly render, ensuring the interpretation channel always produces audible output rather than failing silently.

[0123]In an embodiment, the computer-implemented system is further configured to: (a) detect, by a multi-participant conference interpretation module, a connection of a third and subsequent participant speaking a language different from an existing participant; (b) create, by the multi-participant conference interpretation module, additional speech processing pipeline instances for each new ordered language pair introduced; (c) route, by the multi-participant conference interpretation module, an audio of each participant through a plurality of pipeline instances required to produce interpretation for other participants; (d) deliver, by the multi-participant conference interpretation module, interpreted audio selectively to each participant for adapting a participant to receive interpreted audio only from participants speaking a different language; and (e) serialize, by the multi-participant conference interpretation module, interpreted audio delivery to each participant through a dedicated sequential audio queue of the participant, preventing simultaneous overlapping interpretation audio from multiple sources.
[0124]The multi-participant conference interpretation module is an extension component that enables real-time speech interpretation for conference calls involving three or more participants who speak different languages, scaling the bidirectional interpretation architecture to support multilingual group conversations. The module begins by detecting a connection of a third or subsequent participant speaking a language different from an existing participant—when a new participant joins an ongoing interpreted call (or when a conference is initiated with multiple parties), the module analyzes the new participant's language configuration or detects their spoken language through automatic language identification, determining whether this introduces a new language to the conversation that requires additional interpretation paths. Upon detecting a new language, the module proceeds to create additional speech processing pipeline instances for each new ordered language pair introduced—in a two-party call between Spanish and English speakers, only one language pair (Spanish↔English) exists requiring two pipeline instances (one per direction); when a Mandarin-speaking third participant joins, the module creates additional instances for Spanish↔Mandarin and English↔Mandarin pairs, resulting in six total directional pipelines (Spanish→English, English→Spanish, Spanish→Mandarin, Mandarin→Spanish, English→Mandarin, Mandarin→English); this combinatorial expansion ensures every participant can understand every other participant regardless of language. The module then handles audio distribution by routing an audio of each participant through a plurality of pipeline instances required to produce interpretation for other participants—when the Spanish speaker talks, their audio is simultaneously routed to the Spanish→English pipeline (for the English speaker) and the Spanish→Mandarin pipeline (for the Mandarin speaker); this parallel routing ensures all recipients receive interpretation with minimal additional latency compared to two-party calls. A critical optimization is delivering interpreted audio selectively to each participant for adapting a participant to receive interpreted audio only from participants speaking a different language—the English speaker receives interpreted audio from the Spanish and Mandarin speakers but hears no interpretation when other English speakers talk (if present), preventing the jarring experience of hearing one's own language interpreted back and avoiding unnecessary processing; this selective delivery is managed through participant-to-language mappings that filter which interpretation outputs reach which recipients. Finally, the module ensures audio clarity by serializing interpreted audio delivery to each participant through a dedicated sequential audio queue of the participant, preventing simultaneous overlapping interpretation audio from multiple sources—if the Spanish and Mandarin speakers talk simultaneously, the English speaker would receive two interpreted audio streams at once, resulting in incomprehensible overlapping speech; instead, each participant has their own dedicated sequential audio queue (similar to the sequential audio scheduler 114 in two-party calls) that serializes all incoming interpreted segments, playing them one after another rather than simultaneously; this means the English speaker hears the Spanish speaker's interpreted words followed by the Mandarin speaker's interpreted words in sequence, even if both spoke at the same time, preserving intelligibility at the cost of some temporal dislocation. For example, consider a conference call between a Spanish-speaking sales representative in Mexico City (+52-55-1234-5678), an English-speaking manager in London (+44-20-7946-0123), and a Mandarin-speaking supplier in Shanghai (+86-21-5888-8888): when the Spanish representative says "El producto estará listo la próxima semana" (The product will be ready next week), the multi-participant module routes this audio to two pipelines—Spanish→English produces "The product will be ready next week" for the London manager, and Spanish→Mandarin produces "产品下周准备好" for the Shanghai supplier; if the Mandarin supplier responds "我们可以加快生产" (We can speed up production) while the English manager simultaneously asks "What about shipping?", the Spanish representative's dedicated sequential audio queue receives both interpreted segments but plays them sequentially—first "We can speed up production" (from Mandarin→Spanish), then "What about shipping?" (from English→Spanish)—ensuring the representative hears clear, non-overlapping interpretation from both colleagues rather than a confusing mix of simultaneous translated speech.

[0135]The dual-tone multi-frequency (DTMF) digit signal collection mechanism comprises a comprehensive input capture, validation, and error recovery system that reliably captures telephone numbers entered by the registered owner via their telephone keypad in the outbound dial-in gateway mode. The process begins by activating a tone signal listener on a session initiation protocol (SIP) audio channel—a software component that monitors the real-time audio connection between the owner's telephone and the interpretation system for DTMF signals. The listener employs dual detection modes: it detects in-band tone signals embedded in an audio stream (analyzing the RTP audio packets for the characteristic dual-frequency combinations that define each keypad digit, where each key generates two simultaneous tones from predefined frequency groups 697-941 Hz and 1209-1477 Hz), and it detects tone event data carried in SIP signaling messages (RFC 2833 telephone-event packets or SIP INFO messages that transmit digit information out-of-band, separate from the audio stream). This dual-mode detection ensures reliable digit capture regardless of how the telephone network transmits DTMF—some networks strip in-band tones due to codec compression, while others may not support out-of-band signaling. As digits are detected, the system buffers received digit characters in an order received, maintaining a sequential string that accumulates each keypress (e.g., detecting "0", then "0", then "4", then "4" builds the string "0044"). Collection termination occurs via two mechanisms: the system terminates digit collection upon receipt of a hash character as a designated input terminator (when the owner presses to signal they have finished entering the number, enabling immediate processing without delay), and alternatively terminates digit collection upon expiry of a configurable maximum waiting period measured from a most recently received digit signal (if no is pressed, the system waits a configured duration—typically 10-30 seconds from the last digit—before treating the current buffer as complete, accommodating users who forget or are unable to press the terminator).

Please try again." in the owner's language), playing the error prompt to the registered owner through the audio channel, incrementing a retry counter tracking how many failed attempts have occurred, re-entering digit collection if a retry count is below a configured maximum (allowing the owner another chance to enter the correct number), and terminating the session without initiating outbound call when the retry count reaches the configured maximum (preventing indefinite resource consumption from repeated failures, abandoned sessions, or potential abuse).
