[0141]In an embodiment, when adapted in a deployment configuration, the computer-implemented system is further configured to: (a) before initiating the outbound call, query, by a configurable credit authorization module, a backend authorization server 110 with the virtual telephone number, wherein the backend authorization server 110 evaluates an available credit balance and a subscription status and returns a positive and negative authorization response; (b) upon a negative authorization response, immediately terminate, by the configurable credit authorization module, the session without connecting to the recipient and without deducting any credits; (c) upon a positive authorization response, proceed, by the configurable credit authorization module, with outbound call initiation; (d) upon call termination, report, by the configurable credit authorization module, a call duration to the backend authorization server 110 and deducting credits proportional to the call duration at a configured rate; and (e) enforce, by the configurable credit authorization module, the subscription status as a mandatory authorization gate for adapting at least one of: a suspended and cancelled subscription status causes authorization to fail regardless of the available credit balance.
[0142]The configurable credit authorization module is an optional billing enforcement component that, when adapted in a deployment configuration, implements pre-call credit verification, post-call credit deduction, and subscription status enforcement to enable prepaid or subscription-based monetization of the interpretation service. The phrase "adapted in a deployment configuration" indicates this is a configurable feature that can be enabled or disabled per deployment—organizations operating internal interpretation services may disable it entirely, while commercial service providers would enable it to enforce payment requirements. Before initiating the outbound call, the module queries a backend authorization server 110 with the virtual telephone number, sending an authenticated API request that identifies which account is attempting to place the call. The backend authorization server 110 evaluates an available credit balance (the prepaid monetary amount remaining in the account, e.g., $25.00) and a subscription status (the account's current standing, such as "active", "suspended", or "cancelled") and returns a positive or negative authorization response—positive indicates sufficient credit and valid subscription permitting the call to proceed, while negative indicates insufficient credit or invalid subscription requiring call rejection. Upon a negative authorization response, the module immediately terminates the session without connecting to the recipient and without deducting any credits, ensuring that accounts with exhausted credit or suspended subscriptions cannot consume carrier resources or incur costs; this termination occurs before any outbound SIP INVITE is sent, so the recipient's phone never rings for unauthorized calls. Upon a positive authorization response, the module proceeds with outbound call initiation, allowing the normal call flow to continue with carrier trunk selection and outbound connection. Upon call termination, the module reports a call duration to the backend authorization server 110 and deducts credits proportional to the call duration at a configured rate—for example, if the rate is $0.10 per minute and the call lasted 12 minutes, the module reports 12 minutes and the server deducts $1.20 from the account balance; this post-call deduction model charges only for actual usage rather than pre-authorizing estimated amounts. The module also enforces the subscription status as a mandatory authorization gate, ensuring that a suspended or cancelled subscription status causes authorization to fail regardless of the available credit balance—even if an account has $500 in credit, a suspended status (perhaps due to terms of service violation or payment dispute) blocks all calls until the suspension is resolved; this enforcement mechanism enables service providers to control access beyond simple credit availability. For example, consider a commercial interpretation service deployment: a business customer with virtual number +1-888-555-0199 attempts to place an interpreted call; the credit authorization module queries the backend server, which checks the account and finds $15.00 available credit with "active" subscription status, returning a positive response; the call proceeds and connects for 8 minutes; upon hangup, the module reports 8 minutes duration, and the server deducts $0.80 (at $0.10/minute rate) leaving $14.20 balance; alternatively, if that same customer's subscription had been suspended due to a billing dispute, the server would return negative authorization despite the $15.00 balance, the module would immediately terminate the session with an appropriate message ("Your account is currently suspended. Please contact support."), the recipient's phone would never ring, and no credits would be deducted—demonstrating how subscription status enforcement operates independently of credit balance to provide comprehensive access control.
[0143]The computer-implemented system is further configured to establish real-time bidirectional speech interpretation between a telephone of the registered owner and a destination telephone, by: (a) initializing a first speech interpretation stream for an audio of the registered owner with translation targeting a language of a destination party, with automatic language identification adapted to detect an actual spoken language of the destination party without requiring either party to declare the actual spoken language; (b) initializing a second speech interpretation stream for an audio of the destination party with translation targeting the owner language code; (c) routing an interpreted output to neural speech synthesis with voice dynamically selected per interpreted segment based on an automatically detected output language code; (d) delivering synthesized interpreted audio to each respective party through the sequential audio scheduler 114 that prevents concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously; and (d) upon call termination, archiving an interpretation record.
[0144]The first speech interpretation stream is a unidirectional speech processing pipeline that receives audio from the registered owner, performs speech recognition, translation, and synthesis, and produces interpreted audio for delivery to the destination party. The stream is configured with translation targeting a language of a destination party, initially set to the default target language code from the profile but subject to adjustment based on automatic language detection. Automatic language identification is a speech recognition capability wherein the system continuously analyzes incoming audio to determine the language being spoken, enabling dynamic adaptation without requiring explicit language declaration from either party. In this configuration, the stream translates the owner's speech (in the owner's native language) into the language spoken by the destination party. The automatic detection is particularly important in the outbound context because the destination party's language may not be known with certainty until they answer and begin speaking—the default target language serves as an initial hypothesis that detection can refine or correct mid-call. For example, the Japanese owner speaks Japanese, which the first stream recognizes, translates to Chinese (the expected destination language), and synthesizes as Chinese audio for the destination party; if the destination party turns out to speak English instead of Chinese, the automatic detection system identifies this and triggers a stream reconfiguration to translate Japanese to English instead. 
[0145]The second speech interpretation stream is a unidirectional speech processing pipeline that receives audio from the destination party, performs speech recognition, translation, and synthesis, and produces interpreted audio for delivery to the registered owner. This stream is configured with translation targeting the owner language code, which is known with certainty from the virtual number profile and does not require dynamic detection. The second stream enables the bidirectional nature of the interpretation: while the first stream allows the owner to speak to the destination party in the destination's language, the second stream allows the destination party's responses to be heard by the owner in the owner's native language. The stream continuously processes the destination party's speech—detecting the source language automatically, translating it to the owner language, and synthesizing natural-sounding audio in a voice appropriate for the owner language. For example, when the Chinese-speaking destination party in Beijing answers the call and says "您好，请问有什么可以帮您的？" (Hello, how may I help you?), the second stream recognizes this as Mandarin Chinese, translates it to Japanese "こんにちは、何かお手伝いできますか？", and synthesizes Japanese audio that is delivered to the Japanese owner's telephone.
[0146]The interpreted output is the translated text produced by the speech processing pipeline 112, representing the meaning of one party's speech expressed in the other party's language. Neural speech synthesis converts this translated text into natural-sounding spoken audio using deep learning-based text-to-speech technology. Dynamic voice selection per interpreted segment means the synthesis voice is chosen individually for each translation segment based on the language of that segment, rather than using a single statically-configured voice throughout the call. The automatically detected output language code is the language identifier determined by the speech recognition system for each utterance, which may vary during the call if a speaker switches languages. This dynamic architecture enables seamless handling of mid-call language changes: if the destination party switches from Chinese to English mid-conversation, the system automatically detects this change and selects an English synthesis voice for subsequent segments, ensuring the synthesized speech always matches the detected language rather than producing nonsensical output by forcing Chinese text through an English voice or vice versa. For example, if the destination party initially speaks Chinese, the system uses a Chinese neural voice (e.g., "zh-CN-Neural2-A"); if they switch to English, the system automatically detects this and switches to an English neural voice (e.g., "en-US-Neural2-J") for subsequent segments. 
[0147]The sequential audio scheduler 114 is an audio delivery component that manages the ordered playback of synthesized interpreted speech, ensuring clarity and naturalness by preventing overlapping audio segments. Synthesized interpreted audio refers to the speech audio produced by neural synthesis from translated text, ready for delivery to the receiving participant. The sequential audio scheduler 114 comprises multiple sub-components working in coordination: a bounded input queue that accepts interpreted text sentences, parallel synthesis workers that convert text to audio concurrently (each assigned a unique sequence identifier), an ordered output queue that holds completed audio segments, and a single sequential player that extracts and plays segments one at a time in sequence order. The "prevents concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously" constraint is essential for intelligibility: if multiple translated sentences were played at the same time (due to varying synthesis completion times), the result would be incomprehensible overlapping speech. The sequential audio scheduler 114 ensures that even if sentence 3 finishes synthesis before sentence 2, the player waits for sentence 2 to complete and plays them in order (1, 2, 3) rather than in completion order. For example, if the destination party speaks three rapid sentences, the sequential audio scheduler 114 ensures the Japanese owner hears them in proper sequence—"What is your order number?" plays completely, followed by "Let me check the system," followed by "Please hold for a moment"—without any overlap or reordering.
[0148]In an embodiment, the sequential audio scheduler 114 includes: (a) a bounded sentence input queue with a configurable maximum capacity, wherein sentences received while the bounded sentence input queue is at capacity are discarded without blocking the caller, preventing unbounded memory accumulation during rapid speech events; (b) parallel synthesis worker tasks launched concurrently for each sentence, each assigned a monotonically increasing sequence identifier at queue entry time, wherein concurrent execution adapts synthesis latency for segment N+1 to overlap with playback of segment N rather than adding sequentially; (c) an ordered audio segment queue into which each worker deposits a segment comprising the sequence identifier, a list of synthesized audio frames, and original text after synthesis completes; (d) a single sequential audio player task that reads segments from the ordered audio segment queue one at a time and plays all audio frames of each segment to an audio output interface before reading a next segment, determining that no two interpreted segments are played simultaneously regardless of synthesis completion order; and (e) a graceful shutdown sequence comprising placing a sentinel signal in the ordered audio segment queue to terminate the single sequential audio player task, gathering pending synthesis workers with a timeout, cancelling workers exceeding the timeout, and releasing the audio output interface.
[0149]The sequential audio scheduler 114 is a multi-component audio delivery system that manages the orderly synthesis and playback of interpreted speech segments, ensuring natural conversational flow by preventing audio overlap while maximizing throughput through parallel processing. The scheduler comprises five interconnected components. The bounded sentence input queue with a configurable maximum capacity is a fixed-size buffer (e.g., maximum 10 sentences) that accepts interpreted text segments awaiting synthesis; sentences received while the bounded sentence input queue is at capacity are discarded without blocking the caller, meaning the system drops excess input rather than causing backpressure that would freeze the interpretation pipeline—this design choice prevents unbounded memory accumulation during rapid speech events where a fast-speaking caller might generate sentences faster than synthesis can process them, ensuring system stability under load. Parallel synthesis worker tasks are concurrent processing threads or coroutines launched concurrently for each sentence dequeued from the input queue, with each assigned a monotonically increasing sequence identifier at queue entry time (e.g., sentence 1 gets ID=1, sentence 2 gets ID=2, regardless of which finishes synthesis first); this parallelization means concurrent execution adapts synthesis latency for segment N+1 to overlap with playback of segment N rather than adding sequentially—while segment 5 plays to the listener, segments 6, 7, and 8 can be synthesizing simultaneously, dramatically reducing perceived latency compared to sequential synthesis-then-play architectures. The ordered audio segment queue is a data structure into which each worker deposits a segment comprising the sequence identifier, a list of synthesized audio frames, and original text after synthesis completes—the sequence identifier enables proper ordering even when workers complete out-of-order (e.g., if segment 7 finishes before segment 6, both are deposited but the player knows to play 6 first). The single sequential audio player task reads segments from the ordered audio segment queue one at a time and plays all audio frames of each segment to an audio output interface before reading a next segment, enforcing strict sequential playback and determining that no two interpreted segments are played simultaneously regardless of synthesis completion order—even if segments 6, 7, and 8 all complete synthesis while segment 5 is still playing, the player waits for segment 5 to finish, then plays 6 completely, then 7, then 8, never overlapping. Finally, the graceful shutdown sequence handles call termination cleanly by placing a sentinel signal in the ordered audio segment queue to terminate the single sequential audio player task (a special marker that tells the player to stop waiting for more segments), gathering pending synthesis workers with a timeout (waiting a reasonable period for in-progress synthesis to complete), cancelling workers exceeding the timeout (forcibly stopping any synthesis that takes too long, preventing hung workers from blocking shutdown), and releasing the audio output interface (freeing the audio channel resources for reuse by other sessions). For example, consider a rapid Spanish-to-English interpretation where the caller speaks four sentences quickly: the bounded queue accepts all four (capacity permitting), launches four parallel synthesis workers (IDs 1-4), and while worker 3 happens to finish first (synthesizing "The shipment arrives tomorrow"), it deposits to the ordered queue but the player waits; worker 1 finishes next ("Hello, I have a question"), deposits, and the player immediately begins playing it; worker 2 finishes ("About my recent order"), deposits, and waits; worker 4 finishes ("Can you confirm?"), deposits, and waits; the player finishes segment 1, plays segment 2, then 3, then 4 in perfect order—despite out-of-order synthesis completion—and when the caller hangs up, the shutdown sequence sends the sentinel, waits 2 seconds for any pending workers, cancels stragglers, and releases the audio channel cleanly.
[0150]The interpretation record is a structured data artifact containing a complete transcript of all interpreted speech exchanges during the call, including original utterances, their translations, speaker identification, language codes, and timestamps. Call termination refers to the end of the telephone call, triggered by either party hanging up or by network disconnection. Archiving is the process of persisting the interpretation record to durable storage for future retrieval, analysis, and compliance purposes. The record captures the full bilingual conversation history, enabling businesses to review what was discussed, verify interpretation accuracy, resolve disputes, meet regulatory compliance requirements, and analyze communication patterns. The archival process typically stores records to cloud object storage (such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage) with local filesystem fallback if cloud storage is unavailable, ensuring no records are lost due to transient connectivity issues. Each record is associated with session metadata including the virtual number, caller/destination numbers, call duration, and timestamps. For example, after a 12-minute interpreted call between the Japanese owner and the Chinese destination party, the system archives a JSON record containing 34 utterance entries—each with speaker ID, source language (ja-JP or zh-CN), original text, target language, interpreted text, and timestamp—to "s3://interpretation-records/2024/07/outbound_+18885550199_+861012345678_20240717T091530Z.json" for future reference, quality review, or dispute resolution.

[0152]FIG. 2A-2D is a sequence diagram 200 illustrating an inbound call interpretation mode, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0153]Referring now to FIG. 2A-2D, there is illustrated a flow diagram and sequence diagram 200 depicting the complete inbound call interpretation mode of the virtual telephone number-based real-time bidirectional speech interpretation system. FIG. 2A-2D illustrates the process wherein a foreign-language caller dials a virtual number, the infrastructure intercepts the call, automatic language detection is performed, and bidirectional interpretation is established.
[0154]A foreign-language caller using a standard telephone instrument (landline, mobile phone, or any PSTN-connected device) dials the virtual telephone number. The carrier trunk interface 104 receives the inbound SIP INVITE or PSTN signaling, capturing the caller's originating telephone number from the signaling headers. Upon receiving the inbound call, the session manager 106 creates a real-time communication session with a structured identifier encoding both the virtual telephone number and the caller's originating telephone number in a deterministic parseable format. This structured identifier follows the format "[virtual\_number]---[caller\_number]" using a fixed multi-character delimiter sequence that cannot appear in valid telephone numbers, enabling any component to extract both numbers by simply parsing the session name. The session manager 106 automatically dispatches a speech interpretation agent 108 to the newly created session. Upon joining the session, the speech interpretation agent 108 connects to the real-time communication session and begins initialization procedures without requiring any external trigger or manual intervention. The speech interpretation agent 108 uses its session identifier parser component to split the structured session identifier on the predefined delimiter, extracting the virtual telephone number as the first component and the caller's originating telephone number as the second component. This deterministic extraction enables immediate parameter availability without relying on asynchronous metadata delivery that may experience delays.
[0155]The backend authorization client within the speech interpretation agent 108 queries the virtual number registry database to retrieve the virtual telephone number profile associated with the extracted virtual number. The retrieved profile contains: the recipient forwarding telephone number, the first language code (owner's language), the second language code (caller's expected language), pre-call announcement text, keypad-tone automation configuration, caller identity display settings, credit authorization state, and outbound dial-in authorization configuration. As depicted in the sequence diagram with an "alt" (alternative) block labeled "Optional: Credit Authorization (when credit gating enabled)", when credit gating is enabled in the deployment configuration, the system performs a pre-call credit authorization check by querying the backend authorization server 110 with the virtual telephone number. The backend authorization server 110 evaluates available credit balance and subscription status, returning either a positive authorization response (indicated by a checkmark, permitting the call to proceed) or a negative authorization response (indicated by an "X" with "Denied" label, causing immediate session termination). Upon denial, the call ends with no charge, and a POST /deduct-credits operation is skipped (marked as optional). The pre-call announcement engine retrieves the announcement text from the profile, selects a neural speech synthesis voice from the language configuration registry based on the second language code (caller's language), creates and publishes a dedicated audio channel in the session separate from interpretation audio channels, synthesizes the announcement text into audio frames using the TTS Engine, and streams the frames to the caller's telephone. The sequence diagram 200 shows "Play announcement" as a distinct operation with audio frames flowing to the caller. After the announcement completes, the system validates caller presence through a "Count active participants" operation shown in the sequence diagram within an "alt" block. If at least one participant remains connected (indicated by checkmark and "≥1 participant"), the flow proceeds to "Continue to dial"; if zero participants remain (indicated by "0 parts" condition), the system executes "Abort — no outbound call", terminating the session without ringing the owner's phone and without deducting any credits.
[0156]The carrier trunk selector examines the recipient forwarding telephone number to detect the presence of an international dialing prefix. The sequence diagram shows this as "Outbound SIP → Owner's number (domestic or international trunk)" indicating the decision point. Numbers in local format are routed through the domestic carrier trunk connection; numbers with international prefixes (such as "+" or "00" followed by country code) are routed through the international carrier trunk connection. The system initiates an outbound SIP call to the owner's telephone (the recipient forwarding telephone number) through the selected carrier trunk. The sequence diagram 200 depicts "Ringing" sent to the Owner Phone, followed by "Answer" returned when the owner picks up, establishing the second leg of the interpreted call. Upon owner answer, the speech interpretation agent 108 establishes bidirectional interpretation. The sequence diagram 200 shows a "loop" block labeled "Bidirectional Interpretation" containing the continuous interpretation cycle. Within this loop, a box indicates "Automatic Language Detection ENABLED", emphasizing that the speech recognition component continuously and autonomously identifies the actual language spoken by each participant without requiring any declaration or selection. The sequence diagram 200 shows two parallel interpretation paths: "For Caller's track: lang→[detected] target: [cfg]" processing the caller's audio with translation targeting the owner's language, and "For Owner's track: [cfg]→[cfg]" processing the owner's audio with translation targeting the caller's language.
[0157]Within the bidirectional interpretation loop, the sequence diagram 200 depicts the audio processing flow: "Audio stream" flows from participants to the interpretation agent 108, which performs "ASR → auto-detect lang → translate → TTS" processing. The synthesized interpreted audio then flows as "Interpreted audio" to the TTS Engine, which delivers "Audio stream" to the respective recipient (owner hears interpreted caller speech, caller hears interpreted owner speech). This loop continues throughout the duration of the call, with the sequential audio scheduler 114 ensuring interpreted segments play one at a time without overlap. When either party disconnects (shown as "Disconnect" in the sequence diagram), the system initiates the termination sequence. The sequence shows "POST /deduct-credits (optional)" indicating credit deduction proportional to call duration when credit authorization is enabled, followed by "Delete session" to clean up resources and prevent orphaned resource retention. Prior to session deletion, the interpretation record archival engine archives a structured interpretation record to cloud object storage containing per-utterance entries with participant identifier, source language code, original text, target language code, interpreted text, and entry timestamp.
[0158]The sequence diagram portion of FIG. 2A-2D illustrates the temporal interactions between six principal actors represented as columns: Caller (Foreign Language) shown with a user icon, Carrier Trunk 104 representing the telecommunications interface, Session Manager 106 handling session lifecycle, Interp. Agent (Interpretation Agent 108) orchestrating the interpretation logic, Backend/DB providing data and authorization services, TTS Engine performing speech synthesis, and Owner Phone representing the recipient's telephone. Arrows between these columns depict the flow of messages, API calls, and audio streams, with the vertical axis representing time progression from top (call initiation) to bottom (call termination).

[0160]FIG. 3A-3D is a sequence diagram 300 illustrating an outbound dial-in gateway mode, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure
[0161]Referring now to FIG. 3A-3D, there is illustrated a flow diagram and sequence diagram 300 depicting the outbound dial-in gateway mode of the virtual telephone number-based real-time bidirectional speech interpretation system, which represents a novel feature of the present invention. FIG. 3A-3D illustrates the process wherein an owner dials their own virtual number from any standard phone, performs DTMF destination entry, and establishes an interpreted outbound call — with no internet and no app required. The inbound mode serves foreign-language callers who call the virtual number. However, the owner may need to initiate a call to a foreign-language party without access to internet or smartphone capability. The outbound dial-in gateway reuses the same carrier trunk infrastructure, session management, and speech processing pipeline 112 already deployed for inbound calls, requiring no additional hardware.
[0162]The registered virtual number owner dials their own virtual telephone number from any standard telephone instrument. This includes landlines, basic mobile phones (feature phones), office PBX extensions, hotel room phones, payphones, or any voice-capable device — explicitly requiring no smartphone capability, no internet access, and no application software installation. The carrier trunk interface 104 receives the inbound call via SIP INVITE or PSTN signaling. The session manager 106 creates a real-time communication session with a structured identifier encoding the virtual telephone number and the owner's originating telephone number. The session manager 106 dispatches the speech interpretation agent 108 to the session. As shown in the sequence diagram 300, this is depicted as "Inbound SIP INVITE" followed by "Create session" and "Dispatch agent". When any call arrives at the virtual number, the interpretation agent 108 retrieves the associated profile and compares the call's originating telephone number against the authorized originating number list stored in the profile. A match identifies the session as an outbound dial-in session. An alternative detection mechanism examines a session type marker embedded in the structured session identifier. The sequence diagram 300 depicts this with an "alt" (alternative) block showing the decision point, with the outcome "Session classified as OUTBOUND mode" when the originating number matches the authorized list, versus "Proceed as standard Inbound call" when it does not match.
[0163]The interpretation agent 108 plays an interactive voice response prompt to the owner in the owner's configured language, instructing the owner to enter the destination telephone number using the telephone keypad. The prompt is synthesized using the speech synthesis pipeline with voice selected for the owner's language. The sequence diagram 300 shows "Synthesize IVR prompt in owner's language" sent to the TTS Engine, which returns "Audio frames" that are then delivered as "Play IVR announcement" to the Owner. The system activates a tone signal listener on the owner's audio channel. The dual-tone multi-frequency (DTMF) signals are detected either as in-band audio tones or as SIP protocol signaling messages. Digits are buffered until a designated terminator character ("#") is received or a configurable maximum waiting period elapses. On timeout without a terminator, an error prompt is played and retry opportunities are offered before session termination. The sequence diagram 300 depicts this as a "loop" block containing "DTMF Digit Collection" with operations including "Keypad tone (digit)" from the Owner, "Buffer digit in order" processing, and an "alt" block for validation showing either successful validation proceeding forward, or "Timeout / Empty" triggering "Synthesize error prompt" and retry logic. The loop continues with "Enter →: please retry" until the retry limit is reached.
[0164]If credit gating is enabled in the deployment configuration, a credit authorization check is performed. If credit gating is disabled, this step is bypassed. The sequence diagram shows this as a box labeled "Optional: Credit Authorization (when credit gating enabled)" containing "POST /authorize/vtn/VTN" to the Backend/DB, with a checkmark indicating "Authorized (or feature disabled)" allowing the flow to proceed. A confirmation prompt is synthesized in the owner's language indicating the collected destination number. The sequence diagram 300 depicts "Synthesize confirmation: 'Calling [destination]'" sent to the TTS Engine, returning "Audio frames" that are played to the Owner as "Conf. audio to owner", providing auditory verification of the entered number before proceeding.
[0165]The same carrier trunk selection logic as the inbound mode is applied to the DTMF-collected destination number. An outbound SIP call is initiated to the destination. The sequence diagram 300 shows "Outbound SIP → destination (domestic or international trunk)" indicating the trunk selection decision, followed by "Ringing" sent to the Destination Party column, and "Answer" returned when the destination party picks up. Once the destination party answers, bidirectional interpretation is established using the same per-track processing instance architecture as the inbound mode. The sequence diagram 300 shows a box labeled "Automatic Language Detection ENABLED" emphasizing that the speech recognition component continuously identifies the actual spoken language without requiring either party to declare their language. Two interpretation tracks are initialized: "For Owner Track: [ownerLang] → [destLang]" processing the owner's speech with translation targeting the destination party's language, and "For Dest Track: → [autodetect] → ownerLang" processing the destination party's speech with automatic language detection and translation targeting the owner's language.
[0166]The sequence diagram 300 depicts a "loop" block for bidirectional interpretation containing: "Audio stream" flowing from participants to the Interpretation Agent 108; "ASR → auto-detect lang → translate → TTS" processing within the agent; "Interpreted audio" sent to the TTS Engine; and "Audio stream" delivered to the respective recipient. This loop continues throughout the call duration, with the sequential audio scheduler 114 ensuring interpreted segments play one at a time without overlap. Call termination, credit deduction, and transcript archival follow the same procedure as the inbound mode. The sequence diagram 300 shows "Disconnect" when either party hangs up, followed by "POST /deduct-credits (optional)" for credit deduction when enabled, "POST /archive-transcript" for transcript archival, and finally "Delete session" to clean up resources and prevent orphaned resource retention. Key Advantages include: (a) Universal Device Support — any telephone capable of DTMF tones including fixed landlines, basic mobile phones, and payphones; (b) Zero Internet Requirement; (c) Zero Application Requirement; (d) Authentication by Network-Delivered Identifier; (e) Language Profile Auto-Applied; (f) Infrastructure Reuse — no additional hardware required.
[0167]Unlike the inbound mode (FIG. 2A-2D) where a foreign-language caller dials the virtual number to reach the owner, the outbound dial-in gateway mode reverses this relationship — the owner initiates the call by dialing their own virtual number, enters the destination via keypad tones, and the system places the interpreted outbound call on the owner's behalf. This enables owners without smartphones, internet access, or app installation capability to initiate interpreted calls to foreign-language parties from any location with basic telephone service.

[0169]FIG. 4 is a block diagram 400 illustrating speech processing pipeline variants, including (a) unified single-session pipeline, (b) ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline, (c) ASR-NMT-TTS pipeline, and (d) direct speech-to-speech pipeline, wherein all variants feed into the sequential audio scheduler 114, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[0170]The unified single-session pipeline annotated with "Lowest Latency", comprises a single block labeled "Single Neural Processing Session" with features listed as: Auto Language ID, Recognition, and Translation (same session). Audio frames enter this single processing block, which produces an Event Stream comprising: transcript events (carrying a detected language code) and translation events (distinguished by prefix). The output is labeled "translated text" flowing to the Sequential Audio Scheduler 114. A single continuous processing session receives audio input frames and produces both source-language transcription events and target-language translation events within the same session. Events carry a standardized text prefix distinguishing translations from transcriptions. This configuration eliminates inter-stage transfer latency, achieving the lowest end-to-end latency of the pipeline variants. The ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline annotated with "Conversational Context Awareness", comprises three discrete blocks connected sequentially. The first block is the ASR Module labeled "(source text)" receiving audio frames from the caller. The second block is the Large Language Model with features listed as: Model, conversation context buffer. The third block is the TTS Module labeled "(audio)". The output is labeled "audio / text" flowing to the Sequential Audio Scheduler 114. An automatic speech recognition module converts audio to source-language text. A large language model receives the recognized text together with a conversation context buffer containing recent turns, and produces target-language translation with awareness of conversational context, domain terminology, and cultural register. A speech synthesis module converts the translated text to audio. The conversation context buffer maintains a sliding window of recent conversation turns, removing oldest entries as new turns arrive to maintain bounded context size.
[0171]The ASR-NMT-TTS pipeline annotated with "Specialized Language Pairs", comprises three discrete blocks connected sequentially, structurally similar to pipeline (b) but with a different translation component. The first block is the ASR Module labeled "(source text)" receiving audio frames. The second block is the Neural Machine Translation Module. The third block is the TTS Module labeled "(audio)". The output is labeled "audio / text" flowing to the Sequential Audio Scheduler 114. An automatic speech recognition module converts audio to source-language text. A neural machine translation model translates the text. A speech synthesis module converts the translated text to audio. This configuration may be preferred for specific language pairs where specialized neural machine translation models provide superior quality. 
[0172]The direct speech-to-speech pipeline annotated with "No Text Intermediate", comprises a single block labeled "Neural S2S Translation Model" with the description "(audio in → audio out, no text representation)". Audio frames enter directly and the output is labeled "target audio" flowing to the Sequential Audio Scheduler 114. Unlike pipelines (b) and (c), this variant contains no discrete ASR or TTS stages, and unlike pipeline (a), it produces audio output directly rather than text events. A neural model receives audio input in the source language and directly produces audio output in the target language without generating an intermediate text representation, achieving theoretically lowest possible latency. In deployments using this configuration, transcript archival may use a parallel recognition-only process or archive audio segments directly.
[0173]As depicted on the right side of FIG. 4, all four pipeline variants converge on the same Sequential Audio Scheduler 114 component, shown as a block listing its four sub-components: Bounded Queue, Parallel Synth Workers, Ordered Segment Queue, and Single Sequential Player. Convergence lines from pipelines (a), (b), and (c) carry "translated text" or "audio / text" output, while pipeline (d) carries "target audio" output. All pipeline configurations connect to the same sequential audio scheduler 114, ensuring that regardless of which pipeline variant is deployed, interpreted audio is delivered to the call participants through the same ordered sequential playback mechanism that prevents concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously.
[0174]FIG. 5A-5B is a flow diagram 500 illustrating dynamic mid-call language detection and transparent stream restart, depicting an atomic eight-step restart sequence with audio consumption continuity maintained throughout, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[0175]Referring now to FIG. 5A-5B, there is illustrated a flowchart depicting the dynamic mid-call language detection and transparent stream restart mechanism of the present invention. FIG. 5A-5B illustrates the atomic 8-step restart sequence that executes when a caller switches language during an active call, with audio consumption continuing uninterrupted throughout.
[0176]The transparent mid-call stream restart mechanism enables the system to adapt to caller language changes without interrupting the call or requiring any action from either participant. This mechanism is essential for serving multilingual communities where callers frequently switch languages mid-conversation (code-switching), and for handling scenarios where the initially-configured language assumption is incorrect. The process begins when an Original-Language Transcript Event from Caller Track is received, carrying a detected language code. This event is produced by the speech processing pipeline 112 each time it recognizes an utterance, containing both the transcribed text and an automatically-detected language code identifying which language the caller is actually speaking. The system immediately performs "Update caller.lastDetectedLanguage = detectedCode", storing the most recently detected language for reference. The audio consumption task always reads the current stream reference at the moment of each audio frame push, rather than holding a fixed reference from initialization time. Because the restart sequence updates the stream reference before the next audio frame arrives, the new stream immediately receives audio frames without any gap or frame loss — the restart is transparent to both participants. This design principle ensures zero audio frame loss throughout the entire restart sequence.
[0177]The first diamond decision node evaluates "detectedCode ≠ recipient.currentTargetLanguage?" — comparing the detected language code from the caller's speech against the current translation target language configured on the recipient's speech interpretation stream. If the comparison yields "No — same language" (the detected language matches the current target), the flow exits to a box labeled "No action needed", as no reconfiguration is required. If the comparison yields "Yes — language mismatch", indicating the caller has switched to a different language, the flow proceeds to the guard condition checks. 
On original transcript event from caller track:
	Update caller.lastDetectedLanguage = detectedCode
	If detectedCode != recipient.currentTargetLanguage
		AND detectedCode is supported
		AND detectedCode != recipient.sourceLanguage:
		Schedule: recipient._restartStreamWithTarget(detectedCode)
[0178]The first guard diamond evaluates "Guard: restart already in progress?" — checking whether another restart sequence is currently executing. If "Yes", the flow exits to "Skip — restart pending", preventing race conditions that could corrupt stream state if multiple language-change events trigger simultaneous restarts. If "No", the flow proceeds to the next guard.
[0179]The second guard diamond evaluates "Guard: detected lang supported?" — verifying that the newly-detected language is supported by the configurable speech processing pipeline 112. If "No", the flow exits to "Skip — unsupported lang", as the system cannot create a new processing stream for an unsupported language. If "Yes", the flow proceeds to the final guard. The third guard diamond evaluates "Guard: detected lang = recipient's own source lang?" — checking whether the caller has switched to speaking the same language as the recipient. If "Yes — no translation needed", the flow exits to a box labeled "Caller switched to recipient's language", as interpreting between two speakers of the same language is unnecessary. If "No" (the detected language differs from both the current target and the recipient's native language), all guard conditions are satisfied and the atomic restart sequence begins.
[0180]Before entering the atomic restart sequence, the system executes "Set restart-in-progress guard = true", setting the boolean concurrency guard flag to prevent any concurrent restart attempts during the sequence. The first step of the atomic sequence, shown as "Step 1: Set active stream reference → null (prevents push to closing stream)", sets the active stream reference field to null. This prevents the audio-pushing transcript forwarding task from sending audio frames to the stream that is about to be closed, avoiding errors from pushing to a closing or closed stream. "Step 2: Close old speech processing stream" terminates the current speech recognition and translation session that was configured for the previous language. This releases the resources associated with the old language configuration. "Step 3: Cancel transcript forwarding task" stops the background task that was routing transcription and translation events from the old stream to downstream processing components, preventing stale events from the old stream from being processed.
[0181]"Step 4: Close existing speech synthesis instance" releases the neural speech synthesis voice that was configured for the old target language, freeing resources and preparing for a new synthesis instance matching the newly-detected language. "Step 5: Create new stream targeting detected language" initializes a fresh speech processing stream session configured with translation targeting the newly-detected caller language. This new stream is ready to receive audio frames and produce interpreted output in the correct language pair. "Step 6: Update active stream reference → new stream" (annotated with "Audio frames now route here immediately") updates the active stream reference field to point to the newly-created stream. This is the critical moment where audio continuity is maintained — because the audio consumption task reads this reference at the moment of each frame push (as described in the annotation at the top of the flowchart), subsequent audio frames immediately flow to the new stream without any gap or frame loss.
[0182]"Step 7: Create new synthesis instance for new target language" initializes a new neural speech synthesis voice selected for the newly-detected language, ensuring that synthesized interpreted audio uses a voice matching the correct language and script. "Step 8: Launch new transcript forwarding task" starts a new background task on the new stream to route transcription and translation events to downstream processing, completing the pipeline reconfiguration. After Step 8, the system executes "Clear restart guard (in finally block)" (shown in a yellow-highlighted box), resetting the boolean guard flag in a finally block to ensure it is always cleared regardless of whether the sequence completed successfully or encountered an error, preventing permanent restart lockout. The flowchart terminates at a box labeled "Restart complete. Audio continuity maintained", confirming that the entire atomic restart sequence has completed successfully with zero audio frame loss and no perceptible interruption to either call participant. The caller's speech in the new language is now being recognized, translated, synthesized, and delivered to the recipient in the correct language pair, with the transition having been entirely transparent to both parties.

[0184]FIG. 6A-6B is a database entity diagram 600 illustrating the Virtual Number Profile schema showing all configuration fields and their roles, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[0185]Referring now to FIG. 6A-6B, there is illustrated a database entity relationship diagram depicting the VirtualNumberProfile schema and its relationships to associated data entities within the virtual telephone number-based real-time bidirectional speech interpretation system. FIG. 6A-6B  shows all configuration fields carried by a virtual telephone number and their roles in session initialization.
[0186]The primary entity shown at the top center of FIG. 6A-6B is the VirtualNumberProfile table, which serves as the central configuration store for the entire interpretation system. Each record in this table represents one virtual telephone number and its complete operational configuration. The VirtualNumberProfile entity contains the following fields, each shown with its data type, field name, and description:
[0187](a) assignedNumber (string) — "Virtual phone number (E.164 or local)": This field stores the virtual telephone number itself, formatted in E.164 international format (e.g., "+18885550199") or local format. This is the primary key that uniquely identifies each profile and serves as the language-configuration-profile identifier that callers dial to reach the interpretation gateway. (b) forwardingPhoneNumber (string) — "Owner real telephone number": This field stores the actual telephone number of the registered owner to which inbound interpreted calls are forwarded (e.g., "+442079460123"). In inbound mode, after the caller's announcement and presence validation, the system dials this number to connect the owner to the interpreted call. (c) userLanguage (string) — "Owner language code (e.g. ko-KR)": This field stores the BCP 47 language tag identifying the owner's spoken language (e.g., "ko-KR" for Korean, "en-US" for American English, "ja-JP" for Japanese). This code determines the translation target for the caller's audio stream, the language of IVR prompts in outbound dial-in mode, and the voice selection for synthesized speech delivered to the owner. (d) recipientLanguage (string) — "Expected caller language code (e.g. ar-SA)": This field stores the BCP 47 language tag for the expected caller language (e.g., "ar-SA" for Saudi Arabic, "es-MX" for Mexican Spanish). This code determines the initial translation target for the owner's audio stream, the language of pre-call announcements, and the starting language hint for the automatic language detection system.
[0188](e) preCallAnnouncement (string) — "Text synthesized for caller before connection": This field stores the customizable text message that is synthesized into spoken audio and played to the caller before the outbound connection to the owner is initiated (e.g., "Thank you for calling. Please hold while we connect you with interpretation services."). (f) dtmfEnabled (boolean) — "Enable DTMF IVR automation on connect": This boolean flag controls whether the keypad-tone automation feature is active. When set to true, the system automatically transmits the stored digit sequence to the recipient's SIP participant upon connection, enabling automated navigation of IVR systems at the forwarding destination. (g) dtmfValue (string) — "Stored digit sequence for auto-IVR navigation": This field stores the DTMF digit string (e.g., "1##" or "23#") that is automatically transmitted when dtmfEnabled is true. This enables the system to bypass IVR menus at the owner's phone system, routing directly to the correct extension or department without manual intervention. (h) useCallerNumAsCallerId (boolean) — "Expose caller ID to owner (transparency mode)": This boolean flag controls caller identity presentation. When true, the caller's originating telephone number is displayed to the owner as the caller ID; when false, the virtual telephone number is displayed instead, giving organizations control over caller identity transparency. 
[0189](i) monthlyChargeCredits (integer) — "Subscription cost in credits per billing cycle": This field stores the periodic subscription cost in credit units that is deducted from the account balance at each billing cycle, enabling the system to manage recurring subscription billing. (j) subscriptionStatus (string) — "active | suspended | cancelled": This field stores the current subscription standing, accepting one of three values. When set to "suspended" or "cancelled", all credit authorization checks for this virtual number return a negative result regardless of available credit balance, functioning as a mandatory authorization gate. (k) status (string) — "pending | approved | assigned": This field stores the provisioning lifecycle status of the virtual number, indicating whether it is pending activation, approved for use, or fully assigned and operational. (l) allowOutboundDialin (boolean) — "Enable outbound dial-in gateway mode": This boolean flag controls whether the outbound dial-in gateway feature is enabled for this virtual number. When true, calls from authorized originating numbers are classified as owner-initiated outbound sessions; when false, all calls are treated as inbound foreign-caller sessions regardless of originating number.
[0190](m) outboundIvrPrompt (string) — "Custom IVR prompt in owner language": This field stores the customizable IVR prompt text that is synthesized and played to the owner when they access the outbound dial-in gateway, instructing them to enter the destination number. (n) authorizedCallerNumbers (string) — "JSON list of numbers authorized for outbound mode": This field stores a JSON-formatted array of telephone numbers (e.g., '["+12125551234", "+16465555678"]') that the system recognizes as belonging to the registered owner. Calls originating from any number in this list trigger outbound dial-in gateway mode when allowOutboundDialin is true.
[0191]The InboundCallRecord entity stores call data for each inbound interpreted call. Fields include: id (string — unique record identifier), virtualNumber (string — the virtual number dialed), callerNumber (string — the caller's originating number), callerLanguage (string — the detected caller language code), sessionId (string — linking to the real-time session), direction (string — fixed value "inbound"), durationSeconds (integer — call duration), creditsDeducted (integer — billing amount), startedAt (datetime — call start timestamp), and endedAt (datetime — call end timestamp). The OutboundCallRecord entity stores call data for each outbound dial-in gateway call. Fields include: id (string), virtualNumber (string), destinationNumber (string — the DTMF-collected destination), ownerLanguage (string — the owner's language code), sessionId (string), direction (string — fixed value "outbound"), durationSeconds (integer), creditsDeducted (integer), startedAt (datetime), and endedAt (datetime).
[0192]The TranscriptRecord entity stores per-utterance interpretation data for each call. Fields include: id (string — unique record identifier), sessionId (string — linking to the call session), participantId (string — distinguishing caller from recipient), sourceLang (string — detected source language code), originalText (string — verbatim transcription), targetLang (string — translation target language code), interpretedText (string — translated text), and timestamp (datetime — utterance timestamp). Both inbound and outbound call records link to transcript records, enabling full bilingual conversation retrieval for either call type. The Organization and User entities represent the ownership hierarchy. Each VirtualNumberProfile is "owned by" an Organization, and each User "belongs to" an Organization. This organizational relationship enables access control for transcript search and retrieval-augmented generation, ensuring users can only access transcripts belonging to their own organization.
[0193]FIG. 6A-6B depicts a complete data model wherein the VirtualNumberProfile serves as the central hub: it receives InboundCallRecords (from foreign-language callers), generates OutboundCallRecords (from owner-initiated dial-in gateway calls), and both call record types have associated TranscriptRecords containing the per-utterance bilingual interpretation history. The VirtualNumberProfile is owned by an Organization to which Users belong, forming a hierarchical access control structure. This schema design ensures that the virtual telephone number functions not merely as a routing address but as a comprehensive configuration and data aggregation entity, linking language settings, call records, transcripts, billing, and organizational ownership into a unified data model.
