[0195]FIG. 7 is a block diagram 700 illustrating the sequential audio scheduler 114, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0196]FIG. 7 prevents concurrent interpreted audio interleaving through parallel synthesis and ordered sequential playback. The sequential audio scheduler 114 prevents concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously, which would produce unintelligible overlapping audio in the session. The sequential audio scheduler 114 achieves this by allowing concurrency during the synthesis stage (where text is converted to audio) while enforcing strict sequential ordering during the playback stage (where audio is delivered to the call participant).
[0197]At the top of FIG. 7, a block labeled "Interpreted Text Segment (from speech pipeline)" represents the entry point to the scheduler. Each interpreted text segment is a translated sentence produced by the configurable speech processing pipeline 112, representing one utterance from a call participant that has been recognized, translated, and is ready for speech synthesis. These segments arrive asynchronously and may arrive in rapid succession during fast-paced conversation. The first processing stage is the Bounded Sentence Input Queue, shown as a block annotated with "(max capacity configurable)" and a warning icon indicating "Overflow → silent discard (no blocking, no unbounded growth)." The scheduler comprises a bounded sentence input queue with a configurable maximum capacity — sentences received while the queue is at capacity are silently discarded rather than blocking the caller or accumulating unboundedly. This design choice prioritizes system stability over completeness: during extremely rapid speech where translated sentences arrive faster than synthesis and playback can process them, excess sentences are dropped rather than causing memory exhaustion or backpressure that would freeze the interpretation pipeline. The configurable maximum capacity (e.g., 5, 10, or 20 sentences) can be tuned per deployment based on expected speech rates and available system resources.
[0198]From the bounded input queue, sentences fan out to multiple concurrent processing blocks. FIG. 7 shows three parallel worker blocks: Synthesis Worker #N "(seq_id = N) synthesizes segment N → collects audio frames", Synthesis Worker #N+1 "(seq_id = N+1) runs CONCURRENTLY (latency of N+1 overlaps playback of N)", and Synthesis Worker #N+2 "(seq_id = N+2) runs CONCURRENTLY." Parallel synthesis worker tasks are launched concurrently for each sentence, each assigned a monotonically increasing sequence identifier at queue entry time — concurrent execution enables synthesis latency for segment N+1 to overlap with playback of segment N. The monotonically increasing sequence identifiers (e.g., 1, 2, 3, ...) are assigned at the moment each sentence enters the queue, not at synthesis completion, ensuring correct ordering regardless of which worker finishes first. This parallelization is critical for reducing perceived latency: while the player is delivering segment N to the call participant, segments N+1 and N+2 can be synthesizing simultaneously, so they are ready for immediate playback when segment N completes.
[0199]FIG. 7 shows the Ordered Audio Segment Queue block, annotated with "Entries: (seq_id, audioFrames[], text)" and "Workers deposit in any order → queue maintains insertion order by sequence ID." An ordered audio segment queue into which each worker deposits a segment comprising the sequence identifier, synthesized audio frames, and original text after synthesis completes. Each completed segment contains three elements: the sequence identifier (for ordering), the list of synthesized audio frames (the actual audio data), and the original text (for logging and transcript purposes). Workers deposit segments as they complete synthesis — worker #N+2 may finish before worker #N+1, but the queue maintains correct ordering by sequence ID, ensuring segments are available to the player in the proper sequence regardless of synthesis completion order. Below the ordered queue, FIG. 7 shows the Single Sequential Audio Player block with four operational characteristics listed as bullet points: "Reads ONE segment at a time", "Plays ALL frames before advancing", "No concurrent segment playback", and "Sentinel signal → clean exit." A single sequential audio player task reads segments from the ordered queue one at a time and plays all audio frames of each segment before reading the next, ensuring no two interpreted segments play simultaneously. This is the enforcement point that guarantees sequential delivery: regardless of how many segments are waiting in the ordered queue, the player processes exactly one segment at a time, streaming every audio frame of that segment to the audio output before retrieving the next segment. The "sentinel signal → clean exit" annotation indicates the player's termination mechanism — a special sentinel marker placed in the queue signals the player to stop waiting for more segments and exit cleanly.
[0200]A block labeled "Audio Source Output Interface → Published to session channel" represents the final delivery stage. The single sequential audio player streams each segment's audio frames through this interface, which publishes them to the real-time communication session's audio channel. This is the point where interpreted audio becomes audible to the receiving call participant through their telephone. A block labeled "Graceful Shutdown" depicts the five-step termination sequence that executes when the call ends: "1. Place sentinel in output queue" places the termination marker; "2. Player exits on sentinel" causes the player task to stop; "3. Gather pending workers (timeout)" waits for in-progress synthesis to complete within a time limit; "4. Cancel timed-out workers" forcibly stops any synthesis exceeding the timeout; and "5. Release audio interface" frees the audio output resources for reuse. A dotted arrow labeled "shutdown signal" connects the player to the shutdown block, indicating the flow from normal operation to graceful termination.
[0201]FIG. 8 is a flow diagram 800 illustrating the carrier trunk selection logic, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0202]FIG. 8 illustrates the automatic domestic/international trunk routing based on number format, with per-country override support. If the destination number includes an international dialing prefix (beginning with "+"), the international carrier trunk is selected. If the destination number uses local format without a country prefix, the domestic carrier trunk is selected. Per-country routing configurations may override this default for high-volume destination countries, selecting a dedicated carrier trunk configured for that country.
[0203]A block labeled "Destination Telephone Number (from profile or DTMF collection)" represents the input to the trunk selection logic. This destination number originates from one of two sources: the forwarding telephone number retrieved from the virtual telephone number profile (in inbound interpretation mode), or the destination telephone number string collected via DTMF digit entry (in outbound dial-in gateway mode). The same trunk selection logic applies identically to both operating modes. The first diamond decision node evaluates "Number begins with '+' prefix?" — checking whether the destination telephone number starts with the international dialing prefix character "+". This single-character check provides the primary routing determination: "Yes → International format" branches left to the international processing path; "No → Local format" branches right to the domestic processing path. When the number is in international format, the flow proceeds to a block labeled "Extract country code from +CC prefix", which parses the country code from the beginning of the number following the "+" character. Country codes vary in length from one digit (e.g., "1" for North America, "7" for Russia) to three digits (e.g., "353" for Ireland, "852" for Hong Kong), and the system uses a country code lookup table to determine where the country code ends and the national number begins.
[0204]Following country code extraction, a diamond decision node evaluates "Per-country dedicated trunk configured?" — checking whether the system has a specialized carrier trunk connection for the extracted country code. This branches into three possible trunk selections: (a) If a per-country dedicated trunk is configured (Yes path), the flow selects "Select Per-Country Dedicated Trunk (high-volume destinations)" — a carrier trunk specifically provisioned for calls to that country, typically offering better rates, higher quality, or greater capacity for high-volume destination countries. For example, if the system processes thousands of calls to India daily, a dedicated India trunk may provide superior routing compared to the general international trunk. (b) If no per-country trunk is configured (No path) and the number is in international format, the flow selects "Select International Carrier Trunk" — the default international carrier trunk connection with routing agreements for cross-border call termination. (c) On the domestic path (number in local format without "+" prefix), the flow selects "Select Domestic Carrier Trunk (local PSTN)" — the domestic carrier trunk optimized for calls within the same country as the system's point of presence.
[0205]Following trunk selection, the flowchart shows number formatting steps that vary by trunk type. For the per-country dedicated trunk path, the flow proceeds to "Apply country-specific number formatting" with detailed sub-operations: "Remove +CC prefix", "Add domestic trunk-access digit", and "Special handling for abbreviated service numbers." For calls to countries using a domestic trunk-access prefix system: the system detects the country code from the international dialing prefix; extracts the national number portion; determines whether the national number is a standard subscriber number or a special abbreviated service number based on length and prefix digits; for standard subscriber numbers, prepends the domestic trunk-access digit to form the locally-dialed format; for special abbreviated service numbers, uses the national number without the trunk-access prefix; and applies applicable regulatory caller identity compliance substitution for calls between specific trunk types and destination number formats. For example, converting "+44-20-7946-0123" (UK international) to "020-7946-0123" (UK local) by removing "+44" and prepending the domestic trunk-access digit "0".
[0206]For the international carrier trunk path, a block shows "Apply standard E.164 formatting" — ensuring the number is in standard international format that the international trunk expects. For the domestic carrier trunk path, a block shows "Use local format as-is" — the number is already in local format suitable for domestic routing without modification. The flowchart further shows a "Regulatory Caller ID Compliance Check" block with sub-items: "Country-specific rules", "Trunk-type restrictions", "Substitute as required", and "Caller ID if required." This step addresses telecommunications regulations in various jurisdictions that mandate specific caller identity presentation rules. Some countries require that calls from international trunks to domestic numbers display a specific gateway identifier; others require that calls to certain service numbers present a valid callback number. The system evaluates applicable regulatory rules and substitutes the caller identity field as needed before initiating the outbound call. The flowchart terminates at a block labeled "Initiate Outbound SIP Call on Selected Trunk", indicating that after trunk selection, number formatting, and regulatory compliance checks are complete, the system places the outbound call through the selected carrier trunk with the properly formatted destination number and compliant caller identity.
[0207]FIG. 9 is a flow diagram 900 illustrating the background transcript vector indexing pipeline, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0208]FIG. 9 illustrates the automated archival → vector embedding → semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, with access gated by organizational membership. During each interpreted call, the speech interpretation agent 108 maintains a structured interpretation record containing per-utterance entries. Each entry records: participant identifier; source language code; original-language text; target language code; interpreted text; and entry timestamp. The pipeline operates in two phases: a synchronous archival phase triggered by call termination, and an asynchronous indexing phase executed by background jobs at configurable intervals.
[0209]A block labeled "Call Termination Event" represents the trigger that initiates the archival pipeline. This event fires when either party disconnects from the interpreted call, signaling the end of the conversation and the need to preserve the interpretation record. The flow proceeds to a block labeled "Apply settling period (allow final events to process)." This configurable delay (typically 1-5 seconds) ensures that interpretation events still in transit through the speech processing pipeline 112 and network buffers are captured before the streams are closed. Without this settling period, the final utterances spoken just before hangup would be lost, resulting in an incomplete transcript. The next block shows "Serialize interpretation record:" with sub-items: "per-utterance entries" and "(participant, srcLang, original, tgtLang, interpreted, timestamp)." At this stage, the system converts the in-memory interpretation log maintained during the call into a structured document (typically JSON format), with each entry comprising the participant identifier (caller or recipient), source language code (detected language of the utterance), original text (verbatim transcription in the source language), target language code (translation destination), interpreted text (translated content), and timestamp (precise moment of the utterance).
[0210]A diamond decision node evaluates "Upload to Cloud Storage?" — checking whether cloud object storage (such as Amazon® S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure® Blob Storage) is accessible. Upon call termination, after the settling period, the complete interpretation record is archived to cloud object storage in structured JSON format. If cloud storage is unavailable, the record is saved to a configurable local filesystem fallback path to prevent data loss. The "Success" path leads to a block labeled "Cloud Object Storage (primary archive)", while the "Failure / Unavailable" path leads to a blue block labeled "Local Filesystem (fallback archive)." This dual-path architecture ensures no records are lost due to transient cloud connectivity issues or service outages, with local records synchronized to cloud storage when connectivity is restored.
[0211]Following successful archival (to either destination), the flow proceeds to a block labeled "Mark call record: archived = true, archiveUrl = path." This step updates the corresponding call record in the relational database, setting the archived flag to true and storing the archive URL or file path, enabling the background indexing job to discover which records are available for processing. The flow transitions to the asynchronous indexing phase with a block labeled "Background Job Scheduler (polls DB at configurable intervals)." This scheduler is a separate process that runs independently of individual call sessions, executing at configurable intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes, 15 minutes, or hourly). The scheduler executes a database query shown as "Query: recently-ended calls where indexed = false AND archived = true." This query identifies call records that have been archived (transcript available) but not yet indexed (vector embedding not yet generated), filtering to only process records that are ready for indexing while avoiding reprocessing of previously-indexed records. For each unindexed record, the flow proceeds to "Fetch transcript document from cloud storage (or local)." The system retrieves the archived structured interpretation record from the stored archive URL, downloading the JSON document containing the complete per-utterance bilingual transcript. The next block, highlighted with a brain icon, shows "Generate vector embedding (fixed-dimensionality representation of full transcript content)."
[0212]The system invokes a language model embedding service (such as OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 producing 1536-dimensional vectors, Google's text-embedding-gecko, or similar models) to convert the transcript text into a fixed-dimensionality numerical vector that captures the semantic meaning of the conversation. This vector representation enables similarity-based retrieval where conceptually-related conversations can be found even if they use different words. The flow proceeds to a block labeled "Index into Vector Search Engine:" with sub-items listing the indexed metadata: "embedding vector", "transcript content", "sessionId", "organizationId", "language pair", and "timestamp." 
[0213]The system indexes the vector embeddings with session metadata and organizational identifier into a vector search engine. The vector search engine (such as Pinecone, Weaviate, Elasticsearch with vector capabilities, or Milvus) stores both the embedding vector and the associated metadata, enabling filtered semantic search that combines vector similarity with metadata constraints (e.g., "find similar conversations from the last 30 days in the Spanish-English language pair"). The next block, highlighted with a search icon, shows "Available for:" with two capabilities listed: "1) Semantic similarity search across all org transcripts" and "2) RAG — answer natural language questions using transcript context." The indexed records are made available for semantic similarity search and retrieval-augmented generation query answering, with search results filtered to the authenticated user's organizational boundary.
[0214]The semantic similarity search enables users to find relevant past conversations using natural language queries (e.g., "calls about product returns" finds relevant transcripts even if "returns" was never explicitly spoken), while retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables AI-powered question answering that retrieves relevant transcript segments to ground responses in actual conversation data (e.g., "What were the most common complaints last month?" answered using evidence from indexed transcripts). The final block shows "Access Control: Results filtered by organizationId — users see only their org's transcripts." This organizational boundary enforcement ensures strict data isolation: users authenticated under Organization A can only search and retrieve transcripts belonging to Organization A, even if the same vector search engine contains transcripts from multiple organizations using the shared interpretation platform. This access control is implemented as a metadata filter applied to every search query, ensuring the organizationId in the search filter matches the authenticated user's organizational membership.
[0215]FIG. 10A-10B is a block diagram 1000 illustrating multi-participant conference interpretation, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0216]FIG. 10A-10B shows three or more participants with different languages and selective per-recipient interpreted audio delivery. The multi-participant conference interpretation module extends the bidirectional interpretation architecture to sessions with three or more participants speaking different languages. The diagram illustrates a three-participant conference session with Participant A speaking Korean, Participant B speaking Arabic, and Participant C speaking English, demonstrating how the system creates, routes, and delivers interpretation across all language pairs.
[0217]A region labeled "Multi-Participant Conference Session" containing three participant blocks: Participant A (lang: Korean), Participant B (lang: Arabic), and Participant C (lang: English). Each participant has "audio" output arrows representing their spoken audio entering the system, and "play" input arrows representing interpreted audio being delivered to their telephone. The Speech Processing Pipeline Instances is required for this three-language conference. When a third or subsequent participant connects speaking a language different from any existing participant, the system creates additional speech processing pipeline instances for each new ordered language pair introduced by the new participant. For three participants with three distinct languages (Korean, Arabic, English), the diagram shows six directional pipeline instances: Pipeline: KO→AR "(A's audio → B's language)" translating Korean to Arabic; Pipeline: AR→KO "(B's audio → A's language)" translating Arabic to Korean; Pipeline: AR→EN "(B's audio → C's language)" translating Arabic to English; Pipeline: KO→EN "(A's audio → C's language)" translating Korean to English; Pipeline: EN→AR "(C's audio → B's language)" translating English to Arabic; and Pipeline: EN→KO "(C's audio → A's language)" translating English to Korean.
[0218]Arrows labeled "audio" connect each participant to the pipeline instances that process their speech. Each participant's audio is routed through all pipeline instances required to produce interpretation for all other participants speaking different languages. Participant A's Korean audio routes to both Pipeline KO→AR (for Participant B) and Pipeline KO→EN (for Participant C); Participant B's Arabic audio routes to Pipeline AR→KO (for A) and Pipeline AR→EN (for C); Participant C's English audio routes to Pipeline EN→AR (for B) and Pipeline EN→KO (for A). Interpreted audio is delivered selectively to each participant — a participant receives interpreted audio only from participants speaking a different language, not from participants speaking the same language. Arrows labeled "KO audio" and "EN audio" flow from the respective pipelines to the appropriate participant's scheduler.
[0219]The Per-Recipient Sequential Audio Schedulers is shown in FIG. 10A, each with a "play" output. Scheduler A "(receives KO-targeted audio)" collects all interpreted audio destined for Participant A (from both AR→KO and EN→KO pipelines). Scheduler B "(receives AR-targeted audio)" collects interpreted audio for Participant B. Scheduler C "(receives EN-targeted audio)" collects interpreted audio for Participant C. An annotation states: "Each participant receives interpreted audio only from participants speaking a different language. Per-recipient scheduler prevents simultaneous overlapping interpretation from multiple sources." Interpreted audio delivery to each participant is serialized through that participant's own dedicated sequential audio queue, preventing simultaneous overlapping interpretation from multiple sources. If Participants B and C speak simultaneously, Participant A's scheduler serializes the Korean translations of both utterances, playing them sequentially rather than overlapping.

[0221]FIG. 11 is a flow diagram 1100 illustrating the caller presence validation flow, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0222]FIG. 11 illustrates a post-announcement presence check before any outbound call — preventing ringing the owner for abandoned calls. The flowchart begins at a block labeled "Pre-Call Announcement Playback Complete", indicating the trigger point after the synthesized announcement has been fully delivered to the caller's telephone. The flow proceeds to "Apply settling period (allow audio pipeline to drain)" — a brief configurable delay (typically 1-3 seconds) that accounts for network propagation delays and allows the audio playback pipeline to fully drain, ensuring the system does not misinterpret transient network states as caller disconnection. Next, the system executes "Query session: count active remote participants", interrogating the real-time communication session to determine how many participants remain connected.
[0223]The central diamond decision node evaluates "Participant count > 0?" — branching into two paths. The left path, labeled "0 — caller hung up", indicates the caller disconnected during the announcement and leads to a red "Abort Sequence" block with five steps: "1. Do NOT initiate outbound call" (no SIP INVITE is sent), "2. Owner phone does NOT ring" (the owner is never disturbed), "3. Zero credits charged" (no billing impact), "4. Terminate session" (release all resources), and "5. Log abandoned call" (record the event for analytics). This path terminates at "Session terminated — no charge, no ring." The right path, labeled "≥ 1 — caller present", confirms the caller is still connected and leads to a "Proceed" block: "Initiate outbound call to owner forwarding number", flowing to "Select carrier trunk (domestic or international)" and finally "Outbound SIP INVITE → Owner's phone rings", continuing the normal inbound interpretation call flow. This validation mechanism protects owners from unnecessary disruptions and ensures billing fairness by never charging for calls where the caller abandoned before connection.
[0224]FIG. 12A-12B is a flow diagram 1200 illustrating the acoustic language disambiguation policy, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0225]The acoustic language disambiguation policy prevents systematic language misidentification and consequent speech synthesis silence failures. An annotation at the top right of the flowchart explains the problem: if an acoustically confusable code (e.g., Urdu "ur-IN") is in the hint set alongside Hindi ("hi-IN") and the TTS voice is trained on Devanagari script, the ASR system may misidentify Hindi speech as Urdu, producing Perso-Arabic script text that the Devanagari TTS voice cannot render — resulting in silent audio that breaks the interpretation channel. The flowchart begins at "Configured Language Hint Set (for ASR Language Identification)" and proceeds through six sequential steps. Step 1 — "Include configured caller language code (only if supported by ASR system)" adds the caller's expected language from the virtual number profile, conditionally checking ASR support. Step 2 — "Identify regional context from configured language (e.g., Arabic region → South Asian code-switching contexts)" determines the regional deployment context. Step 3 — "Add dominant regional code-switching language as secondary hint (e.g., add Hindi for multi-region callers with South Asian backgrounds)" includes at least one regionally dominant language to accommodate callers who naturally switch languages. Step 4 — "Evaluate acoustic similarity pairs in hint set" begins the disambiguation analysis.
[0226]A diamond decision node evaluates "Acoustically near-identical pair detected? (e.g., hi-IN and ur-IN share near-identical phonology)" — checking whether any two codes in the hint set are acoustically confusable. If "No confusable pairs", both codes are retained ("Keep both codes in hint set"). If "Yes — confusable pair found", a second diamond evaluates "Does the confusable code use a script incompatible with configured TTS voice?" — if "Script compatible (same or compatible writing system)" both are kept; if "Script incompatible (different writing system → TTS would produce silent audio)", the system executes "Exclude the script-incompatible code from hint set (enforce via language validation function)" — removing the problematic code permanently via a validation function that returns false regardless of configuration. Step 5 — "Validate all hint entries against ASR supported-language list (remove unsupported entries)" filters any remaining unsupported codes. Step 6 — "Deduplicate hint set" removes any duplicate entries. The flowchart terminates at "Final Language Hint Set: Passed to ASR configuration — Language ID enabled with safe candidate set", ensuring the speech recognition component operates with a hint set that cannot produce script-incompatible output causing synthesis silence.

[0243]The present invention with the computer-implemented system is configured to provide the real-time bidirectional speech interpretation over the public telephone network using the virtual telephone number interpretation gateway. The present invention provides a virtual telephone number-based real-time bidirectional speech interpretation system and method that operates entirely at the telecommunications infrastructure layer. No software installation, internet connectivity, or special hardware is required on any end-user telephone device. By intercepting and processing calls at the SIP/PSTN layer rather than within proprietary application platforms, the computer-implemented system overcomes a fundamental limitation of prior art systems that operate at the application layer of proprietary software platforms and require all or at least one of the call participants to install and operate software clients, excluding standard landline telephone users, basic mobile phone users without smartphone capability, payphone users, office PBX fixed-line extension users, users in low-connectivity regions, and any environment where application installation is prohibited or impractical. This architectural advantage ensures universal accessibility across all telephony devices and network types, democratizing real-time interpretation services for the broadest possible user base.
[0244]A fundamental technical concept of the present invention is the use of a virtual telephone number as a complete language configuration profile carrier rather than merely a routing address. When a call arrives at the virtual number, the computer-implemented system retrieves the associated profile and configures the entire interpretation session from stored parameters — eliminating any need for real-time language selection by either caller or recipient. This profile-driven approach provides a decisive advantage over prior art systems that require per-call manual configuration of language parameters by one or both participants, either through an application interface before the call or through interactive menus during the call, a requirement incompatible with calls from standard telephone instruments where no application interface is available. By encoding the entire operational configuration — including language pair, forwarding destination, pre-call announcement, keypad-tone automation, and outbound dial-in authorization — into the virtual telephone number itself, the system achieves fully automatic session initialization without any application interface or per-call configuration.
[0245]The present invention achieves substantially lower interpretation latency compared to prior art sequential pipeline architectures by supporting a unified single-session pipeline in which a single continuous processing session receives audio input frames and produces both source-language transcription events and target-language translation events within the same session, with events carrying a standardized text prefix distinguishing translations from transcriptions, eliminating inter-stage transfer latency and achieving the lowest end-to-end latency of the pipeline variants. Prior art systems suffer from cumulative inter-stage latency because they employ sequential processing pipelines wherein a speech recognition module converts audio to text, a separate translation module converts the text to a target language, and a separate speech synthesis module converts the translated text to audio, introducing cumulative inter-stage latency because each module must complete and transfer its output before the next stage begins, with independent network calls for recognition and translation services being additive in latency. The unified pipeline eliminates these independent network round trips and queuing delays, achieving latency compatible with natural conversational flow.
[0246]The computer-implemented system implements a unique transparent mid-call language detection and atomic stream restart mechanism that enables the computer-implemented system to adapt to caller language changes without interrupting the call or requiring any action from either participant. This is achieved through an audio consumption task that always reads the current stream reference at the moment of each audio frame push, rather than holding a fixed reference from initialization time; because the restart sequence updates the stream reference before the next audio frame arrives, the new stream immediately receives audio frames without any gap or frame loss — the restart is transparent to both participants. Combined with automatic caller language detection wherein the speech recognition component automatically and continuously identifies the actual language spoken by each call participant in real time, with neither caller nor recipient required to declare, select, or configure their language at any point , this provides a seamless interpretation experience for multilingual communities where code-switching behavior is common.
[0247]The sequential audio playback scheduler 114 provides a critical technical advantage by preventing concurrent interpreted audio segments from playing simultaneously, which would produce unintelligible overlapping audio in the session. The sequential audio playback scheduler 114 achieves this through an innovative architecture combining parallel processing with sequential delivery: a bounded sentence input queue with configurable maximum capacity where sentences received while the queue is at capacity are silently discarded rather than blocking the caller or accumulating unboundedly; parallel synthesis worker tasks launched concurrently for each sentence, each assigned a monotonically increasing sequence identifier at queue entry time enabling synthesis latency for segment N+1 to overlap with playback of segment N; an ordered audio segment queue into which each worker deposits a segment comprising the sequence identifier, synthesized audio frames, and original text after synthesis completes; and a single sequential audio player task that reads segments from the ordered queue one at a time and plays all audio frames of each segment before reading the next, ensuring no two interpreted segments play simultaneously. This design achieves the optimal balance between low latency through concurrent synthesis and audio clarity through ordered sequential delivery, ensuring natural conversational flow regardless of speech rate or processing speed variations.

title: Roadside Hazard Detection and Vehicle Warning System and Method Thereof
abstract:
Roadside Hazard Detection and Vehicle Warning System and Method Thereof
The present disclosure relates to a real-time roadside hazard detection and vehicle warning system and a method thereof. The system comprises one or more roadside hazard modules, an alert system, a communication network, and vehicle units associated with approaching vehicles. Each module comprises one or more thermal, infrared, radar, imaging, environmental, or communication sensors configured to detect objects within a predefined roadway range. Upon detecting a hazard, the module generates detection data comprising object presence, location, and classification information and transmits the data through the communication network to the alert system and approaching vehicles. A vehicle-mounted receiver receives the detection data, and a processing unit evaluates collision risk using the received hazard information and locally acquired vehicle sensor data. The processing unit generates an alert signal to notify a driver or an onboard vehicle control system of a potential roadway hazard, thereby improving driver awareness and supporting timely collision avoidance.

specification:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The invention relates to a real-time vehicular safety systems, intelligent transportation systems, roadside monitoring infrastructure, and collision avoidance technologies. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to a roadside hazard detection and communication system, method, and associated vehicle-side response architecture configured to detect stationary, moving, partially occluded, or newly appearing roadway hazards, including cattle, stray animals, wildlife, pedestrians, disabled vehicles, debris, obstructions, and other unidentified obstacles on roadways, especially during night-time or low-visibility conditions, and to communicate real-time warning information to one or more approaching vehicles so as to reduce the likelihood of impact events and secondary collisions.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Intelligent transportation systems and advanced driver assistance systems are increasingly employed in modern vehicles to improve road safety by detecting and monitoring objects present in the vehicle surroundings. Such systems generally utilize cameras, radar sensors, LiDAR sensors, ultrasonic sensors, or combinations thereof to capture environmental information and assist drivers in identifying potential hazards located within the driving path. The detected information may be processed by onboard computing systems to generate warnings or initiate collision avoidance actions.
Existing forward object detection systems are capable of detecting vehicles, pedestrians, animals, and other obstacles located within the sensing range of the host vehicle. These systems generally perform satisfactorily during daytime conditions where sufficient illumination and visibility are available. The generated information enables drivers to react appropriately by applying brakes, steering away from obstacles, or reducing vehicle speed. However, the performance of such systems is substantially affected under adverse environmental conditions, including nighttime driving, fog, rain, haze, dust, smoke, and other low-visibility scenarios. In such conditions, the ability of imaging sensors and computer vision algorithms to accurately detect and classify objects is reduced due to insufficient illumination, poor contrast, occlusion, and environmental interference. This challenge becomes more severe when the detected object comprises cattle, stray animals, wildlife, pedestrians, or irregularly shaped obstacles that share visual characteristics with the surrounding environment.
In conventional traffic environments, the hazard information detected by a leading vehicle is generally restricted to the onboard systems of that vehicle. Consequently, while the leading vehicle may successfully identify a roadway obstacle and initiate a collision avoidance action, while the information regarding the detected hazard is not directly communicated to trailing vehicles. Moreover, a trailing vehicle typically relies upon indirect visual indicators such as brake lights, hazard lamps, turn signals, or sudden changes in the trajectory of the leading vehicle to infer the existence of a potential hazard ahead. Such indicators do not provide sufficient information regarding the type, location, size, distance, or severity of the obstacle detected by the leading vehicle. Furthermore, the leading vehicle often obstructs the field of view of the trailing vehicle, thereby preventing direct observation of the obstacle until the trailing vehicle is in close proximity thereto.
The inability of trailing vehicles to directly perceive hazards detected by leading vehicles, and the delayed recognition of obstacles caused by restricted visibility conditions, the available reaction time for drivers and onboard safety systems is reduced. Consequently, the risk of rear-end collisions and secondary accidents is significantly increased, particularly on highways, rural roads, and poorly illuminated road segments. Various vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication technologies have been proposed to improve information sharing among road users. However, existing systems primarily focus on vehicle status information, traffic management, navigation assistance, and emergency messaging, while providing limited capability for real-time detection and dissemination of information relating to unexpected roadway obstacles located beyond the visual perception of approaching vehicles.
Therefore, there exists a need for an improved roadside hazard detection and communication system capable of detecting cattle, animals, pedestrians, vehicles, and other unidentified obstacles present on roadways, particularly during low-visibility conditions, and transmitting real-time warning information to approaching vehicles. Such a system would enable both leading and trailing vehicles to obtain advanced knowledge of roadway hazards beyond their direct line of sight, thereby improving driver response time, reducing collision probability, and enhancing overall road safety.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The present disclosure overcomes one or more shortcomings associated with conventional vehicle-based hazard detection systems and provides additional advantages discussed throughout the present disclosure. Additional features and advantages are realized through the techniques disclosed herein. Other embodiments and aspects of the disclosure are described in detail herein and are considered a part of the claimed disclosure. 
The present disclosure provides a real-time roadside hazard detection and vehicle warning system configured to detect roadway hazards, including cattle, animals, pedestrians, vehicles, and other unidentified objects present on a roadway, particularly under nighttime, foggy, and other low-visibility conditions. The disclosed system employs roadside sensing modules positioned along a roadway to continuously monitor predefined roadway segments and communicate hazard information to approaching vehicles. By providing advance warning of hazards located beyond the direct line of sight of a driver, the disclosed system reduces collision risk and improves overall road safety. 
In one non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, a method for providing real-time hazard alerts to approaching vehicles is disclosed. The method comprises detecting, by a roadside hazard module, the presence of an object within a predefined detection range of a roadway using one or more sensors. The method further comprises acquiring hazard information associated with the detected object and generating detection data comprising object presence information and object location information. The generated detection data is transmitted to an alert system and one or more approaching vehicles. The method further comprises receiving the detection data by a vehicle-mounted receiver, processing the received detection data, and generating an alert signal configured to notify a driver or an onboard vehicle control system to initiate a collision avoidance action. 
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the one or more sensors comprise at least one of a thermal sensor, an infrared sensor, a radar sensor, an information acquisition device, a communication device, and a Dedicated Short-Range Communication (DSRC) module. 
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the roadside hazard module is installed on a roadway divider, roadway median, roadside structure, or combinations thereof to provide continuous monitoring of a roadway segment. In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the roadside hazard module comprises a processor configured to execute one or more object classification algorithms for identifying cattle, animals, pedestrians, vehicles, and other roadway obstacles under low-visibility conditions.
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the generated detection data further comprises hazard classification information, object distance information, movement information, roadway location information, environmental information, and hazard severity information. The detection data is transmitted through a cloud communication network, a DSRC communication network, a vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication network, or combinations thereof.
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the generated alert signal comprises at least one of a visual alert, an audible alert, a haptic alert, and a control signal for an advanced driver assistance system. The system comprises one or more roadside hazard modules, an alert system, one or more vehicle units, and a communication network configured to exchange hazard information among the roadside hazard modules, alert system, and vehicle units. Each roadside hazard module comprises one or more sensors configured to detect roadway hazards, a processor configured to generate detection data associated with the detected hazards, and a communication device configured to transmit the detection data. Each vehicle unit comprises a receiver configured to receive the detection data, a processing unit configured to evaluate collision risk, and an alert notification unit configured to notify a driver or onboard vehicle control system.
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the alert system comprises a server configured to process hazard information received from the roadside hazard modules and a database configured to store hazard records, event logs, roadway information, and historical hazard data. In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the vehicle unit further comprises one or more imaging sensors, a yaw rate sensor, a brake sensor, and a vehicle speed sensor. The processing unit is configured to fuse received hazard information with locally acquired sensor data to determine a collision risk level associated with a detected hazard. In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, the vehicle unit is configured to provide warning information through at least one of a dashboard display, a heads-up display, an audible alarm, a vibration alert, or an automated driver assistance module.
In another non-limiting embodiment of the present disclosure, a vehicle-mounted apparatus for receiving and responding to roadside hazard information is disclosed. The apparatus comprises a processor, a memory coupled to the processor, a vehicle communication unit, one or more imaging sensors, a yaw rate sensor, a brake sensor, and a vehicle speed sensor. The processor is configured to receive detection data from a roadside hazard module or alert system, process locally acquired sensor data, fuse the received detection data with the locally acquired sensor data, determine a collision risk associated with a detected roadway hazard, and generate an alert or vehicle control signal responsive to the determined collision risk.
The foregoing summary is illustrative only and is not intended to be limiting. In addition to the illustrative aspects, embodiments, and features described above, further aspects, embodiments, and features will become apparent by reference to the accompanying drawings and the following detailed description.
OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION
The main object of the present disclosure is to provide a real-time roadside hazard detection and vehicle warning system configured to detect roadway hazards and communicate hazard information to approaching vehicles for reducing collisions. 
Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a roadside sensing infrastructure capable of detecting cattle, animals, pedestrians, vehicles, and other unidentified objects present on a roadway under low-visibility conditions. 
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a hazard detection system employing thermal sensors, infrared sensors, radar sensors, and communication devices for improving hazard detection accuracy during nighttime, foggy, rainy, or otherwise adverse environmental conditions.
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a mechanism for communicating real-time hazard information from roadside hazard modules to approaching vehicles through vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), Dedicated Short-Range Communication (DSRC), cloud-based communication networks, or combinations thereof. 
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide advance warning of roadway hazards located beyond the direct line of sight of a driver, thereby enabling timely collision avoidance actions. 
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a vehicle-mounted processing system configured to receive hazard information and generate visual, audible, haptic, or automated warning signals for notifying drivers of potential roadway hazards.
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a system capable of integrating externally received hazard information with locally acquired vehicle sensor data to improve collision risk assessment. 
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to reduce the occurrence of rear-end collisions and secondary accidents caused by delayed hazard recognition under nighttime and low-visibility driving conditions.
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a scalable and distributed roadside monitoring architecture capable of continuously monitoring predefined roadway segments and disseminating hazard alerts to multiple approaching vehicles. 
Yet another object of the present disclosure is to improve overall roadway safety by reducing driver reaction time and enhancing situational awareness of hazards present ahead of approaching vehicles.

As used herein, the term “roadway hazard” may include any object, condition, or event that may interfere with, obstruct, or endanger expected vehicular travel along a roadway. By way of example and without limitation, a roadway hazard may include cattle, livestock, stray animals, wildlife, pedestrians, bicycles, stopped vehicles, overturned vehicles, fallen cargo, stones, barriers, construction material, tree branches, flooded regions, smoke regions, or other obstructions. Accordingly, references herein to cattle or animals are merely illustrative examples of a broader class of roadway hazards.
As used herein, the term “roadside hazard module” may refer to any fixed, semi-fixed, or relocatable infrastructure unit configured to sense a roadway region and communicate hazard-related information. Likewise, the term “vehicle unit” may refer to a dedicated onboard module, an integrated vehicle controller, a telematics unit, an advanced driver assistance subsystem, an infotainment-linked processing unit, or any combination of hardware and software capable of receiving and acting upon warning information.
FIG. 1 illustrates a schematic block diagram of a roadside hazard detection and vehicle warning system 100 according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. In the illustrated embodiment, the system 100 generally comprises an alert system 101, a communication network 104, at least one roadside hazard module 110, and at least one vehicle unit 120 associated with an approaching vehicle. The alert system 101 may include one or more servers 102 and one or more databases 103. The communication network 104 may include one or more wired and/or wireless communication infrastructures configured to permit information exchange among the system components.  
The roadside hazard module 110 may be positioned adjacent to or above a roadway segment selected for monitoring. In some implementations, the roadside hazard module 110 is mounted at a location that provides an unobstructed or partially unobstructed view of one or more lanes, shoulders, medians, or merging regions. A plurality of roadside hazard modules 110 may be deployed at intervals along a roadway so that the monitored zones overlap, thereby reducing undetected gaps and improving continuity of hazard tracking between adjacent segments.

A plurality of roadside hazard modules 110 may be deployed at intervals along a roadway so that the monitored zones overlap, thereby reducing undetected gaps and improving continuity of hazard tracking between adjacent segments.
The alert system 101 may receive hazard reports from one or more roadside hazard modules 110 and may perform one or more processing operations such as event verification, event deduplication, vehicle relevance determination, confidence updating, warning-zone generation, record storage, and alert prioritization. In some embodiments, the alert system 101 may also communicate with a roadway operations center, emergency service system, maintenance platform, or analytics platform.
The database 103 may store hazard event records, timestamp information, roadway identifiers, sensor health data, historical detection trends, vehicle acknowledgements, maintenance logs, and learned thresholds for future use. Such storage may be useful for audit trails, incident review, maintenance planning, and tuning of hazard classification models.
The communication network 104 may include cloud connectivity, cellular communication, local wireless communication, Dedicated Short-Range Communications (DSRC), Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X), Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) links, or combinations thereof. In some embodiments, the roadside hazard module 110 may send alerts both to the alert system 101 and directly to vehicles within a predefined local communication radius so as to reduce latency.
The vehicle unit 120 may be installed in a passenger vehicle, commercial vehicle, bus, emergency vehicle, agricultural vehicle, or any other road-going vehicle. The vehicle unit 120 may determine whether a received warning is relevant by considering current vehicle location, travel direction, lane, route, speed, and estimated arrival time at the hazard region. In this manner, warning overload to unaffected vehicles may be reduced.
By way of an example, an animal may enter a rural roadway at night at a location beyond the visible range of a trailing vehicle. The roadside hazard module 110 may detect the animal based on combined thermal, infrared, and radar sensing. Hazard information may then be transmitted through the communication network 104 to the alert system 101 and then to the trailing vehicle before the driver obtains direct visual contact with the animal, thereby increasing available reaction time.
FIG. 2 illustrates a detailed block diagram of the roadside hazard module 110 according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. The roadside hazard module 110 comprises a processor 201 operably coupled to a communication device 202, an information acquisition device 203, a radar sensor 204, a Dedicated Short-Range Communications (DSRC) module 205, an infrared camera 206, and a thermal sensor 207. However, the roadside hazard module 110 is not limited to these specific components and may additionally include visible-spectrum cameras, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors, ultrasonic sensors, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers, local storage, power-conditioning circuits, backup power systems, environmental enclosures, edge accelerators, or self-diagnostic modules. 
The processor 201 may execute one or more software modules, firmware routines, hardware-accelerated routines, or combinations thereof for receiving sensor data, synchronizing multi-sensor inputs, filtering noise, detecting candidate objects, classifying detected objects, tracking object movement, estimating hazard severity, and generating corresponding hazard metadata. In some embodiments, the processor 201 may additionally determine whether the detected object occupies a lane, is approaching a lane, or is likely to remain outside the primary travel path.
The communication device 202 may exchange information with the alert system 101, neighboring roadside modules, maintenance systems, and/or approaching vehicles. The communication device 202 may employ cellular modems, Wi-Fi modules, Ethernet interfaces, fiber links, Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) interfaces, Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) transceivers, or other suitable communication means. The DSRC module 205 may provide low-latency localized communication for rapid dissemination of warning messages to nearby vehicles.
The information acquisition device 203 may collect contextual data used to improve the reliability of hazard evaluation. For example, the information acquisition device 203 may obtain ambient temperature, humidity, time of day, weather condition, visibility condition, roadway illumination level, road surface condition, lane map information, or externally provided environmental data. Such contextual information may be used by the processor 201 to dynamically adjust detection thresholds, confidence weights, or classification logic.
The radar sensor 204 may determine range, radial velocity, movement direction, and positional information for detected objects. The infrared camera 206 may capture infrared imagery of the monitored region and may assist in detecting objects when visible-light contrast is poor. The thermal sensor 207 may identify heat signatures associated with living beings or recently active mechanical objects, thereby assisting in distinguishing warm-bodied hazards from the surrounding environment.
In some embodiments, the roadside hazard module 110 performs sensor fusion by correlating outputs from the radar sensor 204, infrared camera 206, thermal sensor 207, and optionally other sensors. For example, a thermal hotspot detected near a roadway lane may be correlated with radar-based motion information and image-based contour information to determine whether the event likely corresponds to a pedestrian, animal, or false positive. Such fusion may reduce false alarms caused by roadside heat sources, reflections, moving vegetation, or transient background noise.
The roadside hazard module 110 may assign one or more labels to a detected event, such as animal, cattle, wildlife, pedestrian, stopped vehicle, moving vehicle, debris, unknown object, or non-actionable event. The roadside hazard module 110 may further generate a severity score or risk level based on lane occupancy, object size, estimated speed, direction of motion, weather conditions, roadway curvature, vehicle approach speed expectations, and confidence metrics. In some embodiments, alerts may be transmitted only when a threshold event confidence and/or severity criterion is satisfied.
FIG. 3 illustrates a detailed block diagram of a vehicle unit 120 according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. The vehicle unit 120 comprises a system processing unit 320 operably coupled to a vehicle communication unit 321, one or more imaging sensors including camera 301 and camera 302, a yaw rate sensor 303, a brake sensor 304, a vehicle speed sensor 305, an alert notification module 331, and an image display device 332. In other embodiments, the vehicle unit 120 may additionally include a steering angle sensor, inertial measurement unit, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver, map database interface, heads-up display interface, haptic actuator interface, speaker interface, memory, or telematics controller.
The vehicle communication unit 321 may receive warning information from the roadside hazard module 110, the alert system 101, or both. The warning information may include a hazard identifier, location coordinates, roadway segment ID, lane relevance data, object type, distance, approach direction, severity level, confidence level, recommended action, and time validity information. In some embodiments, the warning may further include a reduced-resolution image, symbolic rendering, or geofenced alert boundary.
The system processing unit 320 may combine the externally received warning information with locally generated vehicle data. For example, the cameras 301 and 302 may provide visual context around the vehicle, while the yaw rate sensor 303, brake sensor 304, and vehicle speed sensor 305 may provide current vehicle-state information. By combining these data sources, the system processing unit 320 may determine whether the vehicle is on a collision course, whether the vehicle has sufficient braking distance, and whether a warning or intervention should be escalated.
In one example, if the vehicle is traveling at high speed toward a curve and the received alert indicates that a large animal is occupying the lane beyond the curve, the system processing unit 320 may generate a high-priority warning. In another example, if the alert relates to a hazard in an adjacent carriageway or opposite-direction lane, the system processing unit 320 may suppress or downgrade the warning so as to avoid unnecessary driver distraction.
The alert notification module 331 may generate one or more output modalities depending on the determined hazard level. Such outputs may include dashboard messages, visual icons, heads-up display prompts, spoken alerts, audible tones, seat vibration, steering wheel vibration, or combinations thereof. In some embodiments, the image display device 332 may visually indicate the estimated hazard location relative to the vehicle and may provide lane-specific or directional guidance.
In some implementations, the system processing unit 320 may interact with one or more driver assistance subsystems. For example, the system processing unit 320 may support pre-charging of a braking system, adaptive reduction of cruise speed, enhancement of driver warning urgency, or generation of control suggestions to an autonomous or semi-autonomous driving controller. In other implementations, the vehicle unit 120 may provide an informational warning only, leaving all responsive action to the driver.
FIG. 4 discloses a flowchart of the real-time roadside hazard detection and warning system according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. At an initial stage, the roadside hazard module 110 may monitor a roadway segment and generate hazard detection data 401 after detecting a candidate roadway hazard. The hazard detection data 401 may include object location, lane occupancy, object class, movement vector, estimated speed, severity level, environmental context, confidence score, and time-of-detection data. Subsequently, the roadside hazard module 110 transmits an alert message 402 to the alert system 101. In some embodiments, the roadside hazard module 110 may also directly broadcast or multicast a local warning to nearby vehicles while the alert system 101 performs additional verification. The alert system 101 may evaluate the incoming alert message 402, compare it with prior hazard reports, correlate it with roadway or environmental context, and identify one or more vehicles likely to be affected.

Following verification or prioritization, the alert system 101 may transmit an alert confirmation message 403 to one or more approaching vehicles. The alert confirmation message 403 may include refined hazard information, updated severity information, estimated distance to hazard, warning priority, and recommended driver actions. In some embodiments, the alert system 101 may additionally transmit control data 404 including speed recommendations, lane advisories, route suggestions, warning validity duration, or traffic management data.
After receiving the alert confirmation message 403 and, where applicable, the control data 404, the vehicle unit 120 may process the received information and determine an appropriate warning output. The warning output may vary according to the urgency of the event, the host vehicle state, and the degree of confidence associated with the hazard. For example, a moderate-confidence hazard beyond a long distance may produce an informational alert, whereas a high-confidence lane-occupying hazard at shorter range may trigger an urgent multi-modal warning.
In some embodiments, the vehicle unit 120 may generate a status/data report 405 and transmit the same to the roadside hazard module 110 and/or the alert system 101. The status/data report 405 may include acknowledgment of alert reception, host vehicle speed, host vehicle position, brake status, response timing, communication quality, or locally observed confirmation data. Such feedback may be used to update stored event history, improve hazard model performance, and assess effectiveness of the warning system over time.
The sequence illustrated in FIG. 4 is merely exemplary and should not be construed as limiting. In alternative embodiments, one or more stages may be merged, omitted, repeated, reordered, or executed substantially in parallel. Further, one or more functions described as being performed by the roadside hazard module 110 may instead be performed by the alert system 101, and vice versa, depending on latency requirements, processing capacity, deployment architecture, or communication availability.
In some embodiments applicable to any of the foregoing figures, the roadside hazard module 110 may include a local power supply, solar energy subsystem, battery backup, grid interface, and health monitoring circuitry. The roadside hazard module 110 may be housed in a weather-resistant enclosure configured to withstand environmental exposure. Self-diagnostic data may be periodically transmitted to a maintenance system so as to identify sensor degradation, communication failure, misalignment, or power anomalies.
In some embodiments, machine learning models, rules-based logic, or hybrid decision frameworks may be employed to classify detected objects and estimate hazard relevance. Such models may be trained or tuned to distinguish roadway-relevant events from non-critical background activity, such as moving vegetation, distant heat sources, or off-road animals. The models may operate locally at the roadside hazard module 110, centrally at the alert system 101, or in a distributed arrangement.
In some embodiments, privacy-preserving data handling may be implemented. For example, object metadata may be stored in place of full imagery unless detailed image retention is authorized or required for safety analysis. Similarly, vehicle-originated acknowledgements or telemetry may be anonymized or tokenized before storage.
In some embodiments, the disclosed architecture may be adapted for deployment in animal-crossing corridors, rural roads, mountainous roads, industrial zones, mining roads, toll approaches, construction zones, bridges, tunnels, sharp-curve segments, and fog-prone areas. The same architecture may additionally be adapted to detect floodwater regions, rockfall, stalled vehicles, wrong-way vehicles, fallen cargo, or temporary obstructions.

title: SMART METER ANALYTIC WITH ENERGY CONSUMPTION PREDICTION
abstract: The invention presents a smart meter analytics system based on MATLAB simulation. Historical energy consumption data is imported into the MATLAB workspace. The system performs data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training with the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox and the Deep Learning Toolbox. It compares Linear Regression, Random Forest (TreeBagger), and LSTM networks. Error metrics identify the best-performing model. Graphical plots visualize actual versus predicted consumption along with confusion and error matrices.
specification:
FIELD OF INVENTION

The current invention is about smart grid analytics, artificial intelligence, and energy forecasting systems that use the MATLAB simulation environment. It particularly focuses on modelling, simulating, and predicting smart meter energy consumption through machine learning and deep learning toolboxes in MATLAB.

DEFINITIONS 

MATLAB Simulation, a computational modeling environment, is used for data analysis, algorithm development, and visualization. 
Time-Series Data consists of sequential energy consumption readings collected over time intervals. 
Regression Model is a statistical model used to predict continuous output values. 
Neural Network (LSTM) is a deep learning architecture for forecasting sequential data. 
RMSE and MAE are error metrics used to evaluate prediction accuracy.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION 

Energy utilities need precise short-term and long-term load forecasting. Traditional statistical models do not adjust well to nonlinear patterns in smart meter data. Simulation tools are necessary to confirm prediction accuracy before implementing them in the real world.
Existing approaches use ARIMA, Linear Regression, or standalone Neural Networks. However, these methods do not compare models effectively in a single simulation environment.
The present invention offers a MATLAB-based hybrid simulation framework that combines regression, ensemble learning, and LSTM neural networks. The system assesses models using MAE and RMSE. It also automatically chooses the best prediction model during the simulation.

OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION

•	To simulate smart meter energy data in MATLAB.  
•	To implement several prediction algorithms.  
•	To compare performance with statistical error metrics.  
•	To visualize real-time energy forecasts.  
•	To improve prediction accuracy with hybrid modeling.  

ADVANTAGES OF THE INVENTION

•	Easy implementation using MATLAB toolboxes.
•	Graphical visualization of results.
•	Reliable prediction using hybrid AI models.
•	Simulation before physical deployment.
•	Supports large time series datasets.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The invention presents a smart meter analytics system based on MATLAB simulation. Historical energy consumption data is imported into the MATLAB workspace. The system performs data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training with the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox and the Deep Learning Toolbox. It compares Linear Regression, Random Forest (TreeBagger), and LSTM networks. Error metrics identify the best-performing model. Graphical plots visualize actual versus predicted consumption along with confusion and error matrices.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

The invention is a MATLAB-based smart meter analytics system that predicts energy use with machine learning and deep learning techniques. It processes time-series data gathered from smart meters in a MATLAB simulation environment for testing and analysis.
The system imports energy consumption data, preprocesses it to fix missing values and normalize, and extracts time-based features. The data is then divided into training and testing datasets. A hybrid prediction engine combines linear regression, random forest, and LSTM models. The models are trained using the training data, and predictions are made.
The performance evaluation module calculates error metrics, such as Mean Absolute Error and Root Mean Square Error. Prediction results are shown through actual vs. predicted and error plots in MATLAB figure windows. This system allows for effective forecasting and performance comparison within a single simulation framework.
