TECHNICAL FIELD OF THE INVENTION 
The present invention is related to an electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary-function control system, and more particularly relates to a single-ASIC dual-mode PLC/HMI-arbitrated control architecture with thermal-fault-adaptive pulse-width-modulation regulation, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure.
BACKGROUND 
Electric vehicles, including electric bicycles, e-rickshaws, campus shuttles, low-speed electric vehicles, and last-mile transportation platforms, generally employ multiple electronic control units for managing propulsion and auxiliary vehicle functions. Conventional control architectures commonly use a programmable logic controller for automated, fleet-level, or remotely initiated operations and a human-machine interface for receiving local commands from a vehicle operator. The programmable logic controller and the human-machine interface may independently generate commands for vehicle power, motor operation, headlights, horns, and direction indicators. 
In such conventional architectures, the programmable logic controller and the human-machine interface are frequently connected through separate wiring paths and individual relay or driver circuits. When both control sources attempt to operate the same vehicle function simultaneously, conflicting or overlapping commands may occur. To address these conflicts, existing systems generally employ external arbitration relays, priority encoders, switching circuits, or an additional supervisory microcontroller. These additional components increase circuit complexity, wiring requirements, printed circuit board area, installation effort, and overall manufacturing cost.
The use of multiple control paths also introduces additional electrical interfaces and points of failure. Loose connectors, relay-contact degradation, signal delays, electromagnetic interference, and wiring faults may adversely affect the reliability of the control system. Further, the absence of a deterministic hardware interlock between automated and operator-originated commands may result in uncertain actuator behaviour when conflicting commands are received. Software-based priority selection may also be affected by processor delays, firmware errors, communication failures, or execution hangs.
Conventional electric-vehicle motor-control systems further employ separate circuits or software routines for accelerator processing, brake processing, motor-speed calculation, and pulse-width-modulation generation. In many systems, accelerator and brake commands are evaluated through firmware executed by a general-purpose microcontroller. A failure, delay, or incorrect execution of the firmware may prevent timely reduction of the motor command when a braking input is applied. Consequently, reliance on software-based brake-priority control may reduce the predictability and functional-safety robustness of the propulsion-control arrangement.
Thermal protection in existing motor-control systems is also commonly implemented as an independent analog cut-off circuit, a separate temperature-monitoring controller, or a periodically executed firmware routine. Such arrangements may only disconnect the motor after the temperature reaches a critical limit and may not provide controlled power reduction before complete shutdown. Furthermore, inadequate hysteresis between fault activation and fault clearance may cause repeated switching of the thermal-protection state near the threshold temperature, resulting in unstable motor operation and increased electrical and mechanical stress.
The use of independent motor-control, auxiliary-control, arbitration, and thermal-protection units further increases power consumption, bill-of-materials cost, PCB footprint, and maintenance requirements. Compact electric-vehicle platforms are particularly affected by these limitations because the available installation space, connector capacity, and power budget are restricted. The requirement for separate input and output lines for each controlled function also makes conventional architectures unsuitable for low-pin-count integrated-circuit implementations.
Accordingly, there remains a need for an electric-vehicle control architecture that addresses dual-source command conflicts, excessive wiring and component count, firmware dependency, inadequate brake-priority enforcement, fragmented PWM generation, and delayed or unstable thermal-fault handling, while supporting reliable control of the motor and auxiliary vehicle functions.
SUMMARY 
In an aspect of the present disclosure, a dual-mode electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary-function control system is provided. The system includes a programmable logic controller, a human-machine interface, and a single application-specific integrated circuit controller incorporating an operation-selector state machine, an XOR-based command-arbitration module, a motor-speed calculation module, a pulse-width-modulation generator, and a temperature-monitoring and fault-control module. The operation-selector state machine time-multiplexes eight vehicle-control operations through a shared input/output interface. The command-arbitration module accepts an actuator command when only one command source is asserted and maintains the actuator output inactive when both command sources are simultaneously asserted. The motor-speed calculation module derives a motor-speed word from accelerator and brake values and forces the motor-speed word to zero when the brake value equals or exceeds the accelerator value. The temperature-monitoring and fault-control module reduces the PWM duty cycle during an overheat condition and restores the duty cycle after the temperature reaches a thermal-clear threshold, wherein the control and safety functions are implemented through hardwired digital logic.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the shared input/output interface includes eight dedicated input lines, eight dedicated output lines, and eight bidirectional input/output lines. The operation-selector state machine selects and time-multiplexes the eight vehicle-control operations through the shared interface based on the three-bit operation code.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, corresponding command-bit pairs from the programmable logic controller and the human-machine interface are provided for vehicle-power control, headlight control, horn control, and direction-indicator control. The XOR-based command-arbitration module maintains the respective actuator-control output in an inactive state when both command sources simultaneously assert the corresponding command.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the motor-speed calculation module alternately captures the accelerator value and the brake value from a common four-bit input bus based on a data-selection signal. The motor-speed calculation module determines a saturated difference between the accelerator and brake values and left-shifts the saturated difference to generate the eight-bit motor-speed word.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the pulse-width-modulation generator includes an internal clock-divider arrangement adapted to derive a PWM operating frequency from a system clock. The pulse-width-modulation generator modulates the duty cycle of the motor-control signal according to the eight-bit motor-speed word.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module includes a digital temperature-rise estimator adapted to estimate motor-temperature increase during sustained motor operation and motor cooling during idle or reduced-speed operation.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module maintains the overheat-fault state between the thermal trip threshold of 110°C and the thermal-clear threshold of 105°C. The resulting 5°C hysteresis range prevents repeated activation and clearance of the overheat-fault state near the thermal threshold.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the system further includes a vehicle battery and a voltage-regulation circuit. The vehicle battery supplies a 12 V or 24 V direct-current supply, and the voltage-regulation circuit converts the supplied voltage into a regulated 3.3 V or 5 V logic-level supply for operating the application-specific integrated circuit controller.
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the system further includes an automotive relay interface, a headlight, a horn, and a direction-indicator unit. The automotive relay interface receives actuator-control outputs generated by the XOR-based command-arbitration module and selectively switches electrical power to the headlight, the horn, and the direction-indicator unit.
In an aspect of the present disclosure, a method for dual-mode PLC/HMI-arbitrated control of an electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary functions using a single application-specific integrated circuit controller is provided. The method includes receiving automated and manual command signals, selecting and time-multiplexing one of eight vehicle-control operations, performing XOR-based arbitration between corresponding PLC-origin and HMI-origin command bits, calculating a motor-speed word from accelerator and brake values, forcing the motor-speed word to zero when braking equals or exceeds acceleration, generating a pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal, and operating the brushless direct-current motor through the motor-driver circuit. The method further includes monitoring or estimating the motor-temperature condition, asserting an overheat-fault state at 110°C, reducing the PWM duty cycle by 50%, maintaining the fault until the temperature decreases to 105°C, and thereafter restoring the calculated PWM duty cycle through hardwired digital logic.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
The invention relates to a single-chip electric vehicle motor control and auxiliary-function management system developed in the form of an application-specific integrated circuit. The system is intended to replace a conventional distributed control arrangement in which a programmable logic controller, a human-machine interface, separate relay circuits, a motor-speed controller, a PWM generator, and a thermal-protection unit operate as independent subsystems. By consolidating these functions into a common digital hardware architecture, the invention reduces external wiring, component count, PCB area, control latency, and dependence on supervisory firmware. 
In a typical compact electric vehicle, an external programmable logic controller may be used for fleet-level or automated vehicle commands, while an onboard human-machine interface may be used by the driver to control local functions. Both sources may attempt to operate the same vehicle loads, such as the power circuit, headlight, horn, indicator, or motor-control system. Conventional implementations therefore require additional arbitration relays, priority encoders, or microcontrollers to determine which command source should be accepted. Such arrangements create a fragmented control environment and introduce additional failure points.
The disclosed invention addresses this issue by implementing the command-selection and arbitration process directly within the ASIC. The chip receives command signals from both the programmable logic controller and the human-machine interface. Corresponding command pairs are processed using hardware-level exclusive-OR logic. Accordingly, an actuator output is activated only when one command source is asserted. When both command sources are simultaneously asserted, the output is automatically maintained in a safe inactive condition. This approach prevents simultaneous or conflicting operation without relying on software-based priority routines or external arbitration hardware.
The ASIC further incorporates an operation-selector state machine. A three-bit operation code enables the controller to selectively execute one of eight vehicle-control functions, including power control, headlight control, horn control, indicator control, motor-speed calculation, PWM generation, temperature monitoring, and system reset or status reporting. These functions are time-multiplexed through a shared input and output interface. The arrangement is particularly beneficial for compact and low-pin-count integrated-circuit platforms because multiple vehicle subsystems can be controlled without providing a dedicated set of pins for every function.
For propulsion control, the system receives an accelerator value and a brake value through a shared input bus. The motor-speed datapath subtracts the brake value from the accelerator value and generates a corresponding motor-speed command. When the brake value is equal to or greater than the accelerator value, the calculated motor-speed output is forced to zero. This provides an inherent hardware-level brake override and ensures that the motor is not driven when the braking demand exceeds the acceleration demand. The calculated speed value is subsequently converted into an eight-bit motor-speed word.
The eight-bit motor-speed word is supplied to an integrated pulse-width modulation generator. The PWM generator produces a motor-drive waveform having a duty cycle corresponding to the calculated speed command. The generated PWM signal may be delivered to an external three-phase BLDC motor-driver stage. Since the PWM waveform is generated within the ASIC, a separate PWM controller or external motor-speed-generation circuit is not required.
The invention additionally incorporates a thermal-fault protection mechanism. The thermal subsystem continuously monitors or digitally estimates the temperature condition associated with the motor. When the temperature reaches a predetermined upper threshold, such as 110°C, the ASIC asserts an overheat fault, generates a warning output, and automatically reduces the PWM duty cycle by approximately 50%. The reduced duty cycle limits the power supplied to the motor and thereby assists in controlling further temperature rise.
The thermal fault is not immediately cleared when the temperature falls marginally below the trip threshold. Instead, the system maintains the fault condition until the temperature decreases to a lower reset threshold, such as 105°C. This hysteresis prevents repeated activation and deactivation of the fault state near the threshold temperature. The thermal derating process is carried out autonomously by the hardware and does not require polling, decision-making, or intervention by an external processor.
The invention therefore establishes an integrated vehicle-control architecture in which dual-source command arbitration, actuator control, speed computation, brake-priority enforcement, PWM generation, thermal monitoring, fault indication, and thermal derating are implemented within the same silicon platform. The principal technical contribution lies in combining an eight-operation multiplexed state machine, XOR-based PLC/HMI arbitration, an accelerator-minus-brake motor-speed datapath, and fault-adaptive PWM control in a single low-pin-count ASIC.
In practical deployment, the system may be used in electric bicycles, e-rickshaws, campus shuttles, low-speed electric vehicles, and last-mile transport platforms. A central fleet controller may issue commands through the programmable logic controller, while the driver may operate local functions through the human-machine interface. The ASIC ensures that the two command sources do not simultaneously control the same actuator and that the motor remains protected during excessive thermal loading. Thus, the invention provides a compact, hardware-secured, and operationally resilient EV control solution.
Disclosed is a single-ASIC system for controlling an electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary functions through coordinated PLC and HMI command inputs (hereinafter referred to and denoted as “the system 100”). The system 100 performs hardware-based command arbitration, accelerator-and-brake-based speed calculation, PWM motor driving, and automatic thermal-fault derating within a unified control architecture.
Fig. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a system (100) for dual-mode PLC/HMI-arbitrated control of an electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary functions, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure.
The system (100) includes a programmable logic controller (102), a human-machine interface (104), an application-specific integrated circuit controller (106), an operation-selector state machine (108), an XOR-based command-arbitration module (110), a motor-speed calculation module (112), a pulse-width-modulation generator (114), a temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), a vehicle battery (118), a voltage-regulation circuit (120), a motor-driver circuit (122), a brushless direct-current motor (124), an automotive relay interface (126), a headlight (128), a horn (130), and a direction-indicator unit (132).
The programmable logic controller (102) is adapted to generate automated, fleet-level, or externally initiated control commands for operating one or more electric-vehicle functions. The programmable logic controller (102) produces digital command signals corresponding to vehicle power activation, headlight operation, horn operation, direction-indicator operation, and motor-control functions based on predefined control logic, programmed operating sequences, or instructions received from a centralized vehicle-management arrangement. The programmable logic controller (102) may further provide remote supervisory control for coordinating vehicle operations in a fleet, campus-shuttle, or industrial transportation environment.
The human-machine interface (104) is operatively coupled with the programmable logic controller (102) through a coordinated dual-mode vehicle-control architecture. The human-machine interface (104) is adapted to receive local operator inputs through a touchscreen panel, keypad, switch arrangement, or graphical control console and generate corresponding digital command signals for vehicle power activation, headlight operation, horn operation, direction-indicator operation, accelerator control, brake control, and motor-speed selection. The human-machine interface (104) thereby provides a manual operator-control path complementary to the automated or fleet-level control path provided by the programmable logic controller (102).
The application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) is operatively coupled with the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104) to receive respective automated and manual control commands. The application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) comprises a single-chip digital control core adapted to process the received commands, coordinate electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary-function operations, execute hardware-level command arbitration, calculate a motor-speed value based on accelerator and brake inputs, generate a pulse-width-modulated motor-control output, and implement autonomous thermal-fault protection. The application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) further provides a low-pin-count, state-machine-based hardware architecture that reduces reliance on external arbitration relays, supervisory microcontrollers, and firmware-controlled safety routines.
The operation-selector state machine (108) is operatively integrated within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). The operation-selector state machine (108) is adapted to receive a three-bit operation code and selectively activate one of eight electric-vehicle control operations comprising power control, headlight control, horn control, direction-indicator control, motor-speed calculation, pulse-width-modulation generation, temperature monitoring, and system reset or status reporting. The operation-selector state machine (108) time-multiplexes the selected operations through a shared low-pin-count input/output interface, thereby enabling multiple vehicle-control functions to be implemented within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) without requiring separate dedicated pins for each operation.
The XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) is operatively integrated within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) and selectively activated by the operation-selector state machine (108). The XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) is adapted to receive corresponding command-bit pairs originating from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104) and generate an actuator-control output only when exactly one command bit of each pair is asserted. When both command bits are simultaneously asserted, the XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) maintains the corresponding output in an inactive state, thereby providing hardware-level conflict resolution for vehicle power, headlight, horn, and direction-indicator operations without requiring an external priority encoder, arbitration relay, or supervisory microcontroller.
The motor-speed calculation module (112) is operatively integrated within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) and selectively activated by the operation-selector state machine (108). The motor-speed calculation module (112) is adapted to receive a four-bit accelerator value and a four-bit brake value through a shared time-multiplexed input interface, subtract the brake value from the accelerator value, and generate an eight-bit motor-speed word representative of a requested motor speed. The motor-speed calculation module (112) applies saturation at zero and forces the motor-speed word to zero when the brake value is equal to or greater than the accelerator value, thereby providing a hardware-level brake-priority safety interlock independent of external supervisory software.
The pulse-width-modulation generator (114) is operatively coupled with the motor-speed calculation module (112) and integrated within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). The pulse-width-modulation generator (114) is adapted to receive the eight-bit motor-speed word generated by the motor-speed calculation module (112) and produce a pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal having a duty cycle corresponding to the received motor-speed word. The pulse-width-modulation generator (114) derives a PWM operating frequency from a system clock through an internal clock-divider arrangement, thereby enabling direct speed-command delivery without requiring a separate external PWM-generation circuit.
The temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) is operatively coupled with the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) and integrated within the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). The temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) is adapted to continuously monitor or digitally estimate a motor-temperature condition based on vehicle operating parameters and determine whether the motor-temperature condition reaches a predetermined thermal trip threshold. Upon detecting that the motor-temperature condition reaches approximately 110°C, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) asserts an overheat-fault state, generates a thermal-warning signal, and causes the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) to reduce the PWM duty cycle by approximately 50%. The temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) maintains the overheat-fault state until the motor-temperature condition decreases to approximately 105°C, thereby providing a 5°C hysteresis range that prevents repeated fault activation and clearance near the thermal trip threshold.
The vehicle battery (118) is electrically coupled with the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) through a regulated power-delivery path. The vehicle battery (118) is adapted to supply electrical power required for operating the electric-vehicle control system and may comprise a 12 V or 24 V rechargeable battery pack. The vehicle battery (118) provides a primary direct-current power source for supporting motor-control operations, auxiliary vehicle functions, command-processing operations, and thermal-fault management during vehicle operation.
The voltage-regulation circuit (120) is electrically coupled with the vehicle battery (118) and the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). The voltage-regulation circuit (120) is adapted to receive a battery-level direct-current voltage, such as 12 V or 24 V, and convert the received voltage into a regulated logic-level supply, such as 3.3 V or 5 V, suitable for operating the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). The voltage-regulation circuit (120) may further provide voltage stabilization, filtering, overvoltage protection, and transient suppression to maintain reliable operation of the digital control architecture under varying vehicle-load and battery conditions.
The motor-driver circuit (122) is electrically coupled with the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) and the vehicle battery (118). The motor-driver circuit (122) is adapted to receive the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal from the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) and convert the received low-power control signal into corresponding high-current switching signals suitable for electric-vehicle propulsion. The motor-driver circuit (122) may comprise a three-phase gate-driver arrangement, such as a DRV8305-class or DRV8323-class driver, including switching-control circuitry, current-handling circuitry, and protection circuitry for regulating the electrical power delivered in accordance with the commanded PWM duty cycle.
The brushless direct-current motor (124) is electrically coupled with the motor-driver circuit (122). The brushless direct-current motor (124) is adapted to receive controlled three-phase electrical power from the motor-driver circuit (122) and convert the received electrical power into rotational mechanical output for propelling the electric vehicle. The operating speed and torque of the brushless direct-current motor (124) are regulated in accordance with the switching signals generated based on the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal, while the supplied power is reduced during a detected thermal-fault condition.
The automotive relay interface (126) is electrically coupled with the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) and the vehicle battery (118). The automotive relay interface (126) is adapted to receive low-power actuator-control signals generated by the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) and selectively switch battery-level electrical power for operating one or more electric-vehicle auxiliary loads. The automotive relay interface (126) may comprise electromechanical relays, solid-state relays, transistor-based driver stages, isolation circuitry, flyback-protection elements, and transient-suppression elements adapted to protect the digital control circuitry from inductive switching disturbances and automotive electrical transients.
The headlight (128) is electrically coupled with the automotive relay interface (126). The headlight (128) is adapted to receive selectively switched electrical power and generate forward illumination for the electric vehicle in response to a corresponding headlight-control signal. The headlight (128) may comprise a light-emitting-diode lamp, halogen lamp, or another automotive illumination unit and is maintained in an inactive state when conflicting headlight commands are simultaneously received from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104).
The horn (130) is electrically coupled with the automotive relay interface (126). The horn (130) is adapted to receive selectively switched electrical power and generate an audible warning signal in response to a corresponding horn-control command. The horn (130) may comprise an electromagnetic horn, electronic horn, or another automotive acoustic signalling device and is maintained in an inactive state when simultaneous horn commands are received from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104), thereby preventing conflicting dual-source operation.
The direction-indicator unit (132) is electrically coupled with the automotive relay interface (126). The direction-indicator unit (132) is adapted to receive selectively switched electrical power and generate a visual directional signal indicating an intended turning or lane-change operation of the electric vehicle. The direction-indicator unit (132) may comprise one or more light-emitting-diode lamps, flashing lamps, or automotive signal-light assemblies and is maintained in an inactive state when simultaneous indicator-control commands are received from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104), thereby providing hardware-interlocked dual-source operation.
During operation, the vehicle battery (118) supplies the direct-current electrical power required for operating the system (100). The voltage-regulation circuit (120) receives the battery-level voltage from the vehicle battery (118), converts the received voltage into the regulated logic-level supply, and supplies the regulated voltage to the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106). Upon receiving the regulated voltage and the system-enable signal, the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) performs the initialization and places the vehicle-control outputs in the predefined inactive state.
The programmable logic controller (102) generates the automated, fleet-level, or remotely initiated control commands, while the human-machine interface (104) receives the local operator inputs and generates the corresponding manual control commands. The application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) receives the commands from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104) through the respective input lines. The operation-selector state machine (108) receives the three-bit operation code and identifies the selected operation from the power-control operation, the headlight-control operation, the horn-control operation, the direction-indicator-control operation, the motor-speed-calculation operation, the pulse-width-modulation-generation operation, the temperature-monitoring operation, and the system-reset or status-reporting operation.
When one of the auxiliary-control operations is selected, the XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) receives the corresponding command-bit pair from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104). The XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) generates the actuator-control output when exactly one command source asserts the corresponding command. When the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104) simultaneously assert the corresponding command, the XOR-based command-arbitration module (110) maintains the actuator-control output in the inactive state, thereby preventing the conflicting command sources from simultaneously operating the same vehicle function.
The application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) transmits the accepted auxiliary-control output to the automotive relay interface (126). The automotive relay interface (126) converts the low-power control output into the switched battery-level electrical power. Based on the selected operation, the automotive relay interface (126) supplies the switched electrical power to the headlight (128), the horn (130), or the direction-indicator unit (132). The headlight (128) generates the forward illumination, the horn (130) generates the audible warning signal, and the direction-indicator unit (132) generates the visual turning signal in accordance with the accepted command.
For the motor-control operation, the motor-speed calculation module (112) receives the accelerator value and the brake value through the shared time-multiplexed input interface. The motor-speed calculation module (112) subtracts the brake value from the accelerator value and generates the eight-bit motor-speed word corresponding to the requested speed. When the brake value is equal to or greater than the accelerator value, the motor-speed calculation module (112) forces the motor-speed word to zero, thereby applying the hardware-level brake-priority safety cut-off.
The pulse-width-modulation generator (114) receives the eight-bit motor-speed word from the motor-speed calculation module (112). The pulse-width-modulation generator (114) compares the motor-speed word with the internally generated PWM count and produces the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal having the duty cycle corresponding to the requested motor speed. The motor-driver circuit (122) receives the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal and converts the received low-power signal into the corresponding high-current, three-phase switching signals. The brushless direct-current motor (124) receives the controlled electrical power from the motor-driver circuit (122) and converts the electrical power into the rotational mechanical output for propelling the electric vehicle.
During the motor operation, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) continuously monitors or digitally estimates the motor-temperature condition. When the motor-temperature condition remains below the predetermined thermal trip threshold, the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) operates according to the calculated motor-speed word. When the motor-temperature condition reaches approximately 110°C, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) asserts the overheat-fault state, generates the thermal-warning output, and instructs the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) to reduce the PWM duty cycle by approximately 50%. The reduced PWM duty cycle decreases the electrical power supplied through the motor-driver circuit (122) to the brushless direct-current motor (124), thereby limiting further thermal loading.
The temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) maintains the overheat-fault state while the motor-temperature condition remains above approximately 105°C. When the motor-temperature condition decreases to approximately 105°C, the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116) clears the overheat-fault state and permits the pulse-width-modulation generator (114) to resume the duty cycle corresponding to the calculated motor-speed word. The difference between the thermal trip threshold and the thermal-clear threshold provides the hysteresis and prevents repeated switching of the fault state near the thermal threshold.
When the reset or status-reporting operation is selected, the operation-selector state machine (108) causes the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106) to clear the stored operating states or provide the system-enable and fault-status outputs. Accordingly, the system (100) performs the command acquisition, the operation selection, the dual-source arbitration, the motor-speed calculation, the PWM generation, the motor driving, the auxiliary-load operation, and the thermal-fault-adaptive speed regulation within the single integrated hardware architecture.
Fig. 2 illustrates a flow chart of a method (200) for dual-mode PLC/HMI-arbitrated control of an electric-vehicle motor and auxiliary functions, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure. The method (200) includes the following steps: -
At step 202, supplying, by the vehicle battery (118), electrical power to the system (100) and converting, by the voltage-regulation circuit (120), the electrical power into the regulated logic-level supply for operating the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106).
At step 204, receiving, by the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106), the automated control commands from the programmable logic controller (102) and the manual control commands from the human-machine interface (104).
At step 206, receiving, by the operation-selector state machine (108), the three-bit operation code and selecting one operation from the power-control operation, the headlight-control operation, the horn-control operation, the direction-indicator-control operation, the motor-speed-calculation operation, the pulse-width-modulation-generation operation, the temperature-monitoring operation, and the system-reset or status-reporting operation.
At step 208, comparing, by the XOR-based command-arbitration module (110), the corresponding command bits received from the programmable logic controller (102) and the human-machine interface (104).
At step 210, generating, by the XOR-based command-arbitration module (110), the actuator-control output when exactly one of the corresponding command bits is asserted and maintaining the actuator-control output in the inactive state when both corresponding command bits are simultaneously asserted.
At step 212, transmitting, by the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106), the accepted auxiliary-control output to the automotive relay interface (126) for selectively operating the headlight (128), the horn (130), or the direction-indicator unit (132).
At step 214, receiving, by the motor-speed calculation module (112), the accelerator value and the brake value through the shared time-multiplexed input interface.
At step 216, calculating, by the motor-speed calculation module (112), the motor-speed word by subtracting the brake value from the accelerator value and forcing the motor-speed word to zero when the brake value is equal to or greater than the accelerator value.
At step 218, generating, by the pulse-width-modulation generator (114), the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal having the duty cycle corresponding to the calculated motor-speed word.
At step 220, converting, by the motor-driver circuit (122), the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal into the corresponding high-current switching signals and supplying the controlled electrical power to the brushless direct-current motor (124).
At step 222, monitoring or estimating, by the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), the motor-temperature condition during operation of the brushless direct-current motor (124).
At step 224, determining, by the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), whether the motor-temperature condition has reached the predetermined thermal trip threshold.
At step 226, asserting, by the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), the overheat-fault state and the thermal-warning signal and reducing the duty cycle of the pulse-width-modulated motor-control signal by approximately 50% when the motor-temperature condition reaches approximately 110°C.
At step 228, maintaining, by the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), the overheat-fault state until the motor-temperature condition decreases to approximately 105°C.
At step 230, clearing, by the temperature-monitoring and fault-control module (116), the overheat-fault state and restoring the duty cycle corresponding to the calculated motor-speed word upon the motor-temperature condition decreasing to approximately 105°C.
At step 232, resetting, by the application-specific integrated circuit controller (106), the stored operating states or outputting the system-enable and fault-status information when the system-reset or status-reporting operation is selected.

title: METHOD FOR ON-DEVICE FINANCIAL TRANSACTION EXTRACTION USING MULTI-DIMENSIONAL VECTOR SCORING
abstract:
ABSTRACT
METHOD FOR ON-DEVICE FINANCIAL TRANSACTION EXTRACTION USING MULTI-DIMENSIONAL VECTOR SCORING
A method for extracting financial transaction data from a message is disclosed. The method is performed by a system (100) comprising a weight machine engine (108) and a collision resolution module (112). The method comprises receiving, at a message receiver (102) of a mobile computing device, a message containing text, and extracting, by an evidence extractor (106), a plurality of numeric tokens from the message. The method further comprises computing, by the weight machine engine (108), a multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token, wherein each dimension represents a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a respective semantic classification. The method further comprises performing, by the collision resolution module (112), collision resolution by comparing magnitudes across dimensions, wherein a dimension having a higher magnitude suppresses competing dimensions having lower magnitudes. The method further comprises generating a transaction record (114) based on the collision resolution, wherein the transaction record (114) comprises structured financial data extracted from the message.

specification:
CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS AND PRIORITY
[0001]	The present application does not claim priority from any patent application.
PREAMBLE
[0002]	The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed.
FIELD OF INVENTION
[0003]	The present disclosure relates to mobile financial technology and edge natural language processing, and more particularly to a method for on-device extraction of structured financial transaction data from unstructured text messages using multi-dimensional heuristic vector scoring and deterministic collision resolution.
BACKGROUND
[0004]	The following text of background art is provided for purposes of understanding and is not an admission that any cited document or technique forms part of the prior art under applicable law.
[0005]	Short Message Service (SMS) remains a prevalent medium for receiving transactional notifications in high transaction-volume marketplaces. Financial institutions transmit immediate notifications via SMS regarding debit and credit transactions and balance updates, resulting in fragmented and unstructured ledgers across various banking applications.
[0006]	Existing SMS-parsing solutions may be categorized into template-based or regular expression parsers, or sophisticated systems using cloud-based natural language processing or complex on-device machine-learning models. US Patent No. 10,073,890 B1 discloses a combined semantical-probabilistic algorithm for reference comparison using Naive-Bayes statistical models, which demands heavy computational resources unsuitable for mobile resource constraints. US Patent No. 9,875,486 B2 discloses extracting product purchase information from electronic messages by learning message grammars via generalized suffix trees and trained classifiers, requiring training data and computer or server apparatus. US Patent Application Publication No. 2017/0193465 A1 discloses a server system for purchase transaction data retrieval with unobtrusive side channel data recovery by querying external network sidechannels, which is not offline-capable. US Patent Application Publication No. 2012/0330971 A1 discloses itemized receipt extraction using a trainable receipt-language model whose weights are updated via an accuracy score. US Patent Application Publication No. 2019/0297158 A1 discloses parsing transaction information for extraction and organization using NLP/OCR plus a machine learning model trained on data, targeting refund and return deadlines with backend processing support.
[0007]	Traditional regular expression parsers are reliable but fragile and susceptible to formatting changes, and have difficulty with messages containing multiple number types. Advanced machine learning solutions require large computational resources, may compromise privacy, may cause termination of the device operating system due to excessive memory demands, and function in an unpredictable manner making them unsuitable for financial auditing. There is no current solution that offers deterministic, auditable, and offline-compatible extraction with collision resolution for competing numeric values. The differentiation between semantically similar tokens, such as balance versus transaction amount when preceded by currency symbols, is not addressed by binary matching or single-confidence scoring approaches.
OBJECT
[0008]	In view of the foregoing, and without prejudice to the generality of the disclosure, it is an object of the present invention to provide a method for extracting financial transaction data from unstructured text messages. It is to be understood that the foregoing objects are illustrative and non-limiting; additional objects will be apparent from the description, examples, and claims, and need not be achieved in every embodiment.
[0009]	The object of the present disclosure is to provide a method for extracting financial transaction data from unstructured text messages that operates entirely on a mobile computing device without network transmission. The method aims to employ multi-dimensional heuristic vector scoring to classify numeric tokens by evaluating proximity to currency symbols, action verbs, account masks, and reference indicators. Further, the method seeks to resolve ambiguities between competing numeric values through deterministic collision resolution where higher-scoring dimensions suppress lower-scoring dimensions. The method also aims to provide reproducible results where the same inputs yield the same outputs for audit purposes, while remaining resistant to message format variations without requiring application updates.
[0010]	For the avoidance of doubt, the foregoing objects encompass compositions and manufacturing processes suitable for adoption in jurisdictions where claims to methods of treatment of animals may be restricted; corresponding “use” or “product” claim formats are contemplated without limitation.
SUMMARY
[0011]	The following summary is intended to introduce aspects of the present invention in a simplified form and does not identify all the features or the scope of the claimed invention. The summary is provided to assist in understanding the invention and is to be read in conjunction with the detailed description and accompanying drawings, claims, and abstract. The method further comprises extracting, by an evidence extractor (106), a plurality of numeric tokens from the message. The method further comprises computing, by the weight machine engine (108), a multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token of the plurality of numeric tokens, wherein each dimension of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) represents a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a respective semantic classification. The method further comprises performing, by the collision resolution module (112), collision resolution by comparing magnitudes across dimensions of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token, wherein a dimension having a higher magnitude suppresses competing dimensions having lower magnitudes. The method further comprises generating a transaction record (114) based on the collision resolution, wherein the transaction record (114) comprises structured financial data extracted from the message.
[0013]	The foregoing aspect provides the technical advantage of enabling deterministic extraction of structured financial data from unstructured text messages through evidence-based voting across multiple semantic categories, replacing brittle template matching with magnitude-based arbitration that resolves ambiguities between competing numeric values.
[0014]	According to other aspects of the present disclosure, the multi-dimensional score vector (110) may comprise five dimensions. [0046]	The present invention will now be described in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings illustrating exemplary embodiments.
[0047]	FIG. 1 illustrates a high-level architecture diagram of a system (100) for on-device financial transaction extraction according to various embodiments. The system (100) operates within a mobile computing device and is configured for on-device processing with a zero-knowledge architecture. The method for extracting financial transaction data from a message may be performed entirely on the mobile computing device without network transmission of the message or the transaction record (114).
[0048]	The system (100) comprises a message receiver (102) configured to receive incoming messages from an SMS subsystem of the mobile computing device. The message receiver (102) receives, at the mobile computing device, a message containing text. The message receiver (102) may encapsulate protocol data units (PDUs) with temporary metadata before placing the PDUs into a persistent background queue with guaranteed execution. The message receiver (102) may maintain a short acceptance time to prevent application-not-responding errors on the mobile computing device. In some cases, the message receiver (102) may receive messages from other messaging subsystems or notification services.
[0049]	The system (100) further comprises a background processing worker (104) configured to manage ordered processing of messages received by the message receiver (102). The background processing worker (104) may ensure that PDUs are processed in order while separating threads for transaction processing and user-interface updates. The system (100) may use event-driven background processing that prevents system failure under mobile operating system resource constraints. In some cases, the background processing worker (104) may employ alternative queue management approaches such as priority-based ordering or batch processing.
[0050]	The system (100) further comprises an evidence extractor (106) configured to analyze message content and identify semantic triggers and contextual features. The evidence extractor (106) may extract a plurality of numeric tokens from the message for subsequent scoring operations.
[0051]	The system (100) further comprises a weight machine engine (108) configured to perform multi-dimensional heuristic vector scoring. The weight machine engine (108) serves as a deterministic logic core that converts message strings into structured financial entities. The weight machine engine (108) may compute a multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token, wherein each dimension of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) represents a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a respective semantic classification.
[0052]	The system (100) further comprises a collision resolution module (112) configured to resolve ambiguities between competing numeric values through comparative magnitude analysis of vector dimensions. The collision resolution module (112) may perform collision resolution by comparing magnitudes across dimensions of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token, wherein a dimension having a higher magnitude suppresses competing dimensions having lower magnitudes. The collision resolution module (112) may generate a transaction record (114) based on the collision resolution, wherein the transaction record (114) comprises structured financial data extracted from the message.
[0053]	The system (100) further comprises a local transaction database (116) configured to store transaction records with cryptographic deduplication. The local transaction database (116) may be implemented using a relational database with write-ahead logging for concurrency management. The local transaction database (116) may employ atomic properties of database transactions for speed and consistency in storage operations. The transaction record (114) may be stored in the local transaction database (116) of the mobile computing device. In some cases, the local transaction database (116) may be implemented using alternative database technologies such as key-value stores or document databases.
[0054]	The system (100) further comprises an interface update coordinator (118) configured to manage updates to a user interface of the mobile computing device. The interface update coordinator (118) may provide system notifications for push-based interface updates rather than polling-based updates. The interface update coordinator (118) may update the user interface to display the transaction record (114). The interface update coordinator (118) may present summary and historical information in two separate views with manual adjustment capability. In some cases, the interface update coordinator (118) may employ alternative notification mechanisms such as callback-based updates or reactive data binding.
[0055]	FIG. 2 illustrates a detailed component diagram showing internal configurations of system components according to various embodiments. The message receiver (102) may be configured to receive system broadcasts, encapsulate message protocol data units, and enqueue background work. In some cases, the message receiver (102) may employ alternative message encapsulation formats such as JSON structures or binary serialization.
[0056]	The background processing worker (104) may be configured to dequeue and order messages, invoke an inference engine, persist transactions, and update views. The background processing worker (104) may use the evidence extractor (106) for processing incoming messages. The background processing worker (104) may persist data to the local transaction database (116) and notify the interface update coordinator (118).
[0057]	The evidence extractor (106) may be configured to parse message text and identify amount candidates, reference candidates, account-mask candidates, and date candidates. The evidence extractor (106) may extract a plurality of numeric tokens from the message. When multiple extraction methods return similar candidates, the evidence extractor (106) may select the best candidate by evaluating timestamp proximity, pattern accuracy, and supporting conditions. The system (100) may employ substring caching to avoid duplicate computation during token analysis. In some cases, the evidence extractor (106) may employ alternative candidate identification methods such as machine learning-based token detection or grammar-based parsing.
[0058]	The weight machine engine (108) may be configured to apply fixed weights and thresholds, perform hybrid parse orchestration, classify numeric tokens, compute confidence scores, resolve transaction direction, and generate cryptographic fingerprints. The weight machine engine (108) may operate as a stateless inference engine with fixed compile-time constant weights that are never trained or updated. The weight machine engine (108) may use pre-compiled regular expressions with match-limiting to prevent runaway processing on malformed inputs, providing bounded execution time. The weight machine engine (108) may maintain read-only semantic dictionaries that provide constant-time lookup for classification keywords. The system (100) may achieve thread-safe concurrent processing using immutable word collections for lock-free access. The system (100) may achieve linear-complexity algorithm execution suitable for constrained mobile environments.
[0059]	The weight machine engine (108) may produce several outputs including a numeric token structure comprising a value, start index, and end index. The weight machine engine (108) may also produce a score vector comprising transaction, balance, account, reference, and date dimensions. The weight machine engine (108) may generate a transaction record comprising an amount, type, and payer or payee fingerprint.
[0060]	The weight machine engine (108) may generate a cryptographic fingerprint based on characteristics of the message. The cryptographic fingerprint generation may combine all stable characteristics of a message including content and metadata for duplicate detection. The system (100) may compare the cryptographic fingerprint against stored fingerprints and reject the message as a duplicate responsive to the cryptographic fingerprint matching a stored fingerprint. In some cases, the cryptographic fingerprint may be generated using alternative algorithms such as SHA-256, MD5, or content-based hashing.
[0061]	FIG. 3 illustrates a flowchart for message processing and transaction extraction according to various embodiments. The process may begin when a new message is received at the message receiver (102). Prior to extracting the plurality of numeric tokens, the system (100) may filter the message through a multi-layer rejection architecture.
[0062]	The filtering may comprise rejecting the message responsive to the message matching one or more of a hard-skip pattern, a one-time password pattern, an advertisement pattern, and a fraud indicator pattern. The first decision point may check whether the message matches hard-skip patterns. If a match is found, the message may be dropped and processing may terminate. If the message does not match hard-skip patterns, the process may proceed to check whether the message contains transaction verbs such as debited, credited, or paid. If no transaction verbs are detected, the message may be dropped. If transaction verbs are present, the process may move to another decision point that checks whether the message matches one-time password, advertisement, promotional, or fraud patterns. If a match is detected, the message may be dropped. The system (100) may perform contextual fraud pattern detection as part of the multi-layer rejection architecture. In some cases, the multi-layer rejection architecture may include additional pattern types such as subscription notifications or account alerts.
[0063]	If no rejection pattern match is found, the process may continue to a parsing phase. The parsing phase may begin with extraction of numeric tokens from the message content. The system (100) may employ URL-aware token filtering that removes embedded paths from numeric token candidates before scoring. The system (100) may perform normalization of large numbers by converting regional conventions for word-form large numbers into uniform numeric form. The weight machine engine (108) may perform regional numbering normalization to convert non-standard numeric formats into standardized form. The weight machine engine (108) may employ language filters that reject messages with inconsistent grammar patterns.
[0064]	Each extracted token may then be scored using a five-dimensional scoring mechanism. The process may subsequently identify candidate amounts from the scored tokens. The system (100) may compute a confidence score based on the collision resolution. A confidence evaluation may be performed to determine whether the confidence level exceeds an adaptive threshold. The system (100) may employ adaptive thresholds where validation rules vary based on the quality of supporting evidence, with identifiers, references, or dates raising the requirement. If the confidence does not meet the threshold, the message may be dropped. The transaction record (114) may be generated responsive to the confidence score exceeding the adaptive threshold. In some cases, the adaptive threshold may be determined using alternative methods such as historical accuracy analysis or message source reputation.
[0065]	If the confidence exceeds the adaptive threshold, the process may proceed to extract additional information including date, reference, and account details. The system (100) may perform relative-date resolution by comparing temporal descriptors against message-received timestamps and converting the temporal descriptors to absolute date values. A transaction record may then be created based on the extracted information.
[0066]	The system (100) may determine a transaction direction for the transaction record (114) by performing aggregated keyword analysis of the message. The transaction direction may comprise one of a debit classification and a credit classification. The collision resolution module (112) may apply temporal and inverse context modifiers during global direction identification for transaction classification. The system (100) may implement a branded-noise score dimension that prevents reference-number misclassification as transaction amounts. In some cases, the transaction direction may be determined using alternative methods such as sender identification or message template matching.
[0067]	FIG. 4 illustrates a flowchart for five-dimensional score vector classification applied to numeric tokens according to various embodiments. The process may begin with receiving a numeric token and may proceed to initialize a five-dimensional score vector. The weight machine engine (108) may compute a multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token of the plurality of numeric tokens. Each dimension of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) may represent a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a respective semantic classification. The five dimensions may comprise transaction, balance, account, reference, and date dimensions.
[0068]	The process may then move to analyze a context window surrounding the numeric token. Computing the multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token may comprise analyzing a context window surrounding the numeric token. The context windows used by the weight machine engine (108) may be variable-length depending on the detection purpose being served. In some cases, the context window may span a fixed number of characters or words on either side of the numeric token.
[0069]	Following context window analysis, the system (100) may apply proximity-weighted scoring to evaluate the semantic context of the token. The process may comprise identifying semantic triggers within the context window. The semantic triggers may comprise one or more of currency markers, action verbs, account masks, and reference keywords. The system (100) may apply proximity-weighted scoring to each dimension of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) based on proximity of the numeric token to the identified semantic triggers. The weight machine engine (108) may apply both positive and negative weights to allow active suppression of inappropriate classifications during feature extraction. In some cases, the scoring weights may be configured differently for different message sources or regional formats.
[0070]	The scoring operation may branch into five parallel dimension scoring operations, each evaluating the token against a specific semantic category: transaction dimension scoring, balance dimension scoring, account dimension scoring, reference dimension scoring, and date dimension scoring. After the parallel scoring operations complete, the process may proceed to compare dimension magnitudes across all five dimensions.
[0071]	The collision resolution module (112) may perform collision resolution by comparing magnitudes across dimensions of the multi-dimensional score vector (110) for each numeric token. A dimension having a higher magnitude may suppress competing dimensions having lower magnitudes. The flowchart may then present a decision point that checks whether a currency marker is present, detecting indicators such as Rs. or INR. If a currency marker is detected, the process may apply a currency-priority override mechanism. The system (100) may detect an explicit currency marker adjacent to a numeric token of the plurality of numeric tokens and apply a currency-priority override that grants weighted advantage to a transaction amount classification for the numeric token. The currency-priority override may supersede suppression by competing dimensions. In some cases, the currency-priority override may be triggered by alternative currency indicators such as currency codes or symbol variations.
[0072]	If no currency marker is present, the process may proceed directly to suppress competing dimensions based on the comparative magnitude analysis. Both the currency-priority override path and the direct suppression path may converge at the suppress competing dimensions step. Following the suppression of competing dimensions, the process may assign a classification label to the numeric token based on the dominant dimension score. The flowchart may conclude with the output of a classified token.
[0073]	FIG. 5 illustrates a worked example of the five-dimensional score vector and deterministic collision-resolution mechanism according to various embodiments. An input message text such as "Rs. 15000 Debited From A/c XX1234 on 12-02-06. UPI Ref 887766554433" may be processed through a tokenizer. The tokenizer may extract numeric tokens from the message, identifying values such as 15000, 1234, 12, 02, 06, and 887766554433. In some cases, the tokenizer may employ alternative token extraction approaches such as regular expression matching or character-by-character scanning.
[0074]	The multi-dimensional score vector (110) may comprise five dimensions. The five dimensions may comprise a transaction amount dimension representing a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a transaction amount, an account balance dimension representing a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to an account balance, an account identifier dimension representing a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to an account identifier, a reference dimension representing a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a reference number, and a date dimension representing a likelihood that the numeric token corresponds to a date component.
[0075]	FIG. 5 depicts a transaction score vector (50) showing the score magnitude distribution for the token 15000. The transaction score vector (50) may show the transaction dimension with a high magnitude while the balance, account, reference, and date dimensions have minimal scores. The high magnitude in the transaction dimension may result from the proximity of the currency marker "Rs." to the numeric token 15000.
[0076]	FIG. 5 further depicts a reference score vector (60) showing the score magnitude distribution for the token 887766554433. The reference score vector (60) may show the reference dimension with a high magnitude while the transaction, balance, account, and date dimensions have minimal scores. The high magnitude in the reference dimension may result from the proximity of the reference keyword "Ref" to the numeric token 887766554433.
[0077]	At the collision resolution stage, the dimension of greatest magnitude may win and suppress competing dimensions. The explicit currency marker such as Rs. or INR may grant priority override to the transaction classification. In some cases, the magnitude comparison may employ alternative algorithms such as weighted voting or threshold-based selection.
[0078]	The final structured output produced by the system (100) may comprise an Amount field containing the value 15000, a Type field containing the value Debit, an Account field containing the value XX1234, and a Reference field containing the value 887766554433. In some cases, the output format may include additional fields such as date, time, or merchant information.
[0079]	The concepts, systems, and techniques disclosed herein are not limited to use in the example applications described herein, but rather may be useful in substantially any application where extraction of structured data from unstructured text messages is desired. While particular embodiments and applications of the present disclosure have been illustrated and described in connection with financial transaction extraction from SMS messages, embodiments of the disclosure are not limited to the precise constructions and compositions disclosed herein. The disclosed methods and systems may be applied in the mobile financial technology industry, the personal finance management industry, the banking and payment processing industry, and the edge computing industry. The disclosed methods and systems may also be applied in other industries where on-device text processing with privacy preservation is desired, such as healthcare messaging, logistics notifications, and enterprise communication systems.
[0080]	The disclosed methods and systems may provide several technical effects. The multi-dimensional heuristic vector scoring may enable classification of numeric tokens through evidence-based voting across multiple semantic categories, replacing brittle template matching with magnitude-based arbitration. The deterministic collision resolution may mathematically resolve ambiguities by magnitude comparison of each dimension, where higher-scoring dimensions suppress lower-scoring dimensions. The zero-knowledge architecture may enable processing entirely on-device with no ability to transmit data, eliminating interception and complying with data-protection regulations. The resource-optimized mobile execution may employ stateless, deterministic inference using linear-complexity algorithms suited to constrained environments.
