title: REAL TIME ROAD SIGN DETECTION FOR SPEED CONTROL AND ACCIDENT PREVENTION
abstract: The real-time road sign detection system is made to make the roads safer and to help with driving. It has a camera on the vehicle that takes pictures of the road all the time. These pictures are then looked at using computer programs and deep learning algorithms to find road signs such as speed-limit signs, STOP signs, and warning indications. The information that the system identifies is forwarded to the processing unit for more work and to make decisions. The traffic sign that the system finds is shown on a screen so the driver can see it away. The system also gives the driver warnings that they can see and hear when they need to. If the system sees a speed limit sign it can automatically make the vehicle go slower using a special control unit. The system uses computer vision, small computers and Internet of Things technology to find traffic signs and respond right away. The real-time road sign detection system helps drivers follow the traffic rules reduces mistakes that people make and lowers the chance of accidents on the road. The suggested system provides a reliable and intelligent approach that will make vehicles safe and improve transportation. The real time identification of traffic signs is a very important aspect that can help improve safety on roads. The other advantage of this system is that it helps to have intelligent driving through proper identification of traffic signs.
specification: The suggested project is dedicated to developing a real-time road sign detection system aimed at ensuring road and vehicle safety. There will be a camera installed in the vehicle that would take pictures of the road during the movement of the car. The obtained images are processed by computer vision technologies that detect significant traffic signs such as speed limit signs, STOP signs, and warning signs. After detection, the information is processed and the identified sign is shown on the display screen to inform the driver about the actions he/she needs to perform. It is also possible for the system to give an audio or visual signal to alert the driver. In case of speed limit detection, the system will help control the speed of the vehicle. ,
claims:
Claim 1

A road sign detection system that works in time for controlling vehicle speed and stopping accidents. It has a camera that takes pictures of the road all the time. There is a part that uses image processing and deep learning to find and sort traffic signs from the pictures. A small computer gets the information about the signs that are found. A screen shows the signs that are recognized to the driver. There is a way to make sounds and show lights to warn the driver. A motor control part changes the speed of the car depending on the signs that are seen. All these parts work together to recognize signs as they happen help the driver change speed automatically and make the roads safer, by reducing accidents.
  Claim 2

The real-time road sign detection system according to Claim 1 wherein the image processing and deep learning module is set up to identify categories of road signs including speed-limit signs, STOP signs, and warning indications. Once the traffic sign is detected the system shows the recognized traffic sign, on an LCD display turns on sound alerts to let the driver know and changes the vehicle speed using the motor control unit when a speed limit sign is found which makes driving safer helps follow traffic rules and makes the whole intelligent transportation system work better

title:
Adaptive In-Flight Battery Relay System for Extended
Endurance Autonomous Multirotor Drone Swarms
abstract:
Flight endurance remains the dominant constraint limiting the 
practical deployment of autonomous multirotor drones in persistent 
tasks such as infrastructure inspection, perimeter surveillance, and 
precision agriculture. An adaptive in-flight battery relay system is 
disclosed, in which a fleet of lightweight autonomous carrier drones 
delivers charged modular battery cells to a continuously operating 
working drone through an in-flight docking and hot-swap 
procedure, so that the working drone need never land during a 
mission. The system comprises three cooperating elements: a self
aligning electro-permanent magnetic quick-connect coupling with a 
conical probe-and-funnel geometry that tolerates residual lateral 
misalignment; a predictive dispatch scheduler at a ground station 
that estimates a time-to-depletion for the working drone and 
launches a charged carrier ahead of that deadline; and a 
downwash-aware relative-position stabilization controller that 
models the aerodynamic coupling between two closely spaced 
multirotors and holds the relative offset inside a narrow capture 
window during contact. A modular dual-cell power path allows one 
battery cell to be replaced while a second continues to supply 
power, so that propulsion is never interrupted. By delivering energy 
to the working drone where and while it operates, the invention 
converts flight endurance from a hard per-flight limit into a logistics 
parameter that scales with the number of carrier drones.
specification:
PREAMBLE TO THE DESCRIPTION 
[0001] 
In this disclosure, an adaptive in-flight battery relay system is 
presented for extending the operational endurance of autonomous 
multirotor drones performing persistent tasks such as infrastructure 
inspection, perimeter surveillance, and precision agriculture. A fleet 
of lightweight autonomous carrier drones delivers charged modular 
battery cells to a continuously operating working drone through an 
in-flight docking and hot-swap procedure, so that the working drone 
need never land during a mission. The system comprises a self
aligning electro-permanent magnetic quick-connect coupling with a 
conical probe-and-funnel geometry that tolerates residual lateral 
misalignment during docking; a predictive dispatch scheduler at a 
ground station that estimates a time-to-depletion for the working 
drone and launches a charged carrier ahead of that deadline; and a 
downwash-aware relative-position stabilization controller that 
models the aerodynamic coupling between two closely spaced 
multirotors and holds the relative offset inside a narrow capture 
window during contact. A modular dual-cell power path allows one 
battery cell to be replaced while a second continues to supply 
power, so that propulsion is never interrupted. The proposed relay 
architecture converts flight endurance from a hard per-flight limit 
into a logistics parameter that scales with the number of carrier 
drones, making it a strong candidate for persistent autonomous 
aerial operations. 
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION 
[0002] 
The demand for persistent, uninterrupted aerial coverage is a 
primary area of concern in the modern deployment of autonomous 
multirotor drones. Present-day multirotors are limited to twenty to 
forty minutes of useful flight per battery charge, because lift is 
produced continuously by the rotors and the specific energy of 
currently available battery cells is modest relative to the power 
consumed. For applications that require persistent presence, such 
as continuous monitoring of a pipeline, a solar farm, a construction 
site, a border, or a crop, this ceiling forces the operation to be 
broken into short sorties separated by long ground charging 
intervals. 
[0003] 
Several classes of solution have previously been proposed 
to extend endurance, and each improves one property at the 
expense of another. Increasing on-board battery capacity adds 
mass, so that the marginal endurance gained per additional cell 
diminishes rapidly and can even reverse. Ground battery-swap 
stations reduce turnaround time relative to charging in place, but 
the working drone must still leave its task, land, and return, so 
continuous coverage of the asset is lost during every swap. 
Physical power tethers deliver unlimited energy from the ground but 
confine the drone to a small radius around a tether reel and 
introduce a heavy, drag-inducing cable. Wireless power transfer 
and stationary charging pads remove the physical connector but still 
require the drone to descend onto, or hover precisely over, a fixed 
location, again interrupting the mission. In each case the 
fundamental difficulty is that the energy source is either carried, and 
therefore mass-limited, or fixed to the ground, and therefore 
mobility-limited. 
[0004] 
The present invention overcomes these limitations by making 
the energy source itself mobile and by delivering energy to the 
working drone at its point of operation, without requiring that drone 
to land. The invention comprises three cooperating elements: a self
aligning quick-connect coupling that mechanically corrects residual 
misalignment during an in-flight docking approach; a modular dual
cell power path that keeps the working drone continuously powered 
throughout a battery transfer; and a predictive dispatch scheduler, 
supported by a downwash-aware relative-position controller, that 
ensures a charged carrier drone is always available at the point of 
need. 
[0005] 
Figure 1 shows the overall system architecture. The system 
comprises a ground station, a fleet of carrier drones, and at least 
one working drone. The ground station maintains fleet 
management, predictive dispatch, dock management, and telemetry 
and health monitoring functions, and holds a set of charged carrier 
drones on charging pads, each carrier carrying a modular battery 
cell. When a relay is required, a charged carrier drone is dispatched 
from the ground station and navigates autonomously to rendezvous 
with the working drone in flight. The carrier drone docks with the 
working drone without requiring the working drone to land, transfers 
its charged cell, and the depleted carrier then returns to the ground 
station's automated dock, which provides auto landing assist, 
wireless power transfer, and auto alignment for recharging. 
[0006] 
Figure 2 shows the operational relay sequence in six stages. 
At stage T0, a carrier drone is launched from the ground station 
carrying a charged battery cell. At stage T1, the carrier drone 
autonomously navigates en route toward the working drone. At 
stage T2, the carrier drone performs auto alignment and docks with 
the working drone in flight, without either aircraft landing. At stage 
T3, the depleted cell is released from the working drone and the 
charged cell is engaged, this hot-swap transfer being completed in 
under twenty seconds. At stage T4, the carrier drone undocks and 
the working drone continues its mission seamlessly. At stage T5, 
the depleted carrier drone returns to the ground station base for 
recharging. 
[0007] 
Figure 3 shows the self-aligning quick-connect coupling in 
cross-section. The working drone carries a docking receptacle 
comprising a funnel-shaped recess that provides coarse alignment, 
together with spring-loaded electrical contacts for power and data 
and an electro-permanent magnet ring disposed about the recess. 
The carrier drone carries a self-centering conical probe, mounted 
above its modular battery cell, that provides fine alignment. As the 
conical probe enters the funnel-shaped recess, any residual lateral 
offset between the two aircraft is converted into a centering force by 
the sloped walls of the funnel, so that the sprung contacts seat 
concentrically even when the approach is imperfect. The electro
permanent magnet ring retains the probe within the receptacle 
without continuous electrical power once latched, and releases the 
probe in response to a momentary electrical pulse, so that a loss of 
power cannot strand the two aircraft locked together. 
[0008] 
Figure 4 shows the modular dual-cell power path that 
ensures propulsion is never interrupted during a battery transfer. 
The working drone carries a first modular battery cell, designated 
the reserve cell, and a second modular battery cell, designated the 
hot-swap cell, both electrically coupled through an ideal-diode 
power-OR bus to the flight controller and motors of the working 
drone. During normal flight, the reserve cell remains on the active 
path of the bus at all times. When a relay is performed, the hot
swap cell is disengaged from the standby path and replaced by the 
carrier drone with a charged cell, while the reserve cell continues, 
uninterrupted, to supply the flight controller. Because the reserve 
cell remains connected throughout, there is no instant at which the 
working drone is unpowered, and a failed docking attempt can be 
safely aborted at any stage, with the working drone continuing on its 
reserve cell until a replacement carrier is dispatched. 
[0009] 
Figure 5 shows the predictive dispatch scheduler 
implemented at the ground station, represented as a cyclic state 
machine. The scheduler continuously monitors the working drone's 
state of charge and telemetry, predicts a time-to-depletion from the 
recent power history, dispatches a carrier drone carrying a charged 
cell before that predicted instant, manages the rendezvous and 
docking procedure, executes the hot-swap transfer, and then 
returns to monitoring while the working drone undocks and resumes 
its mission. This loop repeats for the duration of the mission. 
Because the prediction is refreshed continuously, transient 
increases in power demand, such as those caused by wind gusts or 
aggressive manoeuvres, automatically advance the dispatch of the 
next carrier drone. 
[0010] 
Figure 6 shows the downwash-aware relative-position control 
pipeline employed during the final docking approach. The controller 
estimates the aerodynamic downwash produced by the working 
drone's rotors, which would otherwise disturb the carrier drone 
during close proximity flight, and feeds this estimate into a state 
estimation stage and a relative-pose control stage defined in a 
body-frame convention referenced to the working drone. The 
relative-pose control stage drives the carrier drone into a narrow 
capture window before the self-centering probe engages the 
docking receptacle described with reference to Figure 3, so that the 
coupling geometry completes the final alignment. 
[0011] 
The invention provides a number of advantages over 
previously known endurance strategies. Unlike a larger on-board 
battery, the invention adds only the modest mass of a dual-cell 
power path rather than a single oversized battery pack. Unlike a 
ground battery-swap station or a wireless charging pad, the 
invention does not require the working drone to leave its task or to 
descend to a fixed location. Unlike a physical tether, the invention 
imposes no restriction on the mobility of the working drone, since it 
is the carrier drone, and not a cable, that reaches the working 
drone. Because each relay restores the working drone's charge, the 
sustainable duration of a mission is governed by the size of the 
carrier fleet and the rate at which the ground station can recharge 
returned cells, rather than by the capacity of any single on-board 
battery, so that flight endurance is converted from a fixed per-flight 
limit into a logistics parameter that can be provisioned by an 
operator to meet a required mission duration. 
[0012] 
The invention is applicable to a wide range of persistent 
autonomous aerial operations, including infrastructure inspection, 
perimeter and border surveillance, precision agriculture, and 
continuous environmental or asset monitoring, wherever an 
autonomous multirotor drone is required to remain airborne and on 
task for a duration exceeding the endurance of a single on-board 
battery. 
[0013] 
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS 
Figure 1 shows the system architecture of the proposed in
flight battery relay, including the ground station, the carrier drone 
fleet, the working drone, and the automated dock. 
[0014] 
Figure 2 shows the operational relay sequence, from 
dispatch of a carrier drone through in-flight docking and hot-swap 
transfer to the return of the depleted carrier drone to the ground 
station. 
[0015] 
Figure 3 shows a cross-section of the self-aligning probe
and-funnel coupling with electro-permanent magnet retention, by 
which the carrier drone docks with the working drone in flight. 
[0016] 
Figure 4 shows the modular dual-cell ideal-diode power-OR 
bus, by which a reserve battery cell continuously powers the 
working drone while a second cell is hot-swapped. 
[0017] 
Figure 5 shows the predictive dispatch scheduler, 
represented as a cyclic state machine, by which the ground station 
monitors state of charge and dispatches carrier drones ahead of a 
predicted depletion instant. 
[0018] 
Figure 6 shows the downwash-aware relative-position 
control pipeline and body-frame convention used to guide the 
carrier drone into a narrow capture window during the final docking 
approach.  ,
claims:
1. We claim: An in-flight battery relay system for extending the operational 
endurance of an autonomous multirotor drone, the system comprising: 
a working drone configured to perform a mission task while airborne, 
the working drone including a power bus connected to at least two 
modular battery cells arranged such that at least one of the modular 
battery cells remains electrically connected to the power bus at all 
times; a docking receptacle mounted on the working drone, the docking 
receptacle comprising a funnel-shaped recess and an electro
permanent magnet ring disposed about the recess; at least one carrier 
drone configured to carry a charged modular battery cell and having a 
self-centering probe configured to mate with the docking receptacle of 
the working drone during flight; and a ground station in communication 
with the working drone and the at least one carrier drone, the ground 
station being configured to receive telemetry data from the working 
drone indicative of a state of charge, to predict, from the telemetry 
data, a time to depletion of a power reserve of the working drone, and 
to dispatch the at least one carrier drone to rendezvous with the 
working drone in flight, before the predicted time to depletion, so as to 
deliver the charged modular battery cell to the working drone without 
requiring the working drone to land. 
2. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the self-centering probe 
comprises a conical male member configured to engage the funnel
shaped recess of the docking receptacle so as to mechanically correct 
a lateral misalignment between the at least one carrier drone and the 
working drone during a docking approach. 
3. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the electro-permanent 
magnet ring is configured to retain the self-centering probe within the 
docking receptacle without continuous electrical power, and to release 
the self-centering probe in response to a momentary electrical pulse. 
4. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the power bus comprises an 
ideal-diode power-OR bus electrically coupling a first modular battery 
cell and a second modular battery cell to a flight controller of the 
working drone, such that the flight controller draws power from the first 
modular battery cell while the second modular battery cell is 
disengaged and replaced by the at least one carrier drone, thereby 
preventing an interruption in propulsion of the working drone during a 
battery transfer. 
5. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the ground station is further 
configured to recompute the predicted time to depletion continuously 
during the mission task, and to advance a dispatch of the at least one

title: A SPLIT TYPE COMBINED BRAKING SYSTEM
abstract:
A SPLIT TYPE COMBINED BRAKING SYSTEM. A split type combined braking system (100) for a vehicle includes a master cylinder housing (102) having a master cylinder (204) and a piston (604). A brake lever (104) is pivotably mounted on the housing (102) and configured to actuate the piston (604). A piston plunger (222) is pivotably supported relative to the housing (102) and operatively engageable with the piston (604). A combined braking system arrangement (201) includes a CBS plunger (220) operatively connectable at one end to a braking input. The piston plunger (222) has a wedge-shaped projection (504a), and the CBS plunger (220) has a complementary recessed wedge surface (504b), together defining a wedge interface. Actuation of the CBS plunger (220) displaces the piston plunger (222) to actuate the piston (604), while the brake lever (104) independently displaces the piston plunger (222).
Reference figure: FIG. 3
specification:
DESCRIPTION
Background
[0001]	Unless otherwise indicated herein, the materials described in this section are not prior art to the claims in this application and are not admitted to being prior art by inclusion in this section.
Field of the invention:
[0002]	The present invention relates generally to braking system for vehicles. More particularly, the present invention relates to a braking system with a cable-operated combined braking system (CBS) for two-wheelers.
Discussion of the related field:
[0003]	Braking systems are widely used in two-wheeled vehicles to provide effective vehicle deceleration and stopping performance. In such systems, a brake lever operated by a rider generates actuation force within a master cylinder assembly, which in turn transmits the braking force to a corresponding brake mechanism associated with the vehicle wheel. The consistency and smoothness of force transmission from the brake lever to the master cylinder piston significantly influence the overall braking performance and rider control.
[0004]	Many modern two-wheelers incorporate a combined braking system (CBS), in which actuation of a rear brake control partially actuates a front brake . In cable-operated CBS arrangements, the pulling force generated during rear brake actuation is transmitted through a cable to an actuator mechanism associated with the front brake system. Such systems improve braking balance and distribute braking forces between the front and rear wheels, thereby enhancing vehicle stability during deceleration.
[0005]	Although cable-operated CBS arrangements provide the aforementioned advantages, integration of such mechanisms with master cylinder assemblies may introduce certain challenges. In conventional arrangements, the actuator mechanism that transfers force from the CBS cable to the master cylinder piston is typically formed as a single, unitary member that also interfaces directly with the brake lever. Because this single actuator member serves both the CBS actuation path and the brake lever actuation path, actuation of the combined braking system may cause unintended movement of the brake lever, or actuation of the brake lever may cause unintended movement of the CBS actuator, resulting in irregular transmission of force to the master cylinder piston.
[0006]	Furthermore, because a single actuator member is shared between the CBS mechanism and the brake lever in such conventional configurations, the actuation path of the CBS mechanism and the actuation path of the brake lever remain mechanically interdependent. Movement initiated through one actuation path may influence or interfere with the other, resulting in inconsistent engagement of the master cylinder piston and variation in braking response between manual lever actuation and CBS operation. These limitations may adversely affect braking feel, controllability, and overall braking system performance. In particular, the mechanical coupling arising from the shared, unitary construction of the CBS actuator and the lever mechanism may result in unintended lever movement during CBS activation, which may reduce rider comfort and introduce inconsistencies in braking response. Additionally, such coupling may necessitate substantial modification of existing brake lever assemblies to accommodate the CBS mechanism, thereby increasing structural complexity and manufacturing cost.
[0007]	In light of the foregoing, there is a need for a brake actuator assembly for a combined braking system in which the actuation path of the CBS arrangement and the actuation path of the brake lever are structurally separated rather than sharing a single, unitary actuator member, thereby overcoming the shortcomings associated with existing braking system designs.
SUMMARY
[0008]	A braking system for a two-wheeled vehicle includes a master cylinder housing. The master cylinder housing includes a master cylinder and a piston. A brake lever is pivotably mounted on the master cylinder housing. The brake lever is configured to actuate the piston. The braking system further includes a piston plunger. The piston plunger is pivotably supported relative to the master cylinder housing. The piston plunger is configured to be operatively engageable with the piston. The braking system also includes a combined braking system arrangement. 
[0009]	Further, the combined braking system arrangement includes a CBS plunger. The CBS plunger is configured to be operatively connectable, at one end, to a braking input. The piston plunger includes a wedge-shaped projection. The CBS plunger includes a recessed wedge surface that is complementary in shape to the wedge-shaped projection of the piston plunger. The wedge-shaped projection is configured to engage the recessed wedge surface. The engagement between the wedge-shaped projection and the recessed wedge surface defines a wedge interface. When the CBS plunger is actuated, the movement of the CBS plunger is transferred through the wedge interface to displace the piston plunger. The displacement of the piston plunger, in turn, actuates the piston. The brake lever is also configured to displace the piston plunger. Actuation of the brake lever causes displacement of the piston plunger through engagement with the brake lever, independently of the CBS plunger. Thus, the piston can be actuated through movement of the piston plunger either by actuation of the CBS plunger through the wedge interface or by actuation of the brake lever independently of the CBS plunger.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
[0019]	The following detailed description includes references to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of the detailed description. The drawings show illustrations in accordance with example embodiments. These example embodiments, which may be herein also referred to as “examples” are described in enough detail to enable those skilled in the art to practice the present subject matter. However, it may be apparent to one with ordinary skill in the art, that the present invention may be practised without these specific details. In other instances, well-known methods, procedures and components have not been described in detail so as not to unnecessarily obscure aspects of the embodiments. The embodiments can be combined, other embodiments can be utilized, or structural, logical, and design changes can be made without departing from the scope of the claims. The foregoing detailed description is, therefore, not to be taken in a limiting sense, and the scope is defined by the appended claims and their equivalents.
[0020]	In this document, the terms “a” or “an” are used, as is common in patent documents, to include one or more than one. In this document, the term “or” is used to refer to a nonexclusive “or” such that “A or B” includes “A but not B,” “B but not A,” and “A and B,” unless otherwise indicated.
[0021]	Referring to FIG. 1, a split-type combined braking system 100 (hereinafter referred to as the braking system 100) for a vehicle is disclosed. The braking system 100 includes a master cylinder housing 102, a brake lever 104, a plunger assembly 106, and a clamp 108. The master cylinder housing 102 may be configured as a rigid structural body adapted to support hydraulic and mechanical components of the braking system 100, while the brake lever 104 may be  pivotably mounted on the master cylinder housing 102 and configured to be actuated by a rider to generate braking force.
[0022]	The brake lever 104 may include an elongated lever body having a proximal portion positioned adjacent to the master cylinder housing 102 and a distal portion configured to be engaged by the rider during braking. The distal portion of the brake lever 104 may include an enlarged end or ball end configured to provide a comfortable and safe gripping surface for the rider. The brake lever 104 may further include a lever link 110 provided as a rigid member at the proximal portion of the brake lever 104 and protruding toward the master cylinder housing 102. In an embodiment, the lever link 110 may be formed integrally with the brake lever 104 and may be configured to directly contact and actuate a piston plunger 222 upon actuation of the brake lever 104. The plunger assembly 106 may be operatively positioned at the proximal portion of the brake lever 104, between the brake lever 104 and the master cylinder housing 102 and may be configured to transmit mechanical force generated during actuation of the brake lever 104 toward hydraulic components disposed within the master cylinder housing 102. The plunger assembly 106 will be described in greater detail below.
[0023]	The clamp 108 may be provided on the master cylinder housing 102 and may be configured to mount the braking system 100 onto a handlebar of the vehicle. The clamp 108 may define a clamping region configured to receive the handlebar and may include cooperating clamp portions configured to secure the master cylinder housing 102 to the handlebar when tightened. In an alternative embodiment, the clamp 108 may be replaced by any suitable mounting arrangement, such as a bracket, an integrated mounting boss, or a fastener-based mounting interface, depending on the configuration of the vehicle on which the braking system 100 is installed.
[0024]	In an embodiment, the braking system 100 may be mounted on a right side of a handlebar of a two-wheeled vehicle, wherein the brake lever 104 is configured to be actuated by a right hand of the rider, for example to operate a front brake of the vehicle. In an alternative embodiment, the braking system 100 may be mounted on a left side of the handlebar of the two-wheeled vehicle, wherein the brake lever 104 is configured to be actuated by a left hand of the rider, for example to operate a rear brake of the vehicle. In such configurations, the orientation of the master cylinder housing 102, the brake lever 104, and the plunger assembly 106 may be mirrored to suit left-hand or right-hand mounting.
[0025]	Furthermore, the braking system 100 may not be limited to two-wheeled vehicles. In alternative embodiments, the braking system 100 may be mounted on a right side or a left side of a handlebar of a three-wheeled vehicle, or on any other vehicle employing a handlebar-operated or lever-operated braking arrangement, including but not limited to scooters, motorcycles, mopeds, all-terrain vehicles, quadricycles, and electric vehicles. The braking system 100 may therefore be adapted to any vehicle configuration in which a lever-actuated master cylinder is employed, and references herein to a two-wheeled vehicle are intended to be illustrative rather than limiting.
[0026]	Referring to FIG. 2, the braking system 100 is illustrated in a back view showing the combined braking system (CBS) arrangement 201 in association with the master cylinder housing 102. The master cylinder housing 102 may define an internal chamber configured to accommodate a master cylinder 204. The master cylinder 204 may define a cylindrical bore within which a piston 604 is configured to reciprocate to generate hydraulic pressure during operation of the braking system 100.
[0027]	The master cylinder housing 102 may include a fluid reservoir 202a positioned on an upper region of the master cylinder housing 102. The fluid reservoir 202a may define a hollow chamber configured to store hydraulic brake fluid required for operation of the braking system 100. The fluid reservoir 202a may be fluidly connected to the master cylinder 204 through an internal fluid passage formed within the master cylinder housing 102, thereby enabling hydraulic fluid to be supplied to the master cylinder 204 during actuation. The fluid reservoir 202a may be enclosed by a fluid reservoir cover 202b removably secured on top of the fluid reservoir 202a. The fluid reservoir cover 202b may be configured to seal the fluid reservoir 202a so as to prevent leakage and contamination of the hydraulic fluid, while permitting access to the fluid reservoir 202a for inspection and replenishment of the hydraulic fluid.
[0028]	In an embodiment, a hydraulic port 206 may be provided on one side of the master cylinder housing 102. The hydraulic port 206 may define a fluid outlet passage configured to establish fluid communication between the master cylinder 204 and an external brake line connected to a braking mechanism of the vehicle, thereby allowing hydraulic pressure generated within the master cylinder 204 to be transmitted to the braking mechanism.
[0029]	Referring to FIG. 2, the braking system 100 may further include the CBS arrangement 201 positioned adjacent to a bottom region of the master cylinder housing 102. The CBS arrangement 201 may include a CBS cable comprising an outer cable 210 and an inner cable 212 arranged within the outer cable 210, a CBS adjuster nut 208, a CBS bracket 216, a CBS bracket pivot pin 218, and a CBS plunger 220.
[0030]	In an embodiment, the outer cable 210 may be supported relative to the master cylinder housing 102 through the CBS adjuster nut 208. The CBS adjuster nut 208 may include a threaded cylindrical body configured to engage a corresponding threaded portion provided on the master cylinder housing 102, such that the CBS adjuster nut 208 is supported and retained relative to the master cylinder housing 102. The CBS adjuster nut 208 may further include a central passage extending axially therethrough along a longitudinal axis of the CBS adjuster nut 208. One end of the CBS adjuster nut 208 may define a seat configured to receive and abut an end of the outer cable 210, such that the outer cable 210 is retained against the CBS adjuster nut 208, while the inner cable 212 may extend through the central passage and beyond an opposite end of the CBS adjuster nut 208 so as to remain slidable relative to the outer cable 210. The threaded engagement of the CBS adjuster nut 208 may further permit adjustment of cable tension by varying the axial position of the CBS adjuster nut 208 relative to the master cylinder housing 102.
[0031]	The inner cable 212 may extend from the CBS adjuster nut 208 toward the CBS bracket 216. The CBS bracket 216 may be configured as an elongated linkage member positioned adjacent to the master cylinder housing 102. A first end of the CBS bracket 216 may be configured to be connected to a braking input, through engagement with an end portion of the inner cable 212, thereby enabling transmission of movement from the braking input to the CBS bracket 216. The CBS bracket 216 may further include a pivot portion configured to receive the CBS bracket pivot pin 218. The CBS bracket pivot pin 218 may extend through the pivot portion of the CBS bracket 216 and a corresponding portion of the CBS plunger 220, thereby pivotably connecting the CBS bracket 216 to the CBS plunger 220, such that the CBS plunger 220 is operatively connectable to the braking input via the CBS bracket 216.
[0032]	The CBS plunger 220 may be positioned below the piston plunger 222 and adjacent to the master cylinder housing 102. The piston plunger 222 may be positioned adjacent to the proximal portion of the brake lever 104 and may be configured to transmit mechanical force toward the piston 604 disposed within the master cylinder 204. The term split type, as used with reference to the braking system 100, refers to the plunger assembly 106 being configured as two separate, independently pivotable plunger members, namely the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220, rather than as a single, unitary actuator element, such that the piston plunger 222 may be displaced either through the wedge interface upon actuation of the CBS plunger 220, or independently through direct engagement with the brake lever 104, without either actuation path being kinematically dependent on the other. The structural configuration of the CBS plunger 220 and the piston plunger 222, including the interlocking configuration therebetween, is explained in detail in subsequent sections with reference to FIG. 5.
[0033]	Referring to FIG. 3, the braking system 100 is illustrated in a perspective view showing the pivotable mounting of the brake lever 104, the piston plunger 222, and the CBS plunger 220 relative to the master cylinder housing 102. The brake lever 104 may include a mounting hole positioned near the proximal portion of the brake lever 104. The mounting hole may be configured to receive a lever pivot bolt 302, which may extend through the mounting hole of the brake lever 104 and corresponding aligned openings formed in the master cylinder housing 102. The lever pivot bolt 302 may be secured using a lock nut 304, thereby enabling the brake lever 104 to pivot about the lever pivot bolt 302 relative to the master cylinder housing 102 about a pivot axis X-X’ during actuation.
[0034]	The lock nut 304 may be threadedly engaged with an end portion of the lever pivot bolt 302 and may be configured to prevent loosening of the lever pivot bolt 302 due to vibrations encountered during operation of the vehicle, thereby maintaining a secure pivotable connection between the brake lever 104 and the master cylinder housing 102 throughout the service life of the braking system 100.
[0035]	Referring to FIG. 3, the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 may be positioned adjacent to each other between the proximal portion of the brake lever 104 and the master cylinder housing 102. The piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 may be pivotably supported relative to the master cylinder housing 102 through a plunger pivot pin 306. The plunger pivot pin 306 may extend through corresponding pivot portions formed on the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 and through aligned openings provided in the master cylinder housing 102, thereby pivotably supporting the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 relative to the master cylinder housing 102 about a common pivot axis.
[0036]	Through this configuration, the brake lever 104 pivots about the pivot axis X-X’ defined by the lever pivot bolt 302, while the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 pivot about the common pivot axis defined by the plunger pivot pin 306. The pivot axis defined by the plunger pivot pin 306 may be arranged substantially parallel to and spaced apart from the pivot axis X-X’, such that pivoting movement of the brake lever 104 may be transmitted to the piston plunger 222 through contact engagement, while the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 remain independently pivotable relative to the brake lever 104. The pivot axis of the plunger pivot pin 306, designated Y-Y’ (refer FIG. 4A), and the detailed structural configuration of the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 are explained further with reference to FIG.5.
[0037]	Referring to FIGs. 4A and 4B, the master cylinder housing 102 of the braking system 100 is illustrated without the brake lever 104 to show structural features thereof. The master cylinder housing 102 may be configured as a rigid structural body adapted to support hydraulic and mechanical components of the braking system 100. The master cylinder housing 102 may include the fluid reservoir 202a, the master cylinder 204, the hydraulic port 206, the clamp 108, a C-shaped mounting slot 408, a lower mounting plate 410a, an upper mounting plate 410b, and mounting holes 402, 403, 406, and 412.
[0038]	Referring to FIG. 4A, the clamp 108 may be provided on the master cylinder housing 102 and may define a clamping region configured to receive a handlebar of the vehicle along a handlebar line 404. The clamp 108 may include cooperating clamp portions configured to secure the master cylinder housing 102 to the handlebar when tightened, thereby mounting the braking system 100 onto the vehicle.
[0039]	The master cylinder housing 102 comprises the upper mounting plate 410b and the lower mounting plate 410a extending outwardly from one side of the master cylinder housing 102, opposite to the fluid reservoir 202a. The upper mounting plate 410b and the lower mounting plate 410a are arranged in a spaced-apart and parallel configuration so as to define a space 414 there between. The space 414 is specifically configured to accommodate the piston plunger 222, the CBS plunger 220, and at least a portion of the brake lever 104.
[0040]	In an embodiment, the upper mounting plate 410b may be provided with the mounting holes 402 and 406, and the lower mounting plate 410a may be provided with the mounting holes 403 and 412, respectively, aligned correspondingly therewith. The mounting holes 402 and 403 may be aligned along the pivot axis X-X’ and may be configured to receive the lever pivot bolt 302, such that the brake lever 104 is pivotably supported relative to the master cylinder housing 102 within the space 414. The mounting holes 406 and 412 may be aligned along the pivot axis Y-Y’ and may be configured to receive the plunger pivot pin 306, such that the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 are pivotably supported relative to the master cylinder housing 102 within the space 414. The pivot axis X-X’ and the pivot axis Y-Y’ may be arranged substantially parallel to and spaced apart from each other, thereby defining independent pivot locations for the brake lever 104 and for the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220.
[0041]	Referring to FIG. 4B, the fluid reservoir 202a may be positioned on an upper region of the master cylinder housing 102 and may define a hollow chamber configured to store hydraulic brake fluid required for operation of the braking system 100. The master cylinder housing 102 may define an internal chamber configured to accommodate the master cylinder 204, wherein the fluid reservoir 202a may be fluidly connected to the master cylinder 204 through an internal fluid passage formed within the master cylinder housing 102. The hydraulic port 206 may be provided on one side of the master cylinder housing 102 and may define a fluid outlet passage configured to establish fluid communication between the master cylinder 204 and an external brake line of the vehicle.
[0042]	The master cylinder housing 102 may further include a portion protruding downwardly from a bottom region of the master cylinder housing 102 near the hydraulic port 206, thereby forming the C-shaped mounting slot 408. The C-shaped mounting slot 408 may define an open channel having a threaded portion configured to receive and support the CBS adjuster nut 208 of the CBS arrangement 201. Through this configuration, the CBS arrangement 201 may be guided and supported at the bottom region of the master cylinder housing 102, thereby enabling integration of the CBS arrangement 201 with the master cylinder housing 102 without requiring modification of the brake lever 104.
[0043]	Referring to FIG. 5, the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 of the plunger assembly 106 are illustrated in an enlarged view showing an interlocking configuration therebetween. The piston plunger 222 may be configured as an elongated structural member extending generally toward the master cylinder housing 102. The piston plunger 222 may include a plurality of structural portions formed integrally with a body of the piston plunger 222, including a pivot portion 506a, a protruding member 502a, and a wedge-shaped projection 504a.
[0044]	The pivot portion 506a may be formed on an upper region of the piston plunger 222 and may define an opening configured to receive the plunger pivot pin 306. The plunger pivot pin 306 may extend through the pivot portion 506a and through the corresponding mounting holes formed in the upper mounting plate 410b and the lower mounting plate 410a of the master cylinder housing 102, thereby pivotably supporting the piston plunger 222 relative to the master cylinder housing 102 for pivoting movement about the pivot axis Y-Y’.
[0045]	The protruding member 502a may extend from a forward region, in other words, an end region of the piston plunger 222 that faces the piston 604. The protruding member 502a may be configured to engage the piston 604 disposed within the master cylinder 204 and may define a contact surface through which mechanical force is transmitted from the piston plunger 222 to the piston 604.
[0046]	In an embodiment, the piston plunger 222 may further include the wedge-shaped projection 504a extending downwardly from a lower region of the piston plunger 222, in between the pivot portion 506a and the protruding member 502a. The wedge-shaped projection 504a may define an engagement surface configured to interact with a corresponding recessed wedge surface 504b of the CBS plunger 220, thereby establishing a structural interface between the piston plunger 222 and the CBS arrangement 201.
[0047]	Referring to FIG. 5, the CBS plunger 220 may be positioned below the piston plunger 222 and may be configured as an elongated structural member arranged adjacent to the master cylinder housing 102. The CBS plunger 220 may include a plurality of structural portions formed integrally with a body of the CBS plunger 220, including a pivot portion 506b, a recessed wedge surface 504b, and a protruding member 502b.
[0048]	The pivot portion 506b may be formed on an upper region of the CBS plunger 220 and may define an opening configured to receive the plunger pivot pin 306. The plunger pivot pin 306 may extend through the pivot portion 506b of the CBS plunger 220 and through the corresponding mounting holes provided in the upper mounting plate 410b and the lower mounting plate 410a, thereby pivotably supporting the CBS plunger 220 relative to the master cylinder housing 102 about the pivot axis Y-Y’, common to the piston plunger 222.
[0049]	The recessed wedge surface 504b may extend upwardly from an upper portion of the CBS plunger 220. The recessed wedge surface 504b may define an engagement surface configured to interact with the wedge-shaped projection 504a formed on the piston plunger 222. The recessed wedge surface 504b may be shaped with a complementary geometry corresponding to the wedge-shaped projection 504a. The protruding member 502b may extend from a lower portion of the CBS plunger 220 and may be configured to connect with the pivot portion of the CBS bracket 216 through the CBS bracket pivot pin 218, thereby enabling mechanical movement transmitted through the inner cable 212 and the CBS bracket 216 to be transferred toward the CBS plunger 220, thereby actuating the piston plunger 222.
[0050]	Referring to FIG. 5, the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 may be positioned adjacent to each other within the braking system 100, such that a lower region of the piston plunger 222 is arranged above an upper region of the CBS plunger 220. In this configuration, the wedge-shaped projection 504a formed on the piston plunger 222 may be positioned directly above the recessed wedge surface 504b formed on the CBS plunger 220. The wedge-shaped projection 504a may define a contact surface, while the recessed wedge surface 504b may define a corresponding complementary surface. The complementary geometries of the wedge-shaped projection 504a and the recessed wedge surface 504b may thereby define an interlocking wedge interface between the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220.
[0051]	In an embodiment, the wedge-shaped projection 504a may extend downwardly from the body of the piston plunger 222, while the recessed wedge surface 504b may extend upwardly from the body of the CBS plunger 220, such that the two surfaces are positioned in facing engagement. The orientation of these surfaces may allow the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 to interact through surface-to-surface contact along the wedge interface. Through this structural arrangement, the wedge-shaped projection 504a of the piston plunger 222 and the recessed wedge surface 504b of the CBS plunger 220 together define a complementary wedge-type engagement structure or a wedge interface that enables mechanical interaction between the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 within the braking system 100.
WORKING
[0052]	Referring to FIG. 6A, the actuation of the braking system 100 through the CBS arrangement 201 is illustrated. When a pulling force F2 is applied to the inner cable 212 of the CBS arrangement 201, the inner cable 212 is displaced relative to the outer cable 210, which remains supported on the master cylinder housing 102 through the CBS adjuster nut 208. The pulling force F2 may be generated upon actuation of a second brake lever of the vehicle (not shown), the inner cable 212 being operatively connected to the second brake lever, such that application of the second brake lever transmits the pulling force F2 through the inner cable 212 to the braking system 100. The movement of the inner cable 212 is transmitted to the CBS bracket 216 connected to an end portion of the inner cable 212.
[0053]	The CBS bracket 216, which is pivotably connected to the protruding member 502b of the CBS plunger 220 through the CBS bracket pivot pin 218, transfers the transmitted movement toward the CBS plunger 220, thereby pulling the CBS plunger 220 in the direction of movement of the CBS bracket 216. The CBS plunger 220 thereby pivots about the pivot axis Y-Y’ defined by the plunger pivot pin 306 and moves relative to the piston plunger 222, such that the recessed wedge surface 504b of the CBS plunger 220 interacts with the wedge-shaped projection 504a of the piston plunger 222.
[0054]	Due to the complementary wedge geometry between the recessed wedge surface 504b and the wedge-shaped projection 504a, displacement of the CBS plunger 220 causes corresponding displacement of the piston plunger 222 about the pivot axis Y-Y’, in a direction indicated by F1 in FIG. 6A. The displacement of the piston plunger 222 is then transmitted through the protruding member 502a toward the piston 604, thereby causing axial displacement of the piston 604 within the master cylinder 204 and generating hydraulic pressure within the braking system 100.
[0055]	During actuation of the CBS arrangement 201, the brake lever 104 and the lever link 110 remain unaffected, as the displacement of the piston plunger 222 caused by the CBS plunger 220 occurs without imparting movement to the brake lever 104. Conversely, during actuation of the brake lever 104, the CBS plunger 220 and the CBS arrangement 201 remain unaffected. Through this configuration, the braking system 100 enables independent actuation paths for the brake lever 104 and the CBS arrangement 201, wherein both actuation paths ultimately produce displacement of the piston 604 within the master cylinder 204, thereby generating hydraulic pressure within the braking system 100 and ensuring effective transmission of braking force through either actuation path.
[0056]	Referring to FIG. 6B, the actuation of the braking system 100 through the brake lever 104 is illustrated. When a rider applies an input force F3 at a distal end of the brake lever 104, the brake lever 104 pivots about the pivot axis X-X’ defined by the lever pivot bolt 302, in a direction indicated by 606. The corresponding pivoting movement at the pivot region of the brake lever 104 is indicated by 610.
[0057]	As the brake lever 104 pivots in the direction 606, the lever link 110 provided as a rigid member on a proximal portion of the brake lever 104, in other words, formed integrally with the brake lever 104, comes into contact with the piston plunger 222 and applies a mechanical force to the piston plunger 222, thereby causing angular displacement of the piston plunger 222 about the pivot axis Y-Y’ defined by the plunger pivot pin 306.
[0058]	As the piston plunger 222 pivots about the pivot axis Y-Y’, the protruding member 502a of the piston plunger 222 engages the piston 604 disposed within the master cylinder 204. The mechanical force is thereby transmitted from the piston plunger 222 to the piston 604, causing axial displacement of the piston 604 within the master cylinder 204 in a direction indicated by 608. The axial movement of the piston 604 in the direction 608 compresses hydraulic fluid contained within the master cylinder 204, thereby generating hydraulic pressure. The generated hydraulic pressure is transmitted through the hydraulic port 206 to a brake line connected to a braking mechanism of the vehicle, such as a brake caliper assembly, thereby producing braking action at a wheel of the vehicle.
[0059]	During actuation of the brake lever 104, the CBS plunger 220 remains unaffected, as the wedge-shaped projection 504a of the piston plunger 222 moves relative to the recessed wedge surface 504b of the CBS plunger 220 without imparting significant displacement to the CBS plunger 220. Through this configuration, the brake lever 104 actuates the piston 604 through the lever link 110 and the piston plunger 222 independently of the CBS arrangement 201.
[0060]	The braking system 100 described herein provides several technical advantages over conventional braking arrangements. The wedge interface defined between the wedge-shaped projection 504a of the piston plunger 222 and the recessed wedge surface 504b of the CBS plunger 220 enables the piston 604 to be actuated through two independent actuation paths, namely through the brake lever 104 and through the CBS arrangement 201, without mechanical interdependence therebetween. During actuation of the CBS arrangement 201, the displacement of the piston plunger 222 occurs without imparting movement to the brake lever 104, thereby eliminating unintended lever movement and improving rider comfort and braking feel. Conversely, during actuation of the brake lever 104, the wedge-shaped projection 504a moves relative to the recessed wedge surface 504b without imparting significant displacement to the CBS plunger 220, thereby ensuring consistent braking response irrespective of whether braking is initiated manually or through the combined braking system. The surface-to-surface contact along the wedge interface further enables smooth and consistent force transmission while reducing wear and irregular engagement of the piston 604.
[0061]	The pivotable support of the piston plunger 222 and the CBS plunger 220 about the common pivot axis Y-Y′ through the single plunger pivot pin 306 reduces the number of components and pivot locations, thereby simplifying assembly and improving alignment accuracy. The integration of the CBS arrangement 201 at the bottom region of the master cylinder housing 102 through the C-shaped mounting slot 408 enables the cable-operated CBS arrangement to be incorporated without substantial modification of the brake lever 104 or of existing brake lever assemblies, while the CBS adjuster nut 208 permits adjustment of tension of the inner cable 212 to compensate for cable elongation over the service life of the vehicle. The space 414 defined between the upper mounting plate 410b and the lower mounting plate 410a accommodates and protects the actuation components within a compact envelope, thereby enabling the braking system 100 to retain the overall dimensions of a conventional master cylinder assembly and to improve braking balance and vehicle stability through distribution of braking forces between the wheels of the vehicle.
[0062]	The braking system 100 described herein provides a flexible design in which the components and their interconnections may be arranged in various configurations depending on application requirements. Certain components may be added, modified, or omitted while maintaining the intended functionality of the system.
[0063]	Although specific embodiments of the invention have been described for purposes of illustration, it will be appreciated that various modifications, substitutions, and alterations may be made without departing from the spirit and scope of the invention. Accordingly, the description and accompanying drawings are intended to be illustrative rather than limiting.
[0064]	It will be apparent to persons skilled in the art that numerous variations and modifications of the present invention may be made in light of the foregoing description. The terminology used herein is intended for descriptive purposes and should not be construed as limiting the scope of the invention. The foregoing description provides examples of preferred embodiments and should not be interpreted as restricting the scope of the invention. ,

title: A Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction
abstract: The present invention relates to a Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction for automatically identifying and reconstructing contaminated electroencephalography (EEG) signals. EEG recordings are frequently affected by ocular, muscular, motion, and other artifacts, which can reduce signal quality and adversely affect subsequent analysis. The proposed system receives contaminated EEG signals and performs preprocessing, segmentation, and normalization before extracting complementary temporal, frequency, and spatial features. A Transformer-based temporal module captures long-range dependencies in EEG signals, while frequency-domain processing extracts spectral characteristics and spatial learning models relationships among EEG electrode channels. The extracted features are integrated through a multi-domain feature fusion mechanism to generate a comprehensive representation of the EEG signal. An artifact detection module identifies contaminated regions and generates an artifact mask, which guides a reconstruction module in estimating and reconstructing the underlying EEG signal. The proposed framework is designed to reduce artifact contamination while preserving important neural characteristics of the original EEG recording. The reconstructed signals may be evaluated using signal-quality metrics including RMSE, SNR, PSNR, correlation coefficient, SAR, PNR, and RRE. The invention provides an automated and integrated approach for EEG artifact detection and reconstruction and may be applied in neurological disorder analysis, EEG classification, brain-computer interfaces, clinical research, and other EEG.
specification:
Brief Description of the System:

Overview of the Proposed Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction

The proposed invention provides a Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction that automatically identifies contaminated EEG signals and reconstructs the underlying neural activity. The system is designed to address various artifacts, including ocular artifacts, muscle artifacts, motion artifacts, and other signal disturbances that may affect the quality and reliability of EEG recordings.The proposed system receives raw or contaminated EEG signals as input and performs preprocessing to normalize and prepare the signals for analysis. The preprocessed EEG signals are then analyzed using multiple complementary domains, including temporal, frequency, and spatial domains. A Transformer-based temporal processing module captures long-range temporal dependencies in the EEG signals, while frequency-domain analysis extracts spectral characteristics associated with different types of artifacts. A spatial learning module models relationships among different EEG electrode channels.The features obtained from these domains are subsequently integrated through a feature fusion mechanism to generate a comprehensive representation of the EEG signal. An artifact detection module estimates the presence and severity of contamination and generates an artifact mask identifying corrupted signal regions. Based on the detected artifact information, a reconstruction module estimates the underlying clean EEG signal while attempting to preserve important neural characteristics.

Benefits of the Invention

1.	Automated Artifact Detection: The system automatically identifies contaminated EEG segments, reducing the need for manual inspection and intervention. 
2.	Multi-Domain Analysis: The framework simultaneously utilizes temporal, frequency, and spatial information, enabling more comprehensive characterization of EEG signals and artifacts. 
3.	Improved Artifact Identification: The Transformer-based architecture can capture long-range dependencies in EEG signals, helping distinguish artifacts from underlying neural activity. 
4.	Effective EEG Reconstruction: The system reconstructs corrupted EEG segments while attempting to preserve important neural signal characteristics. 
5.	Multiple Artifact Types: The framework can be designed to detect and address different artifacts, including ocular, muscle, motion, and other interference components. 
6.	Reduced Loss of Neural Information: Unlike some conventional filtering approaches, the proposed reconstruction mechanism aims to remove contamination while preserving clinically and physiologically relevant EEG patterns.




Functionalities of the System

The proposed Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction provides the following functionalities:
1.	EEG Signal Acquisition
Receives raw EEG signals from one or more EEG recording channels as input. 
2.	Signal Preprocessing
Performs preprocessing operations such as filtering, normalization, segmentation, and removal of unwanted baseline variations. 
3.	Artifact Identification
Automatically identifies contaminated EEG segments affected by ocular, muscular, motion, and other artifacts. 
4.	Temporal Feature Extraction
Uses a Transformer-based module to learn temporal dependencies and relationships within EEG signals over time. 
5.	Frequency-Domain Analysis
Analyzes spectral characteristics of EEG signals to distinguish normal neural activity from frequency-specific artifacts. 
6.	Spatial Feature Learning
Learns relationships and dependencies between different EEG electrode channels to identify spatial patterns associated with artifacts. 
7.	Multi-Domain Feature Fusion
Combines temporal, frequency, and spatial features into a unified EEG representation. 
8.	Artifact Mask Estimation
Generates an artifact mask indicating the locations or regions of the EEG signal affected by contamination. 
9.	Artifact Severity Estimation
Estimates the degree of contamination in EEG segments to support selective reconstruction. 
10.	EEG Signal Reconstruction
Reconstructs corrupted portions of the EEG signal using information learned from surrounding and multi-domain signal characteristics. 
11.	Neural Information Preservation
Attempts to preserve important EEG characteristics and underlying neural patterns during artifact removal and reconstruction. 
12.	Quality Evaluation
Enables evaluation of reconstructed EEG signals using measures such as RMSE, SNR, PSNR, correlation coefficient, SAR, and reconstruction error. 
13.	Automated End-to-End Processing
Integrates preprocessing, artifact detection, feature learning, artifact localization, and reconstruction into a unified processing pipeline.












4. Best Practices

1. High-Quality EEG Acquisition
EEG signals should be acquired using appropriately positioned and calibrated electrodes with suitable sampling rates to preserve relevant neural information. 
2. Proper Preprocessing
Appropriate filtering, normalization, segmentation, and preprocessing procedures should be applied consistently before artifact detection. 
3. Preservation of Original EEG Information
Preprocessing and reconstruction parameters should be selected to minimize distortion or loss of clinically and physiologically relevant EEG characteristics. 
4.Multi-Domain Feature Analysis
Temporal, frequency, and spatial characteristics should preferably be analyzed together to improve the reliability of artifact detection. 
5.Appropriate Training and Validation Data
The Transformer-based model should be trained and validated using representative EEG datasets containing sufficient variations in subjects, recording conditions, electrode configurations, and artifact types. 
6.Avoidance of Data Leakage
Training, validation, and testing data should be appropriately separated, preferably at the subject level where applicable, to ensure reliable evaluation of model generalization.

5. Objectives of the Invention

The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction capable of automatically identifying and reconstructing contaminated EEG signals while preserving important neural information.
The specific objectives of the invention are:
1.	To provide an automated system for detecting artifacts present in EEG recordings without requiring extensive manual intervention. 
2.	To detect multiple types of EEG artifacts, including ocular/eye-blink artifacts, muscle artifacts, motion artifacts, and other signal contamination. 
3.	To develop a Transformer-based architecture capable of learning long-range temporal dependencies and complex patterns in EEG signals. 
4.	To analyze EEG signals across multiple domains, including temporal, frequency, and spatial domains, for improved artifact characterization. 
5.	To extract frequency-domain characteristics of EEG signals for distinguishing artifact-related spectral components from neural activity. 
6.	To model spatial relationships between EEG electrode channels to improve the identification and localization of artifacts.












6. Proposed Algorithm: 

Algorithm 1: Automatic Artifact Scoring for EEG Windows
Input: Raw EEG signal X
Output: Top 10 artifact-heavy windows
1:  Preprocessing:
2:      • Resample X to 128 Hz
3:      • Bandpass filter between 1–40 Hz
4:      • Segment X into 2 s windows with 1 s overlap
5:  InitializeBlinkScore(w) = 0, EMGScore(w) = 0 for each window w
6:  for each window w do
7:      % Eye-blink (EOG) scoring
8:      Extract low-frequency band B_0.5–3Hz from frontal channels:
            {Fp1, Fp2, AF3, AF4}
9:      Compute BlinkScore(w):
BlinkScore(w) = Σ | B_0.5–3Hz(x(t)) | > 3σ
10:     % Muscle (EMG) scoring
11:     Extract high-frequency band B_20–45Hz from all channels
12:     Compute EMGScore(w):
EMGScore(w) = Σ ( B_20–45Hz(x(t)) )²
13:     % Combined artifact severity
14:     ArtifactScore(w) = BlinkScore(w) + EMGScore(w)
15: end for
16: Rank all windows by ArtifactScore(w) in descending order
17: Select the top 10 highest-scoring windows
18: return Top 10 artifact-heavy windows

Algorithm 2: Training Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Reconstruction Model
Input: Preprocessed EEG windows {Xᵢ}, batch size B, learning rate η
Output: Reconstructed signal
1: Initialize model parameters Θ
2: Define loss weights λ_spec and λ_mask
3: while not converged do
4:     Sample a mini-batch of EEG windows {X₁ … X_B}
5:     % ----- Forward Pass -----
6:     Obtain time-domain features:
F_t = TimeTransformer(X)

7:     Obtain frequency-domain features:
            Z = STFT(X)
F_f = FrequencyAttention(Z)
8:     Obtain spatial-domain features
            F_s = GraphModule(X)  
9:    Fuse multi-domain features:
F_fused = Concat(F_t, F_f, F_s) W_fusion
10:    Estimate artifact mask:
            M = σ(F_fusedW_mask)
11:    Reconstruct clean EEG:
            X̂ = (1 - M) ⊙ X + M ⊙F_fused
12:    % ----- Loss Computation -----
13:    Reconstruction loss:
L_rec = ||X̂ - X||²
14:    Spectral loss:
L_spec = || STFT(X̂) - STFT(X) ||₁
15:    Mask KL-divergence:
L_mask = KL(M* || M)
16:    Total loss:
            L = L_rec + λ_specL_spec + λ_maskL_mask
17:    % ----- Backpropagation -----
18:    Compute gradients ∇Θ L
19:    Update model parameters:
            Θ ← Θ - η ∇Θ L
20: end while 
21: return X̂












7. Summary of the invention:

The present invention relates to an automated Multi-Domain Transformer-Based Framework for EEG Artifact Detection and Reconstruction. The invention provides a computational system for identifying contaminated portions of electroencephalography (EEG) signals and reconstructing the corresponding signal while preserving relevant neural information. In one aspect, the proposed system receives one or more EEG signals as input and performs preprocessing operations including signal filtering, normalization, and segmentation. The preprocessed EEG signals are subsequently analyzed using multiple complementary domains, including temporal, frequency, and spatial domains. A Transformer-based temporal module is configured to learn short-term and long-range temporal dependencies within the EEG signals. A frequency-domain processing module extracts spectral characteristics of the EEG signal, while a spatial learning module captures relationships among different EEG electrode channels. The features obtained from these modules are combined using a multi-domain feature fusion mechanism to generate a comprehensive representation of the EEG signal. Based on the fused representation, an artifact detection module identifies contaminated EEG segments and generates an artifact mask representing the location and/or degree of signal contamination. The artifact information is provided to a reconstruction module, which estimates the underlying clean EEG signal and reconstructs the contaminated portions. The proposed framework is configured to address different types of EEG artifacts, including ocular artifacts, muscle artifacts, motion artifacts, and other signal disturbances. The reconstruction process is designed to reduce artifact components while maintaining important temporal, spectral, and spatial characteristics of the underlying neural activity.The reconstructed EEG signal is evaluated using one or more signal-quality measures, including root mean square error (RMSE), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), correlation coefficient, signal-to-artifact ratio (SAR), percentage noise reduction (PNR), and relative reconstruction error (RRE).The invention provides an integrated and automated approach that reduces dependence on manual artifact identification and combines multi-domain EEG analysis with Transformer-based learning. The resulting reconstructed EEG signals may be used for neurological disorder analysis, EEG classification, brain-computer interfaces, clinical research, and other EEG-based applications.Overall, the invention provides a unified framework that performs EEG signal preprocessing, multi-domain feature extraction, artifact detection, artifact localization, and signal reconstruction to improve the quality and usability of contaminated EEG recordings.
