title: Adaptive Thermoelectric Waste Heat Recovery System for Internal Combustion Engines
abstract:
ABSTRACT
Adaptive Thermoelectric Waste Heat Recovery System for Internal Combustion Engines
The present invention relates to an adaptive thermoelectric waste heat recovery system for an internal combustion engine (101), comprising an exhaust pipe (102), a heat exchanger (103), thermoelectric generator (TEG) modules (104a), a cooling mechanism (105), a power conditioning circuit (106), a DC-DC buck converter (107), a charger module (108) and a battery (109). The heat exchanger (103) captures thermal energy from high-temperature exhaust gases and transfers the thermal energy to a hot side of the TEG modules (104a), while the cooling mechanism (105) maintains a comparatively lower temperature at a cold side thereof to establish a temperature gradient for Seebeck-effect electrical generation. The generated electrical energy is conditioned and stored in the battery (109) and/or supplied to an auxiliary electrical load (110). An ESP32 controller (111) with temperature sensors (112, 113, 114) provides thermal monitoring and adaptive cooling control, while an OLED display (115) and wireless module (116) facilitate system monitoring and communication.
Figure-1
specification:
Adaptive Thermoelectric Waste Heat Recovery System for Internal Combustion Engines
FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates generally to automotive engineering, thermal energy recovery, energy management and thermoelectric power generation, and more particularly to a system and method for recovering waste thermal energy from an internal combustion engine exhaust using thermoelectric generator (TEG) modules. The invention is particularly concerned with improving the conversion of otherwise dissipated exhaust heat into useful electrical energy by maintaining a temperature differential across thermoelectric modules through a heat exchanger and cooling arrangement. The invention further relates to electrical power conditioning, energy storage and controlled delivery of recovered electrical energy to auxiliary loads of an engine or vehicle.
The invention is applicable to heavy-duty diesel vehicles, marine vessels, stationary power plants and other internal combustion engine-based systems where substantial thermal energy is discharged through exhaust gases. The disclosed technical field corresponds to the optimization of waste heat recovery systems involving thermodynamic energy conversion, thermal management, thermoelectric generation and electronic power management. The invention disclosure identifies Automotive/Energy Management Engineering as the technical field and specifically identifies waste heat recovery optimization for internal combustion engines as the specialization.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Internal combustion engines are widely used for propulsion and stationary power generation because of their ability to convert chemical energy contained in fuel into mechanical work. However, the conversion of fuel energy into useful mechanical output is inherently accompanied by substantial thermal losses. A considerable portion of the energy released during combustion is discharged from the engine in the form of high-temperature exhaust gases, while other portions are removed through engine cooling arrangements and radiation from engine components. Consequently, a significant amount of potentially useful energy is continuously dissipated into the environment rather than being utilized for improving the overall energy efficiency of the engine. The disclosed invention identifies this loss of thermal energy through exhaust gases as a principal technical problem.
Conventional waste heat recovery arrangements attempt to extract useful energy from engine exhaust streams, but effective recovery is technically challenging because the exhaust system must continue to permit adequate gas flow while transferring sufficient thermal energy to a recovery device. A further difficulty arises in thermoelectric generation because electrical output from a thermoelectric generator depends upon the temperature difference maintained between its hot and cold surfaces. Merely exposing a thermoelectric module to a hot exhaust stream may therefore result in limited electrical generation if the cold side is not adequately maintained at a lower temperature.
The present disclosure proposes a waste heat recovery arrangement in which an exhaust-mounted heat exchanger receives thermal energy from high-temperature exhaust gases and transfers the recovered heat to thermoelectric generator modules. The TEG modules operate according to the Seebeck effect, whereby a temperature difference between the hot side and cold side generates an electrical voltage. A cooling mechanism is consequently provided to maintain the cold side at a comparatively lower temperature and thereby establish a sustained temperature gradient. The generated electrical energy is subsequently subjected to power conditioning and can be stored in a battery or supplied to auxiliary systems.
The uploaded disclosure does not identify a specific close prior-art patent or publication; the corresponding prior-art table is presently unfilled. Accordingly, no specific prior-art reference is asserted here as being disclosed by the inventors.
There remains a technical need for an integrated waste heat recovery system that not only converts exhaust heat into electrical energy, but also manages the thermal gradient, electrical conversion and energy storage in a coordinated manner so that recovered energy can be practically utilized for engine auxiliary loads.

OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION
1.	To provide an optimized waste heat recovery system capable of capturing thermal energy from high-temperature exhaust gases of an internal combustion engine and converting the captured thermal energy into useful electrical energy using thermoelectric generator modules.
2.	To maintain an effective temperature differential across the TEG modules by transferring exhaust heat to a hot side while actively maintaining the cold side at a comparatively lower temperature through a suitable cooling arrangement.
3.	To provide an integrated electrical energy management arrangement comprising power conditioning, DC-DC conversion, charging and battery storage for supplying the recovered electrical energy to auxiliary loads or retaining the energy for subsequent use.
4.	To improve the overall energy conversion efficiency and practical utilization of recovered waste heat, while providing monitoring and adaptive control of thermal and electrical operating conditions through an electronic controller.


SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The present invention provides an adaptive thermoelectric waste heat recovery system for an internal combustion engine, configured to recover thermal energy otherwise discharged through high-temperature exhaust gases and convert at least a portion of the recovered thermal energy into useful electrical power. The system is particularly configured as an integrated thermal-to-electrical energy recovery arrangement comprising an exhaust-side heat exchanger, one or more thermoelectric generator (TEG) modules, a cooling mechanism, an electronic controller, a power conditioning circuit, a DC-DC buck converter, a charger module and a rechargeable battery. The principal components disclosed in the invention include TEG modules, an ESP32 controller, an OLED display, a battery, a DC-DC buck converter and a charger module.
During operation of the internal combustion engine, combustion of fuel generates mechanical power together with substantial thermal energy. High-temperature exhaust gases transport a portion of this thermal energy through an exhaust pipe. The heat exchanger is positioned along the exhaust path and is configured to absorb thermal energy from the exhaust gases while allowing continued exhaust flow. The heat exchanger transfers the absorbed thermal energy toward the thermoelectric generator modules coupled thereto.
Each thermoelectric generator module has a hot side thermally coupled to the recovered exhaust heat and a cold side associated with a cooling mechanism. The temperature difference established across the thermoelectric module produces an electrical voltage through the Seebeck effect. Maintaining the cold side at a lower temperature is therefore important for establishing a sustained temperature gradient and supporting continuous electrical generation. The generated electrical output is delivered to the power-conditioning arrangement, where the electrical characteristics are regulated before the recovered power is supplied to a load or transferred to the battery for storage.
The system may incorporate an adaptive thermal-gradient control subsystem in which temperature sensing elements associated with the hot and cold sides of the TEG modules provide temperature information to the ESP32 controller. The controller can determine a thermal-gradient condition and selectively regulate the cooling mechanism so that the cold-side temperature is controlled according to the prevailing exhaust temperature and available thermal energy. This provides a technically useful feedback mechanism for maintaining the operating temperature differential rather than relying upon a fixed cooling condition. The adaptive control can further cooperate with the power-conditioning circuit to regulate the recovered electrical output according to battery state and auxiliary-load requirements.
The system thereby integrates thermal capture, thermoelectric conversion, temperature-gradient management, electronic power conditioning and energy storage into a coordinated waste heat recovery arrangement. In one practical application, the system can be installed on a heavy-duty diesel engine, where exhaust heat that would ordinarily be discharged to the surroundings is transferred through the heat exchanger to the TEG modules, converted into electrical energy and subsequently used for auxiliary electrical requirements or stored in the battery. This can improve utilization of otherwise wasted thermal energy without requiring additional fuel consumption for generating the recovered electrical power.
The disclosed validation framework further contemplates component-level testing, signal-quality validation, system integration testing, wireless transmission testing, application validation, and power/endurance testing. 
The invention consequently provides a practical technical architecture for recovering exhaust waste heat and converting it into usable electrical energy while improving thermal-gradient management and enabling controlled storage and utilization of the recovered power.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWING
FIG. 1 illustrates a block diagram of an adaptive thermoelectric waste heat recovery system for an internal combustion engine. The system includes an internal combustion engine (101) coupled to an exhaust pipe (102), a heat exchanger (103) positioned along the exhaust path, and a thermoelectric generator (TEG) module assembly (104) having one or more TEG modules (104a). A cooling mechanism (105) maintains the cold side of the TEG module assembly (104) at a comparatively lower temperature. Electrical output from the TEG module assembly (104) is supplied to a power conditioning circuit (106), a DC-DC buck converter (107), a charger module (108) and a battery (109) for storage and subsequent supply to auxiliary electrical loads (110). An ESP32 controller (111) is associated with temperature sensors (112, 113, 114), an OLED display/user interface (115) and a wireless module (116) for monitoring, data acquisition, display and communication/control functions.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to an optimized waste heat recovery system for an internal combustion engine and, more particularly, to a thermoelectric waste heat recovery arrangement configured to capture a portion of the thermal energy normally discharged through engine exhaust gases and convert the captured thermal energy into useful electrical energy. The invention is particularly suitable for applications involving heavy-duty diesel vehicles, marine vessels and stationary power plants, where internal combustion engines operate for extended periods and consequently reject substantial quantities of thermal energy through their exhaust systems. The invention integrates thermal energy capture, thermoelectric conversion, cooling, electrical power conditioning, energy storage and auxiliary power utilization into a coordinated system. The invention disclosure identifies the principal objective as maximizing the conversion of otherwise wasted thermal energy into useful mechanical or electrical power, thereby improving overall engine thermal efficiency and supporting reduction in fuel consumption and environmental emissions.
Referring to FIG. 1, the system comprises an internal combustion engine (101) that produces mechanical power through combustion of fuel. During operation of the internal combustion engine (101), combustion generates mechanical energy together with a significant quantity of thermal energy. A substantial part of this thermal energy is carried away by high-temperature exhaust gases. Instead of allowing the entire thermal energy associated with the exhaust gases to be discharged unused to the surroundings, the present invention directs the exhaust gases through an exhaust pipe (102) associated with a heat recovery arrangement. The exhaust pipe (102) therefore provides a thermal energy transport path from the internal combustion engine (101) toward the heat exchanger (103). The underlying technical concept of capturing thermal energy from exhaust gases and converting it into electrical energy is expressly disclosed in the invention disclosure.
The heat exchanger (103) is positioned along the exhaust path such that the high-temperature exhaust gases pass through or in thermal proximity to the heat exchanger (103). The heat exchanger (103) is configured to absorb thermal energy from the exhaust gases while maintaining the exhaust flow through the exhaust pipe (102). In an implementation, the heat exchanger (103) can have a thermally conductive structure with an increased heat-transfer surface so that thermal energy is efficiently transferred from the exhaust gases to the thermoelectric generator module assembly (104). The heat exchanger (103) consequently serves as the thermal interface between the exhaust stream and the thermoelectric conversion portion of the system. The disclosed invention specifically states that the heat exchanger is physically mounted along the exhaust path and is intended to absorb thermal energy without obstructing exhaust flow, while providing sufficient surface contact for efficient heat transfer.
The thermoelectric generator module assembly (104) is thermally coupled to the heat exchanger (103). The assembly (104) includes one or more thermoelectric generator modules (104a). The TEG modules (104a) may be implemented using semiconductor thermoelectric material capable of generating electrical energy when a temperature difference is established between opposite surfaces of the module. A first surface or hot side of the TEG module (104a) receives thermal energy transferred from the heat exchanger (103), while an opposite cold side is maintained at a comparatively lower temperature by the cooling mechanism (105). The invention disclosure specifically identifies TEG modules as a principal hardware component and explains that the modules generate electrical energy when subjected to a temperature difference.
The operating principle of the TEG module (104a) is based on the Seebeck effect. When a temperature difference exists between the hot side and cold side of the TEG module (104a), an electrical voltage is generated across the module. Accordingly, the quantity of electrical energy available from the thermoelectric conversion stage is associated with the thermal gradient established across the TEG module (104a). The heat exchanger (103) supplies the thermal input required at the hot side, while the cooling mechanism (105) assists in maintaining the temperature of the cold side at a lower level. This arrangement provides a continuous temperature gradient across the TEG module (104a), thereby enabling sustained thermoelectric energy generation while the engine (101) is operating and suitable exhaust heat is available.
The cooling mechanism (105) is thermally coupled to the cold side of the TEG module assembly (104). The cooling mechanism (105) can, depending upon the implementation, employ air cooling or liquid cooling to remove heat from the cold side. In the illustrated embodiment, the cooling mechanism (105) is represented as a heat-sink-based cooling arrangement with a fan and/or pump. The purpose of the cooling mechanism (105) is not merely to remove heat from the system, but to establish and maintain a useful temperature differential across the TEG module (104a). By maintaining the cold side at a lower temperature relative to the hot side, the cooling mechanism (105) supports the thermoelectric conversion process. The disclosed invention expressly identifies maintaining the temperature difference across the TEG modules as one of its objectives.
Electrical energy generated by the TEG module assembly (104) is supplied to a power conditioning circuit (106). Since the electrical output generated by thermoelectric modules can vary according to the prevailing thermal operating conditions, the power conditioning circuit (106) provides electrical regulation before the recovered power is delivered to a storage unit or electrical load. In the illustrated embodiment, the power conditioning circuit (106) performs suitable rectification and regulation of the electrical output. The conditioned output is then supplied to the DC-DC buck converter (107). The DC-DC buck converter (107) is configured to convert the conditioned electrical output into a suitable voltage level for the subsequent charging stage and/or electrical utilization. The disclosed hardware list specifically identifies a DC-DC buck converter as one of the components of the invention.
The output of the DC-DC buck converter (107) is supplied to a charger module (108). The charger module (108) controls the charging interface between the conditioned thermoelectric power and the battery (109). The battery (109) serves as an energy storage unit for retaining electrical energy generated during periods in which sufficient exhaust heat is available. The stored electrical energy can subsequently be utilized by auxiliary electrical loads (110) associated with the engine or vehicle. Thus, the system does not require the electrical output of the TEG modules (104a) to be consumed instantaneously. Instead, the combination of the power conditioning circuit (106), DC-DC buck converter (107), charger module (108) and battery (109) provides a practical energy-management path through which recovered thermal energy can be converted, conditioned and stored. The disclosure specifically states that conditioned power can be used for charging a battery or supplying auxiliary systems.
The auxiliary electrical loads (110) represent one or more electrical systems associated with the engine or vehicle that can utilize the recovered electrical energy. Depending on the particular application, such auxiliary systems may include suitable low- or medium-power electrical accessories associated with the engine or vehicle. The invention therefore provides an energy recovery pathway in which exhaust heat that would otherwise be lost is converted into electricity and subsequently made available for useful electrical operation. The principal advantage is that the electrical energy is recovered from an existing thermal loss associated with engine operation rather than requiring a separate primary fuel-consuming generation process.
The system further includes an ESP32 controller (111) for data acquisition, monitoring and control. The ESP32 controller (111) provides a computational and supervisory interface between the thermal recovery system and the monitoring hardware. In the illustrated embodiment, a hot-side temperature sensor (112) is associated with the hot region of the TEG module assembly (104), a cold-side temperature sensor (113) is associated with the cold region, and an exhaust temperature sensor (114) is associated with the exhaust path near the heat exchanger (103). The sensors (112, 113, 114) provide temperature information to the ESP32 controller (111) so that the thermal condition of the recovery arrangement can be observed. In particular, the relative hot-side and cold-side temperature information can be used to determine the prevailing thermal gradient across the TEG module (104a).
The ESP32 controller (111) is further coupled to an OLED display or user interface (115). The OLED display (115) can provide an operator-facing representation of monitored system conditions, such as relevant temperature information or operating status. The controller (111) can further communicate through a wireless module (116), represented in FIG. 1 as a Wi-Fi/IoT communication interface. The wireless module (116) permits system information to be transmitted to a remote monitoring or analysis platform where such functionality is implemented. The controller (111), display (115) and wireless module (116) therefore provide a monitoring and communication layer around the thermal and electrical recovery hardware.
In one embodiment, the controller (111) can receive the hot-side temperature from sensor (112), cold-side temperature from sensor (113) and exhaust temperature from sensor (114) and determine whether the thermal gradient is adequate for thermoelectric energy generation. Based upon the monitored condition, the controller (111) can provide monitoring information through the OLED display (115) and/or transmit the information through the wireless module (116). Where an actively controlled cooling arrangement is implemented, the controller (111) can further cooperate with the cooling mechanism (105) to maintain an appropriate cold-side condition. Such control establishes an integrated thermal monitoring arrangement around the TEG module assembly (104) rather than treating thermoelectric conversion as an isolated energy-generating component.
The invention therefore provides a method of recovering waste heat beginning with operation of the internal combustion engine (101) and generation of high-temperature exhaust gases. The exhaust gases travel through the exhaust pipe (102) and transfer thermal energy to the heat exchanger (103). The heat exchanger (103) conducts the transferred heat to the hot side of the TEG module assembly (104). At substantially the same time, the cooling mechanism (105) removes heat from the cold side of the TEG module assembly (104). A temperature difference is thereby maintained across the TEG module (104a), resulting in generation of electrical voltage through the Seebeck effect. The electrical output is then processed by the power conditioning circuit (106), converted by the DC-DC buck converter (107), passed through the charger module (108) and stored in the battery (109) or utilized for auxiliary electrical loads (110). The controller (111) can monitor operating temperatures and system conditions through the sensors (112, 113, 114) and present or communicate relevant information through the OLED interface (115) and wireless module (116).
For example, consider a heavy-duty diesel vehicle operating continuously under a substantial engine load. During operation, the internal combustion engine (101) produces mechanical power and simultaneously generates high-temperature exhaust gases. Instead of allowing the exhaust heat to be entirely rejected through the exhaust pipe (102), the exhaust gases pass through the heat exchanger (103). Thermal energy from the exhaust is transferred to the TEG module assembly (104). The hot side of the TEG module (104a) becomes heated while the cooling mechanism (105) maintains the opposite side at a lower temperature. The resulting thermal gradient generates electrical energy. The generated electrical output is conditioned by the circuit (106), appropriately converted by the DC-DC buck converter (107), processed through the charger module (108) and stored in the battery (109). When required, the stored energy can be supplied to auxiliary electrical loads (110). Meanwhile, the ESP32 controller (111) can monitor the thermal condition using sensors (112, 113, 114) and make the operating information available on the OLED display (115) or through the wireless module (116).
The same principle can be applied to a stationary diesel generator or marine engine. In such an installation, the engine (101) may operate for several hours, continuously producing exhaust heat. The heat exchanger (103) and TEG module assembly (104) can consequently recover a portion of the otherwise dissipated thermal energy over an extended operating period. The recovered electrical energy can be stored in the battery (109) and used for suitable auxiliary electrical requirements. The invention is consequently applicable to heavy-duty diesel vehicles, marine vessels and stationary power plants, as identified in the invention disclosure.
The overall system is intended to improve utilization of wasted thermal energy and increase energy efficiency. The disclosed validation approach contemplates component-level testing before integration, signal-quality validation, system integration testing, wireless transmission testing, application validation and power/endurance testing. The invention disclosure identifies the technology readiness level as experimental proof of concept, indicating that the disclosed architecture is at a proof-of-concept stage.
Accordingly, the invention combines the thermal components (101–105), electrical conversion and storage components (106–110), and monitoring and communication components (111–116) into an integrated waste heat recovery architecture. The cooperation between the heat exchanger (103), TEG module assembly (104) and cooling mechanism (105) provides the fundamental thermal-to-electrical conversion function, while the power conditioning circuit (106), DC-DC buck converter (107), charger module (108) and battery (109) enable practical utilization and storage of the generated energy. The ESP32 controller (111) and associated sensing, display and communication components provide an additional monitoring layer. Thus, the system and corresponding method enable otherwise wasted engine exhaust heat to be captured and converted into useful electrical energy for storage and auxiliary utilization, thereby providing a practical waste heat recovery architecture for internal combustion engine applications.

title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR MONITORING WILDFIRE RISK
abstract: A system (102) and a method (300) for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone are disclosed. The system (102) includes a plurality of sensors (104) including an electromagnetic field sensor (104A) and an air ionization sensor (104B), a suppression unit (110), a communication unit (112), and a control unit (106) communicably coupled thereto. The control unit (106) receives the sensor data, detects an anomaly indicative of a pre-ignition condition, analyzes historical data associated with the anomaly, determines a fire risk score, classifies the monitored zone into a risk category based on the fire risk score, triggers the suppression unit (110) to dispense a fire suppressant, and generates a corresponding alert for transmission through the communication unit (112), enabling a timely intervention prior to a visible ignition of the wildfire.
specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001]	The present disclosure relates to the field of wildfire risk monitoring systems. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to a system and a method for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone using electromagnetic field sensing and air ionization sensing.

BACKGROUND
[0002]	Forest fires cause extensive ecological, economic, and human loss across large geographic regions each year, and the ability to intervene before a fire ignites is materially more valuable than the ability to detect a fire after ignition has already occurred. Conventional wildfire monitoring systems rely predominantly on the detection of smoke, heat, or open flame, by their nature, such systems can only generate an alert once combustion has already commenced. By the time a smoke plume, a thermal signature, or a visible flame is detected by these conventional systems, a fire may have already progressed to a stage where suppression becomes considerably more resource-intensive, time-critical, and, in many terrains, materially less effective.
[0003]	Existing environmental sensing networks that monitor temperature, humidity, and gas concentration are also unable to reliably anticipate the atmospheric and electromagnetic disturbances that frequently precede an ignition event, such as those associated with lightning strikes, underground electrical discharge, or localized electrical faults in remote or forested terrain. These existing networks are further limited by high power consumption, dependence on frequent battery replacement, restricted communication range in dense forest canopies, and an absence of any structured mechanism for correlating instantaneous sensor anomalies with longer-term historical and climatic patterns. Consequently, existing approaches are reactive in nature, responding only after visible signs of fire are already present, and do not provide forest management authorities with an actionable window in which preventive or suppressive measures may be deployed prior to ignition.
[0004]	 There exists, therefore, a need for a wildfire monitoring system that is capable of identifying precursor conditions indicative of an impending ignition event before a fire visibly manifests, that integrates a plurality of sensing modalities into a unified risk assessment, that operates reliably and autonomously over extended durations in remote forested terrain, and that is capable of triggering an appropriate preventive or suppressive response and issuing a timely alert to relevant stakeholders. 

OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE
[0005]	It is an object of the present disclosure to provide a system and a method for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone based on an electromagnetic field measurement and an air ionization measurement.
[0006]	Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a system that determines a fire risk score for a monitored zone by combining a detected anomaly with historical data associated with the monitored zone, and that classifies the monitored zone into a risk category based on the fire risk score.
[0007]	Yet another object of the present disclosure is to provide a system that triggers a suppression unit and generates a corresponding alert for transmission through a communication unit responsive to a risk category associated with a monitored zone.

SUMMARY
[0008]	In an aspect, the present disclosure provides a system for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone. The system includes a plurality of sensors deployed in the monitored zone, including an electromagnetic field sensor and an air ionization sensor, a suppression unit, a communication unit, and a control unit communicably coupled thereto. The control unit receives sensor data, detects an anomaly indicative of a pre-ignition condition, analyzes historical data associated with the anomaly, determines a fire risk score, classifies the monitored zone into a risk category, triggers the suppression unit, and generates an alert for transmission through the communication unit.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
[0009]	FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary architecture of a system for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone, according to embodiments of the present disclosure.
[0010]	FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary block diagram of a control unit of the system, according to embodiments of the present disclosure.
[0011]	FIG. 3 illustrates a flow diagram illustrating a method for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone, according to embodiments of the present disclosure.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
[0012]	The present disclosure relates to the field of wildfire risk monitoring systems, and more particularly to a system and a method for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone using electromagnetic field sensing and air ionization sensing.
[0013]	Throughout the present disclosure, the term "monitored zone" may refer to a geographic region of forested or vegetated terrain that is designated for wildfire risk surveillance, and may be defined by a boundary, a grid cell, or a radius associated with a deployment location of one or more sensors. 
[0014]	The term "pre-ignition condition" may refer to a likelihood, assessed prior to a visible or a detectable combustion event, that ignition of a wildfire may occur within the monitored zone. The term "anomaly" may refer to a measured deviation of one or more sensor parameters from a baseline value or a range of expected values associated with the monitored zone. The term "control unit" may refer to a processing entity that receives data, executes instructions, and generates outputs, and may be implemented as a single processing entity or may be distributed across a plurality of communicably coupled processing entities. Each numerical value, range, or threshold referred to in the present disclosure is provided by way of an illustrative and non-limiting example, and a corresponding parameter may be adjusted or may be recalibrated for a particular monitored zone, a particular terrain, or a particular deployment without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.
[0015]	Various embodiments of the present disclosure will be described with reference to FIGs. 1 to 3.
[0016]	FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary architecture (100) of a system (102) for monitoring wildfire risk in a monitored zone, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[0017]	Referring to FIG. 1, the system (102) may include a sensing unit (104), a control unit (106), an alert unit (108), a suppression unit (110), a communication unit (112), and a power supply unit (114). The system (102) may further be communicably coupled to an external data unit (116) that may be disposed external to the system (102), as illustrated in FIG. 1.
[0018]	In an embodiment, the sensing unit (104) may include a plurality of sensors deployed in the monitored zone. The plurality of sensors may include an electromagnetic field sensor (104A), an air ionization sensor (104B), an environmental sensor (104C), and a thermal sensor (104D), each disposed within the sensing unit (104) as illustrated in FIG. 1. The sensing unit (104) may be communicably coupled to the control unit (106), such that sensor data generated by the plurality of sensors may be received by the control unit (106).
[0019]	In an embodiment, the control unit (106) may be communicably coupled to each of the alert unit (108), the suppression unit (110), the communication unit (112), and the power supply unit (114), as illustrated in FIG. 1. The suppression unit (110) may be deployed in the monitored zone and may be actuable, responsive to a signal received from the control unit (106), to dispense a fire suppressant in the monitored zone. The communication unit (112) may be operative to transmit data associated with the monitored zone to a remote device, and may further be operative to receive data at the control unit (106) from a remote source. The alert unit (108) may be actuable, responsive to a signal received from the control unit (106), to output a perceivable indication associated with a risk category determined by the control unit (106). The power supply unit (114) may supply electrical power to the plurality of sensors of the sensing unit (104) and to the control unit (106).
[0020]	In an embodiment, the external data unit (116) may be communicably coupled to the control unit (106), and may provide external data associated with the monitored zone to the control unit (106). The internal architecture of the control unit (106), including a processor, a memory, and a processing unit having a plurality of functional sub-units, is described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 2 herein below, and a corresponding method performed by the control unit (106) is described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 3 herein below.
[0021]	In some embodiments, the plurality of sensors of the sensing unit (104) may be distributed across the monitored zone at a plurality of spaced-apart locations, such that the monitored zone may be represented as a plurality of zones or grid cells, each zone or grid cell being associated with a corresponding subset of the plurality of sensors. In an illustrative embodiment, a monitored zone spanning approximately 100 square kilometers of forested terrain may be instrumented using approximately 50 spaced-apart sensing nodes, each sensing node incorporating a respective instance of the sensing unit (104) described herein, so as to provide a spatially distributed and redundant coverage of the monitored zone.
[0022]	In some embodiments, the electromagnetic field sensor (104A) may be operative to detect a fluctuation in an electromagnetic field within the monitored zone. The electromagnetic field sensor (104A) may be implemented using a Hall effect sensor, a fluxgate magnetometer, or a magneto-resistive sensor configured to detect low-frequency electromagnetic anomalies. The fluctuation may be associated with a source that may include an electrical discharge, a fault in an electrical distribution line disposed in proximity to the monitored zone, or an atmospheric disturbance. 
[0023]	In some embodiments, the electromagnetic field sensor (104A) may be operative to measure a magnetic field strength within a workable range of approximately 0.2 microtesla to approximately 20 microtesla, where a measured magnetic field strength exceeding approximately 6 microtesla is indicative of a pre-ignition condition within the monitored zone. In some embodiments, the electromagnetic field sensor (104A) may further be operative to detect a variation in an electric field associated with an atmospheric charge accumulation, the electric field variation being indicative of an impending lightning-induced ignition event.
[0024]	In some embodiments, the air ionization sensor (104B) may include a bipolar ion counter or a Gerdien condenser operative to detect a concentration of ionized particles present in an air sample obtained from the monitored zone. The sensor (104B) measures the mobility of small air ions within a workable range of approximately 300 ions per cubic centimeter to approximately 2500 ions per cubic centimeter, where a measured ion concentration exceeding approximately 1500 ions per cubic centimeter is indicative of an atmospheric instability that may precede a spontaneous combustion event or a lightning-induced ignition event within the monitored zone.
[0025]	In some embodiments, the environmental sensor (104C) may include one or more of a temperature sensor operative within a workable range of approximately -10 degrees Celsius to approximately 60 degrees Celsius, a humidity sensor operative within a workable range of approximately 5 percent to approximately 95 percent relative humidity, and a wind speed sensor operative within a workable range of approximately 0 kilometers per hour to approximately 50 kilometers per hour, each generating a respective environmental measurement associated with the monitored zone. In some embodiments, a measured ambient temperature exceeding approximately 35 degrees Celsius, a measured relative humidity below approximately 20 percent, or a measured wind velocity exceeding a threshold value, may each be indicative of an elevated fire likelihood within the monitored zone.
[0026]	In some embodiments, the thermal sensor (104D) may include an infrared imaging sensor operative within a workable range of approximately 20 degrees Celsius to approximately 100 degrees Celsius, and may be operative to generate a thermal measurement associated with a surface or a sub-surface temperature within the monitored zone, the thermal measurement being usable to identify a localized sub-surface heat anomaly that may precede a visible ignition and that may not be attributable to an ambient environmental condition.
[0027]	In some embodiments, the suppression unit (110) may include one or more of a sprinkler apparatus, a fogging apparatus, and a chemical suppressant dispenser. The fire suppressant dispensed may include water, aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF), or a dry chemical powder. The fogging apparatus may be specifically configured to atomize water or chemical agents into a fine mist to increase the surface area of the suppressant for rapid cooling of the monitored zone. The suppression unit (110) positioned at a location within the monitored zone, and may be communicably coupled to the control unit (106) such that the suppression unit (110) may be remotely actuated responsive to the signal received from the control unit (106).
[0028]	In some embodiments, the suppression unit (110) may be actuated by the control unit (106) for an actuation duration within a workable range of approximately 30 seconds to approximately 10 minutes, and may dispense the fire suppressant over a coverage radius within a workable range of approximately 5 meters to approximately 50 meters about the location of the suppression unit (110) within the monitored zone, the actuation duration and the coverage radius each being adjustable by the control unit (106) based on the fire risk score determined for the monitored zone.
[0029]	In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) may transmit data using a communication protocol that may include a low-power wide-area network protocol, a long-range wide-area network protocol, or a combination thereof, and the communication unit (112) may further employ a cellular communication protocol as a fallback communication channel responsive to unavailability of the low-power wide-area network protocol. 
[0030]	In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) may transmit data at a transmission interval within a workable range of approximately 1 minute to approximately 30 minutes, the transmission interval being adaptively adjusted based on a sensor activity level and an available energy level associated with the power supply unit (114).
[0031]	In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) may be operative to transmit data over a transmission distance of up to approximately 15 kilometers in open terrain, and may transmit data as a data packet having a size within a workable range of approximately 20 bytes to approximately 512 bytes. In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) may perform between approximately 1 and approximately 5 retry attempts responsive to a transmission failure occurring during a network outage, so as to provide a resilience against an intermittent communication disruption within the monitored zone. In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) may transmit the alert generated by the control unit (106) through a plurality of communication channels concurrently, the plurality of communication channels including a short messaging service channel, an electronic mail channel, and a cloud-based dashboard channel, such that the alert reaches the remote response device through more than one communication channel substantially concurrently.
[0032]	In some embodiments, the communication unit (112) of a first instance of the system (102) may relay data received from a second instance of the system (102) deployed at a geographically adjacent monitored zone, such that the plurality of spaced-apart sensing nodes referred to with reference to FIG. 1 herein above may form a mesh network extending an effective communication range beyond the transmission distance of an individual communication unit (112), and such that the sensor data or the alert associated with the second instance of the system (102) may reach the remote response device via the first instance of the system (102) responsive to an unavailability of a direct communication path from the second instance of the system (102) to the remote response device.
[0033]	In some embodiments, the power supply unit (114) may include a solar energy source and an associated energy storage element, such that the sensing unit (104) and the control unit (106) may operate autonomously in the monitored zone over an extended duration, which may exceed approximately six months, without requiring a manual battery replacement. In some embodiments, the control unit (106) may further be operative to adjust an operating duty cycle of one or more sensors of the sensing unit (104) based on an available energy level associated with the power supply unit (114), so as to balance an energy consumption of the sensing unit (104) against the reliability of the pre-ignition condition prediction provided by the system (102).
[0034]	In some embodiments, the control unit (106) may operate in a sleep mode for a duration within a workable range of approximately 5 minutes to approximately 30 minutes between successive instances of receiving the sensor data, so as to conserve the electrical power supplied by the power supply unit (114), and the control unit (106) may transition from the sleep mode to an active mode responsive to a firmware-controlled wake interval or responsive to an interrupt signal generated by a sensor of the sensing unit (104) upon the sensor measurement exceeding a preliminary threshold lower than the respective threshold employed by a real-time anomaly detection unit (refer FIG. 2), such that a computational load associated with a processor (refer FIG. 2) may be reduced during a period in which the monitored zone is not exhibiting the anomaly.
[0035]	In some embodiments, the sensing unit (104), the control unit (106), and the suppression unit (110) may each be disposed within a weatherproof enclosure having an ingress protection rating of at least IP65, so as to shield a corresponding hardware component from a weather condition, a moisture condition, or a wildlife-related disturbance associated with the monitored zone.
[0036]	In some embodiments, the external data unit (116) may include a satellite data source, a meteorological data source, or a combination thereof, and the external data associated with the monitored zone may include a satellite-derived fire risk indicator or a forecast weather parameter associated with the monitored zone. In some embodiments, the satellite data source may be updated at a periodic interval, and the external data unit (116) may make available to the control unit (106) an updated instance of the external data responsive to each such periodic interval.
[0037]	In some embodiments, the satellite data source of the external data unit (116) may include a forest fire monitoring service and a moderate-resolution satellite imaging service, such that the external data received at the control unit (106) may include a satellite-derived active fire indicator and a satellite-derived vegetation moisture indicator associated with the monitored zone. In some embodiments, a risk determination unit (refer FIG. 2) may cross-reference the satellite-derived active fire indicator against the anomaly detected by the real-time anomaly detection unit, such that a concordance between a locally sensed anomaly and a satellite-derived indicator may increase a confidence value associated with the fire risk score, whereas an absence of a corresponding satellite-derived indicator may not by itself preclude the fire risk score from reflecting an elevated pre-ignition condition, since a locally sensed electromagnetic or ionization precursor may precede a satellite-detectable thermal signature.
[0038]	FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary block diagram (200) of the control unit (106) of the system (102), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0039]	Referring to FIG. 2, the control unit (106) may include one or more processors (202), one or more memories (204) coupled to the processor (202), and an interface (206). The control unit (106) may further include a processing unit (208) and a database (226).
[0040]	In an embodiment, the memory (204) may store instructions which, on execution by the processor (202), may cause the processing unit (208) to perform one or more operations described herein. The interface (206) may facilitate a communicable coupling between the control unit (106) and each of the sensing unit (104), the alert unit (108), the suppression unit (110), the communication unit (112), and the power supply unit (114) (refer to FIG. 1), and between the control unit (106) and the external data unit (116) (refer to FIG. 1).
[0041]	In some embodiments, the memory (204) may include a non-transitory computer-readable storage medium storing the instructions executable by the processor (202), the non-transitory computer-readable storage medium including one or more of a volatile memory element and a non-volatile memory element. In some embodiments, the processor (202) may include a microcontroller or a microprocessor, and the sensing unit (104) may further include an analog-to-digital converter operative to digitize an analog signal generated by a sensor of the sensing unit (104) prior to the data reception unit (210) (refer to FIG. 2) receiving the sensor data therefrom, such that the electromagnetic field measurement, the air ionization measurement, the environmental measurement, and the thermal measurement may each be represented as a digital value processed by the processor (202).
[0042]	In an embodiment, the processing unit (208) may include a data reception unit (210), a real-time anomaly detection unit (212), a historical data analysis unit (214), a risk determination unit (216), an intervention control unit (218), a risk classification unit (220), an external data integration unit (222), and a feedback recalibration unit (224), each disposed within the processing unit (208) as illustrated in FIG. 2.

title: A BIO-QUANTITATIVE DATA PROCESSING SYSTEM AND COMPUTING FRAMEWORK FOR PSYCHOSOCIAL MEASUREMENT
abstract: The present invention introduces a dopamine-based bio-quantitative framework that enhances the measurement of subjective human experiences. The computing system and framework propose the use of blood (plasma) and 24-hour urine dopamine measurements as objective physiological indicators to complement conventional scales. By developing structured dopamine-based scales, the system translates variations in biochemical levels into proportional indices that reflect changes in psychosocial constructs such as happiness, satisfaction, excitement, opinion, and agreement. This approach enables the integration of biological markers with behavioral data, providing a more grounded and measurable representation of respondents’ emotional and cognitive states in a feasible and scalable method.
specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD
The present invention generally relates to the field of bio-quantitative data processing, biometric computing systems, and psychometric evaluation. More particularly, the invention relates to a computing system and specialized data processing framework configured to receive raw physiological biomarker data specifically peripheral dopamine levels and execute algorithmic mappings to output objective, quantifiable indices of non-pathological psychosocial constructs such as happiness, satisfaction, excitement, opinion, and agreement.

BACKGROUND
Traditional social science research heavily relies on subjective scaling techniques, such as the Likert Scale, Semantic Differential Scale, Thurstone Scale, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS), to measure respondents’ attitudes and emotional states. While these tools convert qualitative responses into numerical data, they inherently restrict respondents’ feelings within predefined psychological intervals, limiting the realism and depth of the captured emotional states. The results of these subjective reports are often susceptible to cognitive bias and self-reporting inaccuracies.

The underlying study further describes conventional social-science scaling approaches including the Likert Scale, Semantic Differential Scale, Guttman Scale, Thurstone Scale, Constant Sum Scaling, Rank-Order Scale, Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and Q-Sort Technique. These approaches are used to record attitudes, opinions, satisfaction, personality-related variables, preference, and other subjective responses at predefined response intervals. The present disclosure provides a biochemical data-based complement to such subjective scaling by converting numerical peripheral dopamine observations into structured proportional indices.

In the clinical domain, psychology utilizes scales like the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) or Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D) to evaluate pathological mental health conditions. However, there is a distinct lack of objective, biologically grounded computing frameworks for measuring standard, non-pathological human experiences in social science, consumer research, and behavioral economics.

Dopamine plays a crucial role in the brain's motivation, reward, and pleasure systems. Current methods for measuring peripheral dopamine, such as blood plasma analysis and 24-hour urinary excretion, are well-established, yielding standard reference ranges such as 0-30 pg/mL for resting adult plasma and 65-400 µg/day for urinary excretion. Prior arts (e.g., WO2006015606A1 or advanced biosensor technologies) strictly apply dopamine measurement to the clinical diagnosis of pathological disease states or claim the physical hardware of chemical detection.

The study identifies several factors capable of influencing peripheral dopamine measurements, including stress, diet, medications, activity, sleep patterns, time of day, posture, and general physiological condition. Accordingly, the computing framework may retain contextual information associated with a measurement and may apply baseline/reference comparison or data-quality validation before generating a proportional index.

The study describes multiple approaches for evaluating dopamine-related activity, including biological samples, neuroimaging, behavioural assessments, pharmacological observations, and self-report surveys. Blood plasma and 24-hour urinary measurements are selected for the disclosed framework because they are comparatively accessible and suitable for repeated or large-scale research, whereas PET imaging and CSF analysis are more specialized or invasive.

There remains a critical unmet need for a technical computing system capable of ingesting routine, non-diagnostic biomarker data through a structured framework to algorithmically generate a proportional index reflecting changes in normal psychosocial constructs.

OBJECTIVES:
An objective of present disclosure provides a bio-quantitative computing system that translates qualitative human responses into quantifiable biometric measures, eliminating the subjectivity of traditional social science surveys.

Another objective of present disclosure provides a data processing system configured to automatically execute a mathematical mapping of blood (plasma) and 24-hour urine dopamine measurements into structured proportional percentage indices.

Yet another objective of present disclosure provides a non-diagnostic, technical evaluation tool that correlates biological markers with psychological constructs without requiring highly invasive techniques like Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) analysis or Positron Emission Tomography (PET).
In yet another objective of present disclosure provides a system that calibrates raw biomarker data against established baselines to isolate psychosocial activation from physiological noise.

SUMMARY
The present invention provides a bio-quantitative data processing system that enhances the measurement of subjective human experiences by introducing an automated, dopamine-based evaluation framework. The system comprises an input interface for receiving raw numerical dopamine biomarker data derived from a subject, a memory unit storing predefined proportional mapping scales, a processor, and an output interface.

An aspects of the present disclosure provides a bio-quantitative data processing system (100) for processing previously acquired peripheral dopamine measurement data and generating a standardized quantitative output associated with a selected behavioural or psychosocial variable, the system comprising: 
(a) an input interface (101) configured to receive numerical peripheral dopamine measurement data together with specimen-modality information and measurement-unit information; 
(b) a non-transitory memory unit (102) storing a machine-readable mapping framework comprising a plurality of predefined numerical intervals associated with respective proportional output values; 
(c) a hardware processor (103) communicatively coupled to the input interface (101) and the memory unit (102), the hardware processor being configured to: 
(i) validate the numerical measurement data using at least the specimen-modality information and measurement-unit information; 
(ii) select, from the mapping framework, a corresponding numerical interval for the validated measurement data; 
(iii) compare the validated measurement data with stored reference or baseline information and, where a baseline is available, determine a baseline-referenced change; (iv) generate a standardized quantitative output corresponding to the selected numerical interval and/or the baseline-referenced change; and 
(d) an output interface (104) configured to output the standardized quantitative output together with associated measurement metadata, wherein the system thereby provides a reproducible machine-readable transformation of the received peripheral dopamine measurement data into a standardized quantitative representation for subsequent correlation, comparison or statistical analysis with the selected behavioural or psychosocial variable.

Another aspects of the present disclosure provides a computer-implemented method of processing previously acquired peripheral dopamine measurement data, the method comprising: 
(a) receiving numerical plasma dopamine and/or 24-hour urinary dopamine measurement data together with specimen-modality and measurement-unit information; 
(b) validating the received measurement data using a hardware processor (103); 
(c) retrieving, from a non-transitory memory (102), a machine-readable mapping framework comprising predefined numerical intervals and respective proportional output values; 
(d) selecting a corresponding interval for the validated measurement data; 
(e) comparing the validated measurement data with stored reference or baseline information and, where a baseline is available, determining a baseline-referenced change; 
(f) generating a standardized quantitative output corresponding to the selected interval or the baseline-referenced change; and 
(g) outputting the standardized quantitative output together with associated measurement metadata for subsequent correlation, comparison or statistical analysis with a selected behavioural or psychosocial variable.

The hardware processor is configured to receive the raw biomarker data (specifically blood plasma or 24-hour urine dopamine levels) and automatically map variations in these biochemical levels into proportional indices, ranging from a 10% to 100% increase level. These outputted indices represent quantifiable changes in psychosocial constructs such as happiness, satisfaction, excitement, opinion, and agreement. By translating continuous biochemical data into categorized computational intervals, the system provides a scalable technical method for objective behavioral analysis, strictly excluded from the clinical diagnosis of disease.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
The present invention will now be described in detail with reference to the computing methodologies and system architecture.

The invention is implemented through a computing system configured to execute the disclosed bio-quantitative processing framework. The system may comprise an input interface, memory unit, hardware processor and output interface. The components may be implemented in a single computing device or distributed across multiple computing devices connected through a communication network.

The input interface is configured to receive a numerical dopamine result. The result may originate from a routine laboratory test, laboratory information system, analytical instrument, imported data file, database, application programming interface or manual entry by an authorized researcher. The computing system therefore processes the measurement result and does not require that the system itself perform the biochemical extraction or analytical assay.

The memory unit stores executable instructions and the Bio-Quantitative Mapping Framework. The mapping framework may be represented using tables, records, arrays, rules, database entries or other machine-readable structures. At minimum, the framework identifies a biological modality, numerical interval and corresponding proportional output.

The hardware processor executes the stored instructions to validate the received data, select the applicable mapping, compare the numerical input with stored interval boundaries, perform optional baseline and normalization operations, and generate the final index.

The output interface may comprise a graphical user interface, display, report generator, database output or machine-readable data stream. The output may contain the generated percentage, category, underlying biomarker value, specimen type and associated psychosocial variable.

For clarity of implementation, PD denotes plasma dopamine concentration expressed in pg/mL. UD denotes 24-hour urinary dopamine excretion expressed in µg/day. PD_base and UD_base denote selected baseline observations, while PD_post and UD_post denote subsequent or post-event observations. A proportional index denotes the percentage value retrieved from the stored mapping framework. An NDI denotes the normalized dopamine index generated in the composite embodiment.

A measurement record may contain a subject identifier, specimen type, numerical measurement, unit, collection date and time, baseline designation, generated percentage, NDI where calculated, category, psychosocial score and optional contextual variables. The record may additionally contain the mapping-framework version used to produce the result.

For plasma processing, the processor receives a dopamine concentration represented in pg/mL and determines that the specimen corresponds to blood plasma. For urinary processing, the processor receives a dopamine excretion value represented in µg/day and determines that the underlying collection represents a 24-hour urine observation.

The processor may verify that the unit and specimen definition correspond to the selected mapping. A record with an unsupported unit or specimen definition may be flagged for review rather than being automatically mapped. The validation record may be retained together with the generated output.

Where a baseline is required but unavailable, the system may operate using the stored reference/mapping framework and identify that the result is reference-based. Where only one of the two modalities is available, the system may process that modality and identify the unavailable modality rather than creating a false dual-modality result.

The memory may store reference information separately from the psychosocial proportional scale. The present disclosure identifies approximately 0-30 pg/mL as a resting adult plasma reference range and 65–400 µg/day as a urinary reference range. The processor may classify a received value as within, below or above the corresponding stored reference interval. This classification is contextual and is not itself a diagnosis or a psychosocial output.

The present study adopts blood (plasma) and urine-based dopamine assessments as the primary biochemical measures, based on considerations of feasibility, cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and suitability for social science research designs. While multiple techniques exist to evaluate dopamine activity, including advanced neuroimaging such as Positron Emission Tomography and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, these approaches present significant practical and ethical constraints when applied to large or non-clinical populations.

Blood and urine dopamine tests are comparatively simple to administer. Plasma dopamine measurement requires only a minimally invasive venous blood sample, while 24-hour urinary dopamine assessment is non-invasive and can be conducted with standard participant instructions. These methods do not require specialized infrastructure beyond routine laboratory facilities, making them highly suitable for field-based data collection and large sample studies. In contrast, PET imaging involves the use of radioactive tracers and sophisticated imaging equipment, and CSF analysis requires lumbar puncture, an invasive procedure that is not appropriate for general population research due to associated risks and participant burden.

Cost considerations further support the selection of blood and urine tests. These methods are significantly more economical than PET and CSF-based approaches, enabling their use in studies with larger sample sizes and repeated measurements. Additionally, blood and urine testing facilities are widely available across clinical laboratories, whereas PET imaging and CSF testing are typically restricted to tertiary care centers and specialized research institutions, limiting their scalability.

Another important factor is interpretability. Blood and urine dopamine measures are reported in standardized numerical formats that are relatively straightforward to analyze in interdisciplinary research contexts. Plasma dopamine levels are typically expressed in picograms per milliliter (commonly within a reference range of approximately 0–30 pg/mL), while urinary dopamine is measured over a 24-hour period (generally within 65–400 µg/day). Urine tests often include related metabolites such as homovanillic acid (HVA), vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), and metanephrines, which provide a structured biochemical profile of catecholamine activity. This numerical clarity facilitates statistical modeling and integration with social science variables.

From a practical standpoint, urine dopamine testing provides a useful indicator of overall catecholamine production and potential excess, whereas plasma dopamine offers a rapid and minimally invasive measure of circulating levels. Both methods are suitable for routine use and repeated assessment, which is advantageous in longitudinal or experimental designs. In contrast, PET and CSF-based measurements are not intended for routine application and are primarily used in specialized clinical or research settings, such as the evaluation of Parkinson's disease and rare neurotransmitter disorders.

Despite these advantages, it is essential to recognize the limitations of blood and urine dopamine measurements. These tests primarily reflect peripheral dopamine activity and do not directly capture central nervous system processes. Consequently, they should be interpreted as indirect indicators rather than precise measures of brain dopamine function. Techniques such as PET imaging provide superior insight into functional brain activity, while CSF analysis offers a closer approximation of central neurotransmitter metabolism.

In summary, the selection of blood and urine dopamine testing in this study is methodologically justified by their practicality, affordability, accessibility, and ease of interpretation. These characteristics make them particularly appropriate for social science research contexts, where large sample sizes and non-invasive data collection are critical. However, interpretations are made with appropriate caution, acknowledging the distinction between peripheral biochemical markers and central neurobiological mechanisms.

System Architecture: The invention operationalizes a bio-quantitative framework through a specialized computing system. The system includes:
1.	Input Interface: Configured to receive quantitative data from standard peripheral biomarker tests. The data comprises numerical values representing plasma dopamine (measured in pg/mL) and 24-hour urinary dopamine (measured in µg/day).
2.	Memory Unit: A non-transitory computer-readable storage medium that hosts the "Bio-Quantitative Mapping Framework." This framework is a database of categorized computational intervals.
3.	Hardware Processor: Configured to execute comparison and normalization algorithms. The processor establishes a baseline for the subject, filters out identified physiological confounders (e.g., standard dietary noise), and compares the isolated raw data against the framework stored in the memory.
4.	Output GUI: A graphical user interface that displays the final psychometric index.

Data Processing Framework - Plasma Dopamine: The system’s memory stores a structured plasma dopamine-based scale that translates biochemical measurements into a proportional index of relative dopamine increase. The processor executes instructions to map the inputted raw plasma data according to the following predefined intervals:
•	30-40 pg/mL corresponds to a 15% increase level.
•	41-50 pg/mL corresponds to a 30% increase level.
•	51-60 pg/mL corresponds to a 45% increase level.
•	61-70 pg/mL corresponds to a 60% increase level.
•	71-80 pg/mL corresponds to a 75% increase level.
•	81-90 pg/mL corresponds to a 90% increase level.
•	91- <100 pg/mL corresponds to a 100% increase level. This linear progression across plasma ranges provides a standardized metric for the system to output a quantitative value reflecting a subject's level of satisfaction or excitement.

Data Processing Framework - Urinary Dopamine: For a broader representation of cumulative physiological arousal, the system's memory stores a 24-hour urine-based scale. The processor maps the inputted raw urinary data according to the following intervals:
•	65-90 µg/day corresponds to a 10% increase level.
•	91-125 µg/day corresponds to a 20% increase level.
•	126-160 µg/day corresponds to a 30% increase level.
•	161-195 µg/day corresponds to a 40% increase level.
•	196-230 µg/day corresponds to a 50% increase level.
•	231-265 µg/day corresponds to a 60% increase level.
•	266-300 µg/day corresponds to a 70% increase level.
•	301-335 µg/day corresponds to a 80% increase level.
•	336-390 µg/day corresponds to a 90% increase level.
•	<391 µg/day corresponds to a 100% increase level. This framework enables the system to generate a stable, cumulative index of psychosocial activation states, reducing the influence of short-term physiological fluctuations. The output is a highly accurate, biometric validation of survey responses.
 
The Proposed Social Science Research Scales through Dopamine Measures  
From the study, a social science research scale is developed based on blood and urine dopamine tests to translate qualitative human responses into quantifiable measures. The respondents’ subjective aspects such as happiness, opinion, satisfaction, excitement, and agreement are interpreted through corresponding increases in dopamine levels obtained from blood (plasma) and 24-hour urine tests. This approach enables the conversion of qualitative perceptions into a structured quantitative framework, where variations in dopamine levels are used as indicative markers of changes in these psychosocial constructs. The proposed scales, presented in Tables 2 and 3, provide a systematic method for linking physiological measures with behavioral and attitudinal outcomes, thereby facilitating more objective analysis in social science research.

Table 1 presents a structured plasma dopamine-based scale that translates biochemical measurements into a proportional index of relative dopamine increase for use in social science analysis. The scale begins at a range of 30–40 pg/mL, corresponding to a 15 percent increase level, and progresses in equal intervals up to values approaching 100 pg/mL, which are assigned a 100 percent increase level. Methodologically, this scaling framework allows researchers to transform continuous biochemical data into categorized intervals that can be more easily integrated with psychosocial variables such as happiness, satisfaction, excitement, opinion, and agreement. The gradual and linear progression of percentage values across plasma ranges provides a standardized metric for comparing respondents based on their physiological dopamine levels. This approach facilitates quantitative modeling, enabling correlation and regression analysis between dopamine levels and subjective constructs. However, it should be noted that plasma dopamine reflects peripheral activity and is sensitive to situational factors such as stress and posture. Therefore, while the scale offers a practical tool for operationalization, it should be interpreted as an indirect indicator of neurobiological influence on behavioral outcomes rather than a direct measure of central dopamine function.

Table 2 outlines a urine-based dopamine scale derived from 24-hour excretion levels, offering a broader representation of total body dopamine production. The scale ranges from 65–90 µg/day, corresponding to a 10 percent increase level, and extends to values approaching 391 µg/day, which represent a 100 percent increase level. The use of multiple graded intervals enables a finer distribution of respondents across dopamine levels, supporting more detailed statistical differentiation in social science research. Compared to plasma measurement, urinary dopamine provides a more stable and cumulative index, reducing the influence of short-term physiological fluctuations. The inclusion of metabolites such as homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid in urine analysis further strengthens its interpretive value as an overall catecholamine profile. Methodologically, this scale enhances the robustness of quantitative analysis by offering a reliable and non-invasive measure that can be applied in large sample studies. It is particularly useful for identifying relative differences in physiological arousal or activation states that may correspond with variations in subjective experiences. Nevertheless, similar to plasma-based measures, urinary dopamine does not directly capture central nervous system activity. As such, the scale should be employed as a proxy indicator, with careful consideration of its limitations when drawing inferences about psychological or behavioral constructs.
