The study establishes a structured approach to integrating physiological measures with social science constructs by developing dopamine-based scales derived from blood (plasma) and 24-hour urine tests. By translating biochemical variations into graded percentage levels, the study provides a systematic framework for quantifying subjective experiences such as happiness, opinion, satisfaction, excitement, and agreement. The findings suggest that blood and urine dopamine measurements can serve as practical proxy indicators for capturing variations in human behavioral and attitudinal responses within a quantitative research design. Compared to advanced techniques such as Positron Emission Tomography and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, the selected methods offer advantages in terms of simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and accessibility, making them suitable for large-scale social science investigations. The developed scales enhance the potential for interdisciplinary research by linking biological markers with psychological and social variables in a measurable and comparable format. However, it is also recognized that these measures primarily reflect peripheral dopamine activity and do not directly capture central nervous system processes. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with appropriate caution, acknowledging the indirect nature of the association between dopamine levels and complex human experiences.

Implications of the study
The study contributes to methodological advancement in social science research by introducing a novel bio-quantitative scaling framework that enables the incorporation of physiological data into behavioral analysis. This approach supports more objective measurement of subjective constructs, thereby reducing reliance on self-reported data alone and enhancing the robustness of empirical findings. The use of blood and urine dopamine tests provides a feasible and scalable option for researchers, particularly in contexts where large sample sizes and field-based data collection are required.

From a practical perspective, the proposed scales can be applied in interdisciplinary domains such as behavioral economics, organizational behavior, consumer research, and public policy studies, where understanding the interaction between physiological states and decision-making processes is increasingly important. The framework also opens avenues for longitudinal studies, allowing researchers to track changes in dopamine levels alongside variations in attitudes and behaviors over time.

At the same time, the study highlights the need for cautious interpretation and further validation. Future research may focus on refining the scaling model, incorporating additional biomarkers, and exploring complementary methods that more directly assess brain function. In particular, integrating biochemical measures with advanced techniques such as PET imaging or clinical assessments in targeted samples may strengthen the explanatory power of the model. Overall, the study provides a foundational step toward bridging biological and social science perspectives through an accessible and methodologically grounded measurement approach.
In view of the foregoing, it is submitted that the present invention represents a pioneering technical leap in the field of biometric computation and psychometric data processing. By engineering a highly specialized and proprietary computing architecture capable of seamlessly translating continuous peripheral biomarker variations into structured proportional indices, the present disclosure successfully solves a long-standing industry deficiency. This automated data processing pipeline unequivocally overcomes the cognitive biases, restrictive intervals, and inherent inaccuracies that have historically plagued conventional social science and consumer research methodologies. 
The invention relies on a system integration comprising a dedicated input interface, an optimized memory unit, and a specialized hardware processor that executes a concrete, physical transformation of biochemical data signals. This constitutes a robust, patentable technological advancement that greatly enhances computational efficiency and biometric data utilization. 
Furthermore, the claimed system is strategically designed for broad commercial, behavioral, and interdisciplinary research applications. The operational matrix of the system is deliberately restricted to the in vitro or ex vivo processing of previously extracted and historical data, thereby operating entirely outside the clinical purview. By ensuring the system does not physically interface with the human body and solely quantifies non-pathological psychosocial states, the present invention provides a highly scalable technological tool that strictly avoids any overlap with methods of diagnosis or treatment under Section 3(i) of the Act. 
In one embodiment, the computing system receives a previously generated laboratory result rather than performing the biochemical assay itself. The input may be received from a laboratory information system, analytical instrument, imported data file, database, application programming interface, or authorized manual entry. The received record may include the specimen modality, numerical value, unit, collection time, baseline designation, and associated contextual variables.
In another embodiment, the processor compares a measurement collected at a later or post-event time with a selected baseline measurement for the same subject. For plasma, PD denotes the dopamine concentration in pg/mL; for urine, UD denotes the 24-hour dopamine excretion in µg/day. Corresponding baseline and post-event values may be retained as PD_base, PD_post, UD_base and UD_post. The processor may determine the change between the baseline and subsequent observation before applying the stored mapping or normalization operation.
The mapping framework may be implemented as a database table, array, lookup structure, rule set, indexed records, or another machine-readable representation. Each mapping record may identify the biological modality, unit, numerical interval, proportional output, category, and optional version identifier. Consequently, the system can maintain reproducibility of outputs when the mapping framework is updated or different versions are used in different research studies.
The processor may perform data-quality checks before mapping. Such checks may include verification of specimen type, measurement unit, numerical validity, supported interval, availability of a baseline, and whether the measurement falls within a validated analytical range. Unsupported or incomplete records may be flagged for review. Where only one modality is available, the system may generate a single-modality result and identify the unavailable modality rather than generating a false dual-modality result.
A composite embodiment may calculate the Normalized Dopamine Index (NDI) from normalized plasma and urinary components. In the demonstrated example, PD_post is 55 pg/mL, UD_post is 180 µg/day, PD_base is 30 pg/mL, UD_base is 120 µg/day, the population standard deviations are σP=10 and σU=40, and the resulting normalized components are ZP=2.5 and ZU=1.5. Applying the disclosed transformation gives f(ZP)=0.924 and f(ZU)=0.818; a weighted combination S=0.4×0.924+0.6×0.818=0.862 corresponds to an NDI of approximately 86.5%, classified as High. The particular example is illustrative of machine execution of the normalization and combination operations.
The study provides analytical and inferential validation information associated with the framework, including plasma LOD of 0.005 pg/mL, plasma LOQ of 0.02 pg/mL, urinary LOD of 0.1 µg/day and urinary LOQ of 0.5 µg/day; intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation; spike recovery of 92–105%; and pilot quality-control results. These values may be retained as validation metadata and may be used by the processor to identify whether an input measurement is within an analytically validated operating range.
In a representative pilot dataset of 50 observations described in the study, the NDI distribution had a mean of 58.2% with a standard deviation of 24.1% and a range of 4.8–98.7%. The study reports a Pearson correlation of r=0.52 (p=0.0002) between NDI and happiness score, a regression coefficient of β=0.045 per 1% NDI with p<0.001 and R²=0.31, and test–retest ICC of 0.76 (95% CI 0.61–0.87) in a subset of 15 participants. These results provide an example of validation of the computational index and do not convert the index into a clinical diagnosis.
The study also reports controls addressing dietary variation, time of day, medication, and self-reported stress. Plasma samples were collected between 08:00 and 10:00 in the reported pilot to reduce circadian variation. Sensitivity analyses reported correlations of r=0.54 after excluding dietary deviations and r=0.51 after excluding participants taking the identified medications, while self-reported stress showed a weak correlation with NDI (r=0.12, p=0.38). Such contextual variables may be stored with measurement records and used for quality-control, stratification, or subsequent statistical analysis.
The generated indices may be used in interdisciplinary research including behavioural economics, organizational behaviour, consumer research, public-policy studies, longitudinal research, and other non-clinical studies in which physiological observations are analyzed together with attitudes or behavioural responses. The system may support repeated observations over time, enabling comparison of changes in dopamine-derived indices with changes in recorded psychosocial variables.
The peripheral dopamine measurements and the resulting indices are intended as indirect or proxy indicators of neurobiological influence and are not represented as direct measurements of central dopamine activity. The framework therefore permits cautious interpretation of associations between peripheral biochemical measurements and complex psychosocial constructs. The disclosed system does not require PET imaging, CSF sampling, or a diagnostic or therapeutic determination.
The disclosure further contemplates longitudinal and comparative studies in which baseline and subsequent measurements are retained in a structured record. A record may include subject identifier, specimen type, measurement, unit, collection date and time, baseline designation, proportional output, NDI, category, psychosocial score, contextual variables, and mapping-framework version, thereby permitting reproducible downstream analysis.
In a preferred implementation, the system receives laboratory-generated plasma dopamine and/or 24-hour urinary dopamine results through a laboratory information system, analytical instrument, imported data file, database interface, application programming interface or authorized manual input. The processor first validates specimen type, unit and numerical validity, then selects the applicable mapping records stored in memory. Where a baseline is available, the processor determines the corresponding baseline-referenced change and may calculate a normalized component. Where both plasma and urinary measurements are available, the processor may generate a composite NDI using the disclosed normalization, transformation and weighting operations. The resulting percentage or NDI, together with associated metadata, is output as a machine-readable record, display, report or database entry.
The preferred implementation does not require the system to collect a biological sample or perform the biochemical assay. The system processes previously acquired numerical measurements and can retain specimen type, measurement unit, collection time, baseline designation, mapping-framework version, generated index and optional psychosocial score as structured data fields.
For avoidance of doubt, the proportional indices and NDI disclosed herein are computational proxy indicators for research and non-pathological psychosocial analysis. They are not represented as direct measurements of central nervous system dopamine activity and are not intended, by themselves, to diagnose, treat, prevent or monitor a disease or medical condition.
The standardized quantitative output may be used as a research index or proxy representation and may be associated with a behavioural or psychosocial variable such as happiness, satisfaction, excitement, opinion or agreement. The output is not required to be a clinical diagnosis, and the system processes previously acquired peripheral measurements rather than requiring the system itself to perform biological sampling or biochemical extraction.

title: BENCHMARK A SCHEDULER IN BAREMETAL SYSTEM
abstract: The present invention relates to a software-based benchmarking method for measuring performance overhead of a bare-metal scheduler in an embedded computing system. The method initializes a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) and a high-resolution hardware timer (100), executes a predefined mathematical operation under a baseline condition (110), records baseline start and end times (120, 140), and determines a baseline execution time t (150). A bare-metal scheduler having an active task and configurable idle tasks is subsequently initialized (170) and executed for a complete cycle (180). The same mathematical operation is executed as the active task, while scheduler start and end times are recorded (190, 200, 210) to determine scheduler execution time T (220). A normalized scheduler overhead is calculated (230) as [(T − t)/t] × 100. The method provides a repeatable and hardware-portable performance metric for scheduler optimization, comparison, regression testing, and embedded-system evaluation across different processor and microcontroller architectures.
specification:
The present invention provides a software-based benchmarking method for quantitatively determining the performance overhead of a bare-metal scheduler. The invention establishes a controlled computational baseline and compares it with the execution of substantially the same computational workload under a scheduler-controlled environment.
The method begins with initialization of a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) and a high-resolution hardware timer (100). A predefined mathematical operation is executed under a baseline condition (110). A baseline start time is recorded (120), the predefined mathematical operation is executed (130), and a baseline end time is recorded (140). The baseline execution time t is subsequently calculated (150) and established as a reference value (160).
[0014]  A bare-metal scheduler is then initialized with at least one active task and a configurable number of idle tasks (170). The scheduler is executed for one complete cycle (180). The scheduler start time and scheduler end time are recorded at (190) and (200), respectively, while the active task executes the same predefined mathematical operation within the scheduler (210). The scheduler execution time T is then determined (220).
[0015]  The invention calculates the normalized scheduler overhead at (230) according to: Overhead % = [(T − t) / t] × 100. The calculated result may be stored, processed and presented through a benchmark report and/or visualization. The HAL separates platform-specific hardware functions from the core benchmarking logic, thereby supporting application across different embedded processor and microcontroller architectures. The disclosed methodology provides a controlled and reproducible metric for evaluating scheduler efficiency, comparing scheduler implementations, performing regression testing, and supporting embedded hardware selection.

title: A Computer-Implemented System for Context-Aware Multi- Stage Cyber Threat Investigation
abstract: The present invention relates to the field of cybersecurity and particularly, to a computer-implemented system and method for context-aware multi-stage cyber threat investigation through dynamic investigation context management and adaptive evidence retrieval. The invention addresses the limitations of conventional SIEM systems that generate isolated security alerts requiring extensive manual investigation. The proposed system comprises functional modules for security event acquisition, event normalization, threat assessment, event correlation, investigation context management, investigation knowledge gap analysis, adaptive evidence retrieval, investigation priority evaluation, investigation report generation, and Security Operations Center dashboard presentation. The system continuously maintains an evolving investigation context by correlating security events, identifying investigation knowledge gaps, retrieving relevant cybersecurity evidence, evaluating investigation priority using contextual information, and generating structured investigation reports. The invention improves investigation continuity, reduces manual investigation effort, enhances contextual understanding of multi-stage cyber threats, and supports efficient cybersecurity investigation and incident response within enterprise Security Operations Center.
specification:
The present invention provides a computer-implemented system and method for context-aware multi-stage cyber threat investigation through dynamic investigation context management and adaptive evidence retrieval. The invention is designed to assist Security Operations Centers (SOCs) in efficiently investigating cybersecurity incidents by continuously maintaining an evolving investigation context, adaptively retrieving relevant cybersecurity evidence, evaluating investigation priority, and generating structured investigation reports. Unlike conventional Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems that primarily generate isolated alerts requiring extensive manual correlation, the proposed invention enables continuous investigation of related security events by maintaining investigation continuity throughout the incident lifecycle.

title: DIRECTION-AWARE SELECTIVE VERTICAL ROUTING FOR PORT-CONSTRAINED 3D NETWORK-ON-CHIP ARCHITECTURE
abstract:
ABSTRACT
DIRECTION-AWARE SELECTIVE VERTICAL ROUTING FOR PORT-CONSTRAINED 3D NETWORK-ON-CHIP ARCHITECTURE
The present invention relates to direction-aware selective vertical routing system and method, for a port-constrained three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture. The system comprises five-port planar routers arranged in a two-dimensional mesh across a plurality of stacked layers, wherein predetermined unused planar ports of selected boundary routers are reassigned to establish vertical inter-layer communication without introducing dedicated UP and DOWN ports, thereby preserving the original five-port router architecture and router radix. The disclosed routing method determines whether packet transmission requires intra-layer or inter-layer communication. For intra-layer communication, deterministic XY routing is performed. For inter-layer communication, the routing method determines the required vertical direction, identifies routers capable of supporting the required vertical traversal, and forwards packets through predetermined gateway routers when direct vertical traversal is unavailable.
specification:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION
[0001]	The invention relates to Network-on-Chip architectures, and more particularly to a direction-aware selective vertical routing technique for extending a conventional two-dimensional mesh router into a three-dimensional communication architecture without increasing router radix. 

BACKGROUND LITERATURE
[0002]	With the rapid advancement of multi-core integrated circuits, Network-on-Chip (NoC) architectures have emerged as an efficient communication paradigm for enabling high-speed data transfer among processing elements, memory modules, and peripheral components within a single chip. Conventional NoC implementations predominantly employ two-dimensional (2D) mesh topologies due to their simple routing structure and ease of implementation. However, as the number of processing cores increases, 2D NoC architectures encounter challenges such as increased communication latency, higher power consumption, network congestion, and limited scalability.
[0003]	To overcome these limitations, three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip architectures have been introduced, wherein multiple silicon layers are vertically stacked and interconnected using vertical interconnect technologies, such as Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs). By enabling communication across stacked layers, 3D NoCs reduce average communication distance, improve bandwidth, and enhance overall system performance while providing better area utilization.
[0004]	Despite these advantages, conventional 3D NoC router architectures generally incorporate dedicated vertical communication ports, such as UP and DOWN ports, in every router to facilitate inter-layer packet transmission. The inclusion of dedicated vertical ports throughout the network increases router complexity, silicon area, power consumption, routing method, and manufacturing overhead. Furthermore, several existing asynchronous NoC router architectures have been primarily developed for two-dimensional communication and require substantial architectural modifications to support efficient three-dimensional routing.
[0005]	Various solutions have been proposed in the prior art to improve communication efficiency in three-dimensional NoC systems. For example, US2009070549A1 discloses a three-dimensional NoC interconnect architecture employing an arc Benes network, hierarchical Global Asynchronous Locally Asynchronous (GALA) configuration, double wishbone two-dimensional torus ring interconnections, and buffer modulation techniques for packet routing. While this approach enhances communication efficiency, it primarily focuses on interconnect organization and routing infrastructure rather than reducing router port requirements.
[0006]	Similarly, IN141/DEL/2013 describes a three-dimensional NoC router architecture incorporating guided flit logic and a crossbar-based routing mechanism that enables simultaneous multi-directional data transmission. The proposed architecture improves routing efficiency and throughput but continues to rely on dedicated routing resources for vertical communication.
[0007]	Further, US2009138581A1 presents a three-dimensional networking design structure that organizes processing elements and networking layers to facilitate communication across stacked integrated circuit layers. Although the disclosed architecture improves interconnection efficiency, it primarily addresses structural organization rather than optimizing router port utilization.
[0008]	Academic research has also contributed to improving NoC routing performance. For instance, the paper entitled "Energy and Performance Evaluation of a Dimension Order Routing Algorithm for Mesh-of-Tree Based Network-on-Chip Architecture" proposes an optimized dimension-order routing algorithm that simplifies router operation and reduces network energy consumption. However, the work is directed toward routing optimisation within existing router architectures and does not address efficient vertical communication using constrained router resources.
[0009]	Another study entitled "Three-Dimensional Hamiltonian Broadcast Wormhole Routing" introduces deadlock-free Hamiltonian broadcast algorithms for wormhole-routed three-dimensional mesh networks. The proposed algorithms improve broadcast communication by efficiently routing flit-based packets in three-dimensional networks while avoiding deadlocks. Nevertheless, the work focuses on routing algorithms and broadcast communication without addressing router microarchitecture or reducing the hardware overhead associated with dedicated vertical ports.
[0010]	Accordingly, the existing literature primarily addresses improvements in three-dimensional interconnection structures, routing algorithms, broadcast mechanisms, or crossbar architectures. Most existing solutions achieve vertical communication by incorporating dedicated vertical interfaces or by extending conventional two-dimensional routers into three-dimensional architectures, resulting in increased hardware complexity and resource utilisation.
[0011]	Three-dimensional NoC architectures have been proposed to overcome these limitations by enabling vertical communication between stacked layers using vertical interconnects such as through-silicon vias. However, conventional 3D NoC routers typically require additional UP and DOWN ports in every router, which increases hardware complexity, silicon area, power consumption, and design overhead. Many existing asynchronous router architectures are also optimized for 2D communication and cannot be extended to 3D without significant redesign. 
[0012]	Accordingly, there remains a need for an improved three-dimensional NoC router architecture that enables efficient inter-layer communication without requiring dedicated vertical ports in every router. There is a further need for a routing mechanism capable of selectively utilising existing directional resources, particularly unused directional ports of boundary routers, to establish vertical communication while reducing hardware complexity, silicon area, power consumption, and design overhead. Such an architecture should be compatible with both synchronous and asynchronous NoC systems while maintaining efficient packet routing performance.
[0013]	Accordingly, there exists a need for a routing architecture that enables efficient 3D communication while maintaining a fixed router port count and minimizing hardware overhead. 

OBJECT OF THE INVENTION
[0014]	An object of the present invention is to provide a three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip (NoC) communication mechanism that reuses unused planar ports of boundary routers to facilitate vertical inter-layer communication without requiring dedicated vertical ports.
[0015]	Another object of the present invention is to preserve the original five-port planar router architecture while enabling communication across multiple layers without increasing the router radix or hardware complexity.
[0016]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a deterministic and sparse inter-layer connectivity scheme by selectively assigning unused planar ports of boundary routers for vertical communication based on router position and layer.
[0017]	Another object of the present invention is to support deterministic XY routing for packet transmission within each layer while enabling direction-aware vertical routing between layers.
[0018]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a routing mechanism that determines the required vertical direction and selectively performs vertical traversal through routers having the appropriate vertical communication capability.
[0019]	Another object of the present invention is to reduce hardware overhead, area, and power consumption associated with providing dedicated vertical communication ports in every router, while maintaining efficient packet delivery in a port-constrained three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip architecture.
[0020]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a routing architecture that efficiently utilizes unused planar ports by reusing the same, while retaining vertical interconnects within the architecture. 
[0021]	Another object of the present invention is to provide a scalable routing architecture that enables efficient inter-layer packet transmission using existing router resources without modifying the fundamental router design.
[0022]	Other objects and advantages of the present invention will be more apparent from the following description when read in conjunction with the accompanying figures, which are not intended to limit the scope of the invention.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
[0023]	The present invention provides a direction-aware selective vertical routing system, a corresponding method for a port-constrained three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture. The system comprises a plurality of five-port planar routers arranged in a two-dimensional mesh across a plurality of layers, each router including North, South, East, West, and Local ports. Unused planar ports of boundary routers are selectively reused to provide vertical inter-layer communication between adjacent layers without requiring dedicated vertical ports, thereby preserving the original five-port router architecture and router radix.
[0024]	The invention provides a port-preserving 3D NoC architecture in which unused planar ports of corner and edge routers are selectively assigned for vertical connectivity according to the router position within the two-dimensional mesh and the layer index. The routing mechanism determines whether a packet is to remain within the same layer or traverse vertically to another layer. When vertical traversal is required, the routing method determines the required vertical direction and checks whether the current router possesses the corresponding vertical traversal capability. If the current router supports the required upward or downward movement, the packet is forwarded through a predetermined reused planar port assigned for vertical communication. Otherwise, the packet is routed to a predefined gateway router having the required vertical traversal capability, after which vertical traversal is performed and deterministic XY routing is resumed in the destination layer until the destination router is reached.
[0025]	The arrangement of the present invention has other features and advantages which will be apparent from or are set forth in more detail in the accompanying drawings, which are incorporated herein, and the following brief description, which together serve to explain certain principles of the present invention.

Throughout the drawings, the same drawing reference numerals will be understood to refer to the same elements and features. The features and advantages of the present proposed system will become more apparent from the following detailed description a long with the accompanying figures, which forms a part of this application.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
[0032]	The present invention will now be described more fully herein after. The embodiments herein and the various features and advantageous details thereof are explained with reference to the non-limiting embodiments in the following description. Descriptions of well-known components and processing techniques are omitted so as to not unnecessarily obscure the embodiments herein. The examples used herein are intended merely to facilitate an understanding of ways in which the embodiments herein may be practiced and to further enable those skilled in the art to practice the embodiments herein. Accordingly, the examples should not be construed as limiting the scope of the embodiments herein.
[0033]	As used herein, the singular forms "a," "an," and "the" include plural reference unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. The term "and/or" means one or all of the listed elements or a combination of any two or more of the listed elements.
[0034]	The terms “preferred” and “preferably” refer to embodiments of the invention that may afford certain benefits, under certain circumstances. However, other embodiments may also be preferred, under the same or other circumstances. Furthermore, the recitation of one or more preferred embodiments does not imply that other embodiments are not useful and is not intended to exclude other embodiments from the scope of the invention.
[0035]	When the term “about” is used in describing a value or an endpoint of a range, the disclosure should be understood to include both the specific value and endpoint referred to.
[0036]	As used herein the terms “comprises”, “comprising”, “includes”, “including”, “containing”, “characterized by”, “having” or any other variation thereof, are intended to cover a non-exclusive inclusion
[0037]	Unless expressly stated otherwise, the terms used herein to describe the routing operations may be used interchangeably where the context permits. For example, the terms “routing method,” “routing process,” and “routing mechanism” may refer to the process by which a packet is forwarded through the disclosed 3D NoC. The term “routing logic” may refer to the decision-making operations or rules employed for performing the routing method. 
[0038]	As used herein, the term ‘packet’ refers to a unit of data transmitted through the 3D NoC from a source router toward a destination router. The packet may include payload data and associated routing information, control information, or other information used for forwarding the packet through one or more routers.
[0039]	Similarly, the terms “vertical communication,” “vertical traversal,” and “inter-layer communication” may refer to transmission of a packet between different layers of the 3D NoC, particularly between adjacent layers. The terms “upward” or “UP” and “downward” or “DOWN” may respectively refer to vertical traversal toward a higher layer and toward a lower layer.
[0040]	The terms “planar routing,” “intra-layer routing,” and “XY routing” may refer to routing of a packet between routers within the same layer. The term “planar (XY) distance” refers to the distance between routers based on their respective X and Y positions, without consideration of their Z coordinates.
[0041]	The terms “reused planar port,” “reassigned planar port,” and “selectively reused planar port” may refer to a planar port that is otherwise unused for planar communication and is assigned or reassigned for vertical communication. Similarly, the terms “gateway router” and “gateway” may refer to a router selected to provide vertical traversal when a current router does not possess the required vertical traversal capability.
[0042]	The terms “predefined” and “predetermined” may be used interchangeably to refer to an assignment, configuration, criterion, or rule established prior to or independently of a particular packet-routing decision. Such assignment, configuration, criterion, or rule may be established based on the topology, router position, layer index, or other design parameters of the 3D NoC.
[0043]	The following is a detailed description of the present disclosure depicted in the accompanying drawings. However, it may be understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art that the present subject matter may be practised without these specific details. In other instances, well-known methods, procedures, and/or components regarding the said method have not been described in detail so as not to obscure the subject matter of the disclosure. The subject matter of the disclosure will be more clearly understood from the following description of the embodiments thereof, given by way of example only with reference to the accompanying drawings, which are not drawn to scale. 
[0044]	Figure 1(a) illustrates the planar routers 10 arranged in a representative 3 × 3 two-dimensional router mesh 12 wherein the routers are classified as corner routers (C), edge routers (E), and interior routers (I) according to their location within the mesh topology. Figure 1(b), depicts a conventional five-port router architecture together with the availability of unused planar ports that are selectively reused for vertical communication in the proposed three-dimensional Network-on-Chip architecture.
[0045]	In an embodiment, intra-layer communication refers to packet transmission between routers located within the same network layer and is performed using deterministic XY routing through the North, South, East, and West ports. Inter-layer communication refers to packet transmission between routers located in different network layers and includes determining a required vertical traversal direction and routing the packet to a designated gateway router for transferring the packet between layers. Thus, the disclosed routing method supports both intra-layer and inter-layer packet communication while retaining the conventional five-port router architecture and avoiding the need for dedicated vertical ports at each router.
[0046]	Figure 1(a) illustrates a representative 3 × 3 two-dimensional mesh, wherein routers are arranged in rows and columns, arranged in a two-dimensional mesh 12 over a plurality of layers. For ease of reference, the routers are classified as corner routers (C), edge routers (E), and interior routers (I) according to their position within the mesh. Corner routers (C) are positioned at coordinates (0,0), (0,2), (2,0), and (2,2); edge routers (E) are positioned along the mesh boundary excluding the corners; and the interior router (I)is positioned at the centre of the mesh.
[0047]	Figure 1(b) further illustrates planar router 10 comprising five directional ports and which is used throughout the disclosed architecture. Each router comprises North, South, East, West, and Local ports, wherein the North ports 14, South ports 16, East ports 18, and West ports 20 provide planar communication with neighbouring routers and the Local port 22 provides packet injection and ejection. The router architecture remains unchanged throughout the disclosed system, such that no additional vertical ports are introduced and the original five-port router architecture and router radix are preserved.
[0048]	The North (N) port 14, South (S) port 16, East (E) port 18, and West (W) port 20 provide communication interfaces between the router and adjacent routers or network nodes. The North port 14 is configured to transmit and receive data packets in a positive Y-axis direction, while the South port 16 is configured to transmit and receive data packets in a negative Y-axis direction. Similarly, the East port 18 is configured to transmit and receive data packets in a positive X-axis direction, and the West port 20 is configured to transmit and receive data packets in a negative X-axis direction. Accordingly, the directional ports enable a data packet received by the router to be forwarded toward a subsequent router or node based on a destination address or routing information associated with the data packet, thereby facilitating packet transfer across a two-dimensional network.
[0049]	The 5-port 2D router includes the local port 22 configured to provide an interface between the router and a locally connected processing element, node, or other network component. The local port 22 facilitates injection of data packets into the network, wherein a packet generated by the locally connected component is supplied to the router for transmission toward a designated destination through one or more directional ports. The local port 22 further facilitates ejection of data packets from the network, wherein a packet received by the router and identified as being destined for the locally connected component is delivered from the router to the corresponding component through the local port.
[0050]	Referring back to Figures 1(a) and 1(b), the relationship between the router type in Figure 1(a) and the availability of unused planar ports from Figure 1(b) is illustrated. As shown, each corner router (C) possesses two unused planar ports because two planar directions terminate at the mesh boundary. Each edge router (E) possesses one unused planar port corresponding to the direction extending beyond the mesh boundary. Interior routers (I) utilise all four planar directional ports for communication with adjacent routers and therefore possess no unused planar ports available for reuse. 
[0051]	The unused planar ports of the boundary routers (C and E) are selectively reused to provide vertical inter-layer communication between adjacent layers without adding dedicated vertical ports, thereby preserving the original five-port router architecture and router radix.
[0052]	The present invention exploits the availability of the unused planar ports of the boundary routers by selectively reusing predetermined unused planar ports to establish vertical inter-layer communication between adjacent layers instead of introducing dedicated vertical ports. The selective reuse is predetermined according to the router position within the two-dimensional mesh and the layer index of the router. The predetermined assignment of the reused planar ports for vertical communication is illustrated with reference to Figure 2, which describes the vertical connectivity established between adjacent layers.
[0053]	Referring to Figure 2, the port reuse mechanism and vertical direction assignment are illustrated for an exemplary 3 × 3 × 3 mesh Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture. The figure shows three layers of stacked two-dimensional mesh layers 26. The stacked configuration of mesh layers 26 comprise a bottom layer 28 where Z = 0, an intermediate layer 30, where Z = 1, and a top layer 32 where Z = 2. Each layer 28, 30, 32 comprises corner routers C, edge routers E, and an interior router I interconnected by planar communication links 34. The planar links 34 utilise the conventional North, South, East and West directional ports 14, 16, 18, 20 respectively, while selected unused planar ports of the boundary routers (C and E) are reassigned to establish vertical communication/ vertical communication links 38a,38b between corresponding routers 10 located in adjacent layers. Interior routers located at coordinate (1,1) utilise all four planar directional ports for intra-layer communication and therefore do not possess unused planar ports for vertical connectivity. The vertical upward/UP communication links 38b are represented by dotted lines and the vertical downward/DOWN communication links 38a are represented by solid lines.
[0054]	In the bottom layer 28 (Z = 0), vertical communication link is configured only in the vertical upward direction/ vertical UP link 38b (solid lines) towards the intermediate layer (I). Each of the four corner routers 10 reuses one predetermined unused planar port to establish an upward vertical connection/ vertical UP link 38b with the corresponding corner router in intermediate layer 30, Z = 1. Among the four edge routers (E), only the edge routers located at coordinates (0,1) and (1,0) reuse their unused planar ports for upward vertical communication, whereas the remaining edge routers (E) at the rest of the coordinates retain their unused ports as unconnected. Thus, only selected boundary routers participate in vertical traversal from the bottom layer.
[0055]	The intermediate layer 30 (Z = 1) serves as the transition layer between upward and downward communication. Each corner router (C) has two unused planar ports wherein the corner router (C) reuses both available unused planar ports. One predetermined unused planar port is assigned for upward communication/ vertical UP link 38b to the corresponding corner router (C) in the top layer (Z = 2) and the other unused planar port is assigned for downward communication/ vertical down link 38a (dotted lines) to the corresponding corner router (C) in the bottom layer (Z = 0). 
[0056]	Furthermore, each edge router (E) possesses only one unused planar port and is therefore assigned a single vertical communication direction. The edge routers (E) located at coordinates (0,1) and (1,0) are assigned upward communication/ vertical UP link 38b, while the edge routers located at coordinates (1,2) and (2,1) are assigned downward communication/ vertical DOWN link 38A  according to a predefined topology. This predetermined assignment distributes vertical traversal capability across the intermediate layer while avoiding the need for every boundary router to support both directions.
[0057]	The top mesh layer 32 (Z = 2) follows an arrangement symmetrical to that of the bottom mesh layer 28. Each corner router (C) reuses one predetermined unused planar port to establish a downward vertical connection/ DOWN vertical link 38a with the corresponding corner router (C) in the intermediate layer. Similarly, only the edge routers (E) located at coordinates (1,2) and (2,1) establish downward vertical links 38a, while the remaining unused planar ports remain disconnected. Accordingly, boundary routers in the top layer support downward traversal only.
[0058]	As further illustrated in Figure 2, the vertical links 38a, 38b are established only between corresponding routers in adjacent layers, thereby forming a sparse and deterministic inter-layer interconnect. The figure also shows that unused planar ports  that are not selected for vertical communication remain unconnected. Consequently, vertical communication is achieved by selectively reusing existing planar router resources instead of introducing dedicated UP and DOWN ports, thereby preserving the original five-port planar router architecture and router radix while reducing additional hardware overhead.
[0059]	Referring to Figure 3, a flowchart 40 illustrating the direction-aware selective vertical routing method executed by the disclosed three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture is shown. The coordinates X and Y represent the planar position of the router, whereas the coordinate Z represents the bottom, intermediate and top layers. The routing process begins when a packet is generated or received at a source router having source coordinates (Xs, Ys, Zs) and is intended for delivery to a destination router having destination coordinates (Xd, Yd, Zd). The routing method initially determines whether the source router and the destination router are located in the same layer by comparing the source layer coordinate (Zs) with the destination layer coordinate (Zd). 
[0060]	When the source router and the destination router are located in the same layer, i.e., Zs = Zd, no vertical traversal is required. The packet is therefore routed using deterministic XY routing within the current layer until the destination router (Xd, Yd) is reached, whereupon packet delivery is completed. 
[0061]	When the source router and the destination router are located in different layers i.e., Zs ≠ Zd, the routing method determines the required vertical traversal direction by comparing the source layer coordinate (Zs) with the destination layer coordinate (Zd). 
[0062]	When the destination layer is positioned above the source layer i.e., Zd > Zs, the required traversal direction is determined as upward communication link i.e., UP. When the destination layer is positioned below the source layer, i.e., Zd < Zs, the required traversal direction is determined as downward communication link, i.e., DOWN. 
[0063]	After determining the required vertical direction, the routing method determines whether the current router possesses vertical traversal capability in the required direction. Stated otherwise, the routing method checks whether the current router supports the required vertical direction.  The vertical traversal capability is determined according to the predetermined assignment of reused planar ports based on the router position within the two-dimensional mesh and the layer index, as described with reference to Figure 2. 
[0064]	If the current router possesses the required vertical traversal capability, the packet is thus forwarded through the pre-assigned reused planar port assigned for upward or downward vertical communication, thereby traversing to the adjacent layer. Following the vertical traversal, the routing logic resumes deterministic XY routing within the newly reached layer. 
[0065]	When the current router does not possess the required vertical traversal capability, router cannot directly provide the required vertical connection. Therefore, the routing method routes the packet using deterministic XY routing to a predefined gateway router that possesses the required upward or downward vertical communication capability. Once the packet reaches the gateway router, the packet traverses to the adjacent layer through the corresponding reused planar port. Following the vertical traversal, the routing method resumes routing in the newly reached layer and, where necessary, performs further vertical traversals until the destination layer is reached.
[0066]	Here, the routing method first identifies all eligible predefined gateway routers supporting the required vertical direction and having the minimum planar (XY) distance from the current router. If only one eligible gateway router satisfies the minimum distance criterion, that gateway router is selected. If multiple eligible gateway routers satisfy the minimum distance criterion, the routing method applies a predetermined deterministic priority rule to select one gateway router for packet forwarding. When multiple eligible gateway routers satisfy the minimum planar (XY) distance criterion, the gateway router having the lowest X-coordinate is selected. If multiple gateway routers still satisfy the criterion, the gateway router having the lowest Y-coordinate is selected. Upon reaching the gateway router, the packet is forwarded through the corresponding reused planar port to the adjacent layer, after which deterministic XY routing is resumed. 
[0067]	Following each routing decision, the routing method logic determines whether the packet has reached the destination router. If the destination router has not yet been reached, the routing process is repeated by continuing planar routing and, where necessary, performing additional vertical traversals until the destination coordinates are reached. Once the packet reaches the destination router, the routing process terminates and packet delivery is completed.
[0068]	Accordingly, the routing method combines deterministic XY routing for intra-layer communication with selective direction-aware vertical traversal through predetermined gateway routers. Since only selected boundary routers participate in vertical communication through reused planar ports, the disclosed method enables deterministic inter-layer packet transmission while preserving the original five-port planar router architecture and router radix without requiring dedicated vertical communication ports.
Illustrative Example - Figure 4
[0069]	Figure 4 illustrates an exemplary operation of the disclosed direction-aware selective vertical routing method for transmitting a packet from a source router 42 located at coordinates (1,1,0) to a destination router 44 located at coordinates (2,2,2) in the 3D Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture. The bold arrows in Figure 4 indicate the routing path followed by the packet, while the circled source and destination routers (42, 44) identify the starting and ending locations of the routing process. The example demonstrates the operation of the routing method in conjunction with the predetermined vertical connectivity established by selective reuse of unused planar ports as described with reference to Figure 2.
[0070]	In the present example, the routing process begins at the source router 42 at (1,1,0) located in the bottom layer (Z = 0). Since the destination router 44 at (2, 1, 2) is located in the top layer (Z = 2), the routing logic determines that inter-layer communication is required. By comparing the source layer coordinate with the destination layer coordinate, the routing method determines the routing method determines that the required vertical traversal direction is UP, since Zd > Zs
[0071]	In the illustrative example, the source router 42 (1,1,0) is an interior router (I) and therefore does not possess unused planar ports for vertical communication. Consequently, the routing method determines that direct vertical traversal cannot be performed from the source router 42 and selects a predefined gateway router capable of supporting upward communication. In the illustrated embodiment, the nearest upward gateway routers are located at coordinates (0,1,0) and (1,0,0). In the illustrated embodiment, the nearest upward gateway routers are located at coordinates (0,1,0) and (1,0,0), both satisfying the minimum planar (XY) distance criterion. Applying the predetermined deterministic priority rule, the router located at coordinate (0,1,0) is selected because it has the lower X-coordinate. The packet is therefore forwarded using deterministic XY routing from the source router 42 to the selected gateway router (0,1,0).
[0072]	Upon reaching the gateway router at coordinate (0,1,0), the routing method determines that the router possesses upward vertical traversal capability according to the predetermined port assignment. The packet is therefore forwarded through the reused planar port assigned for upward communication and traverses vertically to the corresponding router located at coordinate (0,1,1) in the intermediate layer (Z = 1).
[0073]	After reaching the intermediate layer, the routing method again compares the current layer with the destination layer and determines that an additional upward traversal is required to reach Z = 2. However, the current edge router at coordinate (0,1,1) does not possess upward traversal capability in the illustrated embodiment. Accordingly, the routing method identifies a nearest eligible gateway router within the intermediate layer that supports upward communication. In the illustrated routing example, the corner router located at coordinate (0,2,1) is selected as the gateway router. The packet is therefore forwarded using deterministic XY routing from coordinate (0,1,1) to coordinate (0,2,1).
[0074]	The corner router at coordinate (0,2,1) possesses both upward and downward vertical traversal capability. Accordingly, the packet is forwarded through the predetermined reused planar port assigned for upward communication and traverses vertically to the corresponding corner router located at coordinate (0,2,2) in the top layer (Z = 2).
[0075]	After the packet reaches the top layer, the routing method determines that the current layer and the destination layer are the same. Accordingly, no further vertical traversal is required. The routing method resumes deterministic XY routing within the top layer, forwarding the packet eastward from coordinate (0,2,2) through the intermediate routers until the destination router 44 located at coordinate (2,2,2) is reached, thereby completing packet delivery.
[0076]	The foregoing illustrative example therefore demonstrates the operation of the disclosed routing method, wherein the routing method alternates between deterministic XY routing within a layer and selective vertical traversal through predetermined gateway routers. The example illustrates that vertical communication is performed only through routers possessing the required upward traversal capability, while interior routers continue to operate solely as planar routers. Consequently, the disclosed architecture provides deterministic multi-layer packet transmission while preserving the existing five-port planar router architecture and avoiding the introduction of dedicated vertical communication ports.
[0077]	The disclosed routing mechanism therefore, provides deterministic and structured packet forwarding while preserving the original five-port router architecture without modification to the router data path or crossbar structure. Interior routers perform only planar routing, whereas selected boundary routers provide controlled vertical communication through direction-aware mapping of the reused planar ports. Boundary routers in the bottom layer support upward vertical communication, boundary routers in the top layer support downward vertical communication, and boundary routers in intermediate layers provide predetermined upward and/or downward vertical communication according to the router position within the two-dimensional mesh and the layer index. This arrangement enables sparse and deterministic vertical connectivity while reducing hardware overhead and the requirement for dedicated vertical interconnects.
[0078]	Alternative embodiments include that although the embodiment described in the attached document uses a 3 × 3 × 3 mesh for illustration, the same principle may be extended to other mesh sizes and layer counts, provided that boundary routers have unused planar ports that can be selectively reassigned for vertical communication. The gateway selection and vertical reuse pattern may be fixed at design time or encoded in routing method. 
[0079]	The disclosed architecture of the present invention provides several technical advantages. The disclosed direction-aware selective vertical routing system enables three-dimensional (3D) Network-on-Chip communication without increasing the router port count by reusing unused planar ports of boundary routers for selective vertical communication. The system employs sparse vertical connectivity through direction-assigned edge routers and bidirectional corner routers to provide controlled inter-layer communication while restricting vertical traversal to selected boundary routers, thereby reducing hardware overhead and the requirement for vertical interconnect usage. The disclosed routing mechanism integrates deterministic XY routing for intra-layer communication with selective direction-aware inter-layer routing using purely combinational routing decision logic method for deterministic port selection. The invention extends conventional two-dimensional five-port router architectures to three-dimensional communication without structural redesign, is applicable to both synchronous and asynchronous NoC architectures, and reduces area, power consumption, design complexity, and vertical interconnect requirements.
[0080]	While the foregoing written description of the invention enables one of ordinary skill to make and use what is considered presently to be the best mode thereof, those of ordinary skill will understand and appreciate the existence of variations, combinations, and equivalents of the specific embodiment, method, and examples herein. The invention should therefore not be limited by the above-described embodiment, method, and examples, but by all embodiments and methods within the scope of the invention as claimed. ,

title: FERMENTATION-ASSISTED PROCESS FOR THE PRODUCTION OF A FUNCTIONAL WATER-SOLUBLE POLYSACCHARIDE FROM WHEAT BRAN
abstract:
ABSTRACT
FERMENTATION-ASSISTED PROCESS FOR THE PRODUCTION OF A FUNCTIONAL WATER-SOLUBLE POLYSACCHARIDE FROM WHEAT BRAN
A fermentation-assisted process for producing a functional water-soluble polysaccharide from wheat bran is disclosed. Whole wheat grains are hydrated and subjected to controlled fermentation, with partial replacement of the fermentation liquor; the fermented bran is then separated from the endosperm, dried and milled; and the milled bran is subjected to subcritical water extraction, protein removal, alcohol precipitation, ion-exchange chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. Fermenting the intact grain before extraction raises the recovery of water-soluble polysaccharide from about 2.2 per cent in unfermented bran to about 16.7 per cent. The polysaccharide obtained is a branched α-glucan having an α-(1→4)-linked backbone with trace α-(1→6) branching, about 5,859 Da, Mw about 18,205 Da and a hydrodynamic diameter of about 146.6 nm. It acts as an oil-in-water emulsifier, as an anti-syneresis agent in starch systems at low concentration, and as an antioxidant.

specification:
FIELD OF INVENTION
[0001]	The present invention generally relates to the fields of food biotechnology, functional food ingredients and sustainable valorisation of agro-industrial by-products. More particularly, the present invention relates to a fermentation-assisted process for the extraction, purification and production of a functional water-soluble polysaccharide from fermented wheat bran, and to the glucan-rich polysaccharide obtained thereby, exhibiting hydrocolloid, emulsifying, anti-syneresis, antioxidant and prebiotic properties for applications in the food, nutraceutical, pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
[0002]	The present invention relates generally to the field of cereal by-product valorisation, and more particularly to a fermentation-assisted process in which controlled aqueous fermentation of whole wheat grains is integrated with subcritical water extraction and chromatographic purification so as to recover a water-soluble glucan-rich polysaccharide from wheat bran.
[0003]	Wheat bran is one of the most abundant agro-industrial by-products generated during wheat milling and constitutes approximately 14 to 18 per cent of the grain weight, corresponding to a global availability in the order of 0.12 billion tonnes per annum. Wheat bran is rich in dietary fibre, particularly arabinoxylans, cellulose, β-glucans and other structural polysaccharides, cell wall polysaccharides accounting for approximately 55 to 60 per cent of its dry weight. However, the majority of the said polysaccharides are present in insoluble and tightly bound forms within a complex cell wall matrix, wheat bran being predominantly composed of insoluble dietary fibre and containing only a low proportion of soluble dietary fibre. The said tightly bound state limits extraction efficiency, solubility, bioavailability and industrial utilisation, and wheat bran is accordingly used predominantly as low-value animal feed or discarded as agricultural waste, resulting in underutilisation of a valuable biomass resource.
[0004]	Soluble dietary fibre and water-soluble polysaccharides are, by contrast, of considerable interest by reason both of their nutritional characteristics and of their techno-functional attributes, including emulsifying, thickening, water-binding, oil-binding, film-forming and gelling activities which are essential for improving food texture, stability and mouthfeel. There is accordingly an increasing demand for technologies capable of converting wheat bran into high-value functional ingredients possessing improved technological and biological properties.
[0005]	Existing solutions have attempted to address the recovery of wheat bran polysaccharides through chemical, enzymatic, thermal and mechanical treatments. For instance, the patent application published as CN 109206535 A (Jiangsu Yanjiang Agricultural Science Research Institute) discloses a method of preparing high-purity β-glucan from wheat bran by ethanol reflux defatting, sequential alkaline protease, heat-stable α-amylase and neutral protease treatment, repeated ethanol precipitation, DEAE-52 cellulose ion-exchange chromatography, gel filtration on Sephadex G-100, dialysis and freeze drying. Although the said disclosure achieves a high purity, the process relies upon an extended sequence of enzymatic treatments, employs no biological pre-treatment of the substrate, and yields a β-glucan of weight-average molecular mass of the order of 2.5 × 10⁵ Da, which is structurally distinct from the low molecular mass α-glucan of the present invention and for which no emulsifying, anti-syneresis or prebiotic functionality is disclosed.
[0006]	Another existing solution is disclosed in the patent application published as CN 103652945 A (Jiangsu University), which describes hydrothermal extraction of dietary fibre from agro-industrial by-products followed by centrifugation, spray drying and ultrafine milling. Although the said disclosure establishes hydrothermal extraction as a route to soluble dietary fibre, it does not employ any fermentation pre-treatment, does not exemplify wheat bran as the feedstock, and does not proceed to protein removal, alcohol precipitation or chromatographic purification, so that no purified and structurally characterised polysaccharide is obtained.
[0007]	A further existing solution is disclosed in the patent application published as CN 116004742 A (Jiangsu University), which describes increasing the β-glucan and polyphenol content of barley bran by solid-state fermentation with Lactobacillus plantarum. Although the said disclosure establishes that fermentation may be employed as a pre-treatment which raises the soluble glucan content of a cereal bran, the fermentation is conducted upon isolated bran with a defined inoculum, the fermented bran is used directly as such, and no extraction, purification, structural characterisation or functional evaluation of an isolated polysaccharide is disclosed.
[0008]	The patent published as EP 1363504 B1 (Biovelop International BV) discloses a two-stage enzymatic and wet-milling fractionation of cereal brans yielding germ-rich, endosperm-rich and aleurone-rich protein fractions together with soluble hemicelluloses and oligosaccharides, and the patent application published as US 2009/0191308 A1 discloses emulsified cereal bran derivatives obtained by enzymatic digestion followed by addition of lecithin. In the former, no fermentation and no hydrothermal extraction step is employed; in the latter, the emulsifying function is conferred by the added lecithin rather than by the bran polysaccharide itself, and the carbohydrate obtained is characterised only as lower molecular mass dextrins, oligosaccharides and sugars.
[0009]	Non-patent literature has likewise addressed the individual operations separately. The publication titled “Subcritical water extraction-based methods affect the physicochemical and functional properties of soluble dietary fibers from wheat bran” (Food Chemistry, Vol. 298, Article 124987) discloses subcritical water extraction of soluble dietary fibre from wheat bran but employs no fermentation and no chromatographic purification. The publication titled “Characterization and antioxidant activity of wheat bran polysaccharides modified by Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Bacillus subtilis fermentation” (Journal of Cereal Science, Vol. 97, Article 103157) discloses fermentation of isolated wheat bran with a defined inoculum followed by water extraction, Sevag deproteinisation and ethanol precipitation, but employs no subcritical water extraction, no ion-exchange or size-exclusion purification, and reports neither the emulsifying and anti-syneresis functionality nor the α-glucan structure of the present invention. The publication titled “Effect of bioprocessing and particle size on the nutritional properties of wheat bran fractions” (Innovative Food Science & Emerging Technologies, Vol. 25, pages 19-27) discloses bioprocessing of wheat bran for nutritional modification without recovery of an isolated polysaccharide.
[0010]	The approaches known in the art therefore suffer from a number of limitations, including low extraction yields, high processing costs, the use of harsh chemicals and organic solvents, structural degradation of the polysaccharide, environmental burden and inconsistent product quality. Furthermore, many commercially available polysaccharides and hydrocolloids exhibit limited multifunctionality and require additional chemical modification in order to attain desirable emulsifying, stabilising or bioactive properties. Where a biological pre-treatment has been employed it has been applied to isolated bran rather than to the intact grain, has required a defined microbial inoculum, and has not been integrated with a hydrothermal extraction and chromatographic purification train so as to deliver a purified polysaccharide of defined structure.
[0011]	Accordingly, there exists a need for an improved process capable of converting wheat bran into a water-soluble functional polysaccharide at a materially higher recovery than is attainable from native wheat bran, through an integrated route which employs a biological pre-treatment of the intact grain without a defined inoculum, which employs water rather than organic solvents or harsh chemicals as the extraction medium, and which delivers a purified polysaccharide of defined molecular mass, linkage pattern and particle size. There further exists a need for a single wheat-bran-derived polysaccharide ingredient which simultaneously functions as a hydrocolloid, an oil-in-water emulsifier, an anti-syneresis agent, an antioxidant and a prebiotic substrate, thereby serving as a clean-label alternative to synthetic emulsifiers and stabilisers.
[0012]	The present invention addresses the aforementioned technical problems by providing a fermentation-assisted process in which whole wheat grains are subjected to controlled aqueous fermentation, the fermented bran is thereafter separated, dried and milled, and the milled bran is subjected to subcritical water extraction, protein removal, alcohol precipitation and sequential ion-exchange and size-exclusion chromatography, whereby the recovery of water-soluble polysaccharide is raised from about 2.23 per cent in unfermented wheat bran to about 16.74 per cent in fermented wheat bran, and whereby there is obtained a glucan-rich water-soluble polysaccharide having an α-(1→4)-linked backbone with a trace α-(1→6) branching and possessing hydrocolloid, emulsifying, anti-syneresis, antioxidant and prebiotic functionality.

OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION
[0013]	The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a fermentation-assisted process for the production of a functional water-soluble polysaccharide from wheat bran, wherein controlled fermentation of whole wheat grains is integrated with subcritical water extraction and chromatographic purification so as to overcome the low extraction efficiency associated with conventional chemical, enzymatic, thermal and mechanical treatments of wheat bran.
[0014]	Another objective of the invention is to employ controlled aqueous fermentation of the intact wheat grain as a biological pre-treatment which modifies the wheat bran cell wall architecture, increases the accessibility of the bound polysaccharides, effects partial depolymerisation of complex carbohydrate matrices and thereby enhances the release of soluble fibre components.
[0015]	A further objective of the invention is to raise the recovery of water-soluble polysaccharide from about 2.23 per cent obtainable from unfermented wheat bran to about 16.74 per cent obtainable from fermented wheat bran under otherwise identical extraction and purification conditions.
[0016]	Another objective of the invention is to employ subcritical water extraction as the solubilisation step, whereby penetration of water into the bran matrix is enhanced, solubilisation of the polysaccharide is increased and the requirement for organic solvents is reduced, while the structural integrity of the polysaccharide is preserved.
[0017]	A further objective of the invention is to provide a purification train comprising protein removal, alcohol precipitation, ion-exchange chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography, whereby residual salts, proteins, nucleic acids, pigments and low molecular mass compounds are removed and the desired polysaccharide fraction is concentrated.
[0018]	Another objective of the invention is to provide a water-soluble polysaccharide having a glucan-rich composition, an α-(1→4)-linked glucose backbone with traceable α-(1→6) branching, a number-average molecular mass of about 5,859 Da, a weight-average molecular mass of about 18,205 Da and a nanoscale hydrodynamic particle size.
[0019]	A further objective of the invention is to provide a polysaccharide possessing thermal stability sufficient for high-temperature food processing operations, a high water solubility index and a moderate water activity suited to storage stability.
[0020]	Another objective of the invention is to provide a polysaccharide capable of functioning as a natural oil-in-water emulsifier, stabiliser and texture-enhancing agent suitable for clean-label food formulations.
[0021]	A further objective of the invention is to provide a polysaccharide exhibiting anti-syneresis activity in starch-containing systems when incorporated at a low concentration not exceeding about 0.25 per cent w/v, thereby improving the stability, texture and shelf-life of starch-based and processed food products under refrigerated storage.
[0022]	Another objective of the invention is to provide a polysaccharide possessing concentration-dependent antioxidant activity and potential as a prebiotic substrate for beneficial intestinal bacteria, thereby enabling the development of functional foods and nutraceutical products.
[0023]	A further objective of the invention is to provide an environmentally sustainable, industrially scalable and economically viable technology for converting a low-value agro-industrial by-product into a high-value multifunctional ingredient, thereby promoting a circular bioeconomy.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
[0024]	The following summary is provided to facilitate a clear understanding of the new features in the disclosed embodiment and it is not intended to be a full, detailed description. A detailed description of all the aspects of the disclosed invention can be understood by reviewing the full specification, the drawing and the claims and the abstract, as a whole.
[0025]	In one aspect, the present invention provides a fermentation-assisted process for the production of a functional water-soluble polysaccharide from wheat bran, wherein whole wheat grains are subjected to controlled aqueous fermentation, the fermented wheat bran is separated from the remaining grain components, dried and milled, and the milled fermented wheat bran is subjected to subcritical water extraction followed by protein removal, alcohol precipitation and chromatographic purification.
[0026]	In one aspect, the process comprises a grain preparation stage configured to clean wheat grains so as to remove dust, stones, damaged kernels and foreign materials, and to hydrate the cleaned grains in potable or sterile water so as to initiate the biochemical changes necessary for fermentation.
[0027]	In one aspect, the process comprises a controlled fermentation stage configured to maintain the hydrated wheat grains under predetermined conditions of temperature, moisture and duration, wherein naturally occurring microorganisms elaborate cellulases, hemicellulases, glucanases and further carbohydrate-degrading enzymes which partially degrade the cell wall architecture of the wheat bran and convert insoluble dietary fibre components into soluble polysaccharide fractions.
[0028]	In one aspect, the fermentation stage comprises a partial exchange of the fermentation liquor during the fermentation period, whereby accumulated soluble metabolites are removed and the fermentation is sustained over an extended duration without recourse to a defined microbial inoculum.
[0029]	In one aspect, the process comprises a fermented wheat bran separation and drying stage configured to grind the fermented grains, to separate the bran fraction from the endosperm fraction, and to dry and mill the separated fermented wheat bran so as to obtain a uniform powdered substrate.
[0030]	In one aspect, the process comprises a subcritical water extraction stage configured to disperse the fermented wheat bran powder in water and to subject the dispersion to elevated temperature and pressure, whereby the modified polysaccharides are solubilised without recourse to organic solvents.
[0031]	In one aspect, the process comprises a clarification stage configured to remove proteins, peptides, pigments and further soluble impurities from the extract, and a recovery stage configured to precipitate the crude polysaccharide from the clarified extract by addition of a water-miscible precipitating solvent.
[0032]	In one aspect, the process comprises a purification stage configured to subject the crude polysaccharide to ion-exchange chromatography and thereafter to size-exclusion chromatography, and a drying stage configured to recover the purified polysaccharide as a stable powder.
[0033]	In one aspect, the present invention provides a water-soluble fermented wheat bran polysaccharide obtainable by the said process, the said polysaccharide comprising a glucan having an α-(1→4)-linked glucose backbone together with terminal glucose residues and trace α-(1→6) branching, and having a number-average molecular mass of about 5,859 Da and a weight-average molecular mass of about 18,205 Da.
[0034]	In one aspect, the said polysaccharide is characterised by a hydrodynamic particle size of about 146.6 nm with a polydispersity index of about 0.304, a water solubility index of about 100 per cent determined at a loading of 1 per cent w/v, a moisture content of about 6.2 per cent, a hygroscopicity of about 11.67 per cent at 75 per cent relative humidity, a water activity of about 0.56, an oil holding capacity of about 4.06 mL/g and a principal thermal decomposition event occurring at about 322 °C.
[0035]	In one aspect, the said polysaccharide functions as an oil-in-water emulsifier, an emulsion stability index of about 84 per cent and about 89 per cent being obtained at concentrations of about 0.25 per cent and about 0.5 per cent respectively, the said index being the ratio of the emulsifying activity measured 24 hours after preparation to the emulsifying activity measured immediately after preparation.
[0036]	In one aspect, the said polysaccharide functions as an anti-syneresis agent in a starch paste when incorporated at a concentration not exceeding about 0.25 per cent w/v, the degree of syneresis of a refrigerated starch paste being reduced relative to the corresponding paste free of the said polysaccharide, whereas at concentrations above about 0.25 per cent w/v the said polysaccharide interferes with gel formation of the starch and the degree of syneresis is not reduced.
[0037]	In one aspect, the said polysaccharide exhibits concentration-dependent antioxidant activity, the hydroxyl radical scavenging activity rising from about 12 per cent at 1 mg/mL to about 65 per cent at 100 mg/mL, and is a substrate for the growth of Lactobacillus acidophilus and Bifidobacterium species, thereby possessing potential as a prebiotic substrate.
[0038]	In one aspect, the present invention addresses the technical problem of the low recoverability and limited functionality of wheat bran polysaccharides, and provides the technical advantage of an approximately seven-fold increase in the recovery of water-soluble polysaccharide together with a single ingredient combining hydrocolloid, emulsifying, anti-syneresis, antioxidant and prebiotic functionality.
[0039]	In one aspect, the invention enables the sustainable conversion of a low-value milling by-product into a high-value multifunctional ingredient for use in food, nutraceutical, pharmaceutical, cosmetic and bio-based industries.

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
[0040]	The manner in which the present invention is formulated is given a more particular description below, briefly summarized above, may be had by reference to the components, some of which is illustrated in the appended drawing It is to be noted; however, that the appended drawing illustrates only typical embodiments of this invention and are therefore should not be considered limiting of its scope, for the system may admit to other equally effective embodiments.
