DETAILED DESCRIPTION
[0026]	FIG. 1 illustrates a block diagram representation of a conventional 7:3 compressor, wherein seven input bits are reduced into three output bits using cascaded full adders and associated logic structures, thereby demonstrating the presence of ripple-carry propagation and increased logic depth that contribute to higher delay and power consumption. FIG. 2 illustrates simulation waveforms corresponding to the conventional 7:3 compressor, wherein input signal transitions and resulting output responses are depicted over time, highlighting propagation delay, signal transitions, and timing dependencies inherent in conventional compressor architectures. FIG. 3 illustrates a transmission gate-based half adder, wherein complementary transmission gates are utilized to implement sum and carry generation with full voltage swing and reduced transistor count. FIG. 4 illustrates a transmission gate-based OR gate configured to perform logical OR operations, thereby achieving reduced transistor count, lower capacitance, and improved switching efficiency FIG. 5 illustrates a transmission gate-based multiplexer configured to selectively route one of multiple input signals to an output node based on a control signal, wherein the use of transmission gates ensures low-resistance signal paths and full-swing output levels. FIG. 6 illustrates a 6T XOR gate configured to generate exclusive-OR functionality with reduced transistor count, thereby minimizing area and dynamic power consumption while maintaining acceptable delay characteristics. The 14T full adder illustrated in FIG. 7 receives three input bits and simultaneously generates sum and carry outputs using an optimized XOR–XNOR-based sum generation network and carry-generation circuitry, thereby minimizing propagation delay and switching activity.
[0027]	FIG. 8  illustrates a block diagram of the hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure, wherein multiple lower-order compressor blocks, sum generation modules, and carry generation modules are arranged in a hierarchical structure to enable parallel processing of input signals, The present invention shown in FIG. 9 relates to a system 100 for performing high-speed and low-power compression of multiple binary inputs in digital arithmetic circuits, particularly in partial product reduction stages of multipliers. The system 100 is configured to compress seven single-bit input signals X0, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, and X6 into three output signals S0, S1, and S2 representing a binary count of active input bits while maintaining correct weight significance. The system 100 comprises a first novel compressor design embodied as a hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102 and a second novel compressor design embodied as a propagate-generate multiplexer-based compressor 104. The compressors 102 and 104 are distinct and independently operable architectures, each configured to be separately integrated into arithmetic applications through a corresponding multiplier integration module 106. Each compressor design is capable of providing improved processing speed, reduced power consumption, and lower transistor count when implemented within arithmetic circuits.
[0028]	In one embodiment, the hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102 is configured to perform compression using a multi-stage parallel processing architecture that reduces sequential carry propagation. The compressor 102 includes a plurality of lower-order compressor blocks 108, including 3:2 compressors and a 4:3 compressor arranged in a hierarchical structure. The plurality of compressor blocks 108 are configured to receive subsets of the input signals and generate intermediate sum and carry outputs in parallel, thereby reducing dependency between signals and minimizing propagation delay. The compressor 102 further includes a sum generation module 110, a carry generation module 112, and an interconnect network 114, each configured to optimize specific signal paths within the architecture.
[0029]	The sum generation module 110 is configured to generate intermediate and final sum outputs using low-power logic structures. The module 110 includes a plurality of XOR gates 116 implemented as 6-transistor XOR circuits to reduce capacitance and switching activity, XOR-XNOR pair circuits 118 configured to provide complementary logic outputs for efficient signal generation, and a full adder 120 implemented using a 14-transistor configuration. The sum generation module 110 operates by combining subsets of input signals through parallel XOR operations, thereby generating intermediate sum signals minimizing sequential addition stages. The use of reduced transistor-count logic structures ensures lower dynamic power consumption and faster switching characteristics.
[0030]	The carry generation module 112 is configured to produce carry signals independently of ripple-carry propagation. The module 112 includes a plurality of AND gates 122 configured to detect simultaneous high input conditions, OR gates 124 configured to merge carry signals, half adders 126 configured to generate intermediate carry outputs, configured to generate higher-order carry signals. The carry generation module 112 further includes a carry merge network 128 implemented using transmission-gate-based structures, wherein the transmission gates enable full voltage swing and reduce short-circuit current. The independent generation and merging of carry signals ensure that the critical path delay is minimized and signal integrity is preserved.
[0031]	The interconnect network 114 is configured to provide signal routing between the sum generation module 110 and the carry generation module 112. The network 114 includes transmission-gate-based interconnections that ensure reduced parasitic capacitance and improved signal propagation characteristics. The use of transmission-gate-based interconnects enables full-swing signal transmission and minimizes voltage degradation typically associated with pass-transistor logic, thereby enhancing overall circuit reliability.
[0032]	The propagate-generate multiplexer-based compressor 104 is configured to perform compression by first generating propagate and generate signals from the input bits, wherein the generated signals are subsequently utilized in a carry-look ahead mechanism to produce the compressed outputs through multiplexer-based output selection. The compressor 104 includes a partial compression stage 130, a propagate-generate logic module 132, a carry generation unit 134, and a multiplexer-based output selection unit 136. The partial compression stage 130 includes a first 3:2 compressor 138 configured to process inputs X0, X1, and X2 and generate intermediate signals Sum1 and Car1, and a second 3:2 compressor 140 configured to process inputs X3, X4, and X5 and generate intermediate signals Sum2 and Car2. The parallel operation of compressors 138 and 140 reduces the number of active signals and enables simultaneous processing of input subsets.
[0033]	The propagate-generate logic module 132 is configured to generate a propagate signal P and a generate signal G based on the intermediate sums Sum1 and Sum2. The propagate signal P is generated using XOR logic, while the generate signal G is generated using AND logic. The least significant output bit S0 is then generated by combining the propagate signal with the remaining input X6 using an XOR operation. These signals collectively determine whether a carry signal should be propagated or generated internally, thereby eliminating the need for ripple-carry propagation and reducing delay. The carry generation unit 134 is configured to compute a carry signal C0 based on the propagate signal P, the generate signal G, and the remaining input signal X6. The carry signal C0 is generated using a carry-lookahead expression, ensuring that the influence of the seventh input is incorporated without introducing sequential delay. This approach significantly reduces switching activity and improves computational efficiency.
[0034]	The multiplexer-based output selection unit 136 is configured to generate final output signals S1 and S2 using transmission-gate-based multiplexers 142. The multiplexers 142 are controlled by the carry signal C0 and select between intermediate signals generated by intermediate signal generators 144. An intermediate signal generation unit 144 is configured to generate intermediate logic signals U and V, an inverted signal of U, and a combined signal U plus V. A multiplexer-based output selection unit 136 includes transmission-gate-based 2:1 multiplexers 142 configured to generate output signal S1 by selecting between U and the inverted signal of U, and to generate output signal S2 by selecting between V and U plus V, based on the carry signal C0, wherein the propagate-generate multiplexer-based compression architecture 104 eliminates ripple-carry propagation using carry-controlled multiplexing. When the carry signal C0 is in a first logic state, the multiplexers select a first set of signals, and when the carry signal C0 is in a second logic state, the multiplexers select an alternative set of signals. This selection mechanism replaces conventional addition-based output generation, thereby reducing logic depth, minimizing switching transitions, and improving speed.
[0035]	The multiplier integration module 106 is configured to incorporate the compressor modules 102 and 104 into a multiplier architecture, such as a 16×16 grouping and decomposition multiplier. The module 106 includes a partial product generator 150 configured to generate partial products from input operands, a compression tree 152 configured to reduce the partial products using the compressor modules 102 and 104, and a final adder stage 154 configured to produce the final multiplication result. The compressor modules are positioned in high-density columns of the compression tree 152, where multiple partial products converge, thereby reducing the number of reduction stages and improving overall computational efficiency.
[0036]	During operation, the system 100 receives input signals X0 through X6. The input signals are processed by the hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102 in a first compressor design embodiment or by the propagate-generate multiplexer-based compressor 104 in a second compressor design embodiment. The compressors 102 and 104 are distinct and independently implementable architectures configured for separate arithmetic applications.In the hierarchical compressor 102, the inputs are processed in parallel through lower-order compressors to generate intermediate sums and carries, which are subsequently combined to produce final outputs S0, S1, and S2. In the propagate-generate compressor 104, the inputs are partially compressed, propagate and generate signals are formed, LSB output is produced, a carry signal is computed using carry-lookahead logic, and remaining outputs are selected using multiplexers based on the carry signal. Both approaches ensure that the outputs correctly represent the binary count of input logic states while minimizing delay and power consumption.
[0037]	The system 100 provides several technical advantages over conventional compressor architectures. The reduction of ripple-carry propagation reduces critical path delay, while the use of low-transistor-count logic structures reduces power consumption and silicon area. The use of transmission-gate-based interconnects ensures full voltage swing and improved signal integrity. The modular design enables scalability for higher-order compressors and multipliers, making the invention suitable for integration in advanced VLSI systems.
[0038]	The present disclosure is applicable in a wide range of digital systems including microprocessors, digital signal processors, artificial intelligence accelerators, and system-on-chip architectures. The invention can be implemented using standard CMOS fabrication processes and is compatible with both ASIC and FPGA design flows, thereby enabling broad industrial applicability.
[0039]	The present invention relates to improved 7:3 compressor architectures designed for high-speed and low-power arithmetic applications. More particularly, the invention discloses two distinct compressor designs configured to reduce seven single-bit input signals into three output bits in a more efficient manner compared to conventional CMOS, pass-transistor logic (PTL), and hybrid compressor implementations. The proposed architectures are optimized to minimize propagation delay, switching activity, and power consumption while maintaining accurate binary representation of the input bit count.
[0040]	FIG. 10 illustrates a detailed block diagram of the hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102, depicting the interconnection of XOR, AND, and OR gates forming parallel logic paths that reduce sequential carry propagation and reduce critical path delay.
[0041]	FIG. 11 illustrates simulation waveforms of the hierarchical hybrid-logic compressor 102, demonstrating improved timing performance, reduced delay, and stable output transitions in comparison with conventional compressor designs.
[0042]	FIG. 12 illustrates a block diagram of the propagate-generate compressor 104, showing the arrangement of partial compression units, propagate-generate logic modules, carry generation units, and multiplexer-based output selection stages.
[0043]	FIG. 13 illustrates simulation waveforms of the propagate-generate compressor 104, indicating reduced propagation delay, minimized switching activity, and improved signal stability achieved through carry-lookahead and multiplexer-based selection.
[0044]	 FIG. 14 illustrates a 16×16 multiplier system 106 incorporating the proposed compressor architectures within a partial product reduction stage, thereby demonstrating integration of the compressors into a larger arithmetic system. It will be apparent to those skilled in the art that the system 100 of the disclosure may be provided using some or all of the mentioned features and components without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. While various embodiments of the present disclosure have been illustrated and described herein, it will be clear that the disclosure is not limited to these embodiments only. Numerous modifications, changes, variations, substitutions, and equivalents will be apparent to those skilled in the art, without departing from the spirit and scope of the disclosure, as described in the claims. 
ADVANTAGES OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE
[0045]	The present disclosure provides reduced critical path delay due to elimination of sequential carry propagation and adoption of parallel processing logic.
[0046]	The present disclosure achieves lower power consumption by utilizing reduced transistor-count circuits and minimizing switching transitions.
[0047]	The present disclosure ensures full voltage swing and improved signal integrity through the use of transmission-gate-based logic elements.
[0048]	The present disclosure offers reduced logic depth and simplified data paths, thereby improving computational speed.
[0049]	The present disclosure compressor designs are scalable and can be extended for higher-order compression and large arithmetic units.

title: METAMATERIAL ABSORBER WITH THERMOPLASTIC POLYURETHANE SUBSTRATE
abstract:
A metamaterial absorber (100) and a method of manufacturing the same are disclosed. The metamaterial absorber includes a unit-cell structure having a dielectric substrate (104) of thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) and a conductive patterned layer (102) disposed on a first side of the dielectric substrate (104). The conductive patterned layer (102) includes a square-loop resonator (112), a four-petal resonator structure (116) disposed within the square-loop resonator (112), and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure positioned within the four-petal resonator structure (116). A plurality of resistive elements (110) electrically coupled across a plurality of slots (114) formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator (112). An air gap (106) positioned on a second side of the dielectric substrate (104). A conductive ground plane (108) spaced from the dielectric substrate (104) by the air gap (106) and arranged to cooperate with the conductive patterned layer (102) to suppress transmission through the unit-cell structure.

TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001]	The present disclosure relates to electromagnetic wave absorption technologies, and more particularly to metamaterial absorbers, methods of manufacturing the metamaterial absorbers, and computer-implemented methods for designing metamaterial absorbers.
BACKGROUND
[0002]	Metamaterial absorbers have attracted significant interest in a variety of electromagnetic applications, including radar cross-section (RCS) reduction, electromagnetic shielding, antenna systems, wireless communication systems, and sensing platforms. Owing to their ability to manipulate electromagnetic wave propagation through engineered structures, metamaterial absorbers have been investigated for achieving high absorption performance within compact form factors. As the range of applications continues to expand, there is an increasing demand for absorber structures that maintain electromagnetic absorption while being integrated with lightweight, conformal, curved, or mechanically deformable platforms.
[0003]	Existing metamaterial absorbers are often fabricated using rigid substrate materials and planar manufacturing techniques. While such configurations can provide satisfactory electromagnetic performance, rigid substrate materials may restrict integration with non-planar, curved, or deformable surfaces. The rigid nature of the substrate materials becomes increasingly significant in applications requiring lightweight, conformal, or mechanically flexible components. Consequently, efforts have been directed toward developing metamaterial absorber structures to accommodate mechanical deformation while maintaining desirable electromagnetic characteristics.
[0004]	Despite ongoing developments in flexible electromagnetic structures, achieving effective absorption performance in flexible implementations remains challenging. In particular, the performance of the metamaterial absorbers may be influenced by factors such as substrate properties, geometrical constraints, manufacturing considerations, and mechanical deformation. Interactions among substrate properties, geometrical constraints, manufacturing considerations, and mechanical deformation can complicate realisation of absorber structures capable of simultaneously satisfying electromagnetic, mechanical, and practical deployment requirements.
[0005]	In addition to mechanical considerations, the attainment of broad operational bandwidth continues to present a significant challenge in metamaterial absorber design. Conventional approaches for enhancing absorption bandwidth often rely on increased structural complexity, such as multilayer arrangements, incorporation of additional components, or combinations of multiple resonant features. While such approaches may improve broadband response, they can introduce design trade-offs relating to fabrication complexity, weight, thickness, cost, and structural robustness.
[0006]	Accordingly, there exists a need for an improved solution to overcome the above-mentioned problems associated with the existing systems.
SUMMARY

[0008]	According to an aspect of the present disclosure, a metamaterial absorber comprising a unit-cell structure is disclosed. The unit-cell structure comprises a dielectric substrate comprising thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). A conductive patterned layer is disposed on a first side of the dielectric substrate. The conductive patterned layer comprises a square-loop resonator, a four-petal resonator structure disposed within the square-loop resonator, and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure positioned within the four-petal resonator structure. A plurality of slots respectively formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator. A plurality of resistive elements respectively electrically coupled across the plurality of slots so that incident electromagnetic energy coupled into the square-loop resonator is dissipated through the plurality of resistive elements. An air gap positioned on a second side of the dielectric substrate opposite the first side. A conductive ground plane spaced from the dielectric substrate by the air gap and arranged to cooperate with the conductive patterned layer to suppress transmission through the unit-cell structure.
[0009]	According to another aspect of the present disclosure, a method of manufacturing a metamaterial absorber is provided. The method comprises providing a dielectric substrate comprising thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). The method further comprises forming a conductive patterned layer on a first side of the dielectric substrate. The conductive patterned layer comprises a square-loop resonator, a four-petal resonator structure disposed within the square-loop resonator, a centrally disposed circular resonator structure positioned within the four-petal resonator structure, and a plurality of slots respectively formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator. The method further comprises electrically coupling a plurality of resistive elements across the plurality of slots. The method further comprises positioning a conductive ground plane opposite the conductive patterned layer. The method further comprises forming an air gap between the dielectric substrate and the conductive ground plane. The method further comprises assembling the dielectric substrate, the conductive patterned layer, the plurality of resistive elements and the conductive ground plane to form the metamaterial absorber.

The method further comprises providing simulation results to a reinforcement-learning model. The method further comprises iteratively modifying the plurality of geometric parameters using the reinforcement-learning model based on a reward function associated with electromagnetic absorption performance to obtain optimised geometric parameters for designing the metamaterial absorber.

[0027]	Example embodiments of the present inventive concepts will be described below in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings.
[0028]	In some embodiments, the present disclosure provides a metamaterial absorber comprising a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) substrate and a conductive resonator configuration capable of providing broadband electromagnetic wave absorption while maintaining structural flexibility.
[0029]	In some embodiments, the present disclosure provides a metamaterial absorber having a square-loop resonator, a four-petal resonator structure, resistive loading elements, and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure configured to enhance impedance matching and absorption performance over a predetermined microwave frequency band.
[0030]	In some embodiments, the present disclosure provides a metamaterial absorber that can be fabricated using additive manufacturing techniques, including three-dimensional printing of a TPU substrate, thereby enabling lightweight, conformal, and cost-effective absorber structures suitable for curved and wearable platforms.
[0031]	The present disclosure relates to metamaterial absorbers for electromagnetic wave absorption. Conventional metamaterial absorber designs predominantly employ rigid substrates such as FR-4 and Rogers laminates. The rigid substrates limit applicability in complex-shaped structures and flexible configurations. To overcome the inflexibility of rigid substrates, deformable materials such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) have been explored for absorber fabrication. However, PDMS-based absorbers may provide limited bandwidth, mechanical robustness, fabrication scalability, or integration suitability for fully flexible, lightweight platforms suitable for complex geometries.
[0032]	The present disclosure addresses the above-mentioned limitations by providing a metamaterial absorber including a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) substrate. Thermoplastic polyurethane offers flexibility, mechanical stability, and biocompatibility while achieving broadband electromagnetic absorption without requiring rigid printed-circuit-board substrates or multilayer stacking. The TPU substrate enables conformal integration with complex-shaped surfaces and provides structural flexibility for wearable, biomedical, and conformal device applications.
[0033]	In an embodiment, a metamaterial absorber includes a unit-cell structure. The unit-cell structure includes a dielectric substrate comprising thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). A conductive patterned layer is disposed on a first side of the dielectric substrate. The conductive patterned layer includes a square-loop resonator, a four-petal resonator structure disposed within the square-loop resonator, and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure positioned within the four-petal resonator structure. A plurality of slots are respectively formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator. A plurality of resistive elements are respectively electrically coupled across the plurality of slots so that incident electromagnetic energy coupled into the square-loop resonator is dissipated through the plurality of resistive elements. An air gap is positioned on a second side of the dielectric substrate opposite the first side. A conductive ground plane is spaced from the dielectric substrate by the air gap and arranged to cooperate with the conductive patterned layer to suppress transmission through the unit-cell structure.
[0034]	FIG. 1 illustrates an exploded three-dimensional view of a metamaterial absorber 100, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. In an embodiment, the metamaterial absorber 100 may include a conductive patterned layer 102 disposed on an upper surface of a dielectric substrate 104. The conductive patterned layer 102 may include a square-loop resonator having a plurality of slots bridged by corresponding resistive elements 110. A four-petal resonator structure and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure may be arranged within the square-loop resonator to provide a multi-resonant conductive pattern. In a non-limiting example, the conductive patterned layer 102 may include copper, copper alloy, silver, aluminium, conductive ink, or combinations thereof.
[0035]	In an embodiment, the dielectric substrate 104 may include thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). The TPU may provide a flexible support structure for the conductive patterned layer 102. In a non-limiting example, the dielectric substrate 104 may include TPU 87A having a thickness of approximately 0.8 mm. In other non-limiting examples, the thickness of the dielectric substrate 104 may vary depending upon a desired operating frequency range and absorption characteristic. The conductive ground plane 108 may be positioned beneath the dielectric substrate 104. The conductive ground plane 108 may be separated from the dielectric substrate 104 by an air gap 106. In a non-limiting example, the air gap 106 may have a height of approximately 3.7 mm. The conductive ground plane 108 may include copper, aluminium, silver-coated metal, conductive foil, metallised film, or any other electrically conductive layer suitable for suppressing electromagnetic transmission.
[0036]	During operation, incident electromagnetic waves interact with the conductive patterned layer 102 and induce currents within the resonator structures. The resonator structures may be configured to cooperate with the plurality of resistive elements 110, the dielectric substrate 104, the air gap 106, and the conductive ground plane 108 to dissipate electromagnetic energy and thereby reduce reflected electromagnetic energy. The conductive ground plane 108 may be configured to substantially suppress transmission through the metamaterial absorber 100, thereby enabling absorption of incident electromagnetic radiation.
[0037]	In an embodiment, the conductive patterned layer 102, the dielectric substrate 104, the air gap 106, and the conductive ground plane 108 collectively form a layered absorber architecture configured to provide electromagnetic absorption over a predetermined frequency range. In non-limiting embodiments, the metamaterial absorber 100 may be configured for electromagnetic interference (EMI) mitigation, conformal microwave absorption, wearable electronic systems, sensing platforms, radar cross-section reduction applications, or other electromagnetic wave management applications.
[0038]	FIG. 2 illustrates a top view of a unit-cell of metamaterial absorber 100 showing a detailed resonator geometry, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. In an embodiment, the unit-cell may include a square-loop resonator 112. The square-loop resonator 112 may be disposed along a peripheral region of dielectric substrate 104. In a non-limiting example, the square-loop resonator 112 has a side length L1 of approximately 8 mm and a trace width W1 of approximately 3 mm. A slot 114 may be formed at a central region of each side of the square-loop resonator 112. In a non-limiting example, each slot 114 has a length L2 of approximately 5 mm. In an embodiment, a lumped resistive element 110 may be electrically connected across each slot 114 such that the corresponding slot 114 is bridged by the lumped resistive element 110. In a non-limiting example, the lumped resistive elements 110 may include lumped resistors each having a resistance value of approximately 150 ohms, a width W2 of approximately 0.5 mm, and a length L3 of approximately 1 mm. The lumped resistive elements 110 may be configured to provide resistive loading to facilitate dissipation of electromagnetic energy coupled to the square-loop resonator 112.
[0039]	In an embodiment, a four-petal resonator structure 116 may be disposed inwardly of the square-loop resonator 112. The four-petal resonator structure 116 may include four substantially symmetrical petal-shaped conductive portions arranged around a central region of the unit-cell. In a non-limiting example, each petal-shaped conductive portion may be defined by a minor radius D1 of approximately 2 mm and a major radius D2 of approximately 3.4 mm. The four-petal resonator structure 116 may be configured to electromagnetically couple with the square-loop resonator 112 and the centrally disposed circular resonator structure. In a non-limiting embodiment, the substantially symmetrical arrangement of the petal-shaped conductive portions contributes to reduced sensitivity to polarisation of incident electromagnetic waves.
[0040]	In an embodiment, a centrally disposed circular resonator structure may be positioned within the four-petal resonator structure 116. The circular resonator structure may include an outer circular ring 118 and an inner circular ring 120 arranged concentrically with one another. In a non-limiting example, the outer circular ring 118 has a radius r1 of approximately 3.6 mm, and the inner circular ring 120 has a radius r2 of approximately 1.0 mm. An inter-ring spacing S2 of approximately 0.8 mm may be provided between the outer circular ring 118 and the inner circular ring 120. The concentric circular rings define additional resonant paths and are configured to promote electromagnetic coupling within a central region of the unit-cell.
[0041]	During operation, electromagnetic waves incident upon the unit-cell induces surface currents within the square-loop resonator 112, the four-petal resonator structure 116, and the circular resonator structure including the outer circular ring 118 and the inner circular ring 120. Electromagnetic coupling among the resonator structures generates multiple resonant responses across an operating frequency range. The induced currents are partially dissipated through the lumped resistive elements 110, while the cooperative interaction between the resonator structures contributes to enhancement of electromagnetic energy absorption.
[0042]	In a non-limiting example, the unit-cell has a periodicity P of approximately 10 mm and may be repeated in one or more directions to form an array of unit-cells. The geometric arrangement of the square-loop resonator 112, the four-petal resonator structure 116, the circular resonator structure, and the lumped resistive elements 110 collectively provide a compact resonator configuration capable of supporting multi-resonant electromagnetic absorption characteristics.
[0043]	In an embodiment, the dielectric substrate 104 may include thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). In a non-limiting example, the dielectric substrate 104 may include TPU 87A. The TPU 87A may exhibit a relative permittivity of approximately 2.9 and a loss tangent of approximately 0.02 over a microwave frequency range. In a non-limiting example, the dielectric substrate 104 may have a thickness of approximately 0.8 mm, selected based on measured dielectric characteristics of the substrate material. In a non-limiting example, dielectric properties of the TPU substrate may be characterised using a DAK-TL2 measurement kit over a frequency range extending from approximately 0.4 MHz to 20 GHz. As shown in FIG. 3, the dielectric characteristics of the TPU 87A substrate may vary with frequency over the measured frequency range. The measured dielectric response may be utilised for characterising the TPU substrate and may be for electromagnetic design of the metamaterial absorber 100.
[0044]	In a non-limiting example, the unit-cell structure may have a periodicity P of approximately 10 mm and an inter-element spacing S1 of approximately 0.5 mm between adjacent unit-cells. When a plurality of unit-cell structures is arranged in an array, adjacent unit-cells cooperate to provide frequency-selective absorption of incident electromagnetic radiation. The flexible nature of the TPU substrate may permit conformal integration of the metamaterial absorber 100 with curved or non-planar surfaces. Accordingly, the metamaterial absorber 100 may be incorporated into electromagnetic shielding systems, conformal absorber assemblies, wearable electronic platforms, smart textile systems, aerospace structures, radar-signature reduction systems, and other electromagnetic wave management applications.
[0045]	The electromagnetic performance of the metamaterial absorber 100 may be analysed using a full-wave electromagnetic simulator, such as Ansys HFSS v21, operating in the frequency domain and modelling an infinitely periodic array excited by a linearly polarised plane wave. The simulation results may include a reflection coefficient, an absorption coefficient, and angular response characteristics under oblique incidence. In a non-limiting simulated example, the metamaterial absorber 100 may exhibit near-perfect absorption over a frequency range extending from approximately 4.65 GHz to 7.56 GHz with a principal resonance near 5.65 GHz.
[0046]	As shown in FIG. 4a, the reflection coefficient exhibits a minimum value of approximately −43 dB near the resonant frequency, indicating effective impedance matching between the metamaterial absorber 100 and free space. In a non-limiting example, an absorption coefficient A(ω) may be determined using:
A(ω) = 1 − |S11(ω)|²
[0047]	Wherein S11 represents the reflection coefficient. The absorption response illustrated in FIG. 4b demonstrates near-perfect absorption across the operating frequency range. In a non-limiting example, the metamaterial absorber 100 exhibits a minimum reflection coefficient of approximately −43 dB at a resonant frequency, indicative of effective impedance matching and high electromagnetic energy absorption.
[0048]	In an embodiment, the cooperative interaction among the square-loop resonator 112, the four-petal resonator structure 116, the outer circular ring 118, the inner circular ring 120, and the resistive elements 110 may be configured to provide multiple electromagnetic resonances across the operating frequency range. The symmetric arrangement of the four-petal resonator structure 116 may reduce sensitivity to polarisation of incident electromagnetic waves, while the concentric circular resonators may be configured to enhance electromagnetic coupling and field confinement within a central region of the unit-cell. The resistive elements 110 may be configured to facilitate dissipation of induced electromagnetic energy, thereby contributing to broadband absorption performance without requiring multilayer absorber configurations.
[0049]	FIG. 5 illustrates a flow diagram of a method 500 for manufacturing the metamaterial absorber 100, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0050]	At step 502, the method 500 includes providing a dielectric substrate 104 including TPU. In an embodiment, the dielectric substrate 104 includes TPU 87A. In a non-limiting example, the dielectric substrate 104 may be fabricated using a three-dimensional printing process including fused filament fabrication (FFF) utilising TPU 87A filament. The fused filament fabrication process may be performed at a nozzle temperature of approximately 230°C and a layer height of approximately 0.2 mm to produce a flexible dielectric substrate. The dielectric substrate 104 may be configured to provide mechanical support for a conductive resonator structure while eliminating the need for a rigid printed-circuit-board substrate. As shown in FIG. 6, the TPU 87A filament supplied from a filament spool 602 may be processed through the FFF system and deposited in successive layers to fabricate the dielectric substrate 104. The fabricated dielectric substrate 104 may subsequently be utilised as a flexible support structure for the conductive patterned layer 102 during manufacture of the metamaterial absorber 100.
[0051]	At step 504, the method 500 includes forming a conductive patterned layer 102 on a first side of the dielectric substrate 104. The conductive patterned layer 102 may include the square-loop resonator 112, the four-petal resonator structure 116 disposed within the square-loop resonator 112, and a centrally disposed circular resonator structure positioned within the four-petal resonator structure 116. The circular resonator structure may include an outer circular ring 118 and an inner circular ring 120 arranged concentrically with one another. The conductive patterned layer 102 may further includes a plurality of slots 114 respectively formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator 112.
[0052]	In an embodiment, the conductive patterned layer 102 may be formed using a process selected to maintain processing temperatures compatible with the TPU substrate. In a non-limiting example, the conductive patterned layer 102 may be formed by laminating conductive foil onto the dielectric substrate 104 followed by patterning. In another non-limiting example, the conductive patterned layer 102 may be formed using a conductive printing process. In another non-limiting example, the conductive patterned layer 102 may be deposited and patterned on the dielectric substrate 104. The conductive patterned layer 102 may include copper or another electrically conductive material suitable for forming resonator structures.
[0053]	At step 506, the method 500 includes electrically coupling a plurality of resistive elements 110 across the plurality of slots 114. In an embodiment, each resistive element 110 bridges a corresponding slot 114 formed in a corresponding side of the square-loop resonator 112, thereby providing resistive loading to the resonator structure. In a non-limiting example, the resistive elements 110 may include lumped resistors having a resistance value of approximately 150 ohms.
[0054]	In an embodiment, each resistive element 110 may be attached across a corresponding slot 114 using a bonding technique compatible with the dielectric substrate 104. In a non-limiting example, the bonding technique may include conductive adhesive bonding, solder-based attachment processes, or other electrically conductive mounting techniques suitable for establishing an electrical connection between the resistive element 110 and the conductive patterned layer 102.
[0055]	At step 508, the method 500 includes positioning a conductive ground plane 108 opposite the conductive patterned layer 102. The conductive ground plane 108 may be arranged to cooperate with the conductive patterned layer 102 to suppress transmission of incident electromagnetic radiation through the metamaterial absorber 100.
[0056]	At step 510, the method 500 includes forming an air gap 106 between the dielectric substrate 104 and the conductive ground plane 108. In a non-limiting example, the air gap 106 may have a height of approximately 3.7 mm. The air gap 106 contributes to impedance matching and absorption characteristics of the metamaterial absorber 100.
[0057]	In an embodiment, the air gap 106 may be maintained using one or more spacing structures positioned between the dielectric substrate 104 and the conductive ground plane 108. In a non-limiting example, the one or more spacing structures include dielectric spacers, standoffs, low-permittivity support structures, peripheral support frames, spacer rings, or integrally formed support features.
[0058]	At step 512, the method 500 includes assembling the dielectric substrate 104, the conductive patterned layer 102, the plurality of resistive elements 110, and the conductive ground plane 108 to form the metamaterial absorber 100. The resulting multilayer structure may be configured to absorb incident electromagnetic radiation through the cooperative interaction of the conductive patterned layer 102, the resistive elements 110, the dielectric substrate 104, the air gap 106, and the conductive ground plane 108.
[0059]	The method 500 enables fabrication of a flexible metamaterial absorber structure suitable for implementation in electromagnetic absorption, electromagnetic shielding, conformal electronic systems, and other microwave-frequency applications.
[0060]	FIG. 7 illustrates a flow diagram of a computer-implemented method 700 for designing the metamaterial absorber 100, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure.
[0061]	At step 702, the method 700 includes defining a plurality of geometric parameters associated with a conductive resonator structure. In an embodiment, the plurality of geometric parameters include dimensions of the square-loop resonator 112, dimensions of the slots 114 formed through corresponding sides of the square-loop resonator 112, dimensions of the four-petal resonator structure 116, dimensions of the outer circular ring 118 and inner circular ring 120, resistance values of the resistive elements 110, and a height of the air gap 106 may be provided between the dielectric substrate 104 and the conductive ground plane 108.
[0062]	At step 704, the method 700 includes simulating the electromagnetic performance of the conductive resonator structure. In a non-limiting example, the simulation may be performed using a frequency-domain electromagnetic solver configured to model an infinite periodic array of unit-cell structures excited by a linearly polarised plane wave. The simulation results may include a reflection coefficient, an absorption coefficient, impedance characteristics, and other electromagnetic performance parameters associated with the conductive resonator structure.
[0063]	At step 706, the method 700 includes providing the simulation results to a reinforcement-learning model. The reinforcement-learning model may be configured to receive the simulation results and evaluate the electromagnetic performance of the conductive resonator structure based on one or more performance criteria associated with electromagnetic absorption and reflection characteristics of the conductive resonator structure.
[0064]	At step 708, the method 700 includes iteratively modifying the plurality of geometric parameters using the reinforcement-learning model to obtain optimised design parameters for the metamaterial absorber 100. The iterative optimisation process may continue until a predetermined performance criterion or termination condition is satisfied.
[0065]	In an embodiment, the reinforcement-learning model may be configured to optimise one or more parameters associated with the square-loop resonator 112, the slots 114, the four-petal resonator structure 116, the outer circular ring 118, the inner circular ring 120, the resistive elements 110, and the air gap 106.
[0066]	In an embodiment, the reinforcement-learning model may employ a reward function associated with electromagnetic absorption performance. The reward function may be configured to increase with increased absorption performance within a target frequency range and decrease with increased reflection of incident electromagnetic radiation.
[0067]	In one embodiment, the reinforcement-learning model may include a Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm. In another embodiment, the reinforcement-learning model includes a Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) algorithm. Other reinforcement-learning techniques suitable for optimising electromagnetic absorber designs may likewise be employed without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.
[0068]	In an embodiment, the reinforcement-learning model may be configured to iteratively evaluate the simulation results and autonomously tune the plurality of geometric parameters to identify a resonator configuration associated with improved electromagnetic absorption performance.
[0069]	The computer-implemented method 700 enables systematic evaluation and optimisation of resonator geometries, resistive loading characteristics, and absorber configuration parameters, thereby facilitating development of metamaterial absorber structures exhibiting enhanced broadband absorption characteristics over a desired operating frequency range.
[0070]	In a non-limiting example, the optimised geometric parameters obtained using the computer-implemented method 700 are utilised in fabrication of the metamaterial absorber 100 described herein.
[0071]	The metamaterial absorber of the present disclosure provides several technical advantages, including broadband electromagnetic absorption through the cooperative interaction of the square-loop resonator, four-petal resonator structure, concentric circular resonators, and resistive loading elements. The use of the TPU substrate enables a flexible and conformal absorber architecture suitable for integration with curved and non-planar surfaces. The incorporation of resistive elements enhances electromagnetic energy dissipation and impedance matching, while the air-gap-backed ground plane suppresses transmission and contributes to improved absorption performance across the operating frequency range. The metamaterial absorber can be fabricated using additive manufacturing techniques, thereby facilitating lightweight construction, material efficiency, dimensional control, and scalable production. Furthermore, the computer-implemented reinforcement-learning-based design methodology enables systematic optimisation of geometrical parameters, thereby reducing design iterations and facilitating identification of absorber configurations exhibiting improved electromagnetic absorption characteristics.

title: EPOXY-DIPHENYLAMINE-POLYETHYLENE GLYCOL COMPOSITION FOR FABRICATION OF FLEXIBLE MICROFLUIDIC DEVICES AND A METHOD THEREOF
abstract: The invention relates to an epoxy-based composition for manufacturing flexible microfluidic devices. The composition comprises Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA), Diphenylamine (DPA) and Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) in weight ratios ranging from 1:0.25:0.75 to 4:1:4, preferably 4:1:4. The composition is mixed, degassed, cast into moulds and cured under ambient conditions for approximately 24–120 hours to produce transparent, flexible and easily demouldable microfluidic devices containing channels between 50 μm and 500 μm. Experimental evaluation of thirty-eight formulations demonstrated superior flexibility, curing efficiency, groove fidelity and demouldability compared with agarose, alginate and conventional epoxy systems. FTIR characterization confirmed incorporation of DPA and PEG into the cured matrix. The invention enables economical fabrication of microfluidic devices without requiring clean-room infrastructure and is suitable for diagnostic, pharmaceutical, environmental and industrial applications.
specification:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION 
The invention relates to microfluidic device fabrication. More particularly, it relates to a curable epoxy composition comprising Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA), Diphenylamine (DPA), and Polyethylene Glycol (PEG), together with methods of manufacturing flexible, transparent and chemically resistant microfluidic devices without requiring clean-room fabrication facilities.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Microfluidics is a multidisciplinary technology that focuses on the controlled manipulation of fluids at the microscale usually in micrometer dimensions. Microfluidic system enable minute fluid volume manipulation ranging in micro- to nano-litres giving advantages of reduced reagent consumption, faster reaction kinetics with enhanced sensitivity. Microfluidic systems manipulate fluids within channels typically having dimensions between approximately 50 μm and 500 μm. This integration of reaction, transport and detection within compact devices makes microfluidics a versatile platform with immense application potential. Since last twenty years, applications of microfluidic devices in healthcare diagnostics (lab-on-chip system and blood analysis), DNA testing and detection of pathogens; also used in chemical synthesis, pharmaceutical-screening, controlled drug-delivery, quality testing for foods, environmental monitoring and other applications in energy fields thus demonstrating broad-range scientific and industrial application potentials. 
Microfluidic device fabrications need materials which can be easily moulded, cured and optimized for microscale-fluid transport. Conventionally, Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), sodium alginate and agarose have been reported extensively showing innate limitations like- swelling due to organic solvents, inadequate -chemical resistance and -mechanical robustness and reproducibility during large-scale manufacturing. Epoxy-based microfluidic system used today frequently suffer from brittleness, difficult demoulding, inadequate flexibility and poor channel fidelity when fabricated without specialized infrastructure. 
Hence, the need for alternative materials has increased for overcoming these limitations while maintaining biocompatibility, transparency and mechanical robustness. Epoxy resins, when combined with appropriate curing agents and additives provide an effective solution for fabricating durable, transparent and low-cost microfluidic devices.
OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION
The principal objective of the present invention is to provide a curable epoxy-based composition comprising Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA), Diphenylamine (DPA), and Polyethylene Glycol (PEG), and to provide a method for manufacturing flexible, transparent, chemically resistant and easily demouldable microfluidic devices under ambient curing conditions without requiring clean-room fabrication infrastructure.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a cost-effective composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices wherein an epoxy-based composition exhibiting improved flexibility and transparency;
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices with improving demouldability.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices with reproducible fabrication.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices producing chemically resistant microchannels.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices enabling fabrication of approximately 50–500 μm microchannels.
Another objective of the present invention is to provide a composition for manufacturing microfluidic devices suitable for diagnostic and pharmaceutical applications.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
The following detailed description enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. The description is illustrative and is not intended to limit the scope of the invention as defined by the appended claims. Unless otherwise indicated, all percentages are expressed on a weight/weight (w/w) or weight/volume (w/v) basis, as applicable.
The disclosure below describes various embodiments of the present invention relating to a curable epoxy composition comprising Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA), Diphenylamine (DPA), and Polyethylene Glycol (PEG), together with methods of manufacturing flexible, transparent and chemically resistant microfluidic devices without requiring clean-room fabrication facilities.
As used herein, the term “composition” encompasses a product comprising the specified ingredients in the specified amounts, as well as a product resulting directly or indirectly from combining such ingredients.
Unless otherwise stated:
•	DGEBA means Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A.
•	DPA means Diphenylamine.
•	PEG means Polyethylene Glycol.
The principal materials comprise:
•	DGEBA epoxy resin,
•	Diphenylamine curing agent,
•	Polyethylene Glycol,
•	optional glycerol.
The invention particularly relies upon DPA as the curing agent in optimized embodiments.
The invention discloses epoxy-based microfluidic devices fabricated using epoxy resins in combination with suitable curing agents and optional inclusion of plasticizers. In a single embodiment, this formulation comprises epoxy resin, diphenylamine curing agent and polyethlylene glycol plasticizer in a ratio ranging from 1 : 0.25 : 0.75 to 4 : 1 : 4.
In one aspect, the present invention provides a curable composition suitable for manufacturing flexible microfluidic devices. The composition comprises an epoxy resin component, an aromatic amine curing agent component, and a plasticizer component, wherein the combination of these components provides an unexpected balance of transparency, flexibility, curing efficiency, demouldability, and microchannel fidelity.
The inventors have found that systematic variation of the relative proportions of these components results in significant differences in curing behavior and mechanical performance. Following evaluation of multiple formulations, the composition employing Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA), Diphenylamine (DPA), and Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) demonstrated superior performance for fabrication of microfluidic devices under ambient curing conditions. The ratios disclosed herein are expressed as weight ratios unless otherwise specified.
In a preferred embodiment, the epoxy resin comprises Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A (DGEBA) and present in the ratio of 1 to 4. The inventors observed that increasing resin concentration beyond the optimized range generally increased brittleness and reduced effective demoulding, whereas insufficient resin adversely affected structural stability. Accordingly, the disclosed range provides an advantageous balance between mechanical robustness and flexibility.
In another preferred embodiment, the curing agent comprises Diphenylamine (DPA) and present in the ratio of 0.25 to 1. The curing agent initiates crosslinking of the epoxy resin to produce the cured polymer matrix. The inventors found that DPA unexpectedly produced improved flexibility and groove fidelity compared with conventional epoxy curing systems investigated during formulation optimization.
In another preferred embodiment, the plasticizer comprises Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) and present in the ratio of 0.5 to 4. The plasticizer improves flexibility while maintaining adequate structural stability. The inventors observed that PEG significantly improved the flexibility, demouldability, surface smoothness and channel preservation.
In most preferred embodiment, the composition comprises epoxy resin, diphenylamine curing agent and polyethlylene glycol plasticizer in a ratio of 4:1:4, wherein the preferred composition demonstrates, curing within approximately two days, smooth surface formation, easy folding and excellent channel definition.
In certain embodiments, glycerol may optionally be included as an auxiliary plasticizer and present in the ratio of 0.25 to 4, wherein glycerol contributes for temporary flexibility and modification of curing characteristics.
In a preferred embodiment, the composition is manufactured by mixing epoxy resin, diphenylamine curing agent and polyethlylene glycol plasticizer in given ratio, allow to release air bubbles, cast into moulds, cure in ambient conditions and finally demould.
In a preferred embodiment, the composition is manufactured wherein the curing period ranging from 24 hours to 120 hours.
In another preferred embodiment, the composition is manufactured with different types of moulds including glass Petri dishes, butter-paper moulds, plastic cube moulds and 3D printed moulds.
In another preferred embodiment, the composition is manufactured provide microfluidic devices with microchannels wherein the microchannel dimension ranging from 50 μm to 500 μm.
In most preferred embodiment, the composition is manufactured provide microfluidic devices with microchannels wherein the microchannel dimension is 100 μm.
The following non-limiting examples describe the present invention in more detail.

Mold Fabrication and Casting
The prepared mixtures were cast into moulds prepared as different substrates as given below-

After pouring of the formulations, the moulds were left to stand undisturbed for curing at ambient physical conditions (temperature and pressure). According to the formulations prepared at particular ratio and additives, curing times differed from 24-120 hours. 

Evaluation of Agarose and Alginate Substrates
Initial studies for microfluidics fabrication were attempted using agarose and alginate matrices. Agarose, alone or hybrid with starch, resulted in soft and fragile structures that exhibited poor channel clarity, while sodium alginate- cross-linked with CaCl2 resulted in brittle structure with uneven surface lacking transparency and definite channels. These limitations showed that both polymers were unsuitable for reliable microfluidic-device fabrications, thus the need for study on epoxy-based stable systems.  
Epoxy–Hardener Formulation Trials
For optimizing the epoxy-based device fabrication, a systematic set of trials were conducted. Here, standard formulations included resin:hardener ratios of 1:1, 2:1, 1:2 and further extended ratios like- 2.03:1, 3:1 and 4:1 (either in g or mg). Larger batches of the same were prepared in gram for assessing reproducibility, higher resign formulations like- 4:1, 5:1, 6:1 and 7.5:1 were analysed for evaluating the extreme ratios in curing efficiency and brittleness. 
For improvement of de-moulding and flexibility of the formulations, plasticizers were introduced in subsequent tests. Representative compositions included 2:0.5:2, 2:0.5:1, 2:1:2, 2:1:0.5, 2:1:1, and 2:0.75:1 (resin:hardener:PEG). For enhancing softness and groove clarity, loading of higher PEG was examined (4.5:2.26:4.5; 1.75:0.717:1.721; 1.791:0.508:1.758), with additional variations (like 0.945:0.37:1.786; 1.5:0.5; 1.5:0.75:0.25; 1.5:0.5:0.25 and 0.75:0.15:1.1) for transparency balance, flexibility and reduced adhesive properties. Other composition (like 1:0.5:0.5; 1:0.25:0.75 and 0.5:0.05:1.45) were tested for checking curing-consistency and mechanical properties.   
Other cross-linkers/hardeners were also assessed like- diphenylamine (DPA) (in ratios like 4:1:4; 1:0.5:0.5; 1:0.25:0.75; 2:0.2:0; 2:0.3:0 and 1.4:0.15:0.5), pthalic anhydride (2:0.8:0) as an alternate amine-based system.

Analysing the various formulations for effective microfluidic matrix, Formulation # 32 was selected for further analysis. The system was set on the 3D printed moulds showing 100 µm channels and taken onto clear glass slide for further studies. 
3D printed mould with specific design given in Figure 1 was used for casting the various formulations and their further microscopic observations for analysing fine-diameter of the micro-channels for further inlet and outlet setup for further fluid movements (Figure 2A). After curing, the microfluidic chip was de-moulded and mounted between two glass slides with a customized support system (Figure 2B). Expanded polyethylene (EPE) foam was precisely cut to make sandwich system (Figure 2C), allowing inlet and outlet tubing to pass for fluid movement. The system was setup under microscope and observed for fluid movement clearly (Figure 2D, 2E and 2F). The clear micro-channel observation was observed in selected formulation as shown in Figure 3 and final mixture was selected.  Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrosopy (FTIR) was performed for verifying the ceheical composition of selected microfluidic matrix (Formulation 32). The characteristic aromatic C-N band at aproximately 1316cm-1 confirmed the presence of diphenylamine within the cured matrix. The aromatic ring vibrations at 1596 and 1508cm-1 further supported incorporation of DPA, broad hydroxyl stretching and ether-associated bands confirmerd PEG integration (Figure 4). 
The 38 formulations were evaluated and Formulation # 32 (Epoxy:DPA:PEG = 4:1:4) demonstrated as best combination of flexibility, curing efficiency, groove fidelity, transparency and its ease of demoulding and was therefore selected for fabrications of the microfluidic device. This optimized formulation created stable microfluidic channels without the requirement of clean-room fabrication facilities. The fabricated devices showed structural integrity, transparency, flexibility and compatibility with fluid transport systems.
Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrosopy (FTIR) was performed for verifying the ceheical composition of selected microfluidic matrix. The characteristic aromatic C-N band at aproximately 1316 cm-1 confirmed the presence of diphenylamine within the cured matrix. The aromatic ring vibrations at 1596 cm-1 and 1508 cm-1 further supported incorporation of DPA, broad hydroxyl stretching and ether-associated bands confirmerd PEG integration. 
The invention describes a low-cost fabrication method for microfluidic system using optimized epoxy-resin formulations instead of conventional PDMS/Alginate materials. By systematically varying resin-hardener-plasticizer ratios, the study identifies compositions that yield transparent, flexible, chemically resistant and easily de-mouldable microchannels. The resulting device operates without the need for clean-room infrastructure and are applicable in diagnostic, drug testing, environmental monitoring and industrial microfluidic processes. FTIR characterization confirmed the incorporation of diphenylamine curing agent and PEG plasticizer within the epoxy matrix. The optimized composition including Epoxy:DPA:PEG provided superior demouldability and flexibility compared to conventional epoxy formulations

title: EXPLAINABLE MULTI-MODAL DEEP LEARNING FOR EARLY DISEASE PREDICTION USING HEALTHCARE HARDWARE SYSTEMS
abstract:
ABSTRACT
This invention suggests an Explainable Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Early Disease Prediction Utilizing Healthcare Hardware Systems, designed to improve disease detection, risk assessment and Clinical judgments made through incorporating data from wearable devices, medical imagery and Electronic Health Records (EHRs). The system utilizes specialized hardware devices designed for medical use, featuring sensors, to monitor heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen levels (SpO₂), body temperature and physical activity, enabling the continuous gathering of real-time data. While a feature fusion layer generates accurate disease risk predictions, a multi-modal deep learning framework combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for medical image analysis, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for processing temporal sensor data and dense neural networks for assessing electronic health records (EHRs). Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches such as SHAP, LIME and Grad-CAM are used by the system to provide interpretable reasons for prediction outcomes in order to increase transparency and clinician trust. The proposed framework continuously monitors patient health, categorizes risk levels into Healthy, Moderate Risk, High Risk and Critical Risk categories and generates personalized treatment recommendations. By incorporating smart healthcare devices, diverse data processing, advanced deep learning algorithms and open-source AI, the system promotes early identification, proactive health management, improved patient outcomes and tailored treatments.
specification:
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Existing healthcare monitoring systems typically function on segregated data streams and do not have the ability to incorporate data from diverse medical fields. 
(a) Combine data from medical imaging, wearable sensors and electronic health records
(b) Deep learning techniques can be used for accurate early disease prediction
(c) Provide understandable explanations for clinical decision support
(d) Efficient operation can be achieved using healthcare hardware systems designed for real-time monitoring.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The innovation offers a multimodal healthcare intelligence framework that may be explained, consisting of:
• Medical hardware for collecting physiological data.
• Deep learning modules for handling sensor data, medical pictures and EHR data.
• Feature fusion techniques for learning with multiple modalities.
• Explainable AI modules with Grad-CAM, LIME and SHAP.
• An engine that evaluates disease risk and suggests treatments.
The architecture allows for proactive medical intervention by continuously monitoring patient health status and producing interpretable disease forecasts.

System Overview
The proposed design includes:
Data Acquisition Layer
Multi-Modal Deep Learning Layer
Explainability Layer
Disease Prediction Layer
Personalized Treatment Recommendation Layer
Data Acquisition
The system collects physiological parameters from wearable healthcare hardware devices, including:
Heart Rate Monitor
The SpO₂ Sensor
A sensor for blood pressure
Sensor for Temperature
Activity sensor and accelerometer
Diagnostic systems provide medical imaging like CT, MRI, and X-rays, while electronic health records provide the patient's medical history.
Deep Learning Methodology
The framework employs:
• CNN for medical image feature extraction.
• LSTM for wearable sensor time-series analysis.
• Dense Neural Networks for EHR data processing.
A fusion layer combines extracted features to generate comprehensive disease predictions.
Explainable AI Module
The explainability layer makes use of:
• SHAP for the importance of global features.
• LIME for explanations of local predictions.
• Grad-CAM for visualizing image regions. 
These techniques improve transparency and clinician trust.

title: AUTOMATED GARDENING ROVER
abstract: The present invention relates to an automated gardening rover (100). The automated gardening rover (100) comprises a mobile platform (10), a drive assembly (20), a navigation assembly (30), an image acquisition assembly (40), a controller assembly (50), a fluid storage assembly (60), a fluid dispensing assembly (70), a manipulation assembly (80), and a power assembly (90). The navigation assembly (30) generates spatial information for autonomous navigation, while the image acquisition assembly (40) captures images for plant identification. The controller assembly (50) determines gardening operations and controls precision fluid dispensing and planting. A fluid level sensing assembly (61) enables autonomous refill operations, and a communication assembly (95) facilitates remote data exchange.
specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD
The present invention relates to a field of autonomous robotics and smart gardening systems. More particularly, the present invention relates to an automated gardening rover.

BACKGROUND
The increasing adoption of automation technologies in residential, commercial, and agricultural environments has accelerated the development of intelligent systems for performing routine gardening and plant maintenance activities. Gardening operations such as plant watering, seed sowing, plant monitoring, and maintenance are essential for ensuring healthy plant growth and optimum utilization of available resources. Efficient execution of these activities becomes increasingly important in home gardens, nurseries, greenhouses, landscaped areas, and small-scale agricultural fields, where regular monitoring and timely intervention are required.

Conventional gardening systems generally rely on manual labour or stationary irrigation arrangements for plant care. Manual gardening practices are labour-intensive, time-consuming, and often result in inconsistent watering, irregular maintenance, and inefficient utilization of water and other resources. Similarly, fixed irrigation systems such as drip irrigation or sprinkler systems are generally configured to operate according to predetermined schedules or predefined irrigation zones without considering the varying requirements of individual plants or changes in environmental conditions.

Various automated gardening and irrigation systems have been proposed to improve watering efficiency through sensor-based control, weather-responsive scheduling, or remote monitoring. Although such systems provide a certain degree of automation, they are typically restricted to irrigation functions and are generally incapable of autonomously navigating within a gardening area to perform multiple plant care operations. Moreover, existing systems often lack the capability to identify individual plants, assess plant conditions, or selectively perform gardening tasks according to plant-specific requirements.

Some mobile robotic platforms have also been developed for agricultural applications such as lawn mowing, weed removal, crop monitoring, harvesting, or environmental data collection. However, such robotic systems are generally intended for specific agricultural operations, involve complex and expensive hardware configurations, or are designed for large-scale farming environments. Consequently, these systems are not well suited for home gardens, urban gardening environments, or small-scale cultivation where compactness, affordability, and multifunctionality are important considerations.
A recurring limitation associated with conventional gardening systems is the inability to integrate autonomous navigation, intelligent plant recognition, precision irrigation, planting operations, and resource management within a single mobile platform. Existing systems generally perform only isolated functions, require significant user intervention, or lack adaptive decision-making capabilities for responding to changing garden layouts, environmental conditions, plant growth stages, or resource availability. Furthermore, many existing systems require manual replenishment of water, battery charging, or continuous user supervision, thereby reducing operational efficiency and convenience.
Therefore, there exists a need for an improved automated gardening system that provides an efficient, intelligent, and self-sustaining solution for modern gardening applications.

OBJECTIVES
These objectives are provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that are further described below in the detailed description. These objectives are not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor are they intended to be used as an aid in determining the scope of the claimed subject matter.

A primary objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover capable of autonomously navigating within a gardening area to perform one or more plant care operations with minimal human intervention.

Another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover configured to identify individual plants and determine one or more gardening operations based on characteristics associated with the identified plants.

Another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover capable of performing precision watering by selectively dispensing a predetermined quantity of fluid according to plant-specific requirements, thereby improving water utilization.

Another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover having a robotic manipulation assembly configured to perform automated planting operations including formation of a planting cavity, placement of one or more seeds, and closure of the planting cavity.

Still another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover configured to autonomously generate and update a map of a gardening area for facilitating localization, path planning, and obstacle avoidance during traversal.

Yet objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover capable of autonomously navigating to a replenishment location for restoring one or more operational resources upon determining that the resources have fallen below a predetermined threshold.

Another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover configured to modify one or more gardening operations in response to environmental conditions, thereby improving operational efficiency and conserving resources.

Yet another objective of the present invention is to provide an integrated gardening platform that combines autonomous navigation, plant recognition, precision irrigation, and automated planting within a single mobile system.

A further objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover that is compact, modular, scalable, and suitable for deployment in home gardens, nurseries, greenhouses, landscaped areas, and other small-scale agricultural environments.

Another objective of the present invention is to provide an automated gardening rover that improves gardening efficiency, reduces manual labour, enhances resource utilization, and facilitates reliable and intelligent plant care.

SUMMARY
According to one aspect of the present invention, an automated gardening rover is provided. The automated gardening rover comprises a mobile platform, a drive assembly, a navigation assembly, an image acquisition assembly, a controller assembly, a fluid storage assembly, a fluid dispensing assembly, a manipulation assembly, and a power assembly. The drive assembly is configured to propel and steer the mobile platform across a gardening area. The navigation assembly is configured to generate spatial information representative of the gardening area and determine a travel path for the mobile platform. The image acquisition assembly is configured to capture one or more images associated with one or more plants located within the gardening area. The controller assembly is configured to receive the spatial information from the navigation assembly and the one or more images from the image acquisition assembly, identify the one or more plants, determine one or more gardening operations corresponding thereto, and generate one or more control commands. The fluid dispensing assembly is arranged in fluid communication with the fluid storage assembly and is configured to selectively dispense a predetermined quantity of fluid responsive to the control commands generated by the controller assembly. The manipulation assembly is mounted on the mobile platform and is configured to perform one or more planting operations including formation of a planting cavity, placement of one or more seeds, and closure of the planting cavity. The power assembly is configured to supply electrical power to the drive assembly, the navigation assembly, the image acquisition assembly, the controller assembly, the fluid dispensing assembly, and the manipulation assembly. The controller assembly further coordinates autonomous movement of the mobile platform, identification of the one or more plants, execution of the one or more gardening operations, and selective actuation of the fluid dispensing assembly and the manipulation assembly during traversal of the gardening area.

In some embodiments of the present invention, the navigation assembly comprises one or more ranging sensors configured to generate an environmental map of the gardening area and continuously update the environmental map to facilitate localization, path planning, and obstacle avoidance during movement of the mobile platform.
In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the controller assembly is configured to analyse the one or more images captured by the image acquisition assembly to identify at least one of a plant species, a plant condition, a growth stage, or a nutrient deficiency, and determine the one or more gardening operations based thereon.
In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the fluid dispensing assembly dispenses the predetermined quantity of fluid adjacent to a root region of the identified plant in accordance with a watering profile corresponding to the identified plant.
In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the automated gardening rover further comprises a fluid level sensing assembly configured to monitor a quantity of fluid stored within the fluid storage assembly, wherein the controller assembly initiates autonomous navigation of the mobile platform towards a refill station upon determining that the monitored quantity of fluid is below a predetermined threshold.

In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the controller assembly is further configured to resume execution of the one or more gardening operations after replenishment of the fluid storage assembly.

In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the manipulation assembly comprises a multi-axis robotic manipulator configured to sequentially form the planting cavity, deposit the one or more seeds into the planting cavity, and cover the one or more seeds with surrounding soil.

In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the controller assembly is configured to receive one or more environmental inputs and modify execution of the one or more gardening operations in response to the environmental inputs.

In accordance with the embodiments of the present invention, the automated gardening rover further comprises a communication assembly configured to exchange operational data with one or more external devices, receive mission parameters, and transmit operational status associated with the automated gardening rover.
